 1 Device Overview

 1.1 About This Document
     This document contains detailed technical information on peripherals and subsystems of the Alif
     Semiconductor's E7 embedded fusion processor series.
     Device information herein includes details on internal connections, external connectivity options, functional
     descriptions and register guides.
     This document contains also references to third-party technical literature.
     For more information on electrical and mechanical characteristics with specifications, ordering information,
     and peripherals and subsystems available in a particular device, refer to the device series-specific Datasheet.
     For managing software configurations of device resources, power, pins, clocks, DMA requests, interrupts, and
     various other additional settings, refer to the Alif Conductor tool.

 1.2 Device Description
     The families of fusion processors and microcontrollers (MCUs) from Alif Semiconductor create a scalable and
     compatible continuum of highly integrated embedded processor devices for use in low-end to high-end
     intelligent IoT end-point applications. Architected for power efficiency and long battery life, these devices
     deliver high computation and ML/AI capability, multi-layered security, computer vision, and highly interactive
     human-machine interface.
     Individual device selections within a family of devices scale up starting with single-core MCUs, dual-core
     MCUs, triple- core MCU/MPU fusion processors, and quad- core MCU/MPU fusion processors to match
     specific applications. Across all devices are common peripherals, common power management schemes, and
     a common interconnection fabric making it easy to re-use software and hardware over many varied projects.
     This document covers the quad-core E7 embedded fusion processor series from the Ensemble™ family.
     Power efficiency—In addition to the use of FD-SOI silicon technology, aiPM™ provides fine granular control
     over the processing, memory, and peripheral resources of the device, resulting in extreme power
     conservation that consumes only what is needed, when it is needed, at any given instant based on use case.
     Computation and ML/AI—Quad-core design with two Arm® Cortex®-A32 application cores, and two Arm®
     Cortex®- M55 Real- Time core s , with one Real- Time core optimized for extreme low power operation.
     Machine Learning and AI tasks are accelerated by dual Arm Ethos™-U55 neural processing units generating as
     much as 250 GOPS. E7 devices can operate with an RTOS, an OS such as Linux, or both, while using only the
     on-chip memory resources. Additional RAM and Flash memory may be accessed externally through two high-
     speed Octal SPI interfaces supporting XIP mode and HyperBus™ protocol. An in-line AES decryption module
     in each Octal SPI interface ensures the confidentiality of the data and/or code stored in the external memory
     devices.
     Connectivity—E7 devices support many wired interfaces including Ethernet, USB, SDIO, CANFD, MIPI® I3C®,
     I2C, and more.
     Security—An isolated Secure Enclave manages the entire life cycle of the end application from manufacture,
     to deployment, to secure Firmware Over-The-Air updates, and to retirement. A unique Root-of-Trust existing
     in the enclave enables a trusted on- chip platform for key generation, secure storage, secure boot,
     cryptographic acceleration, and more. The Secure Enclave also enables certificate-based secure debugging.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


     Computer Vision—Integrated camera interfaces, including MIPI® CSI-2®, enable easy connection of low-
     power image sensors for AI image classification using the Arm Ethos-U55 NPUs. Biometric ID, face detection,
     object classification, barcode reading, and other vision applications can execute while consuming very little
     energy.
     Human Machine Interface—Integrated color display interfaces, including MIPI DSI®, can drive a wide range
     of display panels with vivid graphics supported by the on-chip 2D graphics processing unit for attractive user
     interfaces. Digital audio inputs and outputs are supported by PDM and I2S interfaces. The Arm Ethos-U55
     NPUs can apply ML inference to audio input streams for key word spotting, speech recognition, failure
     prediction, and more.

 2 Application Processor

 2.1 Arm Cortex-A32

 2.1.1 A32 Overview
     The Arm Cortex-A32 processor is a very efficient, low-power, 32-bit processor. The pair of A32 cores in this
     device is used for application processing and resides in the Application Processor Subsystem (APSS). The APSS
     also includes various memories and peripherals. See the device block diagram (Figure 1-1) for APSS internal
     architecture.
     The A32 processor supports the following main features:
       n Dual-core configuration:
           lSymmetric Multi-Processing (SMP) within the processor cluster
         l CPU core revision: r1p0

       n Full compliance with the Armv8 architecture:
         l A32 instruction set

         l T32 instruction set

         l AArch32 execution state:

           o Supports all exception levels (EL0 to EL3)
           o Provides full compatibility with Armv7

       n Arm TrustZone security technology
       n Arm Neon Advanced SIMD and floating-point architecture
       n Cryptographic extension
       n 8-stage, in-order pipeline with direct and indirect branch prediction
       n Level 1 (L1) memory system that supports separate data and instruction sides:
         l 32KB L1 instruction cache

         l 32KB L1 data cache

         l Memory Management Unit (MMU)

       n Level 2 (L2) memory system that provides cluster memory coherency:
         l 512KB shared L2 cache:

           o L2 data RAM input latency: 1 cycle
           o L2 data RAM output latency: 2 cycles

         l Snoop Control Unit (SCU)

         l Accelerator Coherency Port (ACP)

       n Debug and trace support:
         l Armv8 debug logic

         l Arm CoreSight™ SoC-400 components

         l Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU)

         l Trace infrastructure

         l Debug memory map (v7)

       n Arm AMBA® 4 AXI as the main bus interface
       n Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC) CPU interface to connect to an external distributor (GIC-400)

     Figure 2-1 provides a high-level overview of the A32 implementation in the device.

 3 Real-Time Processor

 3.1 High-Performance Arm Cortex-M55 (M55-HP)

 3.1.1 M55-HP Overview
     The Cortex-M55 High-Performance (M55-HP) processor implements the Armv8.1-M Mainline architecture
     that includes support for the M-profile Vector Extension (MVE), also known as Helium™. The M55-HP
     achieves high compute performance across scalar and vector operations, operating up to 400 MHz.
     The device includes a single M55-HP processor that resides in the High-Performance Real-Time Subsystem
     (RTSS-HP). The RTSS-HP also includes various memories and peripherals. See the device block diagram (Figure
     1-1) for RTSS-HP internal architecture.
     The M55-HP processor supports the following main features:
       n CPU revision: r1p0
       n CPU core logic that includes:
         l In-order, four-stage integer pipeline with early completion of common arithmetic instructions

         l Instruction Fetch Unit (IFU) with 32-bit instruction fetch data width

         l Data Processing Unit (DPU) with 64-bit load/store data width

         l Support for up to 2 × 32-bit vector load operations in parallel

       n Extension Processing Unit (EPU) that works closely with the CPU core to support:
         l Scalar floating-point (VFPv5) operations: half-, single-, and double-precision

         l Vectored operations through MVE (Helium):

           o Integer
           o 128-bit SIMD floating-point: half- and single-precision

       n Double-Precision FPU
       n Support for other Extensions such as:
         l Armv8.1-M Main Extension (16-bit and 32-bit Thumb® instruction set)

         l Armv8-M Security Extension (TrustZone)

         l DSP Extension

         l DSP Debug Extension

         l Reliability, Availability, and Serviceability (RAS) Extension

         l Unprivileged Debug Extension (UDE)

       n Memory architecture that includes:
         l Memory Authentication Unit (MAU) for memory access control:

           o Secure Memory Protection Unit (MPU) supporting 16 regions
           o Non-secure MPU supporting 16 regions
           o Security Attribution Unit (SAU) supporting 8 regions
           o TCM Gate Units (TGU):
             o Instruction TGU (ITGU) protecting 16 address regions, each 16KB in size
             o Data TGU (DTGU) protecting 64 address regions, each 16KB in size

         l Memory system:

           o 32KB L1 Instruction Cache (IRAM)
           o 32KB L1 Data Cache (DRAM)
           o 256KB Instruction TCM (ITCM); access to ITCM is over a single interface
           o 1024KB Data TCM (DTCM); access to DTCM is over four interfaces
           o Master AXI (M-AXI) interface for high latency memory or peripheral access




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                      7
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                        www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


       n Interrupt control:
         l Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC) for low-latency interrupt processing:

           o Supports 480 external interrupts, with 256 priority levels per interrupt

         l Wakeup interrupt control to allow the processor to enter low-power state:

           o Internal Wakeup Interrupt Controller (IWIC)
           o External Wakeup Interrupt Controller (EWIC)

       n Secure and non-secure Vector Table Offset Register (VTOR)
       n Debug and trace support:
         l Full set debug:

           o Breakpoint Unit (BPU) with 8 comparators
           o Data Watchpoint and Trace (DWT) unit with 4 comparators and Performance Monitoring Unit

              (PMU)
         l Trace infrastructure

         l CoreSight-compliant Debug Access Port (DAP):

           o Supports dynamic switching—Serial Wire / JTAG Debug Port (SWJ-DP)

     Figure 3-1 provides a high-level overview of the M55-HP implementation in the device.

 3.2 High-Efficiency Arm Cortex-M55 (M55-HE)

 3.2.1 M55-HE Overview
     The Cortex-M55 High-Efficiency (M55-HE) processor implements the Armv8.1-M Mainline architecture that
     includes support for the M-profile Vector Extension (MVE), also known as Helium™. The M55-HE achieves
     high compute efficiency across scalar and vector operations, operating up to 160 MHz.
     The M55-HE memories are based on ultra-low leakage memory cells which results in low power consumption
     in sleep mode. The choice of TCM retention allows application-optimized tradeoff between current leakage
     during sleep and fast wake-up time.
     The device includes a single M55-HE processor that resides in the High-Efficiency Real-Time Subsystem (RTSS-
     HE). The RTSS-HE also includes various memories and peripherals. See the device block diagram (Figure 1-1)
     for RTSS-HE internal architecture.
     The M55-HE processor supports the following main features:
       n CPU revision: r1p0
       n CPU core logic that includes:
         l In-order, four-stage integer pipeline with early completion of common arithmetic instructions

         l Instruction Fetch Unit (IFU) with 32-bit instruction fetch data width

         l Data Processing Unit (DPU) with 64-bit load/store data width

         l Support for up to 2 × 32-bit vector load operations in parallel

       n Extension Processing Unit (EPU) that works closely with the CPU core to support:
         l Scalar floating-point (VFPv5) operations: half-, single-, and double-precision

         l Vectored operations through MVE (Helium)

           o Integer
           o 128-bit SIMD floating-point: half- and single-precision

       n Double-Precision FPU
       n Support for other Extensions such as:
         l Armv8.1-M Main Extension (16-bit and 32-bit Thumb instruction set)

         l Armv8-M Security Extension (TrustZone)

         l DSP Extension

         l DSP Debug Extension

         l Reliability, Availability, and Serviceability (RAS) Extension

         l Unprivileged Debug Extension (UDE)

       n Memory architecture that includes:
         l Memory Authentication Unit (MAU) for memory access control:

           o Secure Memory Protection Unit (MPU) supporting 16 regions
           o Non-secure MPU supporting 16 regions
           o Security Attribution Unit (SAU) supporting 8 regions
           o TCM Gate Units (TGU):
             o Instruction TGU (ITGU) protecting 16 address regions, each 16KB in size
             o Data TGU (DTGU) protecting 16 address regions, each 16KB in size

         l Memory system:

           o 32KB L1 Instruction Cache (IRAM)
           o 32KB L1 Data Cache (DRAM)
           o 256KB Instruction TCM (ITCM); access to ITCM is over a single interface
           o 256KB Data TCM (DTCM); access to DTCM is over four interfaces
           o Master AXI (M-AXI) interface for high latency memory or peripheral access




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                      11
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


       n Interrupt control:
         l Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC) for low-latency interrupt processing:

           o Supports 480 external interrupts, with 256 priority levels per interrupt

         l Wakeup interrupt control to allow the processor to enter low-power state:

           o Internal Wakeup Interrupt Controller (IWIC)
           o External Wakeup Interrupt Controller (EWIC)

       n Secure and non-secure Vector Table Offset Register (VTOR)
       n Debug and trace support:
         l Full set debug:

           o Breakpoint Unit (BPU) with 8 comparators
           o Data Watchpoint and Trace (DWT) unit with 4 comparators and Performance Monitoring Unit

              (PMU)
         l Trace infrastructure

         l CoreSight-compliant Debug Access Port (DAP):

           o Supports dynamic switching—Serial Wire / JTAG Debug Port (SWJ-DP)

 4 Neural Processing Unit (NPU)
     The Arm Ethos-U55 Neural Processing Unit (NPU) is a Machine Learning (ML) coprocessor that improves the
     inference performance of neural networks (NN).
     The NPU targets 8-bit and 16-bit integer quantized Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Recurrent
     Neural Networks (RNN). The NPU includes a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller that can read and write
     to external memory. The DMA controller reads the neural network description and transfers the input and
     output feature maps.
     The device includes:
       n One NPU coprocessor in the device High-Performance Region—NPU-HP
       n One NPU coprocessor in the device High-Efficiency Region—NPU-HE


 4.1 High-Performance Arm Ethos-U55 (NPU-HP)

 4.1.1 NPU-HP Overview
     The NPU-HP supports the following main features:
       n Up to 204 GOPS performance using up to 256 MAC/cycle
       n Network support: CNN, RNN
       n On-the-fly weight decompression (8-bit weights)
       n 8-bit and 16-bit activations (input data)
       n Activation functions:
         l ReLU, ReLU1, ReLU6, and Leaky ReLU (LReLU)

         l Tanh

         l Sigmoid

         l Configurable Look-Up Table (LUT)

         l None or bypass

       n Element-wise operations:
         l Element-wise ADD and SUB

         l Element-wise Multiplication (MUL)

         l Element-wise Min and Max

         l Element-wise ABS

         l Element-wise Shift Left (SHL) and Shift Right (SHR)

         l Element-wise Count-Leading Zero (CLZ)

       n 48KB of internal shared cache memory (SHRAM)
       n Integrated DMA controller
       n Layer-by-layer visibility with Performance Monitoring Units (PMUs)

     Figure 4-1 provides a high-level overview of the NPU-HP implementation in the device.

 4.1.4.3.12 NPUHP_LOCK Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            Lock Register.
                                            This register is designed for driver use and does not affect NPU functionality.
                                            This register holds a 32-bit value which is cleared to 0 on reset. The register has
        0x2C
                             R/W            special write semantics. Suppose the current register value is 'c' and the newly
     Base address
                                            written register value is 'w':
                                            If (c==0 or w==0), then the register is updated to the newly written value 'w'.
                                            Otherwise, the write is ignored and the value remains unchanged.


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             32-bit value for the lock configuration.
    31-0      LOCK                    R/W          0x0
                                                             To try to claim the lock, write a non-zero ID value and read back to

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                       Alif Semiconductor
                                                                24
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                     E7 Series


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                              see if the value was accepted.
                                                              To release the lock (that contains your non-zero ID value), write 0
                                                              to the lock register.

 4.2 High-Efficiency Arm Ethos-U55 (NPU-HE)

 4.2.1 NPU-HE Overview
     The NPU-HE supports the following main features:
       n Up to 46 GOPS performance using up to 128 MAC/cycle
       n Network support: CNN, RNN
       n On-the-fly weight decompression (8-bit weights)
       n 8-bit and 16-bit activations (input data)
       n Activation functions:
         l ReLU, ReLU1, ReLU6, and Leaky ReLU (LReLU)

         l Tanh

         l Sigmoid

         l Configurable Look-Up Table (LUT)

         l None or bypass

       n Element-wise operations:
         l Element-wise ADD and SUB

         l Element-wise Multiplication (MUL)

         l Element-wise Min and Max

         l Element-wise ABS

         l Element-wise Shift Left (SHL) and Shift Right (SHR)

         l Element-wise Count-Leading Zero (CLZ)

       n 24KB of internal shared cache memory (SHRAM)
       n Integrated DMA controller
       n Layer-by-layer visibility with Performance Monitoring Units (PMUs)

     Figure 4-3 provides a high-level overview of the NPU-HE implementation in the device.

           Offset           Access         Description

    7-4       VERSION_MINOR            R          0x0         This is the n for the P-part of an RnPn release number

           Offset            Access          Description

   31-16 CLEAR_IRQ_HISTORY             R/W          0x0        When bit [k] is set, then the corresponding bit [k] of the NPUHE_

     1        CLEAR_IRQ                R/W          0x0
                                                               Writing 0 has no effect.

              TRANSITION_TO_                                   Write 1 to transition the NPU to running state.
     0                                 R/W          0x0
              RUNNING_STATE                                    Writing 0 has no effect.



 4.2.4.3.4 NPUHE_RESET Register
           Offset            Access          Description
                                             Reset Register.
                                             If this register is written to by a permitted master, then the NPU is reset (clearing all
                                             internal RAMs) and the reset register value is updated. Otherwise, the write to this
         0xC
                              R/W            register is ignored and the NPU is not reset.
     Base address
                                             The value written to this register sets the privilege level used by the NPU when the
                                             NPU acts as an AXI master. The host is permitted to set any level of privilege less
                                             than or equal to the host privilege level.

 4.2.4.3.12 NPUHE_LOCK Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            Lock Register.
                                            This register is designed for driver use and does not affect NPU functionality.
                                            This register holds a 32-bit value which is cleared to 0 on reset. The register has
        0x2C
                             R/W            special write semantics. Suppose the current register value is 'c' and the newly
     Base address
                                            written register value is 'w':
                                            If (c==0 or w==0), then the register is updated to the newly written value 'w'.
                                            Otherwise, the write is ignored and the value remains unchanged.


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             32-bit value for the lock configuration.
                                                             To try to claim the lock, write a non-zero ID value and read back to
    31-0      LOCK                    R/W          0x0       see if the value was accepted.
                                                             To release the lock (that contains your non-zero ID value), write 0
                                                             to the lock register.

                                            0x3: AXI1 port, outstanding counter 3. AXI limits set by NPUHE_AXI_LIMIT3.

 5 2D-Graphics Accelerator (GPU)

 5.1 GPU2D Overview
     The D/AVE 2D Graphics Processing Unit (GPU2D) provides hardware acceleration for sophisticated vector-
     based graphical applications.
     The device includes one GPU2D module.
     The GPU2D supports the following main features:
       n Subpixel accurate rendering
       n Resolutions of up to 2048 × 2048 pixels
       n Operating clock frequency at 400 MHz. GPU render pipeline produces one pixel per clock cycle.
       n 16 blending modes
       n Patterns and gradients with alpha channel on all primitives
       n Render to texture
       n Textures up to 2048 × 1024 pixels
       n Texture blending
       n Bilinear filtering
       n Graphical primitives available:
         l Block Image Transfers (BLIT)—direct and stretch

         l Box

         l Circle—filled or empty (ring)

         l Convex polygon

         l Line

            o Supported caps:
              o Butt
              o Round
              o Square
            o Supported line joins:
              o Bevel
              o Miter
              o Round
            o Supporting different start and end widths

         l Quad

         l Triangle

         l Triangle fan

         l Triangle list

         l Triangle stripe

         l Wedge-filled or empty

       n Graphical primitives attributes:
         l Anti-aliasing

         l Blend modes

         l Color

         l Edge blur

         l Linear alpha gradient

         l Pattern

         l Texture

            o U/V clamp, repeat support
            o No-, linear-, bilinear-filtering support

 5.3 GPU2D Functional Description

                                                        NOTE

       Because GPU2D is delivered with a low-level software driver, this section, as well as the registers
       section, only briefly describe the GPU2D capabilities.
       The static code size of the GPU2D driver is in the range of 90KB to 100KB, depending on the platform
       and the compiler.
       The dynamic memory requirements strongly depend on the actual application.


 5.3.1 GPU2D Block Diagram
     The GPU2D core is a single-clock-domain pipeline structure having four external interfaces:
       n A slave interface for configuration register writes and status reads by a CPU
       n A read-only master interface for Display List (DL) reads from the memory
       n A read-only master interface for texel read from the memory
       n A read/write master interface for framebuffer pixel data from/to memory

     The three master interfaces are merged to a single AXI interface via a 3-to-1 arbiter.
     Internal caches are used to transform the single-token accesses for texel and pixel data to burst accesses to
     enhance performance on the bus.
     Figure 5-3 presents a simplified diagram of the GPU2D main internal blocks and connections.

 5.3.2 GPU2D Interrupt Requests
     GPU2D generates the following interrupts:
       n Enumeration finished interrupt
       n Display list finished interrupt
       n Bus error interrupt

     These interrupts are merged into a single interrupt line. On an interrupt request, the IRQ signal is asserted
     until the CPU resets it by clearing the respective GPU2D_IRQCTL register.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                            78
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                E7 Series


 5.3.3 GPU2D Configuration and Status Interface
     This interface is used to read and write the GPU2D registers. For description of the GPU2D registers refer to
     Section 5.4 GPU2D Registers Guide.

 5.3.4 GPU2D Display List Reader Interface
     The Display List Reader (DLR) fetches a memory block containing instructions on how to set the GPU2D
     control registers and then writes these control registers accordingly.
     Using a DL (also called render buffer) is a way to allow a fully asynchronous operation of CPU and GPU2D. DL
     also gives the best possible system performance.
     Figure 5-4 illustrates the display list mechanism. The display list format is described in Section 5.3.9 GPU2D
     Display List Format.
                                           Figure 5-4 Display List Mechanism

            Applica�on                      Driver                           Buﬀer                GPU2D
                                                                     Buﬀer
                                                                                                                      2DGPU-005




 5.3.5 GPU2D Texture Interface
     For BLIT and texture operations this interface provides GPU2D with the needed pixel data. Pixel formats
     widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits are supported.

 5.3.6 GPU2D Framebuffer Interface
     This interface allows GPU2D to read and write to/from the framebuffer. Pixel format widths of 8, 16, and 32
     bits are supported.

 5.3.7 GPU2D 2D Render Capabilities

 5.3.7.1 GPU2D Anti-aliasing
     GPU2D supports anti-aliasing of graphical primitives. In case of a triangle, the anti-aliasing can be turned on
     or off for every single edge. This mechanism is useful to render polygons with correct outline anti-aliasing.

 5.3.7.3 GPU2D Blend Modes
     GPU2D supports a wide range of color calculation operations. The color calculation is done in the Color Unit
     and Blend Unit.

 5.3.7.3.1 Color Unit
     The following operations can be applied to each color channel (a, r, g, and b) individually:
      REPLACE                   c
      COPY                      x
      INVERT                    1-x
      MULTIPLY                  x*c
      INVMULTIPLY               (1-x) * c
      BLEND                     x * c + (1-x) * d
     Where x is the color channel value (a, r, g, or b); c (color1) and d (color2) are user specified constants.
     The below data type abbreviations are used in Figure 5-6 and Figure 5-7.

  c24          24-bit color
  ca32         32-bit color and alpha

  i16          16-bit integer

 5.3.9 GPU2D Display List Format
     Display lists are stored using direct register-to-value mappings. There is almost no abstraction, so the
     structure of display list is quite simple. As GPU2D registers are always 32 bits wide, list entries had to be at
     least of this size to be efficient. Because register indexes are much smaller (6 to 7 bits), the storage format
     uses a packed notation to reduce the size.

 5.3.9.1 GPU2D Rules
     Display list format follows the next general rules:
         n The list is stored in memory as a stream of 32-bit words.
         n The list contains two different types of words: address word and data word.
         n The stream always starts with an address word.
         n Each address word can specify up to 4 (one byte each) register indexes.
         n The indexes are read and interpreted LSB to MSB (lowest byte first).
         n If less than 4 indexes are required, remaining entries must be filled with 0x80.
         n An address word is followed by 0 to 4 data words, one for each register index.


 5.3.9.2 GPU2D Example
     The following is a C code example of a DL stream.


   C Code Example of a DL Stream
     1       DWORD 0x40302010 // start of list (address word)


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                                83
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                    E7 Series


   C Code Example of a DL Stream
     2      DWORD 0x00000000 // data word 1 (for register offset 0x10)
     3      DWORD 0xFFFFFFAA // data word 2 (for register offset 0x20)
     4      DWORD 0x00000001 // data word 3 (for register offset 0x30)
     5      DWORD 0x00CE0F20 // data word 4 (for register offset 0x40)
     6      DWORD ...   // next address word
     7      DWORD ...   // next data word 1
     8      ...



     This example with DWORDs instructs the GPU2D to execute the following sequence:
         1. Write 0x00000000 into hardware register 0x10.
         2. Write 0xFFFFFFAA into hardware register 0x20.
         3. Write 0x00000001 into hardware register 0x30.
         4. Write 0x00CE0F20 into hardware register 0x40.
         5. Proceed with next stream...

 5.3.9.3 GPU2D Special Cases
     There are a few additional operations besides the filling of register values, for example, waiting for different
     busy signals. All special cases are encoded when using an address word entry equal to or above 0x80 (that is,
     bit 7 set). If a special index is used, no normal indexes must follow after it within the same address word. If a
     special index is used, the data stream continues with the next address word.
     In other words, the behavior is unspecified if an address word contains 'gaps' of special indexes, for example:
     i3, 0x80, i2, i1.
     If the first special index contains the special value 0x80–0xFF, the following (second) index is interpreted by
     the DLR as follows:
         bit 0 set      Display list end
         bit 1 set      Wait for pipeline write to framebuffer cache complete, then issue a full pipeline flush (texture
                        cache and framebuffer cache) and wait for framebuffer cache write to framebuffer complete
                        (necessary before flip)
         bit 2 set      Wait for pipeline write to framebuffer cache complete (necessary before framebuffer format
                        change and alpha channel blending change)

 5.3.10 GPU2D Modes of Operation

 5.3.10.1 GPU2D Synchronization
     The synchronization between CPU and GPU2D can either be done by polling, or by interrupt. For best system
     performance it is recommended to use interrupt synchronization.

 5.3.10.2 GPU2D Register Based
     In the register-based operation mode, the CPU is setting all registers over the peripheral bus. To start a new
     render process, the CPU has to wait until GPU2D is finished. Then, the next render process can be initiated.
     It is recommended to use this mode for debug purposes only.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                     Alif Semiconductor
                                                              84
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                             E7 Series


 5.3.10.3 GPU2D Display List Based
     In this mode, the CPU creates a display list in memory. Such a display list contains a bundle of render
     operations (basically just a list of register settings). Then, the GPU2D DLR executes the display list in parallel
     to the CPU. The memory that stores the display list is required to be accessible from the CPU and GPU2D.
     Note that while the DLR is active, no register writes must be done via the slave bus interface, as they will
     conflict with the commands given by the DLR to the GPU2D rendering core.
     A more detailed description of the display list structure can be found in Section 5.3.9 GPU2D Display List
     Format.

 5.3.11 GPU2D RLE format
     The RLE images comprise of two types of data packets:
       n Run-length packets
       n Raw packets

     The first byte of each packet type contains the Packet Type and the Pixel Count fields. The next field is called
     Pixel Data field and contains the actual pixel value(s).
     For Run-length packets, the Pixel Data field contains a single pixel value to be repeated Pixel_Count + 1
     times.
     For Raw packets, the Pixel Data field has a variable number of pixel values. Pixel Count field in this case
     defines how many pixels follow in the raw (non-RLE) data stream.
     Pixel Count field values of 0 – 0x7F correspond to 1 – 128 count of successive pixels. Zero-data-length packets
     are meaningless and therefore are not allowed.

 5.3.11.1 GPU2D Run-Length Packet
     Table 5-5 shows how Run-length packets are composed.
                                           Table 5-5 Run-Length Packet
     Field Name:       Packet Type            Pixel Count                               Pixel Data
      Field Size:         1 bit                  7 bits                                 1 – 4 bytes
     Field Value:           1                  0 – 0x7F                                <pixel value>

 5.3.11.2 GPU2D Raw Packet
     Raw packets are composed as described in Table 5-6.
                                               Table 5-6 Raw Packet
     Field Name:       Packet Type            Pixel Count                                Pixel Data
      Field Size:         1 bit                  7 bits                        1 – 4 bytes × (Pixel_Count + 1)
     Field Value:           0                  0 – 0x7F                                <pixel values>

 6 Secure Enclave Subsystem (SESS)

 6.1 Security Architecture Overview
      The device contains an advanced Secure Enclave (SE) that is responsible for managing the device security.
      The SE is an isolated subsystem with its own dedicated resources. The isolated subsystem reduces the attack
      surface for the SE along with the minimal software interfaces that are restricted to the Inter-Process
      Communication (IPC) Message Handling Units (MHUs).
      Figure 6-1 presents a simplified diagram of the SE main internal blocks and connections.
                                                          Figure 6-1 Secure Enclave Block Diagram


                            Secure Enclave

  External Interrupts
                                                          Supervisor                          SE UART,
  and Tamper Events                                                                             SDC

                                                                   Private Bus                                 MHUs   Applica�on/Real-Time Core(s)

                                                                                                                                                SECURE-004
                                                Global            Global           M55-HP and            M55-HE and
                                            SRAM and NVM        Peripherals        Ethos-U55              Ethos-U55



      The SE boots first on Power-On-Reset (cold start). It runs the First Stage bootloader code from a private,
      immutable ROM. The SE performs certificate-based integrity and authenticity check on the Second Stage
      bootloader. It is loaded to the SE SRAM (SERAM) and the flow of execution is transferred to it. This
      mechanism enables the secure update of the Second Stage bootloader on the field. The boot process
      continues with processing of the application-specific device configuration. The SE applies configuration
      settings that partition the system resources (memory and peripherals) between the different application
      cores. Next, the SE bootloader performs a signature verification of the installed application binaries. If
      needed, it copies the specified binaries to their designated SRAM regions. Finally, a designated core is
      released from Reset to run its application. This completes the secure boot procedure. The remaining cores
      can be booted by the SE in response to a service request.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                Alif Semiconductor
                                                                           107
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                  www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     The SE is also involved in the process of waking up from STOP mode. When a wakeup event is triggered, the
     SE CPU boots first. It checks if the SERAM is retained and continues the execution flow there. The SERAM
     code maps the wakeup event to an application core and promptly boots it. If the SERAM is not retained, then
     the SE validates the wakeup source and boots the RTSS-HE core. The retention of SERAM in the Secure
     Enclave or the SRAM (M55-HE TCM) in the RTSS-HE offers trade-off options between the leakage current and
     the wakeup time of the device.
     The SE provides traditional security functions such as:
       n Secure boot
       n Secure device configuration
       n HW Root-of-Trust (RoT)
       n Key management
       n Signature validation
       n Crypto operations
       n Life cycle management

     The Supervisor is responsible to:
       n Manage the OEM provisioning process and the Life Cycle State (LCS)
       n Apply the system configuration settings to the security firewalls and security HW in the system
       n Securely boot the Application core (A32) / Real-time cores (M55-HP and M55-HE) as defined by the
         user's configuration file
      Figure 6-2 presents the start-up sequence of the device after a cold POR.

 6.2 Secure Enclave Services
     The SE is an integral part of the device and is responsible for managing the internal security. The SE performs
     device configuration, security and cryptographic services during the start-up of the device and also provides
     runtime security services to the OEM’s application code. These SE services are grouped into four main
     categories as described in the following sections:
       n Section 6.2.1 Secure Provisioning and Programming Service
       n Section 6.2.2 Secure Initialization Service
       n Section 6.2.3 Secure Boot Service
       n Section 6.3 Runtime Security and Cryptographic Services


 6.2.1 Secure Provisioning and Programming Service
     During the start-up of the device (from reset), the SE provides a Secure Provisioning and Programming
     Service via the SE’s dedicated UART that enables the OEM to securely provision their security credentials into
     the device and to securely program the OEM’s configuration settings (or application code) into the device.
     The OEM’s security credentials may be provisioned into the immutable OTP memory of the device only when
     the device is in the OEM Life Cycle State (LCS). The OEM’s signed configuration settings and signed
     application code may be programmed into the NVM MRAM of the device while the device is in the OEM LCS
     and optionally in the Secure LCS. Alif Semiconductor provides a Provisioning and Programming tool and API
     specifications that assist the OEM with this process. For more details, see the Software Reference Manual.

 6.2.2 Secure Initialization Service
     During the start-up of the device, the SE’s Initialization Service configures and initializes the device with the
     OEM’s configuration settings (firewall, pin multiplexing, clock settings, etc.) that were programmed into the
     NVM MRAM of the device. These configuration settings are comprised of the OEM-signed Table of Contents
     (OToC) and the OEM-signed Configuration Settings (OCS). The OToC and OCS are created by the OEM and
     control the secure boot operation and security of the device and are applied to the device by the SE as part
     of the device start-up process. In addition, the SE Initialization Service manages the Secure Debug connection
     with the device and validates the OEM signed certificate to enable the secure debug connection prior to
     booting the processor cores. The OEM has the option to enable or disable the secure debug connection while
     in the Secure or End of Life (EOL) states (see Figure 6-3).
     Figure 6-3 outlines the four Life Cycle States (LCS) of the SE. A LCS can only progress to the next state and
     cannot regress to a prior state. Therefore it is not possible to return to a previous LCS. Each LCS
     enables/disables various security settings and attributes. When the OEM receives the device, the LCS is in the
     OEM state which allows the device to be programmed, debugged and provisioned by the OEM. When the LCS
     advances to the Secure state, the device can no longer be provisioned and the device is considered to be in
     deployed state. In order to exit the Secure state, the OEM software must present a signed certificate to the
     SE in order to advance to the RMA/EOL state. The device is not intended to function in the RMA/EOL state
     and there is no way to exit this final state.

 6.2.3 Secure Boot Service
      The Secure Boot Service is responsible for verifying the signature of a boot image against the security
      credentials provisioned into the device during the Manufacturing LCS. During the start-up of the device, the
      Secure Boot Service is used to securely boot the selected processor cores (A32, M55-HP or M55-HE) with the
      OEM’s signed boot image as specified in the OToC and OCS options. At runtime, the processor core may also
      request the Secure Boot Service to securely boot other processor cores (A32, M55-HP or M55-HE) with other
      signed images. For more details, see the Software Reference Manual.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                           110
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


 6.3 Runtime Security and Cryptographic Services
     The Secure Enclave (SE) supports a variety of Runtime Security and Cryptographic services that enable the
     OEM’s application code to control security functions for the device and request cryptographic operations.
     These runtime services make use of the IPC mechanism between the processor cores and the SE as shown on
     Figure 6-4. Runtime security requests are initiated from a processor core to the SE over the MHU interface
     and replies or notification events are initiated from the SE back to the processor core over the MHU
     interface. For more details, see Section 9.2 Message Handling Unit (MHU).
     The Runtime Security services include the ability for the OEM’s application code to make requests to manage
     the power saving modes for the system cores, manage the secure boot process for processor cores and
     initiate updates for Alif Semiconductor’s internal firmware.
     The Runtime Cryptographic services include the ability of the OEM application code to make requests for
     standard and device-specific cryptographic operations like:
       n Creating keys
       n Using the keys to encrypt or decrypt
       n Return the device certificate
       n Authenticate the device
       n Validate the signature of images against the provisioned keys in the device
       n Secure boot a core
       n Write to MRAM memory
       n Process Alif Semiconductor’s firmware updates

 7 Interconnect

 7.1 Interconnect Overview
     The system interconnect provides the means of connecting bus masters (CPU cores, DMA controllers) to
     memory modules and peripherals. It is based on the Arm AMBA bus architecture utilizing a mix of AXI, AHB
     and APB buses.
     The backbone of the device interconnect is based on an AXI4 bus, featuring multiple master and slave ports.
     The processing subsystems have their own local buses connected as masters to the main AXI bus. The
     memory blocks and the peripheral subsystems connect as slaves to the main AXI bus. Some peripherals (such
     as ETH, SDMMC, and USB) also can act as bus masters and connect via both master and slave ports. The
     master ports serve their DMA controllers to transfer data without CPU intervention, while the slave ports are
     intended for accessing their registers.
     Each master and slave port connects to the main AXI bus through Firewall Components (FC). They enforce
     run-time configurable access rights policy and address translation. Transaction gating is based on master ID,
     transaction type (instruction or data fetch) and TrustZone-defined secure world context. The FC configuration
     settings are set by the SE during the secure boot process. The applications specify their desired access paths
     and address regions in a dedicated region of the on-chip Non-Volatile Memory (NVM), which is MRAM. The
     SE applies these settings during the device boot process.
     The device interconnect supports the following main features:
       n High-performance AXI4 bus protocol
       n 64-bit wide read and write data paths
       n 400 MHz bus clock frequency
       n Burst-based transactions for optimizing bandwidth efficiency
       n TrustZone aware
       n Firewall controller and 14 firewall components to enforce secure policy constraining the bus master’s
         access to the device resources
       n Firewall security monitoring function raising an interrupt when unauthorized access is attempted

     Figure 7-1 provides a high-level overview of the system interconnect implementation in the device.

       For managing software configurations of device resources, power, pins, clocks, DMA requests,
       interrupts, and various other additional settings, refer to the Alif Conductor tool.



 7.2 Interconnect Firewall Functional Description

 7.2.1 Firewall Component
     Each FC has 64KB allocated for its own configuration registers, but only the first 4KB is used and the
     remaining 60KB is reserved and generates a configuration access error if accessed. Any unused address space
     within the 4KB is also reserved and generates a configuration access error if accessed.
     There are some common registers which all FCs have. These are:
         n The FC_CAP0 register that can be used by SW to find out the extension levels for each FC. See also Table
           7-1.
         n The FC_CFG0 to FC_CFG3 registers that can be used by SW to find out how an FC has been configured.


 7.2.1.1 Protection Extension (PE)
     The protection extension enables the FC to split the address space accessed by a bus master. This is achieved
     using regions. Each region defines the access permissions to an address range based on the master which
     issued the transaction.
     Alongside the regions, an FC also implements at least one fault entry. Each fault entry provides details about
     the transaction that has faulted and is automatically added to an internal FIFO. Software accesses the
     individual fault entries using the FE_TAL, FE_TAU, FE_TP, FE_MID, and FE_CTRL registers. When software
     acknowledges a fault entry by setting to 1 the FE_CTRL[ACK] bit, it is removed from the FIFO and the next
     valid fault entry can be read, if such exists. The FE_CTRL register also has other control and status bits
     associated with the fault entry functionality.
     When processing, the FC performs checks on the transactions. Transactions which pass proceed to their
     destination and are referred to as allowed transactions. For transactions which fail, also referred to as
     faulting transactions, the FC blocks the transaction from its destination. This means, the transaction is
     terminated.
     The number of regions implemented in an FC can be found in the FC_CFG1[NUM_RGN] field. A region has
     properties which SW can program using the Region Window Entry (RWE). The RWE_CTRL[RGN_INDX] field
     selects the region to which the RWE refers to.
     A region defines a memory area on which certain masters can perform certain memory operations. A region
     can have the following properties:
         n Base address configured via the RGN_CFG1[BASE_ADDR_H] and RGN_CFG0[BASE_ADDR_L] fields
         n Upper address configured via the RGN_TCFG1[OUTPUT_ADDR_H] and RGN_TCFG0 [OUTPUT_ADDR_L]
           fields
         n Size configured via the RGN_SIZE[SIZE] field
         n One to four Master Permission Entries (MPE), each containing:


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                               Alif Semiconductor
                                                           115
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                  www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


          l Master ID configured via the RGN_MIDn[MST_ID] field
          l Enable controls for combinations of secure and non-secure, privileged and unprivileged, read, write

            and execute accesses configured via the bits shown in Table 7-3
     The base address sets the lower address boundary that the region will match on incoming transactions. The
     base address is considered inclusive to the region, i.e. the address of the incoming transaction must be
     greater than or equal to the base address.
     The upper address sets the upper address boundary that the region will match on incoming transactions. The
     upper address is considered inclusive to the region, i.e. the address of the incoming transaction must be
     lower than or equal to the upper address.
     The base and upper address properties can be either fixed or programmable (software-defined) as shown in
     Table 7-1.
     Both the base and upper address must be an integer multiple of the MNRS. An attempt to program a value
     which is not an integer multiple of MNRS is round down to the nearest integer multiple of MNRS.
     If the base address is set to a value greater than the protection size of the FC, no transactions match against
     the region.
     When the RGN_SIZE[MULNPO2] bit is set to 0, the FC treats the base address as being aligned to the size of
     the region. When MULNPO2 is set to 1, the FC treats the base and upper addresses as being aligned to
     MNRS.
     The size of a region can also be either fixed or programmable (software-defined) as shown in Table 7-1. It can
     be defined as 0 to prevent any transaction matching against the region. If a region size is lower than MNRS or
     greater than MXRS, it is treated as if the size was set to 0.
     There are up to four MPEs per region which allow up to four different permissions to be defined. Each MPE
     defines the access permission for a specific master to that region or in case of MPE0 for any master. The MPE
     is only used if the master ID of the transaction and the MPE match. In case of MPE0, the MPE is also used if it
     is configured to match any master ID via the RGN_MPLn[ANY_MST] bit. The master ID identifies a particular
     master in the device. Table 7-2 shows the master ID mapping.
                                          Table 7-2 Master ID Mapping
                            Master ID                                                Master
                                0                                                      SE
                                1                                                     A32
                               16                                                   M55-HP
                               17                                                    M55-HE
                               32                                   DMA0, CPI, CDC, GPU2D, USB, SDMMC, ETH


     The number of MPEs implemented, per region by an FC, can be discovered using the FC_CFG2[NUM_MPE]
     field. It is also shown in Table 7-1.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       116
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


                                                        NOTE

       If more than four masters must have access to a single area of memory, then SW should define more
       regions with the same base address, size or upper address and use the MPE entries of the additional
       regions. It is valid to define the same area of memory in multiple regions as long as the same master is
       not defined in more than one MPE for the same memory area. The FC generates a programming fault
       if a transaction matches more than one region and MPE pair.


     Table 7-3 shows the master permissions supported by an FC.
                                        Table 7-3 FC Master Permissions
                 Permission (Bit in RGN_MPLn)                                     Description

                            NSUW                                         Non-secure unprivileged write
                            NSUX                                        Non-secure unprivileged execute

                            NSPW                                          Non-secure privileged write
                            NSPX                                         Non-secure privileged execute
                             SUR                                            Secure unprivileged read

     The RGN_CTRL0[EN] bit is present for all FCs. It enables or disables the region specified by the RWE_CTRL
     [RGN_INDX] field. When EN is set to 1, then any write to modify the following region properties generates a
     configuration access error:
       n Base address (RGN_CFG1[BASE_ADDR_H] and RGN_CFG0[BASE_ADDR_L])
       n Size (RGN_SIZE[SIZE])
       n Upper address or translation address (RGN_TCFG1[OUTPUT_ADDR_H] and RGN_TCFG0 [OUTPUT_
         ADDR_L])
       n Translation properties (RGN_TCFG2)

     The RGN_CTRL1[MPE3_EN], RGN_CTRL1[MPE2_EN], RGN_CTRL1[MPE1_EN], and RGN_CTRL1[MPE0_EN] bits
     control whether a transaction can match against the MPE for the associated region. When an MPEx_EN bit is
     set to 1, any write to modify the associated MPE is ignored. The MPE3_EN, MPE2_EN, and MPE1_EN are not
     present for all FCs. Table 7-1 shows the number of MPEs for each FC. This can also be checked when the FC_
     CFG2[NUM_MPE] bit is read.
     Region 0 is the default region and has different behavior than the other regions within the FC. It has the
     following changes to the other regions:
       n The base address is fixed and set to a value of all zeroes
       n The size is fixed and set equal to the FC_CFG2[PROT_SIZE] field
       n The RGN_TCFG2[ADDR_TRANS_EN] bit is 0
       n The RGN_SIZE[MULNPO2] bit is 0




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       117
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


     A transaction only matches against the default region when the default region is enabled, and the transaction
     does not match any other region. If a transaction matches more than one MPE in the default region, then a
     programming error is generated for the transaction.
     In addition, the FC also has a bypass interface which along with the PE_CTRL[BYPASS_MSK] bit control
     whether the FC protection logic is bypassed or not. Software can determine this by reading the PE_BPS
     [BYPASS_ST] bit.


                                                         NOTE

     It is recommended to set the PE_CTRL[BYPASS_MSK] bit to 1 so that the protection logic does not get
     bypassed.


 7.2.1.2 Monitor Extension (ME)
     The FC also has monitor logic that detects errors generated by the transactions of the device masters. It can
     be enabled or disabled using the ME_CTRL[EN] bit. When the FC detects a response to a read transaction,
     which indicates an error has occurred, it can be configured whether to set the read data to all zeroes or a
     value dependent on the master ID of the transaction via the ME_CTRL[RDUM] bit.
     The monitor logic checks the responses on the bus master interfaces of the FC. If the response indicates an
     error, the FC logs the transaction and forwards the response to the issuing master.
     An error detection report contains the following information:
       n Master ID
       n Privilege level
       n Data or instruction
       n Security
       n Read or write
       n Address of transaction

     Each error detection report is automatically added to an internal FIFO. Software accesses the individual error
     detection report using the EDR_TAL, EDR_TAU, EDR_TP, EDR_MID, and EDR_CTRL registers. When software
     acknowledges an error detection report by setting to 1 the EDR_CTRL[ACK] bit, the report is removed from
     the FIFO and the next valid one can be read, if such exists. The EDR_CTRL register also has other status bits
     associated with the error detection report functionality.

 7.2.1.3 Translation Extension (TE)
     The TE allows the FC to modify properties of the outgoing transaction. Translation is only applied after a
     transaction has passed the checks, the region used to perform the checks was configured as a power of 2 in
     size (RGN_SIZE[MULNPO2] set to 0), and the RGN_TCFG2[ADDR_TRANS_EN] bit is set to 1. If the RGN_TCFG2
     [ADDR_TRANS_EN] bit is set to 0, the output transaction address is the same as the incoming transaction
     address.
     The TE adds the following properties to a region:
       n Output transaction memory attribute property—configured by the RGN_TCFG2[MA] field and enabled
         by the RGN_TCFG2[MA_TRANS_EN] bit
       n Output transaction security property—configured by the RGN_TCFG2[NS] field
       n Output transaction instruction property—configured by the RGN_TCFG2[INST] field
       n Output transaction share-ability property—configured by the RGN_TCFG2[SH] field


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                         118
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


       n Output transaction privilege level property—configured by the RGN_TCFG2[PRIV] field
       n Output transaction translation address—calculated by the following formula:
         OTA[63:0] = ITA[63:PROT_SIZE]:TA[PROT_SIZE-1:SIZE]:ITA[SIZE-1:0], where:
         l OTA is the output transaction translation address

         l ITA is the incoming transaction address, zero extended to 64 bits

         l TA is the translation address

         l PROT_SIZE is FC_CFG2[PROT_SIZE]

         l SIZE is RGN_SIZE[SIZE]



 7.2.1.4 Region Size Extension (RSE)
     The RSE allows regions to have a size which is not equal to a power of 2. For example, if there is a 12KB
     memory buffer, the region is defined as 16KB, this means that the memory between 12KB and 16KB is not
     able to be used for another device. However, if the FC supports region size extension, the region can be
     defined to be 12KB and no memory is wasted. Table 7-1 shows which FCs support RSE.

 7.2.1.5 Lockdown Extension (LDE)
     The LDE is implemented at firewall level, with all FCs implementing same features. It allows the FC registers
     to be prevented from being updated. The lockdown states an FC can enter are Open, Partial, and Full
     configured by the LD_CTRL[LOCK] field.
     In Open state all registers can be updated, except for the RWE_CTRL , RGN_CTRL0, RGN_CTRL1, RGN_LCTRL,
     RGN_CFG0, RGN_CFG1, RGN_SIZE, RGN_TCFG0, RGN_TCFG1, RGN_TCFG2, RGN_MIDn, and RGN_MPLn
     registers, when the RWE_CTRL[RGN_INDX] points to a region which is in locked state.
     In Partial lockdown state all registers, except the following, are read-only:
       n RWE_CTRL
       n FE_CTRL
       n EDR_CTRL
       n RGN_CTRL0, RGN_CTRL1, RGN_LCTRL, RGN_CFG0, RGN_CFG1, RGN_SIZE, RGN_TCFG0, RGN_TCFG1,
         RGN_TCFG2, RGN_MIDn, and RGN_MPLn registers, when the RWE_CTRL[RGN_INDX] points to a region
         which is in unlocked state.
     In Full lockdown state all registers, except the following, are read-only:
       n RWE_CTRL
       n FE_CTRL
       n EDR_CTRL

     The LD_CTRL register is read-only, when in Partial or Full lockdown state, and the LD_CTRL[LDI_ST] bit of an
     FC is 1. Any attempt to update a read-only register under these conditions generates a configuration access
     error.

 7.2.1.6 Save and Restore
     There are shadow registers used to preserve the state of certain registers when the associated FC enters a
     non-operational mode. Preserved registers are:
       n PE_CTRL
       n RWE_CTRL
       n ME_CTRL
       n LD_CTRL[LOCK]
       n FW_CTRL
       n FCn_INT_MSK


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                        119
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


       n   For each region, whether activated or not:
           l RGN_CTRL0, RGN_CTRL1

           l RGN_LCTRL

           l RGN_CFG0, RGN_CFG1

           l RGN_SIZE

           l RGN_TCFG0 to RGN_TCFG2

           l RGN_MPLn

           l RGN_MIDn


     In case an FC enters a non-operational mode, the FW_SR_CTRL[SR_PWR] bit determines whether the shadow
     registers are required to retain their values or not. It is recommended that software polls the FW_SR_CTRL
     [SR_RDY] bit whether it became 1 before attempting to program the firewall. When the FW_SR_CTRL[SR_
     RDY] bit is 0 software can only access the FW_SR_CTRL, FC_CAP0, FC_CFG0 to FC_CFG3, PID0 to PID4, and
     CID0 to CID3 registers.

 7.2.2 Firewall Controller
     The FCTLR is a modified FC, which provides access control to all FCs and the save and restore functionality
     described in Section 7.2.1.6 Save and Restore. It also generates interrupts.

 7.2.2.1 Protection Extension (PE)
     The PE functionality supported by the FCTLR is the same as described in Section 7.2.1.1 Protection Extension
     (PE) except for the following differences:
       n Reset value of the PE_CTRL[EN] and PE_ST[EN] bits is 1
       n It always supports at least 3 regions
       n Region 0 is enabled by default



                                                          NOTE

       It is recommended that software never sets the PE_CTRL[EN] bit to 0 when the PE_ST[BYPASS_MSK]
       bit is 1 or PE_BPS[BYPASS_ST] is 0. If this is done, the FCTLR becomes disabled and all transactions will
       fail the protection logic checks, so the software will be unable to perform any other configuration
       accesses to the firewall.

 7.2.2.2 Region Size Extension (RSE)
     The RSE functionality supported by the FCTLR is the same as described in Section 7.2.1.4 Region Size
     Extension (RSE).

 7.2.2.3 Lockdown Extension (LDE)
     The LDE functionality supported by the FCTLR is the same as described in Section 7.2.1.5 Lockdown
     Extension (LDE) except the following additional registers:
       n FW_TMP_TA, FW_TMP_TP, and FW_TMP_MID
       n FCn_INT_ST: can be updated in any lockdown state
       n FCn_INT_MSK: cannot be updated when in Partial or Full lockdown states
       n FW_TMP_CTRL: can be updated in any lockdown state
       n FW_CTRL: cannot be updated when in Partial or Full lockdown states


 7.2.2.3.1 Tamper Interrupt and Tamper Report
     The FCTLR generates configuration access error, tamper report and interrupt when a configuration access
     that has passed the protection logic checks attempts to do one of the following:
       n Update a register of an FC that is in Partial or Full lockdown state, except the RWE_CTRL, FE_CTRL, EDR_
         CTRL, FCn_INT_ST, FW_TMP_CTRL, and LD_CTRL registers
       n Update a register of a region that is in locked state
       n Update the value of the RGN_LCTRL[LOCK] field when it is set to 1 and the FC is in Partial lockdown state
       n Update the value of the RGN_LCTRL[LOCK] field when the FC is in Full lockdown state
       n Change the lockdown state of an FC, when it is in Partial or Full lockdown state, when the LD_CTRL[LDI_
         ST] bit of the FCTLR is 1
       n Access the FW_TMP_CTRL, FW_TMP_TA, FW_TMP_TP, and FW_TMP_MID registers without the correct
         properties or from a master with master ID other than in region 0
     When a tamper report condition occurs, the report is generated only if there is not a valid one, otherwise the
     FW_TMP_CTRL[TR_OVERFLW] bit is set to 1. A tamper report is valid when the FW_TMP_CTRL[TR_VLD] bit is
     set to 1. Software is required to acknowledge the tamper report by writing 1 to the FW_TMP_CTRL[ACK] bit
     only when it has collected the information contained in the FW_TMP_CTRL, FW_TMP_TA, FW_TMP_TP, and
     FW_TMP_MID registers. Once software has acknowledged the tamper report, the values in these registers
     become 0, except if another tamper report is generated in the same cycle.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                       121
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


 7.2.2.4 Interrupts
     The FCTLR receives interrupt requests from the FCs and generates the FW_IRQ. When the FCTLR receives an
     interrupt request that is not masked by a bit in the FCn_INT_MSK registers, it generates an interrupt and
     updates the corresponding status register (FCn_INT_ST) and the corresponding bit in the FW_INT_ST register.
     The FW_IRQ remains asserted as long as any interrupt status field, it is associated with, is set to 1. Changing
     the value of the interrupt mask does not affect any interrupts which have already been asserted.
     For FW_IRQ mapping, refer to Section 11.5 Interrupt Sources Mapping.

 7.3 Interconnect Firewall Programming Guide

 7.3.1 Region Programming
     To program a region software must follow the below steps:
      1. Select the correct region using the RWE_CTRL[RGN_INDX] field.
      2. Program the region base address using the RGN_CFG0 and RGN_CFG1 registers.
      3. Program the region size or upper address using the RGN_SIZE or RGN_TCFG0 and RGN_TCFG1 registers.
      4. Program and enable the translation properties, if required, using the RGN_TCFG2 register. If the region
         is required to perform address translation, software must use the RGN_TCFG0 and RGN_TCFG1 registers
         to define the address translation.
      5. Program the required master permission entries using the RGN_MIDn and RGN_MPLn registers.
      6. Enable the required master permission entries using the RGN_CTRL1[MPE0_EN], RGN_CTRL1[MPE1_EN],
         RGN_CTRL1[MPE2_EN], and RGN_CTRL1[MPE3_EN] bits.
      7. Wait for one of the associated RGN_ST[MPE0_EN], RGN_ST[MPE1_EN], RGN_ST[MPE2_EN], and RGN_ST
         [MPE3_EN] bits to become 1.
      8. Enable the region by setting the RGN_CTRL0[EN] bit to 1.
      9. Wait for the RGN_ST[EN] bit to become 1.

 7.3.2 Update Master Permission Entry
     When the software only updates the MPE, the sequence is as follows:
      1. Select the correct region using the RWE_CTRL[RGN_INDX] field.
      2. Disable the MPE by setting one of the RGN_CTRL1[MPE0_EN], RGN_CTRL1[MPE1_EN], RGN_CTRL1
         [MPE2_EN], and RGN_CTRL1[MPE3_EN] bits to 0. Software may need to unlock the region first.
      3. Wait for the associated RGN_ST[MPE0_EN], RGN_ST[MPE1_EN], RGN_ST[MPE2_EN], and RGN_ST
         [MPE3_EN] bits to become 0.
      4. Update the values in the RGN_MIDn and RGN_MPLn registers.
      5. Enable the MPE by setting one of the RGN_CTRL1[MPE0_EN], RGN_CTRL1[MPE1_EN], RGN_CTRL1
         [MPE2_EN], and RGN_CTRL1[MPE3_EN] bits to 1.
      6. Wait for one of the associated RGN_ST[MPE0_EN], RGN_ST[MPE1_EN], RGN_ST[MPE2_EN], and RGN_ST
         [MPE3_EN] bits to become 1.

 7.3.3 Update Region Address Range or Translation
     When software is required to update any the settings of any region other than MPE, the sequence is as
     follows:
      1. Select the correct region using the RWE_CTRL[RGN_INDX] field.
      2. Disable the region by setting the RGN_CTRL0[EN] bit to 0. Software may need to unlock the region first.
      3. Wait for the RGN_ST[EN] bit to become 0.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                        122
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


      4. Update the required settings in the RGN_SIZE, RGN_CFG0, RGN_CFG1, RGN_TCFG0, RGN_TCFG1, and
         RGN_TCFG2 registers.
      5. Enable the region by setting the RGN_CTRL0[EN] bit to 1. At this point software can also lock, or re-lock
         the region.
      6. Wait for the RGN_ST[EN] bit to become 1.

    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             In case of RSE.0 or PE.1 this field is reserved. It is also reserved for
                                                             the default region in case of PE.2.
                                                             The size of the region
                                                             0x00: 0B
                                                             0x05: 32B
                                                             0x06: 64B
                                                             …
                                                             0x0C: 4KB
                                                             0x0D: 8KB
                                                             …
                                                             0x40: 16KB
    7-0       SIZE                    R/W          0x-
                                                             The legal values this field can be set to depend on the MNRS and
                                                             MXRS.
                                                             If software attempts to set this field to a value greater than 0x40,
                                                             lower than MNRS, or greater than MXRS, the field is set to 0x00
                                                             instead.
                                                             When this field is 0x00 it does not match against any transactions.
                                                             This field is only used if RGN_SIZE[MULNPO2] is 0. Otherwise it is
                                                             ignored.
                                                             This field is functional (R/W) only in case of PE.2 for all regions,
                                                             except for the default one.

                                                             0x0: Address translation is disabled. The output transaction has

                                                             0x1: Address translation is enabled. The output transaction has an
     17       ADDR_TRANS_EN           R/W         0x0        address that is set based on the following formula: OTA[63:0] = ITA

                                                             transaction.

                                                             transaction memory attribute is as defined in the RGN_TCG2[MA]
                                                             field.
                                                             This field is reserved in case of TE.0 or when FC_CFG1[MA_SPT] is
                                                             0x0.
                                                             Output transaction instruction or data
                                                             0x0: Use incoming transaction value
                                                             0x1: Use incoming transaction value
                                                             0x2: Data

   15-14 INST                         R/W         0x0        0x3: Instruction
                                                             This field only affects read transactions. All write transactions are

 7.4.3.34 FW_INT_ST Register
           Offset           Access          Description
        0xD90
                              R             Firewall Interrupt Status Register
     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             Interrupt status for the associated firewall component. There is a
                                                             bit per firewall component indicating if any bit in the
                                                             corresponding FCn_INT_ST register is 1. Any bits associated with a
                                                             firewall component that is not implemented are reserved.
                                                             Bit 0 is for FC0, bit 1 is for FC1, bit 2 is for FC2, etc.
    31-0      FC_INT_ST                R           0x0
                                                             0x0: No interrupt is asserted by firewall component
                                                             0x1: Interrupt is asserted by firewall component
                                                             Note: Software can find out how many firewall components are
                                                             implemented in the firewall by reading the FC_CFG3[NUM_FC]
                                                             field of the firewall controller.
