 8 System Control

 8.1 Power Management

 8.1.1 Power Management Overview
     The device has three operating regions that encapsulate top-level functions from a power consumption
     perspective:
       n Always-On (AON) Region—a group of rudimentary functions that are always powered when a constant
         power source is connected to the VDD_BATT pin.
       n High-Efficiency (HE) Region—a group of compute, sensing, AI functions designed to operate at the
         highest efficiency. Many tasks can be performed in this region to conserve power and/or extend battery
         life before waking up the HP Region.
       n High-Performance (HP) Region—a group of compute, AI, Human-Machine Interface (HMI), and high-
         speed connectivity functions designed to operate at maximum performance. These functions are
         invoked only as required to conserve energy.
     The device block diagram (see Figure 1-1) illustrates these three operating regions and the functions
     available within each of the regions.
     A smart power management scheme named aiPM (autonomous intelligent Power Management) utilizes a
     hierarchy of multiple power domains, multiple internal voltage supplies, and multiple power modes to power
     on, in fine granularity, portions of the device only when they are needed based on use case, and off when not
     needed. Powering on and off portions of the device occurs automatically in hardware as required, but the
     power management policies are configured by software.
     Multiple power domains—There are ten independent power domains in the device, each one with a
     dedicated power controller that is coordinated by digital logic and software configuration for automatic
     transitions—from power-up to full GO mode, and all modes in between. This scheme achieves optimum
     power efficiency based on the dynamic power demand of the device at any given moment in time.
     Multiple voltage supplies—There are internal device voltage supplies consisting of a series of Low Drop-Out
     (LDO) regulators and a dual-mode DC-to-DC buck converter (DC-DC) to generate 0.55 V, 0.8 V, and 1.8 V
     internal voltage rails that are automatically switched on and off as required for optimum performance and
     efficiency.
     Multiple power modes—Below are top-level device modes listed from highest to lowest power
     consumption:
       n GO—any or all processing cores operate up to their max frequency
       n READY—all processing cores are clock gated off, but peripherals can run
       n IDLE—all processing cores are powered off, but some peripherals can run
       n STANDBY—all processing cores are powered off, but a few low-power peripherals can run
       n STOP—entire device is powered off except the AON Region where rudimentary low-power peripherals
         and wake-up sources are active, as well as optional retained SRAM blocks
     The device Power Domains (PD) are managed by a Power Sequence Controller (PSC) and several Power Policy
     Units (PPU). The PSC is a state machine that monitors a fixed set of inputs and automatically acts to turn
     power on or off in power domains at the lower levels. PPUs take inputs from the PSC, inputs from the device
     condition status, and inputs from configuration settings from the application code, then PPUs act
     autonomously to turn on or off power to the domains, and PPUs also control domain clock sources. Thus, the

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                      156
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     operational processes of the PSC and PPUs automatically and dynamically achieve the best power
     consumption based on instantaneous power demand.
     Figure 8-1 illustrates the power domains, control hierarchy, transition possibilities, and relevance to the
     three operating regions of the device. The power-up sequence of the shown regions and domains is:
      1. If VDD_BATT is connected to a constant voltage source, the PD-0 domain and the AON Region are
         Always-On.
      2. The PD-2 domain is first to power up.
      3. The next order of powering up the domains depends on whether the device executes an initial boot
         (cold), or a wake up (warm).
     PDs in each of the three device regions are defined as follows:
       n AON Region
         l PD-0, AON power and control

         l PD-1, SRAM6 to SRAM9 power control

       n HE Region
         l PD-2, High Efficiency Region power and control

         l PD-3, Real Time Subsystem-High Efficiency (RTSS-HE)

         l PD-4, SRAM6 to SRAM9 memory blocks

       n HP Region
         l PD-5, Secure Enclave Subsystem (SESS)

         l PD-6, Shared Peripherals / Shared System Resources (SYST)

         l PD-7, Real Time Subsystem-High Performance (RTSS-HP)

         l PD-8, Debug Subsystem (DBSS)

         l PD-9, Application Processor Subsystem (APSS)

     The device power domains are supplied with voltages from several internal supply sources. Power domains
     that feature SRAM retention have dual voltage supplies.
     The device voltage supply and distribution system is architected to:
       n Implement the aiPM strategy to dynamically power on only what is needed within the most optimum
         region of the device
       n Minimize leakage current in STOP and STANDBY modes
       n Rapidly exit low power modes upon a wake-up event
       n Minimize dynamic current consumption in GO mode

     Figure 8-2 illustrates the voltage distribution inside the device including highly efficient LDO regulators and a
     DC-DC buck converter. Very few external power sources are required because of the power management
     capability within the device to generate multiple voltage rails and to correctly sequence the supplies during
     power up and power down.

 8.1.2 Power Domains
     Figure 8-1 illustrates the power domains, control hierarchy, transition possibilities, and relevance to the
     three operating regions of the device.
     Starting with PD-0, this domain is first to power-on and is always on when a battery or other voltage source is
     connected to the VDD_BATT pin. All functions related to STOP mode reside in PD-0. Within PD-0 is the state
     machine PSC-STOP that monitors device conditions and wake-up inputs to coordinate power-up and power-
     down of PD-2.
     PD-2 is the power source for all functions related to STANDBY mode and for control of the device HE Region.
     PSC-STBY can directly power-up and power-down PD-3 through PD-7 using PPU-3 through PPU-7. Within PD-
     2 is the state machine PSC-STBY that monitors conditions and wake-up inputs to determine the wake-up
     sequence of power domains above PD-2.
     PD-6 is the power source for all shared device resources in the HP Region which are not available in STANDBY
     or STOP mode. PD-8 stays on whenever a debug connection is present. Depending on configuration, PPU-3
     through PPU-7 may autonomously power-on and power-down PD-3 through PD-7 based on software or
     hardware activity.

                                                               161
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                          www.alifsemi.com

 8.1.3 Voltage Supplies
     PMU—The device has an internal Power Management Unit (PMU) block containing two bandgaps, a series of
     LDOs, a DCDC converter, and high frequency clock sources. It is responsible for regulating internal power sup-
     ply voltages and switching on and off LDOs for Tightly Coupled Memory (TCM) retention.
     Three LDOs and an AON bandgap are supplied by VDD_BATT. LDO-0 provides power to optionally retain
     contents of the 4KB Utility SRAM. LDO-1 powers functions within power domain PD-0, including the clock
     sources LFRC and LFXO. LDO-2 provides power to optionally retain the contents of RTSS-HE TCM.
     All remaining LDOs are supplied by VDD_MAIN. LDO-3 supplies a bandgap and a low-power HFRC clock for
     rapid start of processing subsystems (when compared to the HFXO or PLL clock sources). LDO-4 powers the
     MRAM blocks. LDO-5 powers the analog peripheral block. LDO-6 powers the DSI and CSI interface PHYs as
     needed.
     Finally, the DC-DC converter is supplied by VDD_BUCK and it supplies VREG_CORE_0V8 to the device. The
     dual-mode DC-DC automatically switches between a low-power operating range (DC-DC PFM mode) and a
     high-power range (DC-DC PWM mode) to maintain optimum DC-DC conversion efficiency based on the
     device instantaneous power demand.
     There are three functional blocks that have specific voltage requirements: the multi-function I/O pins, system
     debug channels, and analog peripherals and interfaces
     Digital IO—This functional block includes the output drive stage, input buffering, and pullups for digital IO
     functions. Digital IOs are multiplexed for many different peripherals like UART, I2C, SPI, etc.
     Debug—This functional block is powered whenever both VDD_MAIN is present and PD-6 is powered on.
     Analog—This functional block consists of PHY interfaces for USB, DSI, and CSI. Additionally, if precision
     external voltage reference levels are required for device analog peripherals, such as the ADCs, then the pre-
     cision reference should be attached at VREF_P.

 8.1.4 Power Modes
     RUN mode—A processor subsystem is in RUN mode any time the processor core is executing instructions,
     including for(;;) or while(1) loops. This means power and clocks to the core, its TCM, and its subsystem’s local
     peripherals are all enabled. The rest of the device, shared peripherals, and shared memory are available as
     well.
     SLEEP mode—Entering SLEEP mode is simply done by a processor core executing the WFI instruction. While
     in SLEEP mode, the processor core clock is gated. The rest of the processor subsystem and the rest of the
     device continues operation with running clocks. Local and shared peripherals may then generate interrupts
     to resume RUN mode on the core.
     IDLE mode—IDLE mode is when a processor is powered down, that is, CPU is in the OFF state. If RTSS-HE is
     powered down then the LPCPI, LPI2S, LPPDM, and LPSPI in the same subsystem are also powered down.
     LPUART, LPI2C, LPTIMER, LPCMP, LPRTC, and LPGPIO may wake up the device from IDLE mode.
     STANDBY mode—When PD-2 is on, and all higher numbered domains are off (PD-3 and above), the device is
     in STANDBY mode. Using STANDBY mode makes available some clocks and modules that are not available in
     STOP mode. The cost is higher static power relative to STOP mode. The clocks and modules enabled by this
     mode are in the HE Region (PD-2) as shown in Table 8-1.
     STOP mode—When PD-0 is on, and PD-2 and above are off, the device is in STOP mode. The clocks and mod-
     ules enabled by this mode are in the AON Region (PD-0) as shown in Table 8-1.

 8.1.5 Power Supply Supervisors
     The device has integrated supervisory circuits for Brown-Out Reset (BOR), Brown-Out Detect (BOD), and
     Power-On-Reset (POR).
     The POR circuit will hold a device region or the entire device in reset until a sufficient voltage is detected, for
     example, during power-on voltage ramp. There is one POR circuit, VBAT_POR, which monitors the VDD_BATT
     (AON Region) and keeps the entire device in reset during initial power ramp to the device (see Figure 8-3).
     The BOD circuit monitors the VDD_MAIN power supply and generates interrupts when the voltage falls
     below a programmable threshold. The BOR circuit monitors the VDD_MAIN power supply and causes an
     immediate reset to the main SoC when the voltage falls below a programmable threshold. For applications
     utilizing BOD and/or BOR, the minimum device operating voltage on VDD_MAIN is limited to 1.9 V.
     When the BOD threshold is reached, the BOD circuit generates an interrupt to the application CPU cores and
     SE to perform any backup needed before power drops below the threshold. The BOD interrupt can be used
     as a wake-up source from STANDBY and from STOP low-power modes. BOD also triggers a DMA request
     which can help to complete the backup task faster and with lesser CPU load.
     When the BOR threshold is reached and the BOR circuit causes an immediate reset to the main SoC, safe
     operation of the device is not guaranteed.

 8.2 Reset Management

 8.3 Clock Generation and Control

 8.3.1 Clock Generation and Control Overview
     The device clocking scheme includes several clock domains, PLL, clock dividers, clock multiplexers, and four
     oscillators. The PLL has a single clock output.
     The device clock sources are as follows:
       n Low-Frequency Resistor-Capacitor (LFRC) oscillator—a low-power, internal RC oscillator powered by
         VDD_BATT. This oscillator is used during the power-up sequence, with a typical clock frequency accuracy
         of 32.7 kHz ±4%.
       n Low-Frequency crystal Oscillator (LFXO)—a low-power oscillator that can be used with a high-accuracy
         32.768 kHz external crystal. This oscillator is powered by VDD_BATT. It is enabled at power-up and is the
         typical clock source for LPRTC. The LFXO oscillator input may optionally be configured in bypass mode
         for connection to an external 32.768 kHz clock source.
       n High-Frequency Resistor-Capacitor (HFRC) oscillator—a low-power internal RC oscillator that is able to
         generate frequencies of up to 76.8 MHz. When the LFXO clock source is available, the HFRC oscillator
         can be trimmed to reach an accuracy of ±2% or better over temperature. The HFRC oscillator is available
         in all power modes except for STOP mode. This oscillator can be used during a power-up sequence for
         rapid initialization and fast start-up.
       n High-Frequency crystal Oscillator (HFXO)—a power-optimized oscillator that can be used with an
         external crystal with a frequency between 24 MHz and 38.4 MHz. This oscillator is enabled by software
         after initial device configuration and is the source clock for the PLL. The HFXO oscillator input may
         optionally be configured in bypass mode for connection to an external high-speed clock
         source/oscillator.
       n Phase-Locked Loop (PLL)—a power-optimized, fast-locking clock multiplier with fractional mode. It has a
         single clock output used to supply most of the device subsystems, modules, and interconnects.
     Figure 8-5 provides a high-level overview of the clocking scheme implementation in the device.

 8.3.5.3.6 SSI_CTRL Register
           Offset           Access          Description
         0x28
                             R/W            SPI Control Register
     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
   31-12 RESERVED                      R           0x-       Reserved
                                                             SS_IN Value
                                                             One bit for each SPI module:
                                                             - Bit 11: SPI3
                                                             - Bit 8: SPI0
    11-8      SS_IN_VAL               R/W          0x0
                                                             When SS_IN_SEL = 0x1, the programmed SS_IN_VAL is fed to SPI
                                                             module.
                                                             Note: If the corresponding SPI module is configured as a master,
                                                             the associated bit in this field should be set to 0x1.
    7-4       RESERVED                 R           0x-       Reserved
                                                             SS_IN Mode Select
                                                             One bit for each SPI module:
                                                             - Bit 3: SPI3
                                                             - Bit 0: SPI0
                                                             0x0: SS_IN from I/O pin
                                                             0x1: SS_IN from SS_IN_VAL
    3-0       SS_IN_SEL               R/W          0x0
                                                             Note: If the corresponding SPI module is configured as a master,
                                                             the associated bit in this field should be set to 0x1.
                                                             If the corresponding SPI module is configured as a slave, and the
                                                             master device is driving a slave select signal, the associated bit in
                                                             this field should be set to 0x0. If the master device is not driving a
                                                             slave select signal, the associated bit in this field should be set to
                                                             0x1, and the associated bit in SS_IN_VAL field should be set to 0x0.

 8.4 Clock Monitoring System
     The device contains a clock monitoring system. If enabled by the OSC_CTRL[CLKMON_ENA] bit, it checks if
     the clocks from both HFXO and HFRC are running and generates interrupt to SE if these clocks are not active.
     This interrupt is logged in the CGU_IRQ[XTAL_DEAD] bit and also as a read-only status in the OSC_CTRL
     [XTAL_DEAD] bit. It can be cleared by reading the CGU_IRQ[XTAL_DEAD] bit. The clock monitoring system
     does not check frequency, but only if the clocks are running or not.

 8.5 Signal Multiplexing and I/O Buffer Configuration
 8.5.1 Signal Multiplexing
     The device offers a sophisticated signal-to-pin multiplexing scheme. Each I/O pin may be assigned to one of
     up to eight peripheral signals, and vice versa, a peripheral signal may be routed to up to four I/O pins. This
     assignment is pseudo-static and must be performed once during boot time.
     The multiplexed pins are divided into 8-pin groups, also referred to as 'ports'. A pin identifier 'Pn_i' may be
     used, where n is the port number and i is the pin number within that port. A pin may be referenced also with
     the GPIO peripheral's signal name 'GPIOn_i' because it shares the same numbering convention. For more
     information on the GPIO peripheral, see Section 14.1 GPIO Overview.
     MIPI-CSI, MIPI-DSI, USB PHY pins, and power and ground pins have fixed functions and cannot be
     multiplexed.
     Figure 8-6 shows the P0_0 multiplexing as an example. The Pn_i[PINMUX] register bitfield, where n = i = 0,
     selects a peripheral signal to be available on P0_0. The multiplexer switches three signals at a time: IN, OUT,
     and OEN (output enable). OEN could be dynamically driven by the peripheral, for example by the I2C which
     needs to change the Data pin direction very frequently. For many other peripherals OEN could be static, and
     for GPIO it is programmable via its Data Direction register. The analog peripherals are not multiplexed
     between themselves and all three can read P0_0 when [PINMUX] = 7.
                                   Figure 8-6 I/O Signal Multiplexing (P0_0 Example)

 9 Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

 9.1 Hardware Semaphore (HWSEM)

 9.1.1 HWSEM Overview
     The Hardware Semaphore (HWSEM) provides a mechanism for coordinating the concurrency between
     processor cores when they access shared resources—memory regions or peripherals.
     The device includes 16 HWSEM modules with individual interrupt requests. Each of the semaphores can be
     assigned depending on the application needs.
     Each HWSEM module supports the following main features:
       n Acquire, Release, and Reset functions as atomic operation
       n Single-processor access at a time
       n An internal acquisition counter for enabling processor owning of a HWSEM to acquire it multiple times
       n An interrupt assertion once the HWSEM becomes available

     Figure 9-1 provides a high-level overview of the HWSEM module implementation in the device.
                                               Figure 9-1 HWSEM Overview

                                                     HWSEM Logic

                                     Acquire

                                     Reset
                                                    Current Master ID

 9.1.3 HWSEM Functional Description

 9.1.3.1 HWSEM Introduction
     The basic idea of the HWSEM operation is:
       n Each processor in the device has a unique ID, and only one ID is granted access to the shared resource
         (memory or peripheral) at a time.
       n Multiple threads within a single processor reuse the same ID allocated to that processor.
       n The HWSEM count register is reset to zero and gets incremented every time the HWSEM grants a
         software thread (within a single processor) access to a shared resource. For example, if a processor has 3
         threads that need to use the shared resource, then each thread will request and get access to the
         resource, hence the semaphore count register will equal to 3, and then it will get decremented after
         each thread release the resource, till the semaphore count is equal to zero.
       n The interrupt of the HWSEM module is asserted if the module is free, and de-asserted if the module is
         occupied.
     There are two ways to check the availability of a HWSEM module:
       n    Using the HWSEM interrupt
       n    Polling the status of the semaphore
     The interrupt in Figure 9-1 notifies all processor entities that a given HWSEM is free and it can be acquired by
     any CPU. Software algorithms that rely on interrupts are more efficient.
     The use of polling remains an option and the interrupt can be ignored by programming the NVICs or the GIC.

 9.1.3.2 HWSEM Basic Functions
     Every HWSEM module supports the basic functions listed in Table 9-4. Each function is an atomic
     WRITE/READ bus operation from a specific address.
                               Table 9-4 HWSEM Address Offsets of Atomic Functions
   Address Offset       Operation        Function                              Description
           0x0              Write    Request         Putting a request
           0x0              Read     Acquire         Current master ID
           0x4              Write    Release         Releasing resource

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       234
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


   Address Offset        Operation      Function                               Description
         0x4                Read     Check           (Optional) Returns new semaphore count
                                                     (Optional) Reset the semaphore count and current master ID—only
         0x8                Write    Reset
                                                     for debugging
         0x8                Read     No operation    Returns 0

 9.1.3.3 HWSEM Software Programming Sequence
     Use the following sequence to program a HWSEM module:
      1. Request a HWSEM module by writing the processor ID into register with the offset 0x0.
      2. Check the status of the HWSEM request by reading register with the offset 0x0. If the read value
         matches the processor ID the access is granted; otherwise, go to step #1.
      3. Release the HWSEM by writing the processor ID into register with the offset 0x4.
      4. Optional check, read the register with the offset 0x4 to get the current HWSEM count. If the count
         differs from 0, there are other threads in the processor that are still using the resource.

 9.2 Message Handling Unit (MHU)

 9.2.1 MHU Overview
     The Message Handling Unit (MHU) provides point-to-point communication between the Secure Enclave
     processor, the Application processor (A32), and the two Real-Time processors (M55-HP and M55-HE). The
     MHU is an interrupt-based communication between two processing entities.
     The device includes up to 24 unidirectional MHU modules.
     Each of the MHU modules supports the following main features:
       n Two memory mapped register frames—Sender and Receiver
       n Unidirectional communication interface
       n Read and write access—32-bit word aligned
       n Dual transport channels
       n Different transport protocols—Doorbell, Single-Word transfer, and Multi-Word
       n Dedicated interrupt lines for the Sender and Receiver

     The software responsibilities are:
       n To request the Receiver to be powered
       n To ensure that the Sender remains powered until the transfer has been finished
       n To use Ready to Send protocol to send the transfer

     Each processor entity includes only one of the Sender or Receiver frame. To ensure a bi-directional (full-
     duplex) communication between the entities, two MHUs with reversed Sender and Receiver parts are
     implemented, see Figure 9-3.

 9.2.3 MHU Functional Description



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                                 242
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


                                                       NOTE

       Hereinafter, Sender or Receiver refers to a CPU, while Sender frame or Receiver frame refers to a part
       of an MHU.


 9.2.3.1 MHU Introduction
     Figure 9-3 presents the full-duplex communication using MHU modules. Consider unidirectional path in a
     single MHU as a block diagram of an MHU module.

 9.2.3.2 MHU Channel
     Each MHU of the device has 4 channels. The number of channels can be checked in MHU_CFG[NUM_CH]
     field. Each channel occupies eight 32-bit words, in the Sender frame and Receiver frame register maps.
     A channel can be subdivided into 32 flags where each bit of the register controls a different flag or can be
     used as a transfer payload register. The implemented transport protocol determines the use of the channel.
     For more details on Transport Protocols, see Section 9.2.3.6 MHU Transport Protocols.
     The address space that is allocated to channels, which are not implemented, is Reserved and treated as Read
     As Zero / Writes Ignored (RAZ/WI).

 9.2.3.3 MHU Transfer
     Data are transferred between the Sender and Receiver. At its most basic form a transfer is done by:
       n The Sender writes 1 to one or more of the flag bits in a MHU_CHn_SET register.
       n This is reflected in:
         l The corresponding MHU_CHn_ST registers of both Sender and Receiver

         l The corresponding MHU_CHn_ST_MSK register of the Receiver, depending on the current values of

            MHU_CHn_MSK_ST register
       n If any bit in MHU_CHn_ST_MSK register is 1, then the interrupt for the corresponding channel is
         asserted.
       n The Receiver must clear the transfer by writing 1 to one or more flag bits in the MHU_CHn_CLR register.

     The number of transfers used to create a message depends on:
       n Size of the message being sent.
       n Transport protocol that is used.
       n Number of channels that are implemented in the MHU.
       n Number of concurrent transfers between the Sender and Receiver.


 9.2.3.4 MHU Ready to Send Protocol
     To enable the Sender to request that the Receiver enters a state where it can receive a transfer, the Sender
     uses the MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST and MHU_ACCESS_READY registers. The MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST register
     enables the Sender to request that the Receiver enters a state to be able to receive a transfer. The MHU_
     ACCESS_READY indicates whether the Receiver is in a state to receive a transfer.
     When MHU_ACCESS_READY[ACC_RDY] bit is 0, any attempt by the Sender to access any registers of the
     channel windows is treated as follows:
       n   RAZ/WI with no error generated when MHU_RESP_CFG[NR_RDY] bit is 0
       n   RAZ/WI with an error generated when MHU_RESP_CFG[NR_RDY] bit is 1


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                      243
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


 9.2.3.4.1 Software Requirements
     Even when setting MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] to 1, software is still responsible for guaranteeing that
     the transfer has been received by the Receiver using an implementation defined software protocol. An
     example of a sequence is:
      1. Sender configures the MHU to enable the NR2R and R2NR interrupts, by setting the MHU_INT_EN
         [NR2R] and MHU_INT_EN[R2NR] fields to 1.
      2. Sender sets the MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] field to 1.
      3. Sender reads the status of the MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_RDY] field. If it is 1 then it continues to step
         4. Otherwise, the Sender waits for the NR2R interrupt to be triggered.


                                                        NOTE

       A NR2R interrupt is generated due to the Sender setting the MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] field
       to 1, if MHU_ACCESS_READY[ACC_RDY] was already 1. Software must clear this interrupt before
       continuing.


      4. Sender, using one of the transport protocols defined in Section 9.2.3.6 MHU Transport Protocols, sends
         the transfer to the Receiver. While the Sender is performing the steps of the transport protocol, the
         transfer is considered to be outstanding and is not guaranteed to reach the Receiver. While performing
         the transport protocol, the Sender may receive either:
       n   A R2NR interrupt
       n   An error response to an access to a channel window register if MHU_RESP_CFG[NR_RDY] is set to 1
     This indicates that any transfers which were outstanding may have been lost. The Sender must take the
     following action:
      a. Clear the R2NR interrupt and process the fault handler, if an error was generated.
      b. Perform an implementation defined recovery sequence. This sequence can be to resend the transfer
         when the Receiver returns to a state where it is able to receive transfers, or to send other transfers to
         resynchronize the Sender and Receiver.


                                                        NOTE

       When the Receiver enters a state where it cannot receive a transfer, the Receiver may have been
       reset. Therefore, both the Sender and Receiver may need to be resynchronized before continuing to
       communicate.


      5. Sender sets the MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] field to 0 if it has no further transfer to send. If the
         Sender has more transfers to send, it repeats step 4 until it has no more transfers to send.
     The Sender of the transfer may also enter a state where it cannot complete the sending of the transfer. For
     example, the Sender may be reset by a watchdog while writing to the MHU_CHn_SET register. It is the
     responsibility of the Sender and Receiver to clear and ignore any transfers which were from before the
     Sender was reset.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       244
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                      E7 Series


                                                      NOTE

       When the Sender enters a state where it cannot complete sending a transfer, the Sender may have
       been reset. Therefore, both the Sender and Receiver may need to resynchronize before continuing to
       communicate.


 9.2.3.5 MHU Interrupt Requests
     Both Sender and Receiver frames have interrupts. The interrupt of a channel is generated when any bit in the
     corresponding MHU_CHn_ST_MSK register is set to 1.
     An MHU interrupt:
       n Is level-based
       n Remains asserted until all bits in the corresponding MHU_CHn_ST_MSK register are set to 0.

     Each MHU has status, clear, and enable registers to handle the interrupts (MHU_INT_ST, MHU_INT_CLR,
     MHU_INT_EN, and MHU_CHCOMB_INT_ST0/1/2/3).
     The interrupts in MHU are basically generated from:
       n   The Sender
       n   The Receiver
     The Sender frame interrupts are:
       n Not Ready to Ready interrupt (NR2R).
         l This interrupt is asserted when both MHU_INT_EN[NR2R] and MHU_INT_ST[NR2R] bits are 1.

         l MHU_INT_ST[NR2R] bit becomes 1, when:

           o MHU_ACCESS_READY[ACC_RDY] bit goes high and MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] bit is 1.
           o MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] bit goes high and MHU_ACCESS_READY[ACC_RDY] bit is 1.

         l MHU_INT_ST[NR2R] bit becomes 0, when software writes 1 to MHU_INT_CLR[NR2R] bit in the Sender

           frame.
       n Ready to Not Ready interrupt (R2NR)
         l This interrupt is asserted when both MHU_INT_EN[R2NR] and MHU_INT_ST[R2NR] bits are 1.

         l MHU_INT_ST[R2NR] bit becomes 1, when MHU_ACCESS_READY[ACC_RDY] bit goes low and MHU_

           ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] is 0.
         l MHU_INT_ST[R2NR] bit becomes 0, when software writes 1 to MHU_INT_CLR[R2NR] bit in the Sender

           frame.
       n Combined interrupt (CHCOMB)
         l This interrupt is asserted when the Sender frame MHU_INT_EN[CHCOMB] bit is 1 and any of the

           following occur:
           o MHU_CHn_INT_ST[CH_CLR] and MHU_CHn_INT_EN[CH_CLR] bits of any channel are both 1.
           o MHU_INT_ST[NR2R] and MHU_INT_EN[NR2R] bits are both 1.
           o MHU_INT_ST[R2NR] and MHU_INT_EN[R2NR] bits are both 1.

     The Receiver frame interrupts are:
       n Channel Clear interrupt—The MHU_CHn_CLR register relate to the Channel Clear interrupt. This
         interrupt is generated when the Receiver writes to the MHU_CHn_CLR register of the channel,
         irrespective of the value written.
       n Combined interrupt—A combined interrupt output that is set when the Receiver frame MHU_INT_EN
         [CHCOMB] bit is 1 and at least one bit in any channel MHU_CHn_ST_MSK register is 1. To clear the
         combined interrupt, all channel MHU_CHn_ST_MSK bits must be cleared.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                     245
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series



                                                       NOTE

     The Sender is still required to check the value of the MHU_CHn_ST register, as defined by the transport
     protocol, see Section 9.2.3.6 MHU Transport Protocols, when it receives the Channel Clear interrupt.


     The Channel Clear interrupt is only required to be received by the Sender of the original message if the Ready
     to Send interface remains in the state where both signals are 1. This means that software must not set the
     MHU_ACCESS_REQUEST[ACC_REQ] bit to 0 until it has received the clear interrupt.


                                                       NOTE

     It is allowed for the Channel Clear interrupt to be generated when the Ready to Send interface is not in the
     state where both signals are 1.


 9.2.3.6 MHU Transport Protocols
     This section does not define the format of the messages transferred via MHU transport protocols.
     The software is responsible for requesting the Receiver frame of the MHU to be powered. The software does
     this by using the Ready to Send protocol, see Section 9.2.3.4 MHU Ready to Send Protocol. Software is also
     responsible for making sure the Sender frame remains powered until the message has been received by the
     Receiver. How software knows when the Receiver has received the message, depends on the transport
     protocol being used, see Section 9.2.3.6.1 Doorbell, Section 9.2.3.6.2 Single-Word Transfer, or Section
     9.2.3.6.3 Multi-Word Transfer.

 9.2.3.6.1 Doorbell
     Figure 9-5 shows the sequence of events to implement the Doorbell transport protocol. The steps of the
     sequence are:
      1. The Sender writes the optional payload for the transfer to the out-band memory.
      2. The Sender writes 1, to the corresponding bit in the MHU_CHn_SET register. When Sender has sent a
         transfer, it can send other transfers using other flags within the same channel, or any flag within another
         channel, but must not use the same flag bit until the Receiver has processed the transfer.
      3. MHU generates an interrupt to the Receiver.
      4. The Receiver processes the interrupt and reads the transfer payload in the out-band memory, if there is
         a transfer payload.
      5. The Receiver clears the flag by writing 1, to the corresponding bit in the MHU_CHn_CLR register.
      6. The Sender must wait for the bit in the MHU_CHn_ST register (set to 1), to become 0 to know when the
         transfer has been processed by the Receiver. This can be done by either:
         n Polling the MHU_CHn_ST register, checking for the bit set to 1 to become 0.
         n Wait to receive a clear interrupt for that channel, and check that the bit has transitioned to 0.

     This protocol has the following requirements:
       n If there is an out-band memory used, then the location has to be agreed between Sender and Receiver
         and has to be accessible by both.
       n Any MHU_CHn_ST flag bits which are used to indicate a transfer, must not be masked in the Receiver.
         For example, if bits [3-0] of MHU_CHn_ST register are used to indicate 4 different transfers, bits [3-0] of
         MHU_CHn_MSK_ST register must be 0.


                                                          NOTE

       The message format determines whether data, associated with the flag, are transferred in out-band
       memory, or whether the flag bit indicates the full message. If there are out-band data, then the
       location of the data is pre-agreed between the two entities.


 9.2.3.6.2 Single-Word Transfer
     Figure 9-6 shows the required sequence to implement the Single-Word Transfer transport protocol; the
     sequence is:
      1. Using the MHU_CHn_SET register, the Sender writes the in-band payload for the transfer. The in-band
         payload of the transfer can be any value, except all 0s.
      2. The MHU generates an interrupt to the Receiver.
      3. The Receiver receives the interrupt and reads the in-band payload for the transfer in the MHU_CHn_ST
         register.
      4. The Receiver clears the in-band payload for the transfer by writing 1 to each bit of the MHU_CHn_CLR
         register.
      5. To know when the transfer has been processed by the Receiver, the Sender must wait for all bits in the
         MHU_CHn_ST register to read 0. This can be done by either:
         n Polling the MHU_CHn_ST register, checking for the register to read all 0s.
         n Wait to receive a clear interrupt for that channel, and checking that all bits read 0.

                                                          247
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series

                 Sender                            MHU                                                    Receiver




                          Write in-band playload                                    Interrupt generated



                                                         Read MHU_CHn_ST


                                                         Clear transfer playload


                                                                                                                          MHU_004




     This protocol has the following requirements:
       n All transfer payloads must have at least one bit set to 1.
       n The MHU_CHn_MSK_ST register must have at least one bit set to 0.
       n At least one bit, which is set to 1, in the MHU_CHn_ST register and the corresponding bit in the MHU_
         CHn_MSK_ST register is set to 0.


                                                             NOTE

       Software either has all MHU_CHn_MSK_ST bits set to 0 or a single bit has to be used to indicate a
       transfer to the Receiver, and only that bit is required to be 0 in the corresponding MHU_CHn_MSK_ST
       register.


 9.2.3.6.3 Multi-Word Transfer
     Each transfer is made of two or more words. The Sender writes each word of the transfer, but only the final
     word of the transfer is used to indicate to the Receiver, that a transfer is waiting. For this transport protocol,
     the number of channels, that are used, can be 1 or more. It is not a requirement that all words are
     transferred using channels of the MHU, some words of the transfer can be in out-band memory. The location
     of the out-band memory can be either pre-agreed or can be referenced as part of the transfer payload.
     Figure 9-7 shows the sequence of events used to implement the Multi-Word Transfer transport protocol; the
     sequence is:
      1. Sender writes the optional out-band payload to a location in out-band memory. The location in the out-
         band memory is either:
         n Pre-agreed using a software specific implementation.
         n Pointed to via the payload transferred using the channel of the MHU.
      2. Sender writes (N - 1) words of the in-band transfer payload to the channels, using the corresponding
         MHU_CHn_SET register for each channel. The values of these channels are allowed to be zero.
      3. Sender writes the last word of the in-band transfer to the final channel. This value must be nonzero.
      4. MHU generates the interrupt to the Receiver.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                             248
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


      5. Following reception of the interrupt, the Receiver then:
         a. Reads optional out-band payload, if provided.
         b. Reads in-band payload, using the correscponding MHU_CHn_ST register for each channel.
      6. The Receiver clears the in-band payload from all channels by writing 1 to each bit of the corresponding
         MHU_CHn_CLR register for each channel.
      7. Sender waits for all the MHU_CHn_ST registers of the used channels to be read as all 0s, to know that
         the transfer has been processed by the Receiver. This can be done by either:
         a. Polling all MHU_CHn_ST registers of channels used by the transfer to read as all 0s.
         b. Waiting for a clear interrupt for each channel used, and then checking that the MHU_CHn_ST
             registers reads as all 0s.


                                     Figure 9-7 Multi-Word Transfer Transport Protocol

                 Sender                         MHU                         Out-band Memory
                                                                                                       Receiver
                                                      Op�onal out-band playout
                          Write (N – 1) word
                          of in-band playload
                            Write last word
                          of in-band playload




                                                         Read N words
                                                      of in-band playload
                                                         Clear N words
                                                      of in-band playload

                                                                                                                        MHU_005




     The software of the use-case defines:
       n The order in which the Sender writes the out-band and (N - 1) words of in-band payload. However, the
         last word of in-band payload must only be written, after all in-band and out-band payload data are
         guaranteed to be visible to the Receiver.
       n The order in which the Receiver reads the out-band and in-band payload.
       n The order in which the Receiver clears the in-band payload.

     This protocol has the following requirements:
       n MHU_CHn_MSK_ST registers for channels, which are not the last written word of the transfer, have all
         bits set to 1.
       n MHU_CHn_MSK_ST register for channel, used to transfer the last written word, must have at least one
         bit set to 0.
       n At least one bit, which is set to 1, in the MHU_CHn_ST register and the corresponding bit in the MHU_
         CHn_MSK_ST register is set to 0.
       n The order in which words of the transfer are written by the Sender, can be in any order so long as the
         channel which has at least one bit of the MHU_CHn_MSK_ST register set to 0, is the last word to be
         written. The last word to be written to a channel, does not need to be the last word of the transfer, it
         can be the first word. That is, the Sender writes words 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of a 4-word transfer first, then
         writes word 0.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                          249
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


       n   If out-band memory is required, the location of the memory must be accessible by both the Sender and
           Receiver.


                                                        NOTE

       The last channel cleared by the Receiver, is recommended to be a channel with at least one bit of the
       corresponding MHU_CHn_MSK_ST register set to 0. This allows the Sender to wait for only that MHU_
       CHn_ST register to read as all 0s, by either polling or waiting for the clear interrupt for that channel.


                                                        NOTE

     If the number of words in a transfer is greater than the number of channels allocated, the transfer process is
     the same as described in Section 9.2.3.6.2 Single-Word Transfer, except:
       n Sender must write all words of transfer payload, which is stored in out-band memory, before writing the
         last word of transfer payload to the MHU channel.
       n Receiver must read all of the transfer payload, including words stored in out-band memory, before
         clearing the channels in the MHU. There is no requirement to clear the words in the out-band memory.

           Offset           Access         Description
  0x0 + (n × 8 × 0x4)

    Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                            Channel flag status
                                                            Each bit can be used as individual flag or bits can be grouped. The
                                                            usage depends upon the transport protocol used.

                                                            the MHU_CHn_SET register.

                                                            - Clears a bit that is already cleared, the bit remains cleared.

                                                            protocols defined in Section 9.2.3.6 MHU Transport Protocols.

       If the Receiver frame is reset then the content of the MHU_CHn_ST registers in the Sender frame is
       also reset.
       Software is responsible for the handling of lost messages if this occurs.

 9.2.5.3 MHU TX Registers Description

 9.2.5.3.1 MHU_CHn_ST Register
           Offset           Access          Description
  0x0 + (n × 8 × 0x4)
                               R            Channel (n) Status Register; n = 0 to 3, MHU channel index
    Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             Channel flag status
                                                             Each bit can be used as individual flag or bits can be grouped. The
                                                             usage depends upon the transport protocol used.
                                                             Bits in this register are set by writing 1 to the corresponding bit in
    31-0      FLAG_x                    R         0x0
                                                             the MHU_CHn_SET register.
                                                             Bits in this register are cleared by writing 1 to the corresponding
                                                             bit the MHU_CHn_CLR register.
                                                             If software:

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                       Alif Semiconductor
                                                              263
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                        E7 Series


    Bits      Field Name             Access    Reset Value Description
                                                              - Sets a bit that is already set, the bit remains set.
                                                              - Clears a bit that is already cleared, the bit remains cleared.
                                                              - Sets and clears a bit at the same time, the bit remains set.
                                                              It is strongly recommended that software follows the transport
                                                              protocols defined in Section 9.2.3.6 MHU Transport Protocols.



 9.2.5.3.2 MHU_CHn_SET Register
           Offset           Access         Description
  0xC + (n × 8 × 0x4)
                              W            Channel (n) Set Register; n = 0 to 3, MHU channel index
    Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access    Reset Value Description
                                                              Channel flag set
                                                              Write 1 to a bit sets the corresponding bit in the MHU_CHn_ST.
    31-0      FLAG_SET_x               W           0x0
                                                              Writing 0 has no effect.
                                                              Each bit always reads as 0.



 9.2.5.3.3 MHU_CHn_INT_ST Register
           Offset           Access            Description
  0x10 + (n × 8 × 0x4)
                               R              Channel (n) Interrupt Status Register; n = 0 to 3, MHU channel index
     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access    Reset Value Description
    31-1      RESERVED                 R           0x0        Reserved
                                                              Channel Clear Interrupt status bit
                                                              0x0: No Channel Clear interrupt has occurred.
                                                              0x1: A Channel Clear interrupt has occurred
                                                              CH_CLR bit is:
                                                                     n   Set to 1 when the Receiver writes to MHU_CHn_CLR
                                                                         registers.
                                                                         Note: If the Sender domain is not powered on, or is held
     0        CH_CLR                   R           0x0                   in reset at the point the write occurs, then there is no
                                                                         requirement for the field to be set to 1.
                                                                     n   Set to 0 when the Sender writes 1 to the MHU_CHn_INT_
                                                                         CLR[CH_CLR] bit.
                                                              Setting MHU_CHn_INT_ST [CH_CLR] bit to 1 takes priority of
                                                              setting the bit to 0.
                                                              The value of the MHU_CHn_INT_EN[CH_CLR] bit has no effect on
                                                              the value of MHU_CHn_INT_ST register.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                               264

           Offset           Access            Description

     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access    Reset Value Description

 10 Memories

 10.1 Embedded Magnetoresistive Random-Access Memory (MRAM)

 10.1.1 MRAM Overview
     The MRAM module is a type of non-volatile random-access memory which stores information in magnetic
     elements.
     The MRAM operates at 33 MHz clock frequency over 128-bit data bus. The 128-bit (16-byte) word represents
     the minimum sector size for the MRAM. The smaller granularity offers much better efficiency compared to
     the legacy flash memory modules. It takes flash memories longer to be programmed/erased due to their
     much larger sector sizes.
     The MRAM module implements a state machine controlling the erase and programming sequence of 16-byte
     memory blocks. This operation is transparent to the CPU core.
     The MRAM controller implements read cache and write buffer mechanism that enables the concurrent read
     and write operations. This greatly benefits the implementation of multi-core applications that are not
     required to coordinate the access to the MRAM. Up to four bus masters can originate concurrent write
     operations, while the number of concurrent read operations is not limited.
     The MRAM supports the following main features:
       n 5.5MB
       n High endurance (more than 100 000 erase cycles)
       n More than 10 years data retention (at 125 °C junction temperature)
       n 16 ECC bits for each 128-bit data word
       n 2× 16 bytes read cache to accelerate access to frequently used data and non-16-byte aligned read
         requests
       n Built-in state machine controlling 16-byte program/erase cycle (no need of driver)
       n Concurrent write (up to four bus masters) and read operations (no need for synchronization between
         them)
       n DMA write operation with up to 128 bytes in each DMA write cycle data payload


 10.2 Embedded Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM)

 10.2.1 SRAM Overview
     The device contains the following types of on-chip SRAM memories:
       n User SRAM available for all bus masters:
         l Bulk SRAM: SRAM0 and SRAM1

         l M55-HP TCM: SRAM2 (M55-HP ITCM) and SRAM3 (M55-HP DTCM)

         l M55-HE TCM: SRAM4 (M55-HE ITCM) and SRAM5 (M55-HE DTCM), with optional retention

         l Other shared SRAM blocks: SRAM6_A/B, SRAM7, SRAM8, and SRAM9_A/B

       n Processor cache memories:
         l A32 Level 1 cache and Level 2 cache

         l M55-HP Level 1 cache

         l M55-HE Level 1 cache

       n Utility SRAM
         l Located in Always-On domain




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                      274
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                      www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


     It is possible to configure address ranges within SRAM0 and SRAM1 to appear as contiguous address space to
     a given M55 core through configuration of the firewall controllers. For more information on the firewalls, see
     Section 7.2 Interconnect Firewall Functional Description.
     The embedded bulk SRAM is a general-purpose memory to be shared among all applications. It is partitioned
     into two blocks, each having 64-bit wide data bus and providing read/write operation at 400 MHz. The bulk
     memory blocks can be accessed in parallel over the main 64-bit AXI bus running at 400 MHz.
     The TCM is an SRAM block providing high-bandwidth and low latency access. The TCM is primarily used by
     the M55 core it is attached to. Alternatively, it can be shared with other bus masters in the device. For more
     information about TCM, see Section 10.3 Tightly-Coupled Memory (TCM).
     The cache memory is a high-performance SRAM accelerating the CPU access to frequently used instructions
     and data. A32 Level 1 cache memory is dedicated to an individual A32 core. The Level 2 cache is shared
     between the two A32 cores. The M55 processors have Level 1 cache memories dedicated to each M55 core.
     The data retention of SRAM is used for context saving during low power modes.
     The device includes the following quantities of SRAM with their performance characteristics:
       n  User SRAM available to all bus masters:
           13.5MB:
           l

           o 4MB bulk SRAM0 + 2.5MB bulk SRAM1
           o 0.25MB SRAM2 (M55-HP ITCM) + 1MB SRAM3 (M55-HP DTCM)
           o 0.25MB SRAM4 (M55-HE ITCM) + 0.25MB SRAM5 (M55-HE DTCM), with optional data retention
           o 1MB SRAM6_A + 1MB SRAM6_B + 0.5MB SRAM7 + 2MB SRAM8 + 0.25MB SRAM9_A + 0.5MB

               SRAM9_B
         l 400 MHz parallel read/write access

       n Application processor (A32) cache memories:
         l Level 1 Cache: 32KB Instruction and 32KB Data cache per core

         l Level 2 Cache: 512KB shared between the two A32 cores

       n Real-time processors (M55) cache memories:
         l Level 1 Cache: 32KB Instruction and 32KB Data cache per core

       n Utility SRAM:
         l 4KB in Always-On power domain PD-0

         l 100 MHz read/write access (32-bit wide access only)



 10.3 Tightly-Coupled Memory (TCM)

 10.3.1 TCM Overview
     The Tightly Coupled Memory (TCM) is a high-bandwidth and low latency memory. The TCM enables the
     Cortex-M55 cores to perform vector operations with high efficiency and process interrupts with minimum
     latency. The TCM access time is a single clock cycle with no wait states for reads. The TCM interface is based
     on Harvard architecture—it has one instruction memory (ITCM0) bus and four data memory (DTCM0/1/2/3)
     buses, all 32-bit wide.
     Both M55-HP and M55-HE cores can use the ITCM for storing data and can fetch instructions out of the
     DTCM. In this scenario, the TCM access time is slower and vector operations are not supported.
     The Cortex-M55 cores have the following TCM configurations:
       n   M55-HP:
           l 256KB of ITCM and 4 × 256KB of DTCM (total of 1.25MB)
           l 1 × 32-bit ITCM and 4 × 32-bit DTCM memory buses



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       275
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                                                                                   E7 Series


          lSingle-cycle read/write access at 400 MHz
         l Concurrent share of TCM with the other processing entities via AHB slave port

       n M55-HE:
         l 256KB of ITCM and 4 × 64KB of DTCM (total of 512KB)

         l 1 × 32-bit ITCM and 4 × 32-bit DTCM memory buses

         l Single-cycle read/write access at 160 MHz

         l Concurrent share of TCM with the other processing entities via AHB slave port

         l Optional content retention



 10.4 Memory Retention
     The device provides optional memory retention support for the Utility SRAM and M55-HE TCM.
     Utility SRAM Retention
     The Utility SRAM retention can be controlled by the RET_CTRL[BKRAM_RET_MASK] and [BKRAM_RET_
     FORCE] register bits.
     M55-HE TCM Retention
     The memory retention for each M55-HE TCM (ITCM and DTCM) is split into two regions, which can be
     retained individually. The retention of each TCM region is controlled by a dedicated retention rail with its
     own set of control bits in the RET_CTRL register. Figure 10-1 describes the implementation of M55-HE TCM
     retention.

 10.5 External Memory Expansion Options
     The device provides two options to expand the memory using external devices:
       n   1× SDMMC interface
       n   2× OSPI interface
     The SDMMC interface can be used to access embedded or external memory cards with clock frequency up to
     50 MHz. The data bus is up to 8 bits wide. This external memory interface is suitable for expanding the bulk
     data storage capacity in the form of an external flash-based file system. The SDMMC interface supports
     legacy 4-bit cards as well.
     For more information, see Section 16.2 Secure Digital / Embedded Multimedia Card (SDMMC).
     The OSPI interfaces can be used to access external flash memory devices. Each OSPI supports Double Data
     Rate (DDR) mode transferring 8-bit data on both edges of the clock signal. The maximum clock frequency is
     up to 100 MHz, delivering raw DDR bandwidth of up to 200 MB/s.
     The OSPI interface could access the memory in two modes—directly (through register read/write operations)
     or indirectly (through memory-mapped operations). The indirect access supports eXecute-in-Place (XIP)
     mode which translates the instruction fetch operations to proper address and data read transactions. This
     way, the external memory devices expand the available non-volatile memory.
     The OSPI interfaces support legacy Single, Dual, Quad, or Octal SPI flash memory devices.
     Each OSPI interface also supports the HyperBus protocol in direct and indirect modes. This enables the
     integration of external Static or Pseudo-Static RAM devices. See operation limitations in Section 16.1.1
     Cryptographic OSPI Overview.
     Each OSPI interface can be attached to a flash or SRAM devices based on the application needs.
     For more information, see Section 16.1 Cryptographic Octal SPI (OSPI).
     The device includes two AES decoders—one for each OSPI interface. The decoders are implemented in
     hardware and enable on-the-fly decoding of the external memory content. This allows protecting the OSPI
     code or the confidentiality of the data stored in external devices. The decoders effectively add no latency
     while maintaining the overall external memory interface bandwidth.

 11.1 Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC)

 11.1.1 GIC Overview
     The Arm Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC-400) is a high-performance, area-optimized interrupt controller
     that detects, manages, and distributes interrupts to the A32 application processor.
     The GIC module supports the following main features:
       n Supports both cores inside the A32 processor cluster
       n 16 Software Generated Interrupts (SGIs) per core
       n 6 external and 1 internal Private Peripheral Interrupts (PPIs) per core
       n 480 Shared Peripheral Interrupts (SPIs)
       n Interrupt masking and prioritization
       n Interrupt assignment to either of two groups:
         l Group 0 (secure)

         l Group 1 (non-secure)

       n Interrupt virtualization
       n AMBA 4 AXI configuration interface

     Figure 11-1 provides a high-level overview of the GIC implementation in the device.

 11.1.3 GIC Functional Description
     This section provides only a brief description of the GIC functionality. For more information about the GIC
     module, including register descriptions, refer to the Arm® CoreLink™ GIC-400 Generic Interrupt Controller
     Technical Reference Manual.

 11.1.3.1 GIC Functional Blocks
     The GIC includes the following major functional blocks:
       n Distributor (GICD)—common for both A32 cores
       n CPU Interface (GICC)—one per A32 core
       n GIC Virtual Interface Control (GICH)—one per A32 core
       n Virtual CPU Interface (GICV)—one per A32 core


 11.1.3.1.1 GIC Distributor (GICD)
     The GICD detects all interrupt sources, determines the priority of each interrupt, and, for each CPU interface,
     forwards the interrupt with the highest priority to the interface for priority masking and preemption
     handling.
     The GICD provides a programming interface for:
       n Globally enabling the forwarding of interrupts to the CPU interface
       n Enabling or disabling each interrupt
       n Setting the priority level of each interrupt
       n Setting the target processor list of each interrupt
       n Setting each peripheral interrupt to be level-sensitive or edge-triggered
       n Setting each interrupt as either Group 0 or Group 1
       n Sending an SGI to one or more target processors
       n Visibility of the state of each interrupt
       n A mechanism for software to set or clear the pending state of a peripheral interrupt


 11.1.3.1.2 GIC CPU Interface (GICC)
     The GICC provides a programming interface for:
       n Enabling the signaling of interrupt requests by the CPU interface
       n Acknowledging an interrupt
       n Indicating completion of the processing of an interrupt
       n Setting an interrupt priority mask for the processor
       n Defining the preemption policy for the processor
       n Determining the highest priority pending interrupt for the processor

     The GICC also provides the IRQ/FIQ signals to the A32 CPU.
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       287
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


 11.1.3.1.3 GIC Virtual Interface Control (GICH)
     The GICH consists mostly of control and status registers that work with hypervisor software to provide
     software-driven interrupts to guest virtualization-compliant operating system (OS) running on A32 cores.

 11.1.3.1.4 GIC Virtual CPU Interface (GICV)
     The GICV is basically the same as the GICC, except that it connects to the hypervisor interface instead of the
     distributor. As such, this block is the virtualized version of the CPU interface and provides the VFIQ/VIRQ
     signals to the virtualization-compliant A32 CPU.
     The GICV uses the contents of the List registers to determine when to signal virtual interrupts.

 11.1.3.2 GIC Interrupt Sources

 11.1.3.2.1 Software Generated Interrupts (SGIs)
     SGIs are generated by writing to the Software Generated Interrupt Register (GICD_SGIR). A maximum of 16
     SGIs, ID0-ID15, can be generated for each processor interface.
     SGIs are used for inter-process communication. All SGIs are edge-triggered.


                                                        NOTE

       It is recommended to use SGI ID0-ID7 for non-secure interrupts and SGI ID8-ID15 for secure
       interrupts.



 11.1.3.2.2 Private Peripheral Interrupts (PPIs)
     A PPI is an interrupt generated by a peripheral that is specific to a single processor core. There are seven PPIs
     for each CPU interface. All PPIs are active-low level-sensitive.
     The PPI mapping is fixed and can be found in the Arm® CoreLink™ GIC-400 Generic Interrupt Controller
     Technical Reference Manual.

 11.1.3.2.3 Shared Peripheral Interrupts (SPIs)
     SPIs are triggered by events generated on associated interrupt input lines. SPI sources include:
       n   Interrupts coming from the Shared Interrupt Router
       n   Interrupts coming from peripherals local to the Application Processor Subsystem


                                                        NOTE

       For a diagram showing the routing of interrupts in the device, refer to Section 11.3 Shared Interrupt
       Router (IRQRTR).


     The GIC provides support for 480 SPIs in the device. For SPI mapping, refer to Section 11.5.2 GIC400
     Interrupt Map.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        288
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


     SPIs start at ID32. SPIs can be configured to be edge-triggered or active-high level-sensitive. It is strongly
     recommended that SPI inputs are configured according to the trigger type of their associated peripheral
     interrupt, otherwise errors may occur.

 11.1.3.3 GIC Interrupt States
     The GIC supports the following interrupt states:
       n Inactive: An interrupt that is not active or pending
       n Pending: An interrupt from a source to the GIC that is recognized as asserted in hardware, or generated
         by software, and is waiting to be serviced by the target processor
       n Active: An interrupt from a source to the GIC that has been acknowledged by the processor, and is being
         serviced but has not completed
       n Active and pending: The processor is servicing the interrupt and the GIC has a pending interrupt from
         the same source

 11.1.3.4 GIC Interrupt Handling
     The following steps show the interrupt handling flow in the GIC:
      1.      The GIC determines whether an interrupt is enabled (a disabled interrupt has no effect on the GIC).
              Upon interrupt generation, the interrupt is passed to a Finite State Machine (FSM) that controls the
              transitioning from one state to another. If the interrupt was inactive prior to the generation, then it
              transitions to pending state and can be asserted to the host CPU for servicing. If the interrupt was
              already active and gets generated again, it becomes active and pending, which is not a valid state for
              assertion to the CPU.
      2.      For each interrupt that is enabled and pending, the Distributor determines the targeted CPU.
      3.      The Distributor determines the highest priority interrupt and forwards that interrupt to the targeted
              CPU interface.
      4.      The CPU interface compares its internal settings and state with the received interrupt priority. If the
              CPU interface determines that the interrupt may proceed, the IRQ or FIQ line asserts low, signaling
              the interrupt to the host CPU.
      5.      Software must then acknowledge the interrupt by reading the corresponding Interrupt Acknowledge
              Register (GICC_IAR), which returns an ID uniquely identifying the interrupt. This leads to changing
              the interrupt state in the GIC from pending to either active or active and pending (second scenario
              may typically happen for a level-sensitive interrupt), and the interrupt is no longer valid for assertion
              to the CPU. This causes the IRQ or FIQ line to reassert high, deactivating the assertion to the host
              CPU.
      6.      Software handles the interrupt and writes the interrupt ID (the same value returned by the GICC_IAR
              read) to the End-of-Interrupt Register (GICC_EOIR). This notifies the GIC that processing is complete
              and the GIC changes the interrupt from active to inactive. Alternatively, if the interrupt was asserted
              again while active, it is in the active and pending state and an GICC_EOIR write transitions the
              interrupt to the pending state, at which point it is again valid for assertion to the CPU.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                         289
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com

 11.2 Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC)

 11.2.1 NVIC Overview
     The Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC) resides in each of the M55-HP and M55-HE processors, and
     it is closely integrated with the Cortex-M55 core to achieve low-latency interrupt processing. Both NVIC
     modules have the same configuration in the device.
     Each NVIC module supports the following main features:
       n Maintaining the current execution priority of the Cortex-M55 processor
       n Maintaining the pending and active status of all exceptions that are supported
       n Invoking preemption when a pending exception has priority
       n Providing wake-up signals to wake up the Cortex-M55 processor from deep sleep mode
       n Providing support to the Internal Wakeup Interrupt Controller (IWIC) and External Wakeup Interrupt
         Controller (EWIC)
       n Providing priority and exception information to other processor components
       n 480 external interrupts, with 256 priority levels per interrupt

     All the interrupts including the Cortex-M55 core exceptions are managed by the NVIC. For more information
     on the NVIC functionality, refer to the following Arm documentation:
       n     Arm® Cortex®-M55 Processor Technical Reference Manual
       n     Arm® Cortex®-M55 Processor Devices Generic User Guide
     For M55-HP/M55-HE NVIC interrupt mapping, refer to Section 11.5 Interrupt Sources Mapping.

 11.3 Shared Interrupt Router (IRQRTR)

 11.3.1 IRQRTR Overview
     The shared Interrupt Router (IRQRTR) is intended to route interrupt signals from the device peripherals to all
     processing entities. It has an input port wired to the interrupt sources and four output ports connected to
     the Secure Enclave, the Application Processor Subsystem and the two Real-Time Processing interrupt
     controllers.
     The router configuration registers define which interrupt sources are enabled and their destination output
     ports. Once configured, the router can be locked fully or partially so that further changes can be restricted.
     The access to the IRQRTR configuration may be constrained based on the device security policy. In this
     case, the interrupt routing can be indirectly setup by service call to the Secure Enclave.
     The IRQRTR supports the following main features:
       n Manages up to 427 shared interrupts
       n Configures routing of the interrupt signals to up to four processing entities
       n Supports configuration access lockdown
       n Reports tamper interrupts to the Secure Enclave

     Figure 11-3 provides a high-level overview of the IRQRTR implementation in the device.
                                                 Figure 11-3 IRQRTR Overview
                 Device                                 Shared interrupts
