 11.3.3 IRQRTR Functional Description

 11.3.3.1 Software Configuration of Shared Interrupts
     The following IRQRTR registers are associated with the configuration of shared interrupts:
       n IRQRTR_SHD_INT_SEL
       n IRQRTR_SHD_INT_INFO
       n IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG
       n IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL

     The IRQRTR_SHD_INT_SEL register allows software to select the interrupt for which the configuration
     settings in the {IRQRTR_SHD_INT_INFO, IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG, IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL} registers apply. If
     the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_SEL register selects an interrupt which is not implemented, the {IRQRTR_SHD_INT_
     INFO, IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG, IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL} registers are reserved and treated as RAZ/WI (read-
     as-zero; write ignored).
     The IRQRTR_SHD_INT_INFO[ICI_DST] bit field indicates which ICI interfaces the selected interrupt can be
     routed to—that is, the subset of allowed interrupt controllers. This is hardcoded and cannot be changed by
     software. In this device, any shared interrupt is allowed to be routed to any of the following destinations—
     APSS GIC400 (ICI1), M55-HP NVIC (ICI2) and M55-HE NVIC (ICI3). Only the Secure Enclave (ICI0) receives a
     limited number of the shared interrupts.
     The IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG[ICI_EN] bit field configures which ICI interfaces the selected interrupt is routed to.
     It is unpredictable whether the interrupt is routed to the correct destinations if software changes the value in
     the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG[ICI_EN] bit field while the interrupt source is active.


                                                        NOTE

       It is strongly recommended that software disables the interrupt at source, before making any changes
       to the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG[ICI_EN] bit field.


     The IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL[LOCK] bit field defines whether the configuration of the selected interrupt is
     locked or not. For more information, see Section 11.3.3.3 Lockdown Support.

 11.3.3.2 Interrupt Routing Mechanism
     Interrupts received by the IRQRTR are routed to the connected interrupt controllers based on:
       n Subset of allowed interrupt controllers a shared interrupt can be routed to
       n Software configuration for the shared interrupt

                                                       298

     ICIs, is selected using the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG[ICI_EN] bit field.

 11.3.3.3 Lockdown Support
     The IRQRTR supports the ability to lockdown its configuration. Software can lockdown an individual shared
     interrupt configuration or all shared interrupt configurations.

 11.3.3.3.1 Lockdown States
     The IRQRTR supports the following lockdown states:
       n Open—All registers can be updated, except for:
           IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG when the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL[LOCK] bit field is 0x1
           l

       n Partial—All registers can be updated, except for:
         l IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG when the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL[LOCK] bit field is 0x1

         l IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL[LOCK] bit field, which is set to 0x1

         l IRQRTR_CTRL

       n Full—The following registers are read-only:
         l IRQRTR_SHD_INT_CFG

         l IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL


     The IRQRTR_LD_CTRL[LOCK] bit field is read-only if the lockdown interface of the IRQRTR is asserted. An
     asserted lockdown interface prevents the IRQRTR lockdown state from being changed, when it is partial or

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       299
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


     full. It is driven by the [INT_RTR_LOCK] bit of the System Lock Control registers {SYS_LCTRL_ST, SYS_LCTRL_
     SET, SYS_LCTRL_CLR}.

 11.3.3.3.2 Tamper Interrupt
     The IRQRTR reports tamper interrupts using a single level sensitive interrupt output that is mapped to the
     Secure Enclave. It is asserted when either IRQRTR_TMP_ST[TMP_ST_VLD] or IRQRTR_TMP_ST[TMP_SWT_
     OVERFLOW] bit fields are 0x1.

 11.3.3.3.3 Tamper Report Access
     The IRQRTR_TMP_ST register holds information about any transactions that attempt to modify the
     configuration of the IRQRTR in a state of lockdown.
     Access to the IRQRTR_TMP_ST register is only allowed by transactions with the following properties:
       n Secure privileged transactions
       n Transactions from the Secure Enclave

     If an access is attempted without either of the mentioned properties, the IRQRTR performs the actions
     described in Section 11.3.3.3.4 Configuration Access Lockdown.

 11.3.3.3.4 Configuration Access Lockdown
     The following is a list of configuration accesses that cause both a configuration access error and a tamper
     interrupt generation:
       n Update the configuration of an interrupt which is locked (IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL[LOCK] set to 0x1)
       n Unlock a locked interrupt (set IRQRTR_SHD_INT_LCTRL[LOCK] to 0x0 when it is 0x1) when the router's
         lockdown state is partial or full
       n Change the router's lockdown state, when it is partial or full, and the lockdown interface is asserted,
         except for the value of the IRQRTR_SHD_INT_SEL register
       n Update the value of the IRQRTR_CTRL register
       n Access the IRQRTR_TMP_ST register with a transaction that does not have the properties as described in
         Section 11.3.3.3.3 Tamper Report Access
     When any of the above occurs, the IRQRTR does the following:
       n   Generates a configuration access error
       n   Asserts the tamper interrupt, if it is not already asserted, and does either of the following:
           l Generates a tamper report, updating the IRQRTR_TMP_ST register with the address of the

             configuration access and setting the IRQRTR_TMP_ST[TMP_ST_VLD] bit field to 0x1, if that bit field
             was 0x0.
           l Generates a tamper report overflow, setting the IRQRTR_TMP_ST[TMP_ST_OVEFLW] bit field to 0x1,

             if IRQRTR_TMP_ST[TMP_STP_VLD] bit field is 0x1.
     For more information on configuration accesses and configuration access errors, see Section 11.3.3.4
     Configuration Accesses.

 11.3.3.4 Configuration Accesses
     The IRQRTR is configured by 32-bit registers which require word-aligned access. A configuration access can
     become a configuration access error under any of the following conditions:
       n Access is to a reserved location
       n Access is not 32-bit word aligned
       n Access performs any of the actions described in Section 11.3.3.3.4 Configuration Access Lockdown


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       300
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                    E7 Series


     When a configuration access error occurs, the following is done:
         n An error response to the configuration access is generated, if the IRQRTR_CTRL[ERR] bit field is set to
           0x1. Otherwise, the response to the configuration access completes without an error.
         n Read data is set to all zeros
         n Write data is ignored

 11.4 Event Router (EVTRTR)

 11.4.1 EVTRTR Overview
     The device integrates a large number of peripherals that can generate events indicating changes in their
     state, receiving of data or completion of an operation. The Event Router (EVTRTR) is a module that can
     associate an event originated by one peripheral with an action executed by another.
     The function of the EVTRTR is similar to the shared Interrupt Router (IRQRTR), which targets an interrupt
     controller and ultimately a CPU core. Unlike the IRQRTR, the EVTRTR is connecting the event signal to a
     peripheral that executes an action without involving any CPU core.
     Modules generating such event signals include: GPIO, UTIMER, I2C, SPI, UART, and others. The EVTRTR passes
     the signals through edge-detection circuits and gating logic before routing them to specific targets.
     The device includes three Event Routers, each dedicated to a specific target:
       n EVTRTR0, dedicated to DMA0 controller and UTIMER
       n EVTRTR1, dedicated to DMA1 controller
       n EVTRTR2, dedicated to DMA2 controller

     Each EVTRTR provides the following main features:
       n Software generated events
       n Zero wait state for event routing between peripherals in the same clock domain
       n Automatic synchronization of events and triggers between peripherals in different clock domains
       n DMA channel enable, handshake status and type selection

     Figure 11-6 provides a high-level overview of the EVTRTR implementation in the device.
                                             Figure 11-6 EVTRTR Overview

     EVTRTR0 is also referred to as DMA0_MUX and expands the available 32 inputs of DMA0 by exposing the
     DMA channels to 128 different peripheral events via 32 × 4-to-1 multiplexers. The first 16 multiplexed DMA0
     requests are also routed as input triggers to the Universal Timer (UTIMER). This mechanism enables the
     implementation of complex state machines involving the use of peripheral or time-based events that trigger
     data transfers and/or timer triggers.
     EVTRTR1 and EVTRTR2 support 32 input events / output DMA channels each, without implementing events
     multiplexing.

 11.4.3 EVTRTR Functional Description
     For all Event Routers, each of the 32 output channels can be independently enabled via the corresponding
     EVTRTRm_DMA_CTRLn[ENA] field.
     Only for EVTRTR0, which supports 4 groups × 32 events, the EVTRTR0_DMA_CTRLn[SEL] bit field controls the
     event selection for each DMA channel independently by selecting the appropriate group of events. It is
     recommended that event selection is done prior to enabling the channel via the corresponding EVTRTR0_
     DMA_CTRLn[ENA] field.
     The mapping of EVTRTR events to DMA controller inputs is provided in Section 12.3 DMA Events Mapping.

 11.5 Interrupt Sources Mapping

 11.5.1 Shared Interrupt Map
     A shared interrupt in the context of this device is any interrupt that passes through the IRQRTR, before being
     redirected by the router to any of the following interrupt controllers—GIC400, M55-HP NVIC, and M55-HE
     NVIC. All shared interrupts are level sensitive.
     Table 11-22 shows how shared interrupts are mapped to IRQRTR inputs. The IRQRTR_SII[31-0] inputs are
     dedicated to some internal device architecture interrupts, while IRQRTR_SII[426-32] correspond to an
     expansion shared interrupt interface.

 11.5.3 M55-HP Interrupt Map
     Table 11-24 shows the mapping of interrupts to the M55-HP NVIC IRQ inputs. These interrupts are external
     to the M55-HP and represent exceptions [16-495] in the M55-HP exception model. Exceptions [0-15] are
     internal to the M55-HP. For more information about the M55-HP exception model, see the Arm® Cortex®-
     M55 Processor Devices Generic User Guide.


                                                          NOTE

       The M55-HP processor supports a Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) input which represents exception
       number 2 in the M55-HP exception model. The WDT_HP interrupt (WDT_HP_IRQ) is connected to the
       M55-HP NMI input.


  Color-coded legend to Table 11-24:
  Yellow rows          Peripheral interrupts that are directly mapped to the M55-HP NVIC inputs.
  White rows           Peripheral interrupts that pass through the IRQRTR, before being routed to the M55-HP NVIC inputs.
  Grey rows            Unused

 11.5.4 M55-HE Interrupt Map
     Table 11-25 shows the mapping of interrupts to the M55-HE NVIC IRQ inputs. These interrupts are external
     to the M55-HE and represent exceptions [16-495] in the M55-HE exception model. Exceptions [0-15] are
     internal to the M55-HE. For more information about the M55-HE exception model, see the Arm® Cortex®-
     M55 Processor Devices Generic User Guide.


                                                          NOTE

       The M55-HE processor supports a Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) input which represents exception
       number 2 in the M55-HE exception model. The WDT_HE interrupt (WDT_HE_IRQ) is connected to the
       M55-HE NMI input.


  Color-coded legend to Table 11-25:
  Yellow rows          Peripheral interrupts that are directly mapped to the M55-HE NVIC inputs.
  White rows           Peripheral interrupts that pass through the IRQRTR, before being routed to the M55-HE NVIC inputs.
  Grey rows            Unused

 12 Direct Memory Access Management

 12.1 DMA Architecture

 12.1.1 DMA Architecture Overview
     The device features Direct Memory Access (DMA) controllers to offload the CPUs from repeated data
     transfer tasks. The device has the following DMA controllers:
       n USB embedded DMA controller
       n Ethernet embedded DMA controller
       n SDMMC embedded DMA controller
       n DMA0: Can be shared by all of the CPU cores
         l It carries out data transfers from/to ADC, PDM, I2C, I3C, CANFD, SPI, OSPI, and UART.

         l DMA0 also supports multiple DMA triggers like GPIO pin transitions and timer events.

       n DMA1: Dedicated to the RTSS-HP subsystem and serves DMA requests from CMP, QEC, UART, UTIMER,
         and via GPIO9 pins.
       n DMA2: Dedicated to the RTSS-HE subsystem
         l DMA2 can move data from/to the following peripherals: Low Power (LP) peripherals (such as LPUART,

           LPSPI, etc.), ADC, CANFD, and I3C.
         l BOD, LPTIMER, LPCMP, LPCAM_VSYNC, LPCAM_HSYNC, and LPGPIO I/O transitions can trigger DMA

           requests.
     Figure 12-1 gives a high-level overview of the DMA architecture in the device.
                                             Figure 12-1 DMA Architecture

                                                      Peripherals                 Peripherals                               Peripherals




                                                       EVTRTR0                     EVTRTR1                                   EVTRTR2


           USB         Ethernet      SDMMC

                                                        DMA Requests                DMA Requests                              DMA Requests
                                                                        M55-HP                                 M55-HE

                                                                          TCM                                    TCM


        DMA                 DMA        DMA             DMA0                      DMA1                                    DMA2



                                                       AXI




                                                                        OSPI                           Peripherals
                     SRAM                    NVM                       Memory                      (UART, I2C, SPI, etc.)
                                                                                                                                             DMA_ARCH-001




     For DMA requests mapping (peripheral to DMA[0-2] controller), refer to Section 12.3 DMA Events Mapping.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                      358
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                      E7 Series


     The high-speed interface peripherals (USB, ETH, and SDMMC) have their own, embedded DMA controllers.
     They are optimized for the specific needs of these interfaces.
     DMA0, DMA1 and DMA2 are general-purpose, programmable, multi-channel, and TrustZone-aware DMA
     controllers (DMACs). Each DMAC has 32 inputs for accepting DMA requests from various device peripherals
     and triggers (for example, UART Tx and Rx, ADC conversion done, etc). The Event Routers positioned in front
     of the DMA controllers provide support for DMA handshaking between peripherals and DMACs. Additionally,
     EVTRTR0 provides 32 × 4-to-1 programmable multiplexers, which expose the 32 DMA0 inputs to 128 possible
     DMA requests from peripherals, thus providing an increased flexibility. Each DMA controller supports 8
     internal data channels (FIFOs). All channels can perform independently programmed transactions including
     different data lengths, source and destination addresses, single or burst transfers.
     DMA0 controller can be shared by all of the CPU cores. The security privilege of each channel is run-time
     programmable. DMA0 initiates transactions on the main AXI bus with its unique Stream ID. Each of the 32
     request interfaces can generate an interrupt request signal. The interrupts are shared over the Interrupt
     Router (IRQRTR) with all of the CPU cores.
     DMA1 and DMA2 controllers are assigned to the M55-HP and M55-HE CPU cores, respectively. They reside in
     their domains and share their AXI-bus Stream IDs (and security policy). The DMA1 and DMA2 request
     interfaces can generate individual interrupt requests, attached locally to their respective M55 cores.

 12.2 DMA Controllers

 12.2.1 DMA Controllers Overview
     The device includes three copies of the general-purpose DMA Controller (DMAC):
       n DMA0 can be shared among all CPU cores
       n DMA1, dedicated to the RTSS-HP
       n DMA2, dedicated to the RTSS-HE

     For more information about DMA controllers integration in the device, see Section 12.1.1 DMA Architecture
     Overview.
     Figure 12-2 provides a high-level overview of the DMA controllers in the device.
                                                     Figure 12-2 DMAC Overview

                            Device


                                       Clocks
                                                                                 AXI



                                                          DMA[0-2]               APB

                                                                                 Secure

                                     DMA Requests/                               Non-secure

                                                                                              DMA-016




     Each DMAC supports the following main features:
       n Flexible instruction set for programming DMA transfers
       n Transfer types:
         l Memory-to-memory

         l Memory-to-peripheral

         l Peripheral-to-memory

         l Scatter-gather

       n 32 peripheral request interfaces (DMA_Req/DMA_Ack)
       n 8 DMA channels (VFIFOs)
       n Flagging of various DMA events using 33 interrupt signals
         l 32 interrupts, one per DMA request interface

         l One data abort interrupt

       n Dual slave interfaces, secure and non-secure, for accessing registers
       n Programmable security state for each DMA channel
       n Arm TrustZone technology
       n 4 active AXI read transactions
       n 4 active AXI write transactions
       n 32 deep internal data buffer (MFIFO)
       n 4 lines in the instruction cache with 8 words in a line

 12.2.3.1 DMAC Operation
     The instruction processing block included in the DMAC enables it to process program code that controls a
     DMA transfer. The program code is stored in a region of the system memory that the DMAC accesses using
     its AXI master interface. The DMAC stores instructions temporarily in the Instruction Cache.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                   Alif Semiconductor
                                                               364
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                      www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     The DMAC supports eight DMA channels. Each channel is capable of supporting a single concurrent thread of
     a DMA operation. In addition, a single DMA manager thread exists and it initializes the DMA channel threads.
     The DMAC executes up to one instruction for each AXI clock cycle. To ensure that it regularly executes each
     active thread, it alternates by processing the DMA manager thread and then a DMA channel thread. DMAC
     uses a round-robin process when selecting the next active DMA channel thread to execute.
     The DMAC uses variable-length instructions that consist of 1 to 6 bytes (see Section 12.2.3.14 Instruction
     Set). Each DMA channel has a separate Program Counter (PC) register. When a thread requests an instruction
     from an address, the cache performs a look-up. If a cache hit occurs, then the cache immediately provides
     the data. Otherwise, the thread is stalled while the DMAC uses the AXI master interface to perform a cache
     line fill. If an instruction is greater than 4 bytes, or spans the end of a cache line, the DMAC performs multiple
     cache accesses to fetch the instruction.


                                                         NOTE

     When a cache line fill is in progress, the DMAC enables other threads to access the cache, but if another
     cache miss occurs, this stalls the pipeline until the first line fill is complete.


     When a DMA channel thread executes a load or store instruction, the DMAC adds the instruction to the
     relevant read or write queue. The DMAC uses these queues as an instruction storage buffer prior to issue the
     instructions on the AXI bus. The DMAC also contains a Multi First In, First Out (MFIFO) data buffer. The buffer
     use is to store data that DMAC reads, or writes, during a DMA transfer.

 12.2.3.2 DMAC Interfaces

 12.2.3.2.1 APB Slave Interfaces
     The APB interfaces allow an access to status registers and also direct execution of instructions in the DMAC.
     The DMAC supports the following APB slave interfaces:
       n Non-secure APB slave interface—applications running in Normal World can access the DMAC through
         this interface and will configure its operation executing non-secure transactions (ns [non-secure] bit = 1).
       n Secure APB slave interface—supports Arm TrustZone and the security attributes of the applications
         using the DMA controllers. The M55 CPUs running trusted code in Secure World will be able to initialize
         the DMAC operations that perform secure transactions (ns bit = 0).

 12.2.3.2.2 AXI Master Interface
     The DMAC contains a single 64-bit AXI master interface that enables the transfer of data from a source AXI
     slave (peripheral or memory) to a destination AXI slave (peripheral or memory). AXI interface is also used for
     DMAC instruction reads from the main memory.

 12.2.3.2.3 Peripheral Request Interface
     The peripheral request interfaces (DMA Request/DMA Acknowledge) support the connection of DMA-
     capable peripherals to enable memory-to-peripheral and peripheral-to-memory DMA transfers, without
     intervention from a CPU. For more information, see Section 12.2.3.5 Peripheral Request Interface.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        365
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                      E7 Series


 12.2.3.2.4 Interrupt Interface
     The interrupt interface enables efficient communications of events to a CPU. The DMAC signals 33 interrupts,
     one per DMA request interface, and one data abort interrupt. For more information, see Section 12.2.3.6
     Using Events and Interrupts and Section 12.2.3.7 Aborts.

 12.2.3.3.1 Stopped
     In this state, the thread has an invalid PC and it is not fetching instructions. Depending on the thread type,
     DMA manager thread or DMA channel thread can move the thread to the Executing state by:
              DMA manager thread       DMAC waits for an instruction from CPU.
              DMA channel thread       Programming the DMA manager thread to execute DMAGO for a DMA
                                       channel thread in the Stopped state.

 12.2.3.3.2 Executing
     In this state, the thread has a valid PC and therefore the DMAC includes the thread when it arbitrates. The
     thread can then change to one of the next-listed states under the presented conditions:
              Stopped                  When the DMA manager thread executes DMAEND
              Cache missed             When the instruction cache does not contain the next instruction for
                                       either the DMA manager thread or the DMA channel thread
              Updating PC              When the DMAC calculates the address of the next access in the cache
              Waiting for event        When a thread executes DMAWFE
              At barrier               When a DMA channel thread either:
                                             n Executes DMARMB, DMAWMB, or DMAFLUSHP
                                             n Updates control registers that affect alignment, see Section
                                                12.2.3.12.3 Updating DMA Channel Control Registers During a
                                                DMA Cycle.
              Waiting for peripheral   When a DMA channel thread executes DMAWFP
              Killing                  When a DMA channel thread executes DMAKILL
              Fault completing         For a DMA channel thread when either:
                                             n The thread executes an undefined or invalid undefined/invalid
                                                instruction or
                                             n An AXI bus error occurs during an instruction fetch or data
                                                transfer
              Faulting                 For the DMA manager thread when either:
                                             n The thread executes an undefined or invalid undefined/invalid
                                                instruction or
                                             n An AXI bus error occurs during an instruction fetch

                                       For a DMA channel thread when a watchdog timeout abort occurs.
              Completing               When a DMA channel thread executes DMAEND


 12.2.3.3.3 Cache Miss
     In this state, the thread is stalled and the DMAC is performing a cache line fill. After the DMAC completes the
     cache fill, the thread returns to the Executing state.

 12.2.3.3.4 Updating PC
     In this state, the DMAC is calculating the address of the next access in the cache. After the DMAC has
     calculated the PC, the thread returns to the Executing state.

 12.2.3.3.5 Waiting for Event
     In this state, the thread is stalled and is waiting for the DMAC to execute DMASEV using the corresponding
     event number. After the corresponding event occurs, the thread returns to the Executing state.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                               Alif Semiconductor
                                                          367
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                              E7 Series


 12.2.3.3.6 At Barrier
     In this state, a DMA channel thread is stalled and the DMAC is waiting for transactions on the AXI bus to
     complete. After the completitio of the AXI transactions, the thread returns to the Executing state.

 12.2.3.3.7 Waiting for Peripherals
     In this state, a DMA channel thread is stalled and the DMAC is waiting for the peripheral to provide the
     requested data. After the peripheral provides the data, the thread returns to the Executing state.

 12.2.3.3.8 Faulting Completing
     In this state, a DMA channel thread is waiting for the AXI master interface to signal that the outstanding load
     or store transactions are completed. After the transactions completion, the thread moves to the Faulting
     state.

 12.2.3.3.9 Faulting
     In this state, the thread is stalled indefinitely. The thread moves to the Stopped state when the DMA_
     DBGCMD register instructs the DMAC to execute DMAKILL for that thread.

 12.2.3.3.10 Killing
     In this state, a DMA channel thread is waiting for the AXI master interface to signal that the outstanding load
     or store transactions are completed. After the transactions completion, the thread moves to the Stopped
     state.

 12.2.3.3.11 Completing
     In this state, a DMA channel thread is waiting for the AXI master interface to signal that the outstanding load
     or store transactions are completed. After the transactions completion, the thread moves to the Stopped
     state.

 12.2.3.4 Using the Registers
     A CPU can access the registers that Section 12.2.4 DMA Controllers Registers Guide describes. Using these
     registers, a CPU can:
       n Access the status of the DMA manager thread
       n Access the status of the DMA channel threads
       n Enable or clear interrupts
       n Enable events
       n Issue an instruction for the DMAC to execute by programming the following registers:
         l DMA_DBGCMD register

         l DMA_DBGINST0 register

         l DMA_DBGINST1 register



 12.2.3.4.1 Issuing Instructions to the DMAC
     When the DMAC is processing a thread, it can only executes the following limited subset of instructions:
              DMAGO                 Starts a DMA transaction using a DMA channel that is specified
              DMASEV                Signals the occurrence of an event, or interrupt, using an event number
                                    that is specified
              DMAKILL               Terminates a thread



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                        368
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


     For more details about the full set of instruction, see Section 12.2.3.14 Instruction Set.
     Software is responsible to ensure the appropriate APB interface, depending on the security state. For
     example, if the DMAC is in the secure state, the software must issue the instruction using the secure APB
     interface, otherwise the DMAC ignores the instruction. Both the secure APB interface and the non-secure
     APB interface can start or restart a DMA channel when the DMAC is in the non-secure state.


                                                        NOTE

     If the instructions using the debug instruction registers (DMA_DBGINST0/1) or the DMA_DBGCMD register
     are issued when the debug is not idled (the state can be checked in the DMA_DBGSTATUS register), the
     DMAC ignores the instructions.


     The following sequence shows the necessary steps to start a DMA channel thread using the debug instruction
     registers:
      1. Create a program for the DMA channel.
      2. Store the program in a region of system memory.
       Program a DMAGO instruction as follows:
      3. Poll the DMA_DBGSTATUS register to ensure that debug is idle, that is, the DMA_DBGSTATUS bit is 0.
      4. Write to the DMA_DBGINST0 register and enter the:
         n Instruction byte 0 encoding for DMAGO
         n Instruction byte 1 encoding for DMAGO
         n Debug thread bit to 0. This selects the DMA manager thread.
      5. Write the DMAGO instruction byte [5-2] data to the DMA_DBGINST1 register. Software must set these
         four bytes to the address of the first instruction in the program, that was written to system memory in
         Step 2.
       Program the DMAC to execute the instruction that the DMA_DBGINST0/1 contain by:
      6. Writing 0 to the DMA_DBGCMD register. The DMAC starts the DMA channel thread and sets the DMA_
         DBGSTATUS bit to 1. After the DMAC completes execution of the instruction, it clears the DMA_
         DBGSTATUS bit to 0.

     Both buses use the VALID and READY handshake.

          n Signal when it completes the requested single transfer,
          n Signal when it completes the requested burst transfer or
          n Issue a flush request.


 12.2.3.5.1 Mapping to a DMA Channel
     The DMAC can assign a peripheral request interface to any of the DMA channels. When a DMA channel
     thread executes DMAWFP, the value programmed in the peripheral [4-0] field specifies the peripheral
     associated with that DMA channel.

 12.2.3.5.3 Request Acceptance
     Active request is when the DMAC has not started the requested AXI data transfers.
     For each peripheral interface, the DMAC has a request FIFO that it uses to capture the requests from a
     peripheral. To store the state of an active request from the peripheral, the request FIFO uses two bits to
     store the state of:
                 DRTYPE_<x>[0]          Indicates the request type, burst or single.
                 DRLAST_<x>             Indicates if the peripheral is requesting the last data transfer of the DMA
                                        transfer.
     When a request FIFO is full then the DMAC sets the corresponding DRREADY_<x> LOW to signal that the
     DMAC cannot accept any requests sent from the peripheral.

 12.2.3.5.4 Peripheral Length Management
     The peripheral request interface enables a peripheral to control the quantity of data that a DMA cycle
     contains, without the DMAC being aware of how many data transfers it contains. The peripheral controls the
     DMA cycle by using:
          n   DRTYPE[1:0] to select a single or burst transfer
          n   DRLAST to notify the DMAC when it commences the final request in the current series.
     When the DMAC executes a DMAWFP peripheral instruction, the DMAC halts execution of the thread and
     waits for the peripheral to send a request. When the peripheral sends the request, the DMAC sets the state
     of the request flags depending on the state of the following signals:
                 DRTYPE_<x>[1:0]        The DMAC sets the state of the REQUEST_TYPE flag
                                        DRTYPE_<x>[1:0] = 00b REQUEST_TYPE<x> = Single.
                                        DRTYPE_<x>[1:0] = 01b REQUEST_TYPE<x> = Burst.
                 DRLAST_<x>             The DMAC sets the state of the REQUEST_LAST flag:
                                        DRLAST_<x> = 0 REQUEST_LAST<x> = 0.
                                        The DMAC acknowledge bus.


                                                             NOTE

     If the DMAC executes a DMAWFP single or DMAWFP burst instruction then the DMAC sets:
          n The REQUEST_TYPE<x> flag, where x is 0 or 1, to Single or Burst, respectively.
          n The REQUEST_LAST<x> flag to 0.




     DMALPFE is an assembler directive that forces the associated DMALPEND instruction to have its NF bit set to
     0. This creates a program loop that does not use a loop counter to terminate the loop. The DMAC exits the
     loop when the REQUEST_LAST flag is set to 1.
     The DMAC conditionally executes the following instructions, depending on the state of the REQUEST_TYPE
     and REQUEST_LAST flags:

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                             371
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                      www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                   E7 Series


              DMALD, DMAST,                When these instructions use the optional B|S suffix and the REQUEST_
              DMALPEND                     TYPE flag does not match then the DMAC executes a DMANOP.
              DMALDP<B|S>,                 The DMAC executes a DMANOP if the REQUEST_TYPE flag does not
              DMASTP<B|S>                  match the B|S suffix.
              DMALPEND                     When the NF bit is 0 and the REQUEST_LAST flag is set, the DMAC
                                           executes a DMANOP if the REQUEST_LAST flag is set.
     Use the DMALDB, DMALDPB, DMASTB and DMASTPB instructions if the DMAC has to issue a burst transfer
     when the DMAC receives a burst request, that is, DRTYPE_<x>[1:0] = 01b. The values in the DMA_CCRn
     register control the amount of data that the DMAC transfers.
     Use the DMALDS, DMALDPS, DMASTS and DMASTPS instructions if the DMAC has to issue a single transfer
     when the DMAC receives a single request, that is, DRTYPE_<x>[1:0] = 00b. The DMAC ignores the value of the
     SRC_BURST_LEN and DST_BURST_LEN fields in the DMA_CCRn register and sets the ARLEN[3:0] or AWLEN
     [3:0] buses to 0x0.
     Example program for peripheral length management
     The code below shows a DMAC program that transfers 64 words from memory to peripheral zero, when the
     peripheral sends a burst request, that is, DRTYPE_<x>[1:0] = 01b. When the peripheral sends a single request,
     that is, DRTYPE_<x>[1:0] = 00b, then the DMAC program transfers one word from memory to peripheral
     zero.
     To transfer the 64 words, the program instructs the DMAC to perform 16 AXI transfers. Each AXI transfer
     consists of a 4-beat burst (SB = 4, DB = 4), each beat of which moves a word of data (SS = 32, DS = 32).

      3      DMAMOV SAR ...
      4      DMAMOV DAR ...

     18        DMALP 15

     20           DMASTB

 12.2.3.5.5 DMAC Length Management
     DMAC length management is when the DMAC controls the total amount of data to transfer. The peripheral
     uses the peripheral request interface to notify the DMAC when the peripheral requires the DMAC to transfer
     data to or from the peripheral. The DMA channel thread controls how the DMAC responds to the peripheral
     requests.
     The following constraints apply to DMAC length management:
       n   The total quantity of data for all the single requests from a peripheral must be less than the quantity of
           data for a burst request for that peripheral.

                                                                     NOTE

                The DMA_CCRn register controls how much data is transferred for a burst request and a
                single request.
                Recommendation: Do not update a DMA_CCRn register when a transfer is in progress for
                channel n.


       n   When the peripheral sends a burst request then the peripheral must not send a single request until the
           DMAC acknowledges that the burst request is completed.
     Use the DMAWFP single instruction when the program thread has to halt its execution until the peripheral
     request interface receives any request type.
     The DMAC operates as follows dependent on the request type of the head entry in the request FIFO:
              Single                     The DMAC pops the entry from the FIFO and continues program
                                         execution.
              Burst                      The DMAC leaves the entry in the FIFO and continues program execution.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                  Alif Semiconductor
                                                               373
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                 E7 Series


                                                            NOTE

       The burst request entry remains in the request FIFO until the DMAC executes a DMAWFP burst
       instruction or a DMAFLUSHP instruction.


     Use the DMAWFP burst instruction when the program thread has to halt its execution until the peripheral
     request interface receives a burst request. The DMAC operates as follows dependent on the request type of
     the head entry in the request FIFO:
              Single                   The DMAC removes the entry from the FIFO and program execution
                                       remains halted.
              Burst                    The DMAC pops the entry from the FIFO and continues program
                                       execution.


     Use the DMALDP instruction when the DMAC has to send an acknowledgement to the peripheral when the
     DMAC completes the AXI read transfers. Similarly, use the DMASTP instruction when the DMAC has to send
     an acknowledgement to the peripheral when the DMAC completes the AXI write transfers. The DMAC uses
     the DATYPE_<x>[1:0] bus to signal a transfer acknowledgement to peripheral <x>.


                                                            NOTE

       The DMAC sends an acknowledgement for a read transaction when RVALID and RLST are HIGH and for
       a write transaction when BVALID is HIGH. If the system is able to buffer AXI write transfers then it
       might be possible for the DMAC to send an acknowledgement to the peripheral but the transfer of
       write data to the end destination is still in progress.


     Use the DMAFLUSHP instruction to reset the request FIFO for the peripheral request interface. After the
     DMAC executes DMAFLUSHP, the DMAC ignores peripheral requests until the peripheral acknowledges the
     flush request. This enables the DMAC and peripheral to synchronize with each other.


     Example program for DMAC length management
     The below code shows a DMAC program that can transfer 1027 words when a peripheral signals 16
     consecutive burst requests and three consecutive single requests.

   DMAC Length Management
      1   # Set up for AXI burst transfer (4-beat burst, so SB4 and DB4), (word data width, so SS32 and DS32)
      2     DMAMOV CCR, SB4 SS32 DB4 DS32
      3     DMAMOV SAR, 0x02020202
      4     DMAMOV DAR, 0x04040404
      5
      6      # Initialize peripheral '0'
      7      DMAFLUSHP 0
      8      # Perform peripheral transfers
      9      # Burst request loop to transfer 1024 words
     10      DMALP 16
     11         # Wait for the peripheral to signal a burst request. DMAC transfers 64 words for each burst request

   DMAC Length Management
     12        DMAWFP 0, burst
     13        # Set up loop for burst request: first 15 of 16 sets of transactions
     14        DMALP 15
     15        DMALD
     16        DMAST
     17        DMALPEND
     18        # Perform final transaction (16 of 16). Send the peripheral acknowledgement of burst request completion
     19        DMALD
     20        DMASTPB 0
     21      # Finish burst loop
     22      DMALPEND
     23      # Set up for AXI single transfer (word data width, so SS32 and DS32)
     24      DMAMOV CCR, SB1 SS32 DB1 DS32
     25      # Single request loop to transfer 3 words
     26      DMALP 3
     27        # Wait for the peripheral to signal a single request. DMAC to transfer one word
     28        DMAWFP 0, single
     29        # Perform transaction for single request and send completion acknowledgement to the peripheral
     30        DMALDS
     31        DMASTPS 0
     32      # Finish single loop
     33      DMALPEND
     34      # Flush the peripheral, in case the single transfers were in response to a burst request
     35      DMAFLUSHP 0
     36      DMAEND

 12.2.3.6 Using Events and Interrupts
       Program the DMA_INTEN register to specify the type of each event-interrupt resource—either an event or an
       interrupt.
       During the execution of a DMASEV instruction, the DMAC modifies the event-interrupt resource type. The
       DMAC operates as follows dependent on the event-interrupt resource type set in the DMA_INTEN register:

               Event                           The DMAC generates an event for the specified event-interrupt resource.
                                               When the DMAC executes a DMAWFE instruction for the same event-
                                               interrupt resource then it clears the event.
               Interrupt                       The DMAC sets IRQ<EVENT_NUM> HIGH, where EVENT_NUM is the
                                               number of the specified event-resource. To clear the interrupt write to
                                               the DMA_INTCLR register.

 12.2.3.6.1 Using an Event to Restart DMA Channels
       If the DMA_INTEN register is programmed to generate an event, use the DMASEV and DMAWFE instructions
       to restart one or more DMA channels.
       DMAC Executes DMAWFE Before DMASEV
       To restart a single DMA channel perform:




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                                       Alif Semiconductor
                                                                             377
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


         1. The first DMA channel executes DMAWFE and then stalls while it waits for the event to occur.
         2. The other DMA channel executes DMASEV using the same event number. This generates an event, and
            the first DMA channel restarts. The DMAC clears the event, one ACLK cycle after it executes DMASEV.
     Software can program multiple channels to wait for the same event. For example, if four DMA channels have
     all executed DMAWFE for event 12, then when another DMA channel executes DMASEV for event 12, the
     four DMA channels all restart at the same time. The DMAC clears the event, one clock cycle after it executes
     DMASEV.
     DMAC Executes DMASEV Before DMAWFE
     If the DMAC executes DMASEV before another channel executes DMAWFE then the event remains pending
     until the DMAC executes DMAWFE. When the DMAC executes DMAWFE it halts execution for one ACLK
     cycle, clears the event and then continues execution of the channel thread.
     For example, if the DMAC executes DMASEV 6 and none of the other threads have executed DMAWFE 6 then
     the event remains pending. If the DMAC executes DMAWFE 6 instruction for channel 4 and then executes
     DMAWFE 6 instruction for channel 3, then:
         1. The DMAC halts execution of the channel 4 thread for one ACLK cycle.
         2. The DMAC clears event 6.
         3. The DMAC resumes execution of the channel 4 thread.
         4. The DMAC halts execution of the channel 3 thread and the thread stalls while it waits for the next
            occurrence of even.

 12.2.3.6.2 Interrupting a CPU
     The DMAC provides the IRQ[x] signals (where x = 0 to 31) for use as active-high level-sensitive interrupts to
     CPUs. If the DMA_INTEN register is programmed to generate an interrupt, after the DMAC executes
     DMASEV, it sets the corresponding IRQ[x] HIGH.
     CPU can clear the interrupt by writing to the Interrupt Clear Register (DMA_INTCLR).


                                                            NOTE

         Executing DMAWFE does not clear an interrupt.


     It is recommended to insert a memory barrier instruction before the DMASEV if software use the DMASEV
     instruction to notify a CPU when the DMAC completes a DMALD or DMAST instruction. Otherwise the DMAC
     might signal an interrupt before the completion of the AXI transfers.
     For example:

   Example of DMASEV Use
     1        DMALD
     2        DMAST
     3     # Issue a write memory barrier
     4     # Wait for the AXI write transfer to complete before the DMAC can send an interrupt
     5        DMAWMB
     6     # The DMAC sends the interrupt
     7        DMASEV 0




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                            378
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


 12.2.3.7 Aborts

 12.2.3.7.1 Abort Types
     An abort type is:
       n Precise
       n Imprecise

     When the abort occurs and the DMAC provides an abort handler with the precise state of the DMAC, the
     abort is of a precise type. Otherwise, it is imprecise type.
     The DMAC operates according to the abort types as folows:
              Precise               The DMAC updates the DMA_DPC register with the address of the
                                    instruction that created the abort.
              Imprecise             The DMA_DPC register might contain the address of an instruction that
                                    have not caused the abort to occur.

 12.2.3.7.2 Abort Sources
     The DMAC signals a precise abort under the following conditions:
       n A DMA channel thread in the non-secure state attempts to program its DMA_CCRn register and to
         generate a secure AXI transaction.
       n A DMA channel thread in the non-secure state executes DMAWFE or DMASEV for an event that is set as
         secure. For the security state of an event after reset, see Section 12.2.2.2 DMAC State after Reset.

                                                             NOTE

                For each event, the DMA_INTEN register controls if the DMAC generates an event or an
                interrupt.


       n A DMA channel thread attempts to execute DMAST but the DMAC calculates that when it eventually
         performs the store, the MFIFO contains insufficient data to enable it to complete the store.
       n A DMA channel thread in the non-secure state executes DMAWFP, DMALDP, DMASTP, or DMAFLUSHP
         for a peripheral request interface that is set as secure. For the security state of a peripheral request
         interface (see Section 12.2.2.2 DMAC State after Reset).
       n A DMA manager thread in the non-secure state executes DMAGO to attempt to start a secure DMA
         channel thread.
       n The DMAC receives an ERROR response on the AXI master interface when it performs an instruction
         fetch.
       n A thread executes an undefined instruction.
       n A thread executes an instruction with an operand that is invalid for the configuration of the DMAC.



                                                        NOTE

       When the DMAC signals a precise abort, the instruction that triggers the abort is not executed.
       Instead, the DMAC executes a DMANOP.


     The DMAC generates imprecise abort under the following conditions:
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                       379
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


       n The DMAC receives an ERROR response on the AXI master interface when it performs a data load.
       n The DMAC receives an ERROR response on the AXI master interface when it performs a data store.
       n A DMA channel thread executes DMALD or DMAST, and the MFIFO is too small to hold the required
         amount of data.
       n A DMA channel thread executes DMAST but the thread has not executed sufficient DMALD instructions.
       n A DMA channel thread locks up because of resource starvation, and this causes the internal watchdog
         timer to time out.

 12.2.3.7.3 Watchdog Abort
     The DMAC can be locked up if one or more DMA channel programs are running and the MFIFO is too small to
     satisfy the storage requirements of the DMA programs.
     Inner logic prevents the DMAC from remaining in a state where is unable to complete a DMA transfer.
     The DMAC detects a lockup when all of the following conditions occur:
       n Load queue is empty.
       n Store queue is empty.
       n All of the running channels are prevented from executing a DMALD instruction either because the MFIFO
         does not have sufficient free space or another channel owns the load-lock.
     When the DMAC detects a lockup, it generates an interrupt and can also abort the contributing channels. The
     DMAC behavior depends on the state of the WD_IRQ_ONLY bit in the DMA_WD register.
     If:
              WD_IRQ_ONLY = 0      The DMAC aborts all of the contributing DMA channels and sets IRQ_
                                   ABORT HIGH.
              WD_IRQ_ONLY = 1      The DMAC sets IRQ_ABORT HIGH.


     For more information see Section 12.2.3.12.4 Resource Sharing Between DMA Channels and DMA_WD
     register.

     The architecture of the DMAC is not designed to recover from an abort. Terminating a thread when an abort
     occurs requires a use of software. Figure 12-12 shows the operating states for the DMA channel and DMA
     manager threads after an abort occurs.

     DMA Manager Thread
     The thread immediately moves to the Faulting state and the DMAC sets IRQ_ABORT HIGH.
     The external agent can respond to the assertion of IRQ_ABORT by:
       n Reading the status of the DMA_FSRD register to determine if the DMA manager is Faulting. In the
         Faulting state, the DMA_FSRD register provides the cause of the abort.
       n Reading the status of the DMA_FSRC register to determine if a DMA channel is Faulting. In the Faulting
         state, the DMA_FSRC register provides the cause of the abort.
     To enable a thread in the Faulting state to move to the Stopped state, the external agent must:
      1. Program the DMA_DBGINST0 register with the encoding for the DMAKILL instruction.
      2. Write to the DMA_DBGCMD register.

                                                             NOTE

                If the aborted thread is secure, the external agent must use the secure APB interface to
                update these registers.


     After a thread in the Faulting state executes DMAKILL, it moves to the Stopped state.

 12.2.3.8 Security Usage
     When the DMAC exits from reset, it configures the security for:
       n DMA manager thread: The DNS bit in the DMA_DSR register returns the current security state of the
         DMA manager thread.
       n Events and interrupts: The INS bit in the DMA_CR3 register returns the security state of the event-
         interrupt resources.
       n Peripheral request interfaces: The PNS bit in the DMA_CR4 register returns the security state of these
         interfaces.
     See Section 12.2.2.2 DMAC State after Reset for secure state configuration after resets.
     Additionally, each DMA channel thread contains a dynamic non-secure bit, CNS, that is valid when the
     channel is not in the Stopped state.

 12.2.3.8.1 DMA Manager Thread—Secure State
     If the DNS bit is 0, the DMA manager thread operates in the secure state and it only performs secure
     instruction fetches.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       382
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                 E7 Series


     In secure state, a DMA manager thread processes:
              DMAGO                DMA manager thread uses the status of the ns bit, to set the security
                                   state of the DMA channel thread by writing to the CNS bit for that
                                   channel.
              DMAWFE               DMA manager thread halts execution of the thread until the event
                                   occurs. When the event occurs, the DMAC continues execution of the
                                   thread, irrespective of the security state of the corresponding INS bit.
              DMASEV               DMA manager thread sets the corresponding bit in the DMA_INT_
                                   EVENT_RIS register, irrespective of the security state of the
                                   corresponding INS bit.


 12.2.3.8.2 DMA Manager Thread—Non-Secure State
     If the DNS bit is 1, the DMA manager thread operates in the non-secure state, and it only performs non-
     secure instruction fetches.
     In non-secure state, a DMA manager thread processes:
              DMAGO                The DMAC uses the status of the ns bit, to control if it starts a DMA
                                   channel thread. If:
                                   ns = 0     The DMAC does not start a DMA channel thread and instead
                                              it:
                                              1. Executes a NOP.
                                              2. Sets the DMA_FSRD register.
                                              3. Sets the DMAGO_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRD register.
                                              4. Moves the DMA manager to the Faulting state.
                                   ns = 1     The DMAC starts a DMA channel thread in the non-secure
                                              state and programs the CNS bit to be non-secure.
              DMAWFE               The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding INS bit, in the DMA_CR3
                                   register, to control if it waits for the event. If:
                                   INS = 0    The event is in the secure state. The DMAC:
                                              1. Executes a NOP.
                                              2. Sets the DMA_FSRD register.
                                              3. Sets the MGR_EVNT_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRD register.
                                              4. Moves the DMA manager to the Faulting state.
                                   INS = 1    The event is in the non-secure state. The DMAC halts
                                              execution of the thread and waits for the event to occur.
              DMASEV               The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding INS bit, in the DMA_CR3
                                   register, to control if it creates the event-interrupt. If:
                                   INS = 0     The event-interrupt resource is in the secure state. The
                                               DMAC:
                                               1. Executes a NOP.
                                               2. Sets the DMA_FSRD register.
                                               3. Sets the MGR_EVNT_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRD register.
                                               4. Moves the DMA manager to the Faulting state.
                                   INS = 1     The event-interrupt resource is in the non-secure state. The

AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                    www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                               E7 Series


                                               DMAC creates the event-interrupt.



 12.2.3.9 DMA Channel Thread—Secure State
     When the CNS bit is 0, the DMA channel thread is programmed to operate in the secure state and it only
     performs secure instruction fetches.
     In secure state, a DMA channel thread processes the following instructions:
              DMAWFE               The DMAC halts execution of the thread until the event occurs. When the
                                   event occurs, the DMAC continues execution of the thread, irrespective
                                   of the security state of the corresponding INS bit, in the DMA_CR3
                                   register.
              DMASEV               The DMAC creates the event-interrupt, irrespective of the security state
                                   of the corresponding INS bit, in the DMA_CR3 register.
              DMAWFP               The DMAC halts execution of the thread until the peripheral signals a
                                   DMA request. When this occurs, the DMAC continues execution of the
                                   thread, irrespective of the security state of the corresponding PNS bit, in
                                   the DMA_CR4 register.
              DMALDP, DMASTP       The DMAC sends a message to the peripheral to communicate that data
                                   transfer is completed, irrespective of the security state of the
                                   corresponding PNS bit, in the DMA_CR4 register.
              DMAFLUSHP            The DMAC clears the state of the peripheral and sends a message to the
                                   peripheral to resend its level status, irrespective of the security state of
                                   the corresponding PNS bit, in the DMA_CR4 register.


     When a DMA channel thread is in the secure state, it enables the DMAC to perform secure and non-secure
     AXI accesses.

 12.2.3.10 DMA Channel Thread—Non-Secure State
     When the CNS bit is 1, the DMA channel thread is programmed to operate in the non-secure state and it only
     performs non-secure instruction fetches.
     In non-secure state, a DMA channel thread processes the following instructions:
              DMAWFE               The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding INS bit, in the DMA_CR3
                                   register, to control if it waits for the event. If:
                                   INS = 0    The event is in the secure state. The DMAC:
                                              1. Executes a NOP.
                                              2. Sets the appropriate bit in the DMA_FSRC register that
                                              corresponds to the DMA channel number.
                                              3. Sets the CH_EVNT_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRn register.
                                              4. Moves the DMA channel to the Faulting completing state.
                                   INS = 1    The event is in the non-secure state. The DMAC halts
                                              execution of the thread and waits for the event to occur.
              DMASEV               The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding INS bit, in the DMA_CR3
                                   register, to control if it creates the event. If:
                                   INS = 0    The event-interrupt resource is in the secure state. The
                                              DMAC:

                                                        384
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                  www.alifsemi.com

                                             1. Executes a NOP.
                                             2. Sets the appropriate bit in the DMA_FSRC register that
                                             corresponds to the DMA channel number.
                                             3. Sets the CH_EVENT_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRn register.
                                             4. Moves the DMA channel to the Faulting completing state.
                                 INS = 1     The event-interrupt resource is in the non-secure state. The
                                             DMAC creates the event-interrupt.
              DMAWFP             The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding PNS bit, in the DMA_CR4

                                 PNS = 0     The peripheral is in the secure state. The DMAC:

                                             4. Moves the DMA channel to the Faulting completing state.
                                 PNS = 1     The peripheral is in the non-secure state. The DMAC halts

              DMALDP, DMASTP     The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding PNS bit, in the DMA_CR4

                                             1. Executes a NOP.

                                             3. Sets the CH_PERIPH_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRn register
                                             4. Moves the DMA channel to the Faulting completing state.
                                 PNS = 1     The peripheral is in the non-secure state. The DMAC sends a
                                             message to the peripheral to communicate when the data
                                             transfer is complete.
              DMAFLUSHP          The DMAC uses the status of the corresponding PNS bit, in the DMA_CR4
                                 register, to control if it sends a flush request to the peripheral. If:
                                 PNS = 0     The peripheral is in the secure state. The DMAC:
                                             1. Executes a NOP.
                                             2. Sets the appropriate bit in the DMA_FSRC register that

                                 PNS = 1     The peripheral is in the non-secure state. The DMAC clears

     When a DMA channel thread is in the non-secure state, and a DMAMOV CCR instruction attempts to
     program the channel to perform a secure AXI transaction, the DMAC:

      1. Executes a DMANOP.
      2. Sets the appropriate bit in the DMA_FSRC register that corresponds to the DMA channel number.
      3. Sets the CH_RDWR_ERR bit in the DMA_FTRn register.
      4. Moves the DMA channel thread to the Faulting completing state.

 12.2.3.11 Constraints and Limitations of Use

 12.2.3.11.1 DMA Channel Arbitration
     The DMAC uses a round-robin scheme to service the active DMA channels. To ensure that the DMAC
     continues to service the DMA manager, it always services the DMA manager prior to servicing the next DMA
     channel.
     It is not possible to alter the arbitration process of the DMAC.

 12.2.3.11.2 DMA Channel Prioritization
     The DMAC responds to all active DMA channels with equal priority. It is not possible to increase the priority
     of a DMA channel over any other DMA channels.

 12.2.3.11.3 Instruction Cache Latency
     When a cache miss occurs, the latency to service the request is mainly dependent on the read latency of the
     AXI bus. The latency that the DMAC adds is minimal.

 12.2.3.11.4 AXI Data Transfer Size
     The DMAC can only perform data accesses up to the width of the AXI data bus. Programming the SRC_
     BURST_SIZE or DST_BURST_SIZE fields to be larger than this leads to a precise abort generation from the
     DMAC. For more information about abort, see Section 12.2.3.7.2 Abort Sources.

 12.2.3.11.5 AXI Bursts Crossing 4K byte Boundaries
     The AMBA AXI and ACE Protocol Specification does not permit AXI bursts to cross 4K byte address
     boundaries. Programming the DMAC with a combination of burst start address, size, and length that would
     cause a single burst to cross a 4K byte address boundary, causes the DMAC to generate a pair of bursts with a
     combined length equal to that specified. This operation is transparent to the DMAC channel thread program
     so that, for example, the DMAC responds to a single DMALD instruction by generating the appropriate pair of
     AXI read bursts.

 12.2.3.11.6 AXI Burst Types
     The DMAC generates only fixed-address or incrementing-address burst types for data accesses. It does not
     generate wrapping-address bursts for data accesses or for instruction fetches.

 12.2.3.11.7 AXI Write Addresses
     The DMAC can issue multiple outstanding write addresses up to the write issuing capability. The DMAC does
     not issue a write address until it has read in all of the data bytes required to fulfil that write transaction.

 12.2.3.11.8 AXI Write Data Interleaving
     The DMAC does not generate interleaved write data. All write data beats for one write transaction are
     outputed before any write data beat for the next write transaction.
