 13.2.4.1.1 Counter Control Block
      Each channel timer counter can be configured:
        n For sawtooth and triangle wave counter rising or falling
        n To start, stop and clear through registers or via triggers
        n As a free-running counter or trigger sources to advance the clock

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                     Alif Semiconductor
                                                                    469
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


       n To capture timer counter value at rising, falling, or toggling of the triggers
       n To use single or double buffer transfers at overflow or underflow

     Channel timer counters can be started, stopped, cleared, incremented or decremented via various
     programmable events from the following few types of sources:
       n 16 global trigger inputs rising or falling (valid for UTIMER channels only)
       n 12 QEC trigger inputs rising or falling (valid for QEC channels only)
       n 2 channel inputs in total of 8 various combinations:
         l Channel input on driver A rising while channel input on driver B = 0

         l Channel input on driver A falling while channel input on driver B = 0

         l Channel input on driver A rising while channel input on driver B = 1

         l Channel input on driver A falling while channel input on driver B = 1

         l Channel input on driver B rising while channel input on driver A = 0

         l Channel input on driver B falling while channel input on driver A = 0

         l Channel input on driver B rising while channel input on driver A = 1

         l Channel input on driver B falling while channel input on driver A = 1

       n 4 fault trigger inputs
       n 2 pause trigger inputs

     Any combination of these input events can be programmed to cause a timer counter to start.
     The associated registers to these input events are the UTIMERn_START_0/1_SRC, UTIMERn_STOP_0/1_SRC,
     UTIMERn_CLEAR_0/1_SRC, UTIMERn_UP_0/1_SRC, UTIMERn_DOWN_0/1_SRC, UTIMERn_TRIG_CAPTURE_
     SRC_A_0/1, UTIMERn_TRIG_CAPTURE_SRC_B_0/1, UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_A and UTIMERn_COMPARE_
     CTRL_B registers. To enable the source, write a 1 to the respective bits of the UTIMERn_START_0/1_SRC
     register.
     Note that the decoding of the QEC_TRIGGERS[11-0] for the UTIMERn_START_0_SRC register for example, is
     as follows:
       n QEC0_X pin is used for UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[TRIG0_RISING] and UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[TRIG0_
         FALLING] bits;
       n QEC0_Y pin is used for UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[TRIG1_RISING] and UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[TRIG1_
         FALLING] bits;
       n QEC0_Z pin is used for UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[TRIG2_RISING] and UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[TRIG2_
         FALLING] bits.
       n Similarly, for the other QEC[1-3]_X, QEC[1-3]_Y, and QEC[1-3]_Z pins.
       n The UTIMERn_START_0_SRC[31-24] bits are not used by the QEC channels.

     All channel timer counters can also be individually or simultaneously started, stopped and cleared by writing
     a 1 to each bit of the global counter registers (UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START, UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP,
     UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR). Writing a 0 to the bits of these registers has no effect.
     The status of a running timer counter can be checked by reading the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_RUNNING register.
     The output enable signal of the drivers of each channel is controlled by the global register UTIMER_GLB_
     DRIVER_OEN.

 13.2.4.1.2 Capture and Compare Block
     The channel counter value can be captured at rising, falling, and toggling of the triggers. Buffer value is
     transferred at trigger event, overflow or underflow along with the capture events.
     Each UTIMER channel has two compare blocks with its output compare driver A and B, respectively. Compare
     A drives UTIMER UT[0-11]_T0 pins and compare B drives UTIMER UT[0-11]_T1 pins. Each of the two compare

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                         470
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                     E7 Series


     blocks have 3 compare registers. For compare block A, these are UTIMERn_COMPARE_A, UTIMERn_
     COMPARE_A_BUF1, UTIMERn_COMPARE_A_BUF2, and for B—UTIMERn_COMPARE_B, UTIMERn_
     COMPARE_B_BUF1, and UTIMERn_COMPARE_B_BUF2. When these registers match the timer counter value
     they form 6 internal compare match events (their values at compare match hereinafter referred to as A to F),
     as it follows:
       n Value A = UTIMERn_COMPARE_A register
       n Value B = UTIMERn_COMPARE_B register
       n Value C = UTIMERn_COMPARE_A_BUF1 register
       n Value D = UTIMERn_COMPARE_A_BUF2 register
       n Value E = UTIMERn_COMPARE_B_BUF1 register
       n Value F = UTIMERn_COMPARE_B_BUF2 register

     Along with the events of timer counter overflow and timer counter underflow they define when the buffer
     value is transferred to the UT[0-11]_T0 and UT[0-11]_T1 pins. Note that the output signals on the pins are
     controlled only by the matches of the timer counter to the UTIMERn_COMPARE_A and UTIMERn_COMPARE_
     B registers.
     Each driver can also be set to 0 or 1, or to toggle at cycle end through the compare control registers
     UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_A and UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_B, respectively. A compare match event can
     cause either rise, fall or toggle of a driver.

 13.2.4.1.3 Output Control Block
     A duty cycle function can be enabled for both drivers using the UTIMERn_DUTY_CYCLE_CTRL[DC_ENABLE_A]
     and UTIMERn_DUTY_CYCLE_CTRL[DC_ENABLE_B] register bits. Duty cycle for a driver can be forced to 0 or 1
     through the UTIMERn_DUTY_CYCLE_CTRL[DC_FORCE_A] and UTIMERn_DUTY_CYCLE_CTRL[DC_FORCE_B]
     bits. The function can also be enforced to 0% and 100% duty cycle at overflow and underflow.

 13.2.4.2 UTIMER Interrupt Requests
     Each UTIMER channel has 8 interrupt requests, and each UTIMER QEC channel has 2 interrupt requests, that
     can be routed as interrupt requests to processors. Some requests can be shared among channels to enable
     the implementation of complex state machines that can operate in a deterministic manner.
     Read the UTIMERn_CHAN_INTERRUPT register to detect what event submitted the interrupt. Write a 1 to
     each bit of this register to clear the interrupt. Use UTIMERn_CHAN_INTERRUPT_MASK register to mask each
     interrupt separately or all together.

 13.2.4.3 UTIMER DMA Requests
     UTIMER channels [0-7] can trigger a DMA transfer. To clear DMA requests when driver A is the source,
     program the UTIMERn_DMA_CLEAR_SRC_A_1 register. Program the UTIMERn_DMA_CLEAR_SRC_B_1
     register when driver B is the source. To enable or disable the DMA_CLEAR functionality, write the UTIMERn_
     COMPARE_CTRL_A/UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_B[DMA_CLEAR_EN] bit. Similarly, program the respective *_
     SRC_A/B_0 registers when the 16 global input triggers are the source.

 13.2.4.4 UTIMER Buffers
     The UTIMER module can be programmed to use buffers. To enable buffer operation the UTIMERn_BUF_OP_
     CTRL register needs to be configured. Single and double buffer operation can be performed in two different
     modes.
     Figure 13-11 presents a simplified diagram of the double buffer operation and compare buffering.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                     471
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                              E7 Series


                            Figure 13-11 UTIMER Double and Compare Buffering Block Diagram




     In the case of pointer buffering, different values can be loaded into the pointer at events such as overflow or
     underflow. In a single buffering operation the value is loaded from buffer 1 into the pointer. In a double
     buffering the value from buffer 1 is loaded into the pointer and buffer 2 is loaded into buffer 1. The processor
     can write to buffer 1 or buffer 2 during operation to load new values.
     In the case of compare buffering, new values are compared to the timer counter value when there is a
     compare match. The buffer values are transferred in the same way as in the pointer buffering case.
     In the case of capture buffering, the counter value is captured when there is an event to cause a capture.
     Figure 13-12 presents a simplified diagram of the capture buffering.
                                  Figure 13-12 UTIMER Capture Buffering Block Diagram

                                               Capture

                                               Buﬀer 2


     If capture buffering is enabled, on subsequent capture events the new captured value is loaded into the
     UTIMERn_CAPTURE_A register (example for channel event input A), and the previous value is loaded into
     UTIMERn_CAPTURE_A_BUF1, and the previous value of UTIMERn_CAPTURE_A_BUF1 is loaded into
     UTIMERn_CAPTURE_A_BUF2.
     A fixed buffering is used when the counter is programmed as a sawtooth or triangle one shot mode. To
     program the holding register, force a value from UTIMERn_COMPARE_A_BUF2 (example for channel input A)
     to the holding register by writing the UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL[FORCE_COMPARE_BUF_OP] = 0x1. At counter
     overflow/underflow (depending the programming) value of buffer 1 is loaded into the UTIMERn_COMPARE_
     A, and value of buffer 2—into the holding register. At counter compare, value of buffer 2 is loaded into a
     holding register, and the holding register—into the UTIMERn_COMPARE_A.
     Figure 13-13 presents a simplified diagram of the fixed buffering for input channel A.

 13.2.4.5 UTIMER Modules Used as QEC
     QEC channel [12-15] are used to implement a quadrature encoder interface. Quadrature encoders are used
     for high-accuracy rotor position sensing in electrical motors, or for digital potentiometers. The two input
     signals on channel input A and B from a quadrature encoder sensor are sampled on the rising, falling or both
     edges of the clock. The counting direction is adjusted accordingly depending the relative phase-shift between
     the two input signals. This way the timer counter directly holds the angular position of the motor or of the
     potentiometer.
     In addition to the two channel event inputs A and B (used to control incrementation/decrementation of the
     timer counter), the quadrature encoders have a third, zero signal, which occurs once per revolution and is
     used for zero point calibration. This means that whenever zero pulse is detected, the timer counter can be
     programmed to be reset.
     Figure 13-14 shows the counting sequence in QEC mode with input signals being sampled on both clock
     edges.

 13.2.5 UTIMER Programming Guide
     The following steps should be performed to set up the channel:
      1. Enable the timer counter by UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL = 0x1.
      2. Enable start, stop, and clear of the channel by writing the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START, UTIMER_GLB_
         CNTR_STOP, and UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR global registers.
      3. Turn off the interrupt masks (optional) through the UTIMERn_CHAN_INTERRUPT_MASK register.
      4. Turn off the channel output enable (optional) through the UTIMER_GLB_DRIVER_OEN register.
      5. Turn on the channel clock enable through the UTIMER_GLB_CLOCK_ENABLE register.


                                                       NOTE

       The programming sequences in this section should be used as example setups only. The sequences
       consist of control registers that must be set to enable/disable operation and other example register
       values that could get any value from 0x0000_0000 to 0xFFFF_FFFF, as desired.


 13.2.5.1 Example Setup for Up Timer
     To set up the up timer the following sample programming sequence could be used:
      1. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 250. This is the maximum value at which the timer
         counter resets.
      2. Enable timer counter with counter direction up and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x1.
      3. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                       474
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


      2. After some time stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the
         UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
      3. Clear the associated timer counter by writing 1 in the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR[CHANNEL_NUM] bit
         field.
      4. Check channel status in case there is an overflow, timer counter is upward, and both drivers A and B are
         0's, by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_STATUS = 0x4000_8040. A check only for an overflow could be
         validated also by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_INTERRUPT[OVER_FLOW] bit = 0x80. An overflow for an
         up counter sawtooth is when timer counter reaches the pointer value.

 13.2.5.2 Example Setup for Down Timer
     To set up the down timer the following sample programming sequence could be used:
      1. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 180. When a down counter sawtooth reaches 0 it goes to
         this value.
      2. Enable timer counter with counter direction down and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x101.
      3. Initialize the timer counter to 180 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0xB4.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      2. After some time stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the
         UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
      3. Clear the associated timer counter by writing 1 in the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR[CHANNEL_NUM] bit
         field.
      4. Check channel status in case there is an underflow, counter is downward, and both drivers A and B are
         0's, by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_STATUS = 0x4000_0080. A check only for an underflow could be
         validated also by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_INTERRUPT[UNDER_FLOW] bit = 0x40. An underflow for a
         down counter sawtooth is when timer counter reaches 0.

 13.2.5.3 Example Setup for Triangle Wave Timer
     To set up a triangle wave timer the following sample programming sequence could be used:
      1. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 180. In a triangle wave counter this is the maximum
         value the timer counter can reach.
      2. Enable timer counter and a triangle wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL = 0x11.
      3. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      2. After some time stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the
         UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
      3. Clear the associated timer counter by writing 1 in the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR[CHANNEL_NUM] bit
         field.
      4. Check channel status through the UTIMERn_CHAN_STATUS register in case there is a crest, a trough, or
         drivers A and B are both 0's. A check only for an overflow and underflow could be validated also by
         reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_INTERRUPT = 0xC0. A crest for a triangle wave counter is when timer
         counter reaches the pointer value. A trough for a triangle wave counter is when timer counter reaches 0.

 13.2.5.4 Example Setup for Triangle Wave Timer with Buffering
     There is a buffer operation at trough where pointer value updates at trough. Triangle wave timer buffering
     can also be set up with buffer operation at overflow or underflow. To select buffering type (normal or one
     shot), write in the UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL[CNTR_TYPE] bit field.
     To set up a triangle wave timer buffering the following sample programming sequence could be used:
      1. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 1000. This is the maximum value of the timer counter.
      2. Enable triangle counter with counter direction up at start and a triangle wave by writing the UTIMERn_
         CNTR_CTRL = 0x10001.
      3. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
      4. Set value of buffer 1 to 500 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR_BUF1 = 0x1FC.
      5. Set value of buffer 2 to 250 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR_BUF2 = 0xFA.
      6. Set double buffer operation for triangle wave by writing the UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL = 0x20_0002.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                         476
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


      2. After some time write a new value to buffer 2, that is 750, by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR_BUF2 =
         0x2EE.
      3. After some time stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the
         UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
      4. Clear the associated timer counter by writing 1 in the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR[CHANNEL_NUM] bit
         field.
      5. Check channel status for overflow and underflow, validating them by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_

 13.2.5.5 Example Setup for Up/Down Counter via Triggering
     To set up an up/down counter via triggering the following sample programming sequence could be used:
      1. Enable timer counter by writing UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL = 0x1.
      2. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
      3. Set rising trigger 0 to count up by writing the UTIMERn_UP_0_SRC = 0x1.
      4. Set falling trigger 1 to count down by writing the UTIMERn_DOWN_0_SRC = 0x8.
      5. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 1000.
      6. Disable buffer operation by writing UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL = 0x0.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Exercise the triggers and read the timer counter to see changes.
      2. Clear the associated timer counter by writing 1 in the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR[CHANNEL_NUM] bit
         field.
      3. Check channel status for overflow and underflow, validating them by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_
         INTERRUPT = 0xC0.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                                     477
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


                                                       NOTE

       When incrementing/decrementing the counter via triggers or channel events, a trigger or a channel
       event programmed to clear the counter has no effect. As a workaround, rather than programming the
       UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL register to 0x0000_0001, program it to 0x0000_0011 (triangle mode enabled).
       With this value, the programmed triggers or channel events will clear the counter properly, since the
       explicit incrementing/decrementing of the counter does not allow a classic triangle behavior (that is,
       automatically going back down after the peak). In addition, the UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR value should be
       set high enough such that it would not be reached, and the counter would not reverse direction.


 13.2.5.6 Example Setup for Down Counter with Capture at Triggers
     To set up a down counter with capture operation at triggers the following sample programming sequence
     could be used:
      1. Enable timer counter with counter direction down and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x101.
      2. Initialize the timer counter to 2000 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x7D0.
      3. Set up the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 0x7D0.
      4. Set timer counter value is captured A and the capture event had occurred due to a Trigger 2 rising
         (UTIMERn_TRIG_CAPTURE_SRC_A_0 = 0x10).
      5. Set timer counter value is captured B and the capture event had occurred due to a Trigger 3 falling
         (UTIMERn_TRIG_CAPTURE_SRC_B_0 = 0x80).
      6. Enable double buffer operation in capture by writing the UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL = 0xA_0001.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      2. Exercise the appropriate triggers to rise and fall.
      3. After some time stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the
         UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
      4. Clear the associated timer counter by writing 1 in the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_CLEAR[CHANNEL_NUM] bit
         field.
      5. Read the UTIMERn_CAPTURE_A register. Read also the UTIMERn_CAPTURE_A_BUF1 and UTIMERn_
         CAPTURE_A_BUF2 register.
      6. Read the UTIMERn_CAPTURE_B register. Read also the UTIMERn_CAPTURE_B_BUF1 and UTIMERn_
         CAPTURE_B_BUF2 register.
      7. Check channel status for an underflow, and capture A and B had occurred due to a trigger source, by
         reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_STATUS = 0x43.

 13.2.5.7 Example Setup for Up Counter with Compare to Drive Outputs
     To set up an up counter with compare operation to drive outputs the following sample programming
     sequence could be used:
      1. Remove the interrupt masks by writing the UTIMERn_CHANNEL_INTERRUPT_MASK = 0x0.
      2. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 1000. This is the maximum value of the up counter.
      3. Enable timer counter with counter direction up and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x1.
      4. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                      478
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


      5. Write the compare value UTIMERn_COMPARE_A = 0x40.
      6. Initialize driver A to 0, driver value to toggle at compare match and at cycle end by writing the
         UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_A = 0x090F.
      7. Enable double buffering in compare by writing the UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL = 0x500_0004.
      8. Compare on driver A, buffer 1 compare value is UTIMERn_COMPARE_A_BUF1 = 300.
      9. Compare on driver A, buffer 2 compare value is UTIMERn_COMPARE_A_BUF2 = 500.
     To control the timer counter:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      2. Delay for some time looking for output drivers toggling as the timer counter advances.
      3. Stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_
         STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
     To continue controlling the compare block:
      1. Initialize driver A to 1, driver value to retain at compare match and to toggle at cycle end by writing the
         UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_A = 0x091C.
      2. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      3. Delay for some time looking for output drivers toggling as the timer counter advances.
      4. Stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 1 to the respective bits of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_
         STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.
     Continue with other programming options to see output drivers changing:
       n Initialize driver A to 1, driver value to retain at compare match and at cycle end by writing the UTIMERn_
         COMPARE_CTRL_A = 0x0910.
       n Initialize driver A to 1, driver value to 0 at compare match, 1 at cycle end and 1 when counting stops by
         writing the UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_A = 0x0959.
     To program driver B perform the same procedures with the corresponding registers for B:
       n UTIMERn_COMPARE_B;
       n UTIMERn_COMPARE_CTRL_B;
       n UTIMERn_COMPARE_B_BUF1;
       n UTIMERn_COMPARE_B_BUF2;
       n control bits for driver B in UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL register.

     Figure 13-18 shows the diagram of an up counter with compare functionality to drive outputs and sawtooth
     wave.

 13.2.5.8 Example Setup for Triangle Counter with Dead-Time
     To set up a triangle counter with compare operation to variable outputs the following steps should be
     performed:
      1. Disable buffering feature by writing UTIMERn_BUF_OP_CTRL = 0x0.
      2. Enable dead-time and buffering in dead-time by writing UTIMERn_DEAD_TIME_CTRL = 0x3.
      3. Set dead-time in counter direction up by writing UTIMERn_DT_UP = 48.
      4. Transfer this buffer value to UTIMERn_DT_UP register at trough by writing UTIMERn_DT_UP_BUF1 = 49.
      5. Set dead-time in counter direction down by writing UTIMERn_DT_DOWN = 50.
      6. Transfer this buffer value to UTIMERn_DT_DOWN register at trough by writing UTIMERn_DT_DOWN_
         BUF1 = 51.
     To configure the timer counter:
      1. Enable timer counter with counter direction up and a triangle wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL
         = 0x11.
      2. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
      3. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 256.
     To configure the compare registers:
      1. Set for driver A—driver value to toggle at compare match and driver out by writing the UTIMERn_
         COMPARE_CTRL_A = 0x0903.
      2. Initialize driver B to 1, driver value to toggle at compare match and driver out by writing the UTIMERn_
         COMPARE_CTRL_B = 0x0903.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                       481
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                                                         E7 Series


      3. Compare on driver A, compare value is UTIMERn_COMPARE_A = 192.
      4. Compare on driver B, compare value is UTIMERn_COMPARE_B = 512.
      5. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      6. Exercise the appropriate triggers and read the timer counter value through UTIMERn_CNTR register to
         see changes.
      7. After some time stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 0 to the respective bits of the
         UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.

     To configure the timer counter:
      1. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 500.
      2. Enable timer counter with counter direction up and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x1.
      3. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
     The programmatic source enables should be guaranteed turned off. To do this configure the following
     registers:
      1. Turn off the channel timer counter through UTIMERn_START_1_SRC[PGM_EN] = 0x0.
      2. Stop the channel timer counter through UTIMERn_STOP_1_SRC[PGM_EN] = 0x0.
      3. Clear the channel timer counter through UTIMERn_CLEAR_1_SRC[PGM_EN] = 0x0.
     To configure timer counter starts/stops via triggers:


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                                       Alif Semiconductor
                                                                  483
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


      1. Set rising edge of trigger 0 to cause the timer counter to start by writing the UTIMERn_START_0_SRC =
         0x3.
      2. Set falling edge of trigger 0 to cause the timer counter to stop by writing the UTIMERn_STOP_0_SRC =
         0x2.
      3. Drive channel input A rising while channel input B = 0 to cause the timer counter to clear by writing the
         UTIMERn_CLEAR_1_SRC = 0x1.
      4. Write the compare value UTIMERn_COMPARE_A = 0x40.
     To configure timer counter starts/stops via input driver A and B events:
      1. Drive rising and falling edges of trigger 0 to see timer counter starting and stopping. Also, drive the input
         driver A and B events to cause starting and stopping.
     Configure timer counter to increment and decrement via events:
      1. Turn off timer counter control and enable timer counter by writing UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL[CNTR_EN] =
         0x0000_0001.
      2. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 250.
      3. Drive channel input A rising while channel input B = 0 to start the timer counter to increment through
         UTIMERn_UP_1_SRC = 0x0001.
      4. Drive global events input 0 to decrement by writing the UTIMERn_DOWN_0_SRC = 0x0001.
      5. Set driver value to retain at compare match; look for a compare match by writing the UTIMERn_
         COMPARE_A = 0x1800.
     Toggle global trigger input to decrement timer counter, toggle input driver A and B to increment timer
     counter.
     Compare can still be done in increment and decrement mode, and can generate interrupts or output signals.

 13.2.5.10 Changing Count Direction
     To configure the timer counter:
      1. Enable global programmatic start by writing the UTIMERn_START_1_SRC = 0x8000_0000.
      2. Enable global programmatic stop by writing the UTIMERn_STOP_1_SRC = 0x8000_0000.
      3. Enable global programmatic clear by writing the UTIMERn_CLEAR_1_SRC = 0x8000_0000.
      4. Set the pointer value to UTIMERn_CNTR_PTR = 250.
      5. Enable timer counter with counter direction up and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x1.
      6. Initialize the timer counter to 0 by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR = 0x0.
     Start the timer counter, reprogramming counter direction while counter is operational causes direction
     change at overflow or underflow time depending upon current direction. To configure this follow the
     procedure:
      1. Write 1 to the respective bit of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_START[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field depending of
         the desired channel timer counter to run.
      2. After some time, enable timer counter with counter direction down and a sawtooth wave by writing the
         UTIMERn_CNTR_CTRL = 0x103.
      3. Wait for some time before changing.
      4. Enable timer counter with counter direction up and a sawtooth wave by writing the UTIMERn_CNTR_
         CTRL = 0x3.
      5. Wait for some time before changing.
      6. Stop the associated channel timer counter by writing 0 to the respective bits of the UTIMER_GLB_CNTR_
         STOP[CHANNEL_NUM] bit field.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        484
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                                                  E7 Series


      7. Check channel status for overflow and underflow, validating them by reading the UTIMERn_CHAN_
         INTERRUPT = 0xC0.

 13.3 Real-Time Subsystem Watchdog Timer (WDT_RTSS)

 13.3.1 WDT_RTSS Overview
     The Real-Time Subsystem Watchdog Timer module, hereinafter referred to as WDT_RTSS, is a timer based on
     a 32-bit down-counter. The basic function of the WDT_RTSS is to count for a fixed period, during which it
     expects to be serviced by the system, indicating normal operation. The WDT_RTSS provides a mechanism to
     detect errant system behavior and recover from an unknown state by causing non-maskable interrupt of the
     system if the count period elapses without intervention.
     The device includes up to two WDT_RTSS modules:
       n   WDT_HP: Dedicated to the Arm Cortex-M55 High-Performance (M55-HP) processor
       n   WDT_HE: Dedicated to the Arm Cortex-M55 High-Efficiency (M55-HE) processor
     The WDT_RTSS module supports the following main features:
       n 32-bit down-counter
       n Counter decrements by one on each positive watchdog clock edge
       n Configurable NMI generation upon watch period expiration



                                                      NOTE

       Chip-level reset associated with the NMI timeout event must be implemented within the WDT_RTSS
       NMI interrupt handler routine firmware.


     Figure 13-26 provides a high-level overview of the WDT_RTSS implementation in the device.

 13.3.3 WDT_RTSS Functional Description
     Figure 13-28 shows the operation flow of the WDT_RTSS.
                                       Figure 13-28 WDT_RTSS Operation Flow Diagram

                                 Counts down
                                 without
   Watchdog is programmed        re-program
        by wri�ng the                               Counter                 WDT_WDOGCONTROL               Yes     WDT_IRQ is
                                                                                                                                     WDT_RTSS-003
     WDT_WDOGLOAD                                 reaches zero                [INTEN] bit = 1?                     asserted




     The WDT_RTSS module is based on a 32-bit down-counter that is initialized from the WDT_WDOGLOAD
     register. The counter decrements by one on each positive edge of the WDOGCLK clock signal. The value
     programmed in the WDT_WDOGLOAD register defines the so-called watch period.
     When the counter reaches 0, the counter is stopped and the WDT_RTSS module generates interrupt request
     (WDT_IRQ) to the processor system it is implemented in. The interrupt generation is enabled together with
     the counter via the WDT_WDOGCONTROL[INTEN] register bit.
     The interrupt signal is typically used to alert the processor system. The system can attempt to take corrective
     action that includes refreshing the watchdog within the next watch period by clearing the interrupt through
     the WDT_WDOGINTCLR register. If the refresh is successful, the system returns to the previous normal
     operation and the watch period is refreshed to the start.
     The WDT_RTSS also supports a feature to prevent rogue software from disabling the watchdog functionality.
     This is achieved by writing a value of 0x1ACC_E551 to the WDT_WDOGLOCK register in order to enable the
     write access to all other registers. Writing any other value in the WDT_WDOGLOCK register disables write
     accesses.

 13.4 Application Subsystem Watchdog Timer (WDT_APSS)

 13.4.1 WDT_APSS Overview
     The Application Subsystem Watchdog Timer, hereinafter referred to as WDT_APSS, is based on a 64-bit
     compare value and comparator. The WDT_APSS uses the generic timer system counter as the time base
     against which the decision to trigger an interrupt is made. The compare value can either be loaded directly or
     indirectly on an explicit refresh or timeout refresh.
     The device includes up to two WDT_APSS modules:
       n WDT_AP is the non-secure timer in the APSS
       n WDT_AP_S is the secure timer in the APSS

     The WDT_APSS module supports the following main features:
       n 64-bit comparator
       n Counter decrements by one on each generic timer system counter clock
       n Configurable NMI generation upon watch period expiration:
         l WDT_AP provides two interrupts routed to the A32 GIC

         l WDT_AP_S provides one NMI routed to the A32 GIC and a second interrupt routed to the Secure

           Enclave
       n Configurable CPU reset upon watch period expiration

     Figure 13-29 provides a high-level overview of the WDT_APSS implementation in the device.

 13.4.3 WDT_APSS Functional Description

 13.4.3.1 WDT_APSS Introduction
     The basic function of the WDT_APSS is to count for a fixed period of time, during which it expects to be
     refreshed by the system indicating normal operation. If a refresh occurs within the watch period, the period
     is refreshed to the start. If the refresh does not occur, the watch period expires, then an initial interrupt is
     raised and a second watch period begins.
     The initial interrupt alerts the system. The system can attempt to take corrective action that includes
     refreshing the watchdog within the second watch period. If the refresh is successful, the system returns to
     the previous normal operation. If it fails, then the second watch period expires and a second interrupt is
     generated. The second interrupt can be fed to a higher-privileged software to take any necessary executive
     actions.
     The WDT_APSS module uses the generic timer system counter as the timebase against which the decision to
     trigger an interrupt is made.


                                                      CAUTION
       The WDT_APSS must be disabled when the system counter is being updated, or the results may have
       unpredictable behaviour.


     The WDT_APSS module is based on a 64-bit compare value and comparator. The compare value can either be
     loaded directly (which causes watchdog explicit refresh) or indirectly on a timeout refresh.
     The 64-bit compare value is loaded in the WDT_WCV register. In addition, a 48-bit zero-extended offset value
     should be loaded in the WDT_WOR register.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        537
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                             E7 Series


     When the input generic timer system count value becomes greater than the compare value, the first watch
     period expires. This triggers a timeout refresh of the WDT_APSS and the following initial interrupt is
     generated depending on the WDT_APSS module in use:
       n     WDT_AP_IRQ0 interrupt from the WDT_AP
       n     WDT_AP_S_IRQ0 interrupt from the WDT_AP_S
     Upon this timeout refresh, the compare value in the WDT_WCV register is loaded with the sum of the WDT_
     WOR register value and the current timer system count value. A new comparison and new watch period
     begins.
     If the second watch period also expires and timeout refresh occurs again, then the current compare value is
     retained in the WDT_WCV register and the WDT_AP generates the WDT_AP_IRQ1 interrupt, while the WDT_
     AP_S asserts an interrupt to the Secure Enclave. This way the compare value records the time that these
     interrupts are asserted.
     The interrupt signals are not cleared in the case of a timeout refresh.
     An explicit refresh occurs, if a successful write in one of the WDT_WRR, WDT_WOR or WDT_WCS registers is
     performed prior to the generic timer system count value exceeding the compare value in WDT_WCV register.
     In the case of an explicit refresh, the interrupt signals are de-asserted. The compare value is then loaded with
     the sum of the zero-extended WDT_WOR register and the current timer system count value, and a new
     comparison begins.
     The interrupt signals are also de-asserted when the WDT_APSS is disabled either on a cold reset or through
     the WDT_WCS[WATCHDOG_ENABLE_BIT] register bit. The status of the interrupts can be read in the WDT_
     WCS [WATCHDOG_SIGNAL_STATUS_BITS] bit field.

 13.4.4 WDT_APSS Registers Guide
     This section describes the two WDT_APSS register frames. One is for the refresh register, called Refresh
     Frame, and the other containing the status and setup registers, called Control Frame.

 13.5 Low-Power Real-Time Counter (LPRTC)

 13.5.1 LPRTC Overview
     The Low-Power Real-Time Counter (LPRTC) module is a configurable high-range binary counter, which can
     generate an interrupt on a user-specified interval.
     The device includes one LPRTC module located in the PD-0 power domain, allowing it to run even when the
     device is in the lowest power state and power is present on VDD_BATT.
     The LPRTC module supports the following main features:
       n 32.768 kHz typical reference clock
       n 32-bit incrementing counter
       n 16-bit programmable prescaler
       n Interrupt generation upon programmed count match
       n Counter wrap mode
       n The LPRTC interrupt can be used as a wake-up source from STANDBY and STOP low-power modes



                                                      NOTE

       All Low Power peripherals are single-master accessible, including LPRTC. Ensure that application
       software manages access to these LP peripherals such that no more than one bus master (CPU or
       DMA) attempts access at a time, using semaphores or similar techniques.


     The LPRTC module can be utilized for the following use cases:
       n Real-time clock—to keep track of the current time
       n Long-term exact chronometer—to keep track of time from now up to 136 years in the future (when
         clocked with a 1 Hz clock signal)
       n Alarm function—to generate an interrupt after a programmed number of cycles
       n Long time base counter—when clocked with a kHz range clock signal from either LFXO or LFRC

     Figure 13-31 provides a high-level overview of the LPRTC implementation in the device.

 13.5.3.1 LPRTC Introduction
     Figure 13-33 presents a simplified diagram of the LPRTC main internal blocks and connections.

 13.5.3.2 LPRTC Clocks
     The LPRTC uses two clocks:
       n   LPRTC_CLK: Counter clock
       n   PCLK: APB bus clock; free-running

 13.5.3.3 LPRTC Reset Condition
     The LPRTC is reset only upon applying power (VDD_BATT or VDD_MAIN) to the device.


                                                                NOTE

       Regular device resets do not affect the LPRTC.


     After a reset, counters and all configuration registers return to their default states, such as all zeros. Interrupt
     generation is disabled at reset. If the LPRTC counter is not disabled, the counter increments as soon as the
     reset is removed.
     After a reset and before the interrupt enable is set prior to using the LPRTC, following shall be programmed:
       n The counter load value in LPRTC_CLR register
       n The counter match value in LPRTC_CMR register
       n The counter enable bit: LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_EN]


 13.5.3.4 LPRTC Up Counter
     The LPRTC has a programmable, 32-bit binary up counter. The up counter increments on successive positive
     edges of the input counter clock (LPRTC_CLK). When the LPRTC_CLR register is programmed and counting is
     enabled, the counter is loaded with a start value that allows it to increment. When the counter reaches its
     maximum value (all bits are high), it wraps to 0 and then continues incrementing.
     The sequence of events for the counter is:

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                 Alif Semiconductor
                                                               544
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                    www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                        E7 Series


      1. User programs a new load value by writing to the LPRTC_CLR register.
      2. LPRTC_CLR register value is transferred into the counter clock domain.
      3. Transferred value is loaded into the counter.
      4. Counter increments from the loaded value on the positive edge of the counter clock.
     The LPRTC counter can be enabled or disabled through the LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_EN] register bit. The counter
     value can be read at any time through the LPRTC_CCVR register and is always the latest safe counter value.
     The counter may increment while the count is read, but the value that is read back is coherent.


                                                                NOTE

       Coherency is where bits within a register are logically connected. For instance, part of a register is
       read at time 1 and another part is read at time 2. Being coherent means that the part read at time 2 is
       at the same value it was when the register was read at time 1. Coherency enables a value to be read
       that is an accurate reflection of the state of the counter.


     LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_WEN] register bit is implemented to enable the counter to wrap when a match occurs,
     instead of waiting until the maximum count is reached. The counter wraps to 0 in the forced wrap mode.

 13.5.3.5 LPRTC Prescaler Counter
     The LPRTC implements a 16-bit prescaler counter in front of the up counter to allow its increment with rates
     lower than the LPRTC_CLK rate, as shown in Figure 13-34.
                                          Figure 13-34 LPRTC Counter with Prescaler(1)
                                                            LPRTC Counter Logic
          LPRTC_CLK                                                                  LPRTC_CLK
                         16-bit LPRTC                                                                         LPRTC_CNT
               Reset      Prescaler                                                      Reset 32-bit LPRTC
                                                                                               Up Counter
                           Counter                             Counter
                                        LPRTC_PSCLR_CNT        Prescaler    LPRTC_PSCLR_CNT_EN
   LPRTC_PSCLR_EN                                               Value - 1

                                                                                                              RTC-005




     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The prescaler can be enabled or disabled through the LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_PSCLR_EN] register bit. When the
     prescaler is enabled, it runs on the LPRTC_CLK and provides the prescaler count. The prescaler generates an
     enable pulse when the counter counts LPRTC_CPSR[COUNTER_PRESCALER_VALUE] - 1. This enable signal is
     used as the clock enable to the LPRTC counter and allows it to be updated at a rate less than the LPRTC_CLK
     rate.
     For instance, if the LPRTC is running on a 32.768 kHz clock, a 1 Hz clock can be generated from the counter by
     enabling the prescaler and by setting the prescaler value to 32768. Figure 13-35 illustrates this use case.

     The following points should be considered while configuring the prescaler:
       n When LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_PSCLR_EN] bit = 0x0 (disabled prescaler):
           lThe prescaler is reset to zero. This helps in aligning the prescaler with the LPRTC counter, when the
            LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_PSCLR_EN] bit is set again.
         l The LPRTC counter runs in normal mode with LPRTC_CLK without the prescaler logic.

       n The load option is not available for the prescaler.
       n When appropriate, both LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_EN] and LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_PSCLR_EN] bits must be set high
         in a single write. This ensures that both the LPRTC counter and the prescaler are in synchronization.
       n The LPRTC_CPSR register should be programmed with the appropriate value before enabling the LPRTC_
         CCR[LPRTC_PSCLR_EN] bit.
       n Re-programming the LPRTC_CPSR register during a normal prescaler operation (that is, when LPRTC_CCR
         [LPRTC_PSCLR_EN] = 0x1) is not recommended as this may lead to the following scenarios:
         l If the programmed LPRTC_CPSR register value is less than or equal to the LPRTC_CPCVR register value,

            the prescaler wraps immediately to zero and the LPRTC counter is incremented.
         l If the programmed LPRTC_CPSR register value is greater than the LPRTC_CPCVR register value, the

            prescaler increments up to the prescaler value and then wraps to zero and in turn increments the
            LPRTC counter (normal counter and prescaler behavior as defined previously).

 13.5.3.6 LPRTC Match Register and Interrupt Generation
     The LPRTC module has a single interrupt request line: LPRTC_IRQ.
     The LPRTC_CMR match register can be programmed and is compared to the internal counter. An interrupt is
     generated when the match register and the internal counter are equal, provided that interrupt generation is
     enabled by setting LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_IEN] = 0x1. This interrupt can be then masked or unmasked through
     the LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_MASK] register bit, which provides the user control of sending interrupts externally.
     The match register can be read at any time.
     The counter value is transferred between clock domains each time it changes. When the transferred counter
     value matches LPRTC_CMR register value, the rising edge of the match causes an interrupt to be generated in
     the PCLK domain. The interrupt has an active-high polarity and is kept active until it is cleared by reading the
     LPRTC_EOI[LPRTC_EOI] bit or until the counter is disabled.
     The interrupt status bit is not polarity sensitive. Interrupt is active when the status is read as 1; otherwise, it
     is inactive. The interrupt status can be read at any time:
       n Masked interrupt status: LPRTC_STAT register
       n Raw interrupt status: LPRTC_RSTAT register



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                                546
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                         E7 Series


     Note that if the LPRTC_RSTAT register indicates that a pending interrupt exists because a masked interrupt
     has been generated (LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_MASK] = 0x1), then caution should be taken when programming
     LPRTC_CCR register. That is, if both the LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_MASK] and LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_EN] bits are set to
     0, then the interrupt asserts for one clock period. To avoid this scenario, the following two-step process can
     be used:
      1. Set LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_EN] = 0 to clear the interrupt.
      2. Set LPRTC_CCR[LPRTC_MASK] = 0 to unmask any future interrupts.
      Figure 13-36 shows the LPRTC interrupt generation diagram.

 13.6 System Timers

 13.6.1 System Timers Overview
     The system timer is composed of one counter and several timer modules. The counter provides count value
     to the timer modules, which generate interrupts when a certain timer condition is met.
     The device includes two system timers – REFCLK_TMR and S32KCLK_TMR. The REFCLK_TMR system timer is
     clocked by SYST_REFCLK and has four timer modules – REFCLK_CNT_BASE[0-3]. The S32KCLK_TMR system
     timer is clocked by S32K_CLK and has two timer modules – S32KCLK_CNT_BASE[0-1].
     Each system timer supports the following main features:
       n Provides a uniform view of system time
       n Provides 64-bit up counters and 32-bit down counters
       n Has 64-bit wide counter and compare registers
       n Supports virtual time by offsetting the real time via dedicated registers
       n Can be incremented by larger amounts at a lower frequency (for example, increment by 4 at 4 times
         lower frequency)
       n Has individual interrupt output for each timer module (CNT_BASEn)

     Figure 13-37 provides a high-level overview of the system timers implementation in the device.

 13.6.3 System Timers Functional Description

 13.6.3.1 Components of the System Timer
     The components of the system timer are:
       n Counter module – This module controls the counter. It has two register blocks – control (CNT_
         CONTROL) and status (CNT_READ).
       n Timer control module – This module provides control and status registers for each timer. It has a single
         register block – CNT_CTL.
       n Timers – Each of these n modules provides a privileged view of timer n. Each module has a single
         register block – CNT_BASEn.

 13.6.3.2 Counter Module (CNT_CONTROL and CNT_READ)
     The counter module controls the counter via the registers in the CNT_CONTROL block.
     The CNTCR[EN] bit enables or disables the counter. When the CNTCR[EN] bit is set to 0x1, counter is enabled.
     Otherwise, it is disabled. The CNTCR[HDBG] bit enables or disables the halt-on-debug feature. When the
     CNTCR[HDBG] bit is set to 0x1 and the halt-on-debug is activated, the counter halts. Otherwise, it ignores the
     halt-on-debug request. The CNTSR[DBGH] bit indicates whether the counter is halted because of a halt-on-
     debug request.
     The CNTCR[FCREQ] field specifies the index of the CNTFIDn register that holds the counter new frequency.
     Changing the value of CNTCR[FCREQ] requests a change to the counter update frequency. The CNTSR[FCACK]
     field indicates the current update frequency of the counter. When the frequency has changed, the CNTSR
     [FCACK] field is updated with the corresponding index of the CNTFIDn register to indicate the new frequency.
     The FCACK field can be polled to determine when a requested change to the update frequency has been
     made.
     The CNTCVL and CNTCVH registers hold the current counter value. The counter must be disabled before
     writing to these registers, otherwise the effect of the write operation is unpredictable.
     The CNTFID0 register defines the base frequency of the counter. This is the maximum frequency at which the
     counter updates. However, the counter can increment at a lower frequency than the base frequency, using a
     correspondingly larger increment. For example, it can increment by four at a quarter of the base frequency.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                      555
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


     When the counter operates at a lower frequency than the base frequency, the increment applied at each
     counter update is given by equation (13-1).
                                                                                                             (13-1)
     The CNTFIDn registers define an alternative frequency of the counter that must be an exact divisor of the
     base frequency. The last CNTFIDn register is a zero-word end marker. Its value is 0x0. The CNTFID0 and
     CNTFIDn registers specify the frequency in Hz.
     In addition, the CNT_READ block includes a read-only copy of the CNTCVL and CNTCVH registers.

 13.6.3.2.1 Frequency Change Accuracy
     To ensure that the frequency change does not affect the overall accuracy of the counter, it has the following
     behavior:
       n When changing from higher to lower frequency the counter:
         1. Continues running at the higher frequency until the count reaches an integer multiple of the required
            lower frequency.
         2. Switches operation at the lower frequency.
       n When changing from lower to higher frequency the counter:
         1. Waits until the end of the current lower-frequency cycle.
         2. Makes the increment required for operation at that lower frequency.
         3. Switches operation at the higher frequency.

 13.6.3.3 Timer Control Module (CNT_CTL)
     The CNT_CTL block provides control and status registers for each of the CNT_BASEn blocks.
     The CNTTIDR[FnFEL0] bits show if each timer (CNT_BASEn) has only privileged (FnFEL0 = 0x0) or both
     privileged and unprivileged (FnFEL0 = 0x1) views. The CNTTIDR[FnFVI] bits show if each timer (CNT_BASEn)
     has virtual capability (FnFVI = 0x1) or not, and the CNTTIDR[FnFI] bits show if CNT_BASEn is implemented
     (FnFI = 0x1) or not.
     The CNTNSAR[NSn] bits control if the registers from CNT_BASEn and registers CNTACRn, CNTVOFFn_LO, and
     CNTVOFFn_HI are also accessible by non-secure accesses (NSn = 0x1).
     The bits in the CNTACRn register control the accessibility of the following registers from CNT_BASEn:
       n CNTACRn[RWPT] controls CNTP_CVAL_LO, CNTP_CVAL_HI, CNTP_TVAL, and CNTP_CTL
       n CNTACRn[RWVT] controls CNTV_CVAL_LO, CNTV_CVAL_HI, CNTV_TVAL, and CNTV_CTL
       n CNTACRn[RVOFF] controls CNTVOFF_LO and CNTVOFF_HI
       n CNTACRn[RFRQ] controls RD_CNTFRQ
       n CNTACRn[RVCT] controls CNTVCT_LO and CNTVCT_HI
       n CNTACRn[RPCT] controls CNTPCT_LO and CNTPCT_HI

     The CNTNSAR register is accessible only by SE.
     The CNTVOFFn_LO and CNTVOFFn_HI registers hold the virtual offset for CNT_BASEn. This is the offset
     between real time and virtual time. In other words, these registers define the virtual offset between the
     physical count and the virtual count. The CNTVOFFn_LO and CNTVOFFn_HI registers also provide the read-
     write copy of the CNTVOFF_LO and CNTVOFF_HI registers for the corresponding CNT_BASEn as the
     CNTVOFF_LO and CNTVOFF_HI are read-only registers.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                      556
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                               E7 Series


 13.6.3.4 Timers (CNT_BASEn)
     Each CNT_BASEn register block provides its own set of memory-mapped counter, timer, and associated
     interrupt. Each timer is based around a 64-bit compare value (CNTP_CVAL_HI and CNTP_CVAL_LO) that
     provides a 64-bit unsigned up counter. Each timer also provides an alternative view of the compare value,
     called timer value (CNTP_TVAL), that appears to operate as a 32-bit down counter. Equation (13-2) shows the
     relation between these counters.
                                                                                                                     (13-2)
          Where:
          CVAL = (CNTP_CVAL_HI[31:0] to CNTP_CVAL_LO[31:0])
          PCT = (CNTPCT_HI[31:0] to CNTPCT_LO[31:0])
          TVAL = CNTP_TVAL
     If enabled (CNTP_CTL[ENABLE] = 0x1), each timer generates an interrupt when CNTP_CTL[ISTATUS] = 0x1 and
     CNTP_CTL[IMASK] = 0x0. CNTP_CTL[ISTATUS] = 0x1 indicates that the timer condition is met which means
     that (CNTPCT_HI[31:0] to CNTPCT_LO[31:0]) - (CNTP_CVAL_HI[31:0] to CNTP_CVAL_LO[31:0]) is greater than
     or equal to zero.

 13.6.3.5 Register Reset Values
     The CNTCR[FCREQ], CNTCR[EN], and CNTSR[FCACK] fields reset to 0x0. These reset values apply only on
     power-up or after reset. All other registers have a value that is unknown.

 13.6.4.3 CNT_CONTROL Registers Description

 13.6.4.3.1 CNTCR Register
           Offset           Access          Description
         0x0                                Counter Control Register
                             R/W
     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
   31-18 RESERVED                      R          0x0       Reserved
                                                            Frequency change request.
                                                            Specifies the index of the CNTFIDn register that holds the counter
    17-8      FCREQ                   R/W         0x0       new frequency. Changing the value of this field requests a change
                                                            to the counter update frequency. Any non-required most-
                                                            significant bits are read-only and reserved.
    7-3       RESERVED                 R          0x0       Reserved
                                                            Scale Enable.
                                                            This bit can only be changed when the counter is disabled (when
                                                            CNTCR[EN] = 0x0). If the value of CNTCR[SCEN] changes when
                                                            CNTCR[EN] = 0x1 then the counter value becomes unknown and
     2        SCEN                    R/W          0x-      remains unknown on future ticks of the clock.
                                                            0x0: Scaling disabled. The counter value is incremented by 0x1 for
                                                            each counter tick.
                                                            0x1: Scaling enabled. The counter value is incremented by CNTSCR
                                                            [SCALEVAL] for each counter tick.
                                                            Halt-on-debug.
                                                            Controls whether a halt-on-debug request halts the system
                                                            counter.
     1        HDBG                    R/W          0x-
                                                            0x0: The counter ignores the halt-on-debug request.
                                                            0x1: When the halt-on-debug request is activated the counter
                                                            halts.
                                                            Counter enable.
     0        EN                      R/W         0x0       0x0: System counter disabled
                                                            0x1: System counter enabled



 13.6.4.3.2 CNTSR Register
           Offset           Access          Description
         0x4                                Counter Status Register
                              R
     Base address

AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                      www.alifsemi.com

    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                            Frequency change acknowledge.
    31-8      FCACK                    R          0x0       Specifies the index of the CNTFIDn register that holds the counter
                                                            new frequency.
    7-2       RESERVED                 R          0x0       Reserved
                                                            Indicates whether the counter is halted because of a halt-on-
                                                            debug request.
     1        DBGH                     R           0x-
                                                            0x0: Counter is not halted.
                                                            0x1: Counter is halted.

                             R/W
     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                            Scale Value.
                                                            When counter scaling is enabled, this field is the amount added to
    31-0      SCALEVAL                R/W          0x-
                                                            the counter value for every counter tick. Counter tick is defined as
                                                            one period of the current operating frequency of the counter.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                              559
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                    E7 Series


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             This field is expressed as an unsigned fixed point number with an
                                                             8-bit integer value and a 24-bit fractional value. It can only be
                                                             changed when the counter is disabled (when CNTCR[EN] = 0x0). If
                                                             the value of this field changes when CNTCR[EN] = 0x1, then the
                                                             counter value becomes unknown and remains unknown on future
                                                             ticks of the clock.

     0        ENSYNC                  R/W         0x0

                                                            Note: This register is only available in the REFCLK_CNT_CONTROL

                                                            (CNTPCT_HI[31:0] to CNTPCT_LO[31:0]) - (CNTP_CVAL_HI[31:0] to
                                                            CNTP_CVAL_LO[31:0]) is greater than or equal to zero. This means
                                                            that CNTP_CVAL_HI and CNTP_CVAL_LO act like a 64-bit up
                                                            counter timer.
                                                            When the timer condition is met, the CNTP_CTL[ISTATUS] bit is set
                                                            to 0x1, and if CNTP_CTL[IMASK] = 0x0, an interrupt is generated.
                                                            When CNTP_CTL[ENABLE] = 0x0, the timer condition is not met,
                                                            but CNTPCT_HI and CNTPCT_LO continue to count.

 14 General-Purpose Input/Output Module

 14.1 GPIO Overview
     The General-Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) module provides means for driving and reading from digital I/O
     pins when they are not used by other peripheral (like UART, I2C, etc.). GPIO module can be used for tasks like
     lighting LEDs or reading the state of push-buttons, switches, etc. The GPIO module also offers switch contact
     debounce and interrupt capabilities.
     The device includes up to sixteen GPIO modules with support of up to 128 I/O pins in total. The I/O signals
     are distributed as follows:
       n   GPIO[0-14]: 8 I/O signals each
       n   LPGPIO: 8 I/O signals
     The I/O pins are typically powered by VDD_IO_1V8 with the exception of 8 I/O pins, which are powered by
     the VDD_IO_FLEX rail that can range from 1.8 V to 3.3 V.
     The GPIO modules are integrated in two power domains:
       n Power Domain PD-6: GPIO[0-14]
       n Power Domain PD-0 (AON): LPGPIO

     Each GPIO module supports the following main features:
       n Data register allows driving and reading each GPIO pin individually
       n Data Direction register selects pin direction – input or output
       n Debounce function driven by the 32-kHz clock for switch/push-button contacts debouncing
       n Individual interrupt generation for every pin of GPIO[0-14] and LPGPIO
       n Common (combined) interrupt generation for the pin events of LPGPIO
       n The LPGPIO interrupt can be used as a wake-up source from STANDBY and STOP low-power modes



                                                         NOTE

       All Low Power peripherals are single-master accessible, including LPGPIO. Ensure that application
       software manages access to these LP peripherals such that no more than one bus master (CPU or
       DMA) attempts access at a time, using semaphores or similar techniques.




                                                         NOTE

       For digital I/O buffer features, please refer to Section 8.5 Signal Multiplexing and I/O Buffer
       Configuration.

 14.4.2 GPIO Clocks
     The GPIO module uses three clocks:
       n PCLK: APB clock for the bus interface unit.
       n PCLK_INTR: APB clock that is used for detection of edge-sensitive interrupts and for synchronization of
         level-sensitive interrupts. It is synchronous to PCLK.
       n DBCLK: Debounce clock. Used to remove glitches from GPIO inputs.


 14.4.3 GPIO Interrupt Requests
     The GPIO can be programmed to accept external signals as interrupt sources on any of its pins, when
     configured as inputs. An interrupt can be selected to occur on either of the following events:
       n High level
       n Low level
       n Rising edge
       n Falling edge
       n Both edges

     The GPIO_INTTYPE_LEVEL, GPIO_INT_POLARITY, and GPIO_INT_BOTHEDGE registers control interrupt
     generation settings.
     The interrupts can be masked by programming the GPIO_INTMASK register. The interrupt status can be read
     before masking (so called raw status) and after masking.
     Either individual interrupts (GPIOn_IRQm) or a single combined interrupt (LPGPIO_COMB_IRQ) can be
     generated. See Section 14.2 GPIO Internal Connections for details. In order to mask the combined interrupt,
     all individual interrupts have to be masked. The single combined interrupt does not have its own mask bit.
     Whenever the GPIO is programmed for interrupts (via the GPIO_INTEN register), the data direction must be
     set to input (via the GPIO_SWPORTA_DDR register) and the GPIO_SWPORTA_CTL register must be set to
     Software mode for interrupts to be latched. If the GPIO_SWPORTA_DDR register is reprogrammed to output,
     or the GPIO_SWPORTA_CTL register is programmed to enable Hardware mode, then any pending interrupts
     are not lost. However, no new interrupts are generated.


                                                        NOTE

       The GPIO data direction is input by default after POR.


     Figure 14-7 illustrates how the interrupts are generated for one GPIO signal.

                                                                                                               GPIO-005

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The combined interrupt LPGPIO_COMB_IRQ is generated by OR logic that includes all bits of the LPGPIO
     interrupt bus. When only the combined interrupt request is used, then the GPIO_INTSTATUS register must be
     read in the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) to find the source of the interrupt. When the individual interrupts
     lines are connected directly to the interrupt controller, then the GPIO_INTSTATUS register does not have to
     be read by the ISR.
     For edge detected interrupts, the ISR can clear the interrupt by writing a 1 to the GPIO_PORTA_EOI register
     for the corresponding bit to disable the interrupt. This write also clears the interrupt status and raw status
     registers. It is recommended to clear the interrupt source prior to writing to the GPIO_PORTA_EOI register.
     Writing to the GPIO_PORTA_EOI register has no effect on level sensitive interrupts.
     If level sensitive interrupts cause the processor to interrupt, then the ISR can poll the GPIO_RAW_INTSTATUS
     register until the interrupt source disappears, or it can write to the GPIO_INTMASK register to mask the
     interrupt before exiting the ISR. If the ISR exits without masking or disabling the interrupt prior to exiting,
     then the level sensitive interrupt repeatedly requests an interrupt until the interrupt is cleared at the source.
     If the LPGPIO_COMB_IRQ is used and the interrupt service routine reads the GPIO_INTSTATUS register to
     find multiple pending interrupt requests, then it is up to the software to prioritize these pending interrupt
     requests. There are no restrictions on the number of edge detected interrupts that can be cleared
     simultaneously by writing multiple 1 to the GPIO_PORTA_EOI register.

     With level sensitive interrupts, there is a choice of whether they are synchronized to the interrupt clock
     PCLK_INTR or are entirely combinational. The selection is done by programming the GPIO_LS_SYNC register.
     When the GPIO_LS_SYNC[GPIO_LS_SYNC] bit is not set, there is no guarantee that the interrupt lines are
     synchronous to PCLK_INTR. A processor status register may need to be set to indicate asynchronous
     interrupts.
     When the GPIO_LS_SYNC[GPIO_LS_SYNC] bit is set, all level-sensitive interrupts are synchronized to the
     PCLK_INTR clock.

 14.4.4 GPIO Debounce Operation
     The external signal is debounced to remove any spurious glitches that are less than one period of the
     debouncing clock.
     Figure 14-11 shows a diagram of the debounce circuitry. The polarity of the input signal detection is
     controlled by the memory-mapped register, GPIO_INT_POLARITY. For a falling edge or active low sensitive
     input, the input is then inverted and the same debounce logic is used as for rising-edge or active-high level-
     sensitive interrupts.

     The signals must be active for a minimum of two cycles of the debounce clock to guarantee that they are
     registered. Any input pulse widths less than a debounce clock period are bounced. A pulse width between
     one and two debounce clock widths may or may not propagate, depending on its phase relationship to the
     debounce clock. If the input pulse spans two rising edges of the debounce clock, it is registered. If it spans
     only one rising edge, it is not registered.
     The PCLK and DBCLK signals are assumed to be asynchronous to each other.
                                                                NOTE

       The use of the debounce circuitry increases interrupt latency by two clock cycles of the debounce
       clock.

 14.4.5 GPIO Controlling External Pins
     The configuration of data direction for the GPIO signals is under software control. The direction of the device
     I/O pin is controlled by a write to the GPIO_SWPORTA_DDR register. When configured as an output, the data
     written to the GPIO_SWPORTA_DR register drives the output buffer of the corresponding I/O pin.

 14.4.6 GPIO Reading External Pins
     The data on the external GPIO signal is read from the GPIO_EXT_PORTA register. A read of this register
     provides either the data on the GPIO_EXT_PORTA[0-7] or the content of the GPIO_SWPORTA_DR register,
     depending on the value of GPIO_SWPORTA_DDR register:
       n Input—Reads the value of the I/O
       n Output—Reads the data register

     The GPIO_EXT_PORTA register is read-only, meaning that it cannot be written by software.
                                                                NOTE

       The maximum data rate that can be read back on consecutive reads from GPIO_EXT_PORTA[0-7] must
        be less than PCLK/2. Two PCLK cycles per read access is required due to the non-pipelined nature of
       the APB.

 15.1 Controller Area Network (CANFD)

 15.1.1 CANFD Overview
     The Controller Area Network (CANFD) module performs serial communication according to the CAN protocol.
     The CAN bus interface uses the basic CAN principle and meets all constraints of the CAN Specification 2.0B
     active. The CANFD module supports both classic CAN and CAN with Flexible Data-rate (FD) specifications.
     The device includes up to one CANFD module.
     The CANFD module supports the following main features:
       n CAN specifications:
           CAN 2.0B (up to 8 bytes payload, verified by Bosch reference model)
           l

         l CAN FD (up to 64 bytes payload, ISO 11898-1:2015 or non-ISO Bosch)

       n Free programmable data rates:
         l Data rates up to 10 Mbps

         l CAN FD rates are limited by the transceiver and the clock frequency of the CAN controller

       n Programmable baud rate prescaler (1 to 1/256)
       n One receive buffer and two transmit buffers—primary transmit buffer (PTB) and secondary transmit
         buffer (STB):
         l Buffer size: 640 words

         l Number of buffer slots: 16

       n 3× independent and programmable internal 29-bit acceptance filters
       n Extended features:
         l Single Shot Transmission mode (for PTB and/or for STB)

         l Listen-Only mode

         l Loop Back mode (internal and external)

         l Transceiver Standby mode

       n Extended status and error report:
         l Capturing of last occurred Kind Of Error (KOER) and arbitration lost position

         l Programmable Error Warning Limit

       n 32-bit synchronous Host controller interfaces
       n Configurable interrupt sources
       n Dual port memory block for frame buffer
       n CiA 603 32-bit timestamping
       n Compatible with AUTOSAR
       n Optimized for SAE J1939
