 15.1.4 CANFD Functional Description

 15.1.4.1 CANFD Block Diagram
     The CAN core is a serial communications controller that performs serial communication according to the CAN
     protocol. The CAN protocol uses a multi-master bus configuration for the transfer of frames (communication
     objects) between nodes of the CAN network and manages the error handling without any burden on the
     CPU. For more information about the CAN Protocol, refer to Section 15.1.4.2 CAN Protocol.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                            601
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                   E7 Series


     The CAN controller allows setting up economic and reliable links between various components (for
     example: different sensors—temperature, pressure, humidity, and so forth). The CPU accesses the CAN
     controller to control the transmission or reception of frames through the two wire CAN bus interface
     (TXD and RXD).
     Figure 15-4 presents a simplified diagram of the CANFD main internal blocks and connections.
                                                      Figure 15-4 CANFD Block Diagram




                                                                                                                          CAN Bus Transceiver
                                                                             Error                                 TXD
                                  Host Interface           Transceiver    Management      Bit
                                                              Logic          Logic      Timing                     RXD
                                                               (TL)                      Logic
                                                                            (EML)
                                Acceptance Filters                                       (BTL)                     STBY
                                     (ACF)
                                                           Recep�on        Interface


           Controller
                                                            Decoder       Management
                                  Receive Buﬀer                              Logic
    Host                             (RBUF)                  (RDEC)          (IML)

                              Secondary    Primary
                               Transmit    Transmit
                                Buﬀer       Buﬀer
                                 (STB)       (PTB)
                                      (TBUF)
                                                         CAN Controller
                        CAN Controller Wrapper                                                         CANFD-003




     The CAN Controller has the following basic blocks:
           n Host Interface
             The host interface includes control and status register bits. This includes the registers in Section 15.1.5
             CANFD Registers Guide except for the RBUF, TBUF and ACF registers.
           n Acceptance Filters (ACF)
             The ACF consists of the control logic for acceptance filtering and the filter memory blocks. For more
             information about the number of the acceptance filters, refer to Section 15.1.1 CANFD Overview.
           n Receive Buffer (RBUF)
             The RBUF contains the memory for the receive buffer. For more information about the number of the
             RBUF slots, refer to Section 15.1.1 CANFD Overview.
           n Transmit Buffer (TBUF)
             The TBUF consists of Primary Transmit Buffer (PTB) and Secondary Transmit Buffer (STB). The PTB has a
             higher priority than the STB. A PTB transmission suspends an STB transmission and is executed first. The
             CAN protocol rules require that an STB transmission that is written to the CAN bus must not be
             interrupted. Therefore, the PTB transmission starts afterwards (after the interframe space). For more
             information about the number of the TBUF slots, refer to Section 15.1.1 CANFD Overview.
           n Transceiver Logic (TL)
             The TL consists of the CAN protocol state machine. The TL controls all functions for the reception and
             transmission of frames:
             l Checking of received bits and transferring to the receive buffer

             l Generation of bits to transmit to the CAN bus (ID, RTR, IDE, DLC, Data, CRC, and so forth)

             l Arbitration

             l Stuff bit handling

             l Error handling

             l Generation of error and overload frames



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                                 602
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


       n Error Management Logic (EML)
         The EML consists of counters for receive and transmit errors. The counters are controlled depending on
         the corresponding type of errors (Bit Error, Stuff Error, Form Error, CRC Error, and Acknowledgment
         (ACK) Error).
       n Bit Timing Logic (BTL)
         The BTL monitors the CAN bus and synchronizes the internal actions to the bit stream on the bus. Hard
         synchronization is executed if a recessive-to-dominant bus line transition occurs at the beginning of a
         message. Re-synchronization takes place on further recessive-to-dominant transitions during the
         reception of messages.
         The timing registers (refer to Section 15.1.4.9 CAN Bit Time) control the time segments to compensate
         propagation delay times and phase shifts and define the sample point (SP).
         The BTL also includes a baud rate prescaler. The external system clock is divided by a programmed value.
         The resulting period is called Time Quanta (TQ).
       n Reception Decoder (RDEC)
         The RDEC stores and decodes the header bits of the received messages. This information is needed on-
         the-fly for the protocol handling and is later stored into the receive buffer.
       n Interface Management Logic (IML)
         The IML controls the behavior of the entire CAN controller depending on the commands (register
         settings). The IML generates the addresses for the message buffers and provides interrupts and status
         information to the host controller.

 15.1.4.2 CAN Protocol
     The CAN communication is organized in frames. Two types of frames exist—standard and extended frames.
     For CAN 2.0B the maximum data payload is up to 8 bytes while for CAN FD up to 64 bytes can be transmitted
     using one frame.
     All CAN nodes are equal in terms of bus access. There is not super-node because the CAN is a multi-master
     bus. The data addressing is done using message identifiers. In the CAN network, only one node has to
     transmit messages with a certain identifier. All nodes receive all messages and the node host controller has
     to decide if it was addressed by the appropriate message identifier.
     To reduce the load of the host controller, the CAN controller can use acceptance filters. These filters compare
     all received message identifiers to user-selectable bit patterns. Only if a message passes an acceptance filter,
     it is stored in the receive buffer and signaled to the host controller.
     The identifiers of the CAN frames are also used for bus arbitration. The CAN protocol machine stops
     transmission of a message with a low-priority identifier when a message with a higher priority identifier is
     transmitted by another CAN node. The CAN protocol machine automatically attempts to re-transmit the
     stopped message at the next possible transmit position.
     The CAN 2.0B specification defines data bit rates up to 1 Mbit/s. For the CAN FD specification, there is not
     fixed limitation. For CAN FD the standard defines a bit rate switching. If enabled, the transmission of the
     frame payload can be done at a higher speed while the frame headers are transmitted at a lower speed.

 15.1.4.3 Classic CAN 2.0B and CAN FD
     The CAN controller supports both classic CAN and CAN FD. CAN FD is a downward-compatible extension of
     the classic CAN 2.0B protocol. Every CAN FD node is able to receive and transmit classic CAN frames.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       603
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                           E7 Series


                                                                  NOTE

       CAN FD functionality can be enabled or disabled by using the CANFD_CTRL[FD_ENA] bit.


     The host controller firmware can select at run-time for every frame if the frame is transmitted as a classic
     CAN or CAN FD frame. This is done using the configuration bits in the transmit buffer. For received frames
     the status bits in the receive buffer signal if a received frame is a classic CAN or CAN FD frame.
     Table 15-6 presents the main differences between CAN 2.0B and CAN FD protocols.

     For CAN FD ISO frames, the stuff count is transmitted as a part of the CRC field. For CAN FD non-ISO frames,

     frames. Therefore, ISO and non-ISO frames are incompatible.
     The CAN protocol machine in the CAN controller automatically transmits and receives the frames and
     embeds the appropriate control and status bits. The host controller is required to select the desired frame
     type (IDE, RTR, FDF), chose the identifier, and set the data payload.

 15.1.4.3.1 CANFD Upward Compatibility
     The CAN controller supports protocol exception event with frame ignore.
     The CAN specification includes reserved bits (see Figure 15-5) for protocol extension. This has been used to
     build the CAN FD specification on top of the CAN 2.0B specification. The reserved bits are transmitted low
     (dominant) if not used. The CAN 2.0B specification defines the behavior for the case that a reserved bit is
     high (recessive) to accept this and proceed with the frame. Therefore, if a CAN FD frame (which has a
     different and unexpected form compared to a CAN 2.0B frame) is received by a CAN 2.0B node that uses this
     behavior, results in an error frame by the CAN 2.0B node which destroys the frame. This behavior is called
     CAN FD intolerant.
     To be upward compatible to new protocol specifications, a so-called protocol exception event shall take place
     if a node detects a reserved bit high (recessive). This holds for CAN 2.0B as well as for CAN FD nodes. The
     protocol exception event results in no action for a receiver. The receiver just ignores this frame, does not
     generate an acknowledge (ACK), waits for bus idle, and may transmit or receive the next frame. For a CAN
     2.0B node, this is called CAN FD tolerant and enables coexistence of CAN 2.0B and CAN FD frames within one
     CAN network.

 15.1.4.4.1 Receive Buffer
     To reduce the load of the received frames for the host controller, the CAN controller uses acceptance filters.
     The CAN controller checks the message identifier during acceptance filtering. If the received frame matches
     the filter criteria of one of the acceptance filters, then it is stored in the Receive Buffer (RBUF), which has
     FIFO-like behavior.
     Depending on the number of the available message slots, the host controller does not need to read the
     incoming messages immediately. The CAN controller is able to generate interrupts upon every received
     message, when the RBUF is full or filled to a user-selectable almost full limit. Because of the FIFO-like
     behavior, the host controller always reads the oldest message from the RBUF.
     For more details about the RBUF registers refer to Section 15.1.4.11 CANFD RBUF and TBUF Registers.

 15.1.4.4.2 Transmit Buffer
     For frame transmission purposes, two Transmit Buffers (TB) are available. The Primary TB (PTB) has a higher
     priority but is able to buffer only one frame. The Secondary TB (STB) has a lower priority. It can act in FIFO or
     in priority mode. The priority decision between PTB and STB is fixed and fully independent from the CAN bus
     arbitration. The CAN bus arbitration is a priority decision based on the frame identifiers.
     The STB can be programmed to transmit one or all stored frames. In FIFO mode with every transmission, the
     oldest frame inside the STB buffer is transmitted first. In priority mode, the frame with the highest priority
     inside the STB buffer (based on the frame identifier) is transmitted first.
     A frame located in the PTB has always a higher priority for the CAN protocol machine than the frames in the
     STB regardless of the frame identifiers. A PTB transmission stops and delays an STB transmission. The STB
     transmission is automatically restarted after the PTB frame has been successfully transmitted.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                               Alif Semiconductor
                                                               606
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     A PTB transmission starts at the next transmit position that is possible by the CAN protocol (after the next
     interframe space). Because of this, an STB transmission that has won the arbitration and is actually
     transmitted is completed before.
     Interrupting STB transmissions using a PTB transmission happens in the following cases:
      1. The STB is programmed to output all stored frames and the host controller decides to command a PTB
         transmission before all STB transmissions are completed.
      2. The STB is programmed to output a single frame and the host controller decides to command a PTB
         transmission before the STB transmission is completed.
     If the host controller waits until each programmed transmission is completed, then it can easily decide which
     buffer shall transmit the next frame. As a disadvantage, a message with a low-priority identifier may block
     more important messages. Then the host could abort the message (refer to Section 15.1.4.4.3 Aborting a
     Transmission).
     For more details about the TBUF registers, refer to Section 15.1.4.11 CANFD RBUF and TBUF Registers.

 15.1.4.4.2.1 Transmit Buffer Application Example in FIFO Mode
     In the example (see Figure 15-7) a CAN node is used for sensor measurements. In the example, sensor
     measurements are decided to be handled with low priority. Therefore, frame identifiers with low priority are
     used for the CAN frames carrying the sensor data.
     The host controller automatically acquires measurement results and places them as CAN frames in the STB.
     Because of high traffic at the CAN bus, it may happen that the sensor data frames cannot be transmitted
     immediately and several frames remain in the STB for some time. Later, if there is less traffic on the CAN bus,
     they are transmitted.
     In the situation where several frames remain in the STB, an event may happen that forces the host controller
     to output an important high-priority frame. In such a situation, the host can use the PTB. A frame in the PTB
     is always transmitted before all frames in the STB.
     The advantage of having two transmit buffers is the option to keep all messages. No message has to be
     aborted (discarded) in case of a high-priority event.
     The given application example is explained step by step in Figure 15-7. In this figure, LPF_x is the abbreviation
     of low priority frame and HPF means high priority frame. The LPF_1 is blocked by other higher priority frames
     from other CAN nodes in the first part of the figure. The host controller puts a fourth frame into the STB
     (LPF_4) and then decides to output the HPF. Meanwhile, the CAN bus was free to transmit LPF_1 which is
     followed by HPF, LPF_2 and so on.

                                                        607
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                    E7 Series


               Figure 15-7 Buffer Application Example (Transmit Secondary ALL (CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] = 1))

                         LPF_4                         LPF_4

                         LPF_3                         LPF_3                              LPF_4                        LPF_4

                         LPF_2                         LPF_2                              LPF_3                        LPF_3

  PTB              STB   LPF_1    PTB            STB   LPF_1         PTB   HPF      STB   LPF_2   PTB            STB   LPF_2


                  to CAN bus                    to CAN bus                 to CAN bus                            to CAN bus

    Bus blocked with frames             Bus free for LPF_1                 Bus free for HPF             Bus free for LPF_2
       of higher priority
                                                                                                                                  CANFD-006




        The priority decision between the PTB and STB is done by the CAN protocol machine, but the CAN protocol
        itself uses another independent priority decision mechanism which is called bus arbitration. For the CAN bus
        arbitration, the frame identifier defines the priority level.
        In the application example, it would be possible to place a frame with a very low-priority identifier in the PTB
        while higher priority frames remain in the STB. For the decision between PTB and STB always the PTB wins
        regardless of the frame identifier. It is the task of the host controller to place frames with meaningful
        identifier priorities in the appropriate buffers.

 15.1.4.4.2.2 Transmit Buffer Application Example in Priority Mode
        When the STB is in priority mode, the CAN controller automatically changes the order of the frames inside
        the STB. As a result, the frame with the highest priority is transmitted first. The priority decision is the same
        as for the CAN bus arbitration and therefore a frame identifier with a lower value has a higher priority.
        Regardless of that the PTB has always the highest priority.
        Reordering the frames inside the STB is done automatically as soon as a new frame is prepared for
        transmission and written to the STB. As a result, the frame with the highest priority is selected for
        transmission. The host controller needs to write a new frame into the STB while the priority mode is active.
        In general, a frame with a higher priority never interrupts an active transmission. For example in Figure 15-7
        in the leftmost part, the frame LPF_1 is currently under transmission while LPF_4 is written to the STB. Even
        if LPF_4 has a higher priority than LPF_1, still LPF_1 is transmitted until it loses arbitration on the bus. Then
        after the node has lost the arbitration, LPF_4 is selected for transmission because of its priority.
        Priority reordering is automatically done in background but takes some time. During heavy load when a lot of
        new frames with different priorities are written to the STB and the node loses arbitration or there are errors
        on the CAN bus, it may cause that not the frame with the highest priority is selected. This may happen if this
        frame has been written too shortly before the deadline for the decision which frame is next. But this is a very
        rare condition and in general, the host should not care about this.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                               608
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     If two frames with the same priority are written to the STB, then the oldest frame is transmitted first
     regardless of any reordering with other lower or higher prioritized frames.

 15.1.4.4.3 Aborting a Transmission
     In a situation where a message in a transmit buffer cannot be sent due to its low priority, the buffer would be
     blocked for a long time. In order to avoid this, the host controller can withdraw the transmission request and
     abort the message. Aborting is possible for PTB and STB as well as for single or all frame transmission.

 15.1.4.5 CANFD Time-Stamping
     The CAN controller supports CiA 603 32-bit time-stamping by means of an auxiliary free-running counter
     (CANFD_CNT).
     CiA 603 defines rules to read out the CANFD_CNT counter value as well as to modify the counter. The CAN
     controller includes the mechanism of time-stamping, the register to store one transmission time-stamp (TTS),
     and the memory to store reception time stamp (RTS) for all received messages.
     The time-stamping function can be enabled in the CANFD_TIMECFG[TIMEEN] register bit. If disabled, TTS and
     RTS are invalid.
     Time-stamps are acquired at the SOF or EOF segment of a CAN or CAN FD frame where the frame is taken to
     be valid. The setting of CANFD_TIMECFG[TIMEPOS] register bit determines the time-stamping position.


                                                        NOTE

       In the case of software-based time-stamping, which relies on the reception and transmission
       interrupt, the time-stamping at EOF is preferred.


     CiA 603 is supposed to support time-stamping and time-synchronization of AUTOSAR (refer to Section
     15.1.4.6 AUTOSAR and SAE J1939). For AUTOSAR one node in the CAN network is a time master. The time
     master transmits a synchronization message (SYNC message). The time-stamp of the SYNC message is
     acquired by the time master and all time slaves. The difference in the time between the event of
     commanding the SYNC message until the time when the SYNC message actually gets transmitted is
     transmitted in a follow-up (FUP) message by the time master. Therefore, the CAN controller supports only
     one time-stamp for transmitted frames (TTS) but individual time-stamps for all received frames (RTS).
     Generation of a time-stamp for transmitted frames can be enabled or disabled for each frame individually
     using bit TTSEN inside a TBUF slot (see Section 15.1.4.11.2 CANFD TBUF Registers).
     The CANFD_CNT is 64-bit counter and increments with the TIMER_CLK clock. The CANFD_CNTR_LOW register
     holds bits [31:0] of the counter value and register CANFD_CNTR_HIGH register stores bits [63:32].
     The CAN controller uses the 32-bit value accumulated in the CANFD_CNTR_LOW register when a time-stamp
     is acquired. This allows for up to 1μs precision. The CANFD_CNTR_HIGH register can be used by software for
     compensation of different levels of precision from different nodes in a CAN network by doing precision
     adaption if necessary.
     The CANFD_CNT can be started by setting the CANFD_CNTR_CTRL[CNTR_START] register bit. After the
     counter is stopped via the CANFD_CNTR_CTRL[CNTR_STOP] bit, it can resume counting by asserting again bit
     [CNTR_START]. When counting is resumed, the counter continues from the value it had prior to being
     stopped.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       609
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


     When CANFD_CNT increments beyond its maximum value, the counter registers will overflow, and the
     counter will start over from zero automatically. The counter registers CANFD_CNTR_LOW and CANFD_CNTR_
     HIGH can be cleared by setting the CANFD_CNTR_CTRL[CNTR_CLEAR] bit.

 15.1.4.6 AUTOSAR and SAE J1939
     Both AUTOSAR and SAE J1939 are software stacks which can be used with the CAN controller.
     SAE J1939 uses extended IDs (29 bits). For easy handling, the acceptance filters can be configured to accept
     only extended IDs (CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AIDE] and CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AIDEE] bits).

 15.1.4.7 CANFD General Operation

 15.1.4.7.1 Acceptance Filters
     To reduce the load of the received frames for the host controller, the CAN controller uses acceptance filters.
     The CAN controller checks the message identifier during acceptance filtering. The length of each acceptance
     filter is 29 bits. For more information about the number of the acceptance filters, see Section 15.1.1 CANFD
     Overview.
     If a message passes one of the filters then it is accepted. When accepted, the message is stored into the
     receive buffer and finally, the CANFD_RTIF[RIF] bit is set if the CANFD_RTIE[RIE] bit is enabled. If the message
     is not accepted, the CANFD_RTIF[RIF] bit is not set and the receive buffer FIFO pointer is not increased.
     Message that is not accepted is discarded and overwritten by the next message. A stored valid message is
     never overwritten by any not accepted message.
     Independently of the acceptance filtering result, the CAN controller checks every message on the bus and
     sends an acknowledge or an error frame to the bus.
     The Acceptance Mask (AMASK) defines which bits shall be compared while the Acceptance Code (ACODE)
     defines the appropriate values. Setting mask bits to 0 enables the comparison of the selected acceptance
     code bits with the corresponding message identifier bits. Mask bits that are set to 1 are disabled for the
     acceptance check and this results in accepting the message.
     The identifier bits are compared with the corresponding acceptance code bits as follows:
       n   Standard: ID(10-0) with ACODE(10-0)
       n   Extended: ID(28-0) with ACODE(28-0)
     For example: If the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AMASK_X] bit 0 is set to 0 and all other CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK
     [AMASK_X] bits are set to 1 then the value of the last ID bit has to be equal to the CANFD_ACF_0_3_CODE
     [ACODE_X] bit 0 for an accepted message. All other ID bits are ignored by the filter.
     Figure 15-8 gives an example of acceptance filtering using several filters. In this example the filter 0 and 1 are
     enabled by the appropriate AE_n bits in the CANFD_ACF_EN_z registers (where n = 0 to 7 and z = 0 to 1). All
     other filters are disabled and therefore do not accept any messages. For the enabled filters the combination
     of the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AMASK_X] and CANFD_ACF_0_3_CODE[ACODE_X] bit fields settings defines if
     a message is accepted (like in the example for filter 0) or not accepted (like in the example for filter 1).




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                        610
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


                                       Figure 15-8 Example of Acceptance Filtering

                                                                 Message




                            AE_0                          AE_1                                         AE_n




                    AMASK_0                         AMASK_1                                      AMASK_n
                       +                               +                                            +
                    ACODE_0                         ACODE_1                                      ACODE_n

                                                                                                                     CANFD-007




     Note that disabling a filter by setting AE_n bit to 0, blocks messages. In contrast to this disabling, a mask bit
     in the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AMASK_X] bit field disables the check for this bit which results in accepting
     messages.
     The definitions of the acceptance mask and acceptance code alone do not distinguish between standard or
     extended frames. If the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AIDEE] bit is set to 1 then the value of the CANFD_ACF_0_3_
     MASK[AIDE] bit defines which frame type is accepted. Otherwise if the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AIDEE] bit is
     set to 0 both frame types are accepted.
     After Power-on Reset (POR), the CAN controller accepts all messages. Filter 0 is enabled by setting the
     CANFD_ACF_EN_0[AE_0] bit to 1, all bits in the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AMASK_0] bit field are set to 1 and
     the CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AIDEE] bit is set to 0. All other filters are disabled. Filter 0 is the only filter that
     has defined reset values for AMASK/ACODE while all other filters have undefined reset values.

 15.1.4.7.2 Message Reception
     The received data is stored in the receive buffer as shown in Figure 15-9. The receive buffer has FIFO-like
     behavior. Every received message that is valid and accepted sets the CANFD_RTIF[RIF] bit to 1 if the CANFD_
     RTIE[RIE] bit is enabled. The CANFD_RCTRL[RSTAT] bit field is set depending of the fill state. When the
     number of the filled buffers is equal to the programmable value in the CANFD_LIMIT[AFWL] bit field then the
     CANFD_RTIF[RAFIF] bit is set if the CANFD_RTIE[RAFIE] bit is enabled. In case, when all buffers are full, the
     CANFD_RTIF[RFIF] bit is set if the CANFD_RTIE[RFIE] bit is enabled.

     The receive buffer always maps the message slot containing the oldest message to the RBUF registers.
     The maximum payload length for CAN 2.0 messages is 8 bytes and for CAN FD messages 64 bytes. The
     individual length of each message is defined by the Data Length Code (DLC). The receive buffer provides slots
     for each message and the host controller is required to set the CANFD_RCTRL[RREL] bit to jump to the next
     receive buffer slot. All RBUF bytes of the actual slot can be read in any order.
     If the receive buffer is full, the next incoming message is stored temporarily until it passes for valid (6-th EOF
     bit). Then if the CANFD_RCTRL[ROM] bit is set to 0 the oldest message is overwritten by the newest or if the
     CANFD_RCTRL[ROM] bit is set to 1, the newest message is discarded. In both cases the CANFD_RTIF[ROIF] bit
     is set if the CANFD_RTIE[ROIE] bit is enabled. If the host controller reads the oldest message and sets the
     CANFD_RCTRL[RREL] bit before a new incoming message becomes valid then no message is lost.

 15.1.4.7.2.1 Handling Message Receptions
     Without acceptance filtering, the CAN controller signals the reception of every frame and the host is required
     to decide if it is addressed. This results in a big load on the host controller. It is possible to disable the
     interrupts and use the acceptance filters to reduce the load on the host controller.
     For a basic operation, the CANFD_RTIF[RIF] bit is set to 1 if the CANFD_RTIE[RIE] bit is enabled and the CAN
     controller has received a valid message. To reduce the number of the reception interrupts it is possible to use
     the CANFD_RTIE[RAFIE] and CANFD_RTIF[RAFIF] bits (Receive Buffer Almost full Interrupt) or the CANFD_
     RTIE[RFIE] and CANFD_RTIF[RFIF] bits (Receive Buffer Full Interrupt) instead of the CANFD_RTIE[RIE] and
     CANFD_RTIF[RIF] bits (Reception Interrupt). The almost full limit can be set using the CANFD_LIMIT[AFWL] bit
     field.
     Reading the Receive Buffer (RB) is done as follows:
      1. Read the oldest message from the RB FIFO using the RBUF registers.
      2. Release the RB slot with the CANFD_RCTRL[RREL] bit set to 1. This selects the next message (the next
         FIFO slot). The RBUF is updated automatically.
      3. Repeat these actions until the CANFD_RCTRL[RSTAT] bit signals an empty RB.
     For more information about the number of the RB slots, see Section 15.1.1 CANFD Overview.
     If the RB FIFO is full and a new received message is recognized as valid (6-th EOF bit) then one message is lost
     (see the CANFD_RCTRL[ROM] bit). Before this event, no message is lost. This gives enough time for the host
     controller to read at least one frame from the RB after the RB FIFO has been filled and the selected interrupt
     has occurred. To enable this behavior the RB includes one more hidden slot. This hidden slot is used to
     receive a message, validate and check if it matches the acceptance filters before an overflow occurs.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                        612
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                      www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                              E7 Series


 15.1.4.7.3 Message Transmission
     Before starting any transmission, at least one of the transmit buffers (PTB or STB) has to be loaded with a
     message (see Figure 15-10). The CANFD_TCMD[TPE] bit signals if the PTB is locked and the CANFD_TCTRL
     [TSSTAT] bit field signals the fill state of the STB. The TBUF registers provide access to both the PTB as well as
     to the STB.
     Below is the recommended programming flow:
      1. Set the CANFD_TCMD[TBSEL] bit to the desired value to select either the PTB or the STB.
      2. Write the frame to the TBUF registers.
      3. For the STB set the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit to 1 to finish loading of this STB slot.
                     Figure 15-10 Schematic of PTB and STB in FIFO Mode (Empty PTB and 6 STB Slots)
                                                         PTB                   CANFD_TCMD[TBSEL]

     The maximum payload length for CAN 2.0 messages is 8 bytes and for CAN FD messages is 64 bytes. The
     individual length of each message is defined by the DLC. For remote frames (RTR bit) the DLC becomes
     meaningless, because remote frames always have a data length of 0 bytes. The host controller is required to
     set the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit to jump to the next STB slot. All TBUF bytes can be written in any order.
     Setting the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit to 1 is meaningless if the CANFD_TCMD[TBSEL] bit set to 0 selects the
     PTB. In this case, the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit is automatically cleared and does no harm.
     The CANFD_TCMD[TPE] bit should be set to start a transmission when using the PTB. To use the STB, the
     CANFD_TCMD[TSONE] bit has to be set to start a transmission of a single message or the CANFD_TCMD
     [TSALL] bit to transmit all messages.
     The PTB has always a higher priority than the STB. If both transmit buffers have the order to transmit, the
     PTB message is always sent first regardless of the frame identifiers. If a transmission from the STB is already
     active, it is completed before the message from the PTB is sent at the next possible transmit position (the
     next interframe slot). After the PTB transmission is completed or aborted, the CAN controller returns to
     process other pending messages from the STB.
     When the transmission is completed, the following transmission interrupts are set:
       n For the PTB, the CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] bit is set if the CANFD_RTIE[TPIE] bit is enabled.
       n For the STB using the CANFD_TCMD[TSONE] bit, the CANFD_RTIF[TSIF] bit is set if one message has been
         completed and the CANFD_RTIE[TSIE] bit is enabled.
       n For the STB using the CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bit, the CANFD_RTIF[TSIF] bit is set if all messages have been
         completed and if the CANFD_RTIE[TSIE] bit is enabled. In other words: the CANFD_RTIE[TSIE] bit is set if

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                        613
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


           the STB is empty. Therefore, if the host controller writes an additional message to the STB after the
           TSALL transmission has been started then the additional message is also transmitted before the CANFD_
           RTIF[TSIF] bit to be set.
     It is meaningless to set the CANFD_TCMD[TSONE] bit or the CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bit while the STB is empty.
     In such a case the CANFD_TCMD[TSONE] bit respectively the CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bit is reset automatically.
     No interrupt flag is set and no frame is transmitted.

 15.1.4.7.3.1 Message Transmission Abort
     When a message in a transmit buffer cannot be sent due to its low priority, this would block the buffer for a
     long time. In order to avoid this, the host controller can withdraw the transmission request by setting the
     CANFD_TCMD[TPA] or CANFD_TCMD[TSA] bit respectively, if the transmission has not yet been started.
     Both the CANFD_TCMD[TPA] and CANFD_TCMD[TSA] bits source a single interrupt flag: the CANFD_RTIF[AIF]
     bit. The CAN protocol machine executes an abort only if it does not transmit anything to the CAN bus.
     Therefore, the following is valid:
       n   There is no abort during bus arbitration.
           l If the node loses arbitration, the abort is executed afterwards.

           l If the node wins arbitration, the frame is transmitted.


       n   There is no abort while a frame is transmitted.
           l If a frame is transmitted successfully then a successful transmission is signaled to the host controller.

             In this case no abort is signaled. This is done by the appropriate interrupt and status bits.
           l After an unsuccessful transmission where the CAN node does not receive an acknowledge, the error

             counter is incremented and an abort is executed.
           l If there is at least one frame left in the STB, while the host has programmed all frames to be

             transmitted (the CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bit is set to 1), then both the completed frame as well as the
             abort is signaled to the host.
     Because of these facts aborting a transmission may take some time depending on the CAN communication
     speed and frame length. If an abort is executed, this results in the following actions:
       n   The CANFD_TCMD[TPA] bit releases the PTB which results in the CANFD_TCMD[TPE] bit set to 0. The
           frame data is still stored in the PTB after releasing the PTB.
       n   The CANFD_TCMD[TSA] bit releases one single message slot or all message slots of the STB. This
           depends on whether the CANFD_TCMD[TSONE] bit or the CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bit is used to start the
           transmission. The CANFD_TCTRL[TSSTAT] bit field is updated accordingly. Releasing a frame in the STB
           results in discarding the frame data because the host cannot access it.
     Setting both the CANFD_TCMD[TPA] and CANFD_TCMD[TSA] bits simultaneously is not recommended. If the
     host controller decides to do it anyway, then the CANFD_RTIF[AIF] bit is set and both transmissions from PTB
     and STB are aborted if possible. As already stated, if one transmission is completed before the abort can be
     executed, this results in signaling a successful transmission. Therefore, the following interrupt flags may be
     set if enabled:
       n CANFD_RTIF[AIF] (once for both PTB and STB transmission abort)
       n CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] and CANFD_RTIF[AIF]
       n CANFD_RTIF[TSIF] and CANFD_RTIF[AIF]
       n CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] and CANFD_RTIF[TSIF] (very seldom, only happens if the host does not handle the
         CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] bit immediately)
       n CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] and CANFD_RTIF[TSIF] and CANFD_RTIF[AIF] (rare situation—only happens if the host
         does not handle the CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] and CANFD_RTIF[TSIF] bits immediately)

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                         614
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


     To clear the entire STB, both the CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] and CANFD_TCMD[TSA] bits need to be set. In order
     to detect if a message cannot be sent for a long time because it loses arbitration, the host may use the
     CANFD_ERRINT[ALIF] and CANFD_ERRINT[ALIE] bits.

 15.1.4.7.3.2 Full STB
     After writing a message to the STB, the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit set to 1 marks a buffer slot filled and
     jumps to the next free message slot. The CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit is automatically reset to 0 by the CAN
     controller after this operation.
     If the last message slot has been filled and therefore all message slots are occupied then the CANFD_TCTRL
     [TSNEXT] bit stays set until a new message slot becomes free. While the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit is set to
     1, then writing to TBUF is blocked by the CAN controller.
     When a slot becomes free, then the CAN controller automatically resets the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit to 0.
     A slot becomes free if a frame form the STB is transmitted successfully or if the host requests an abort (the
     CANFD_TCMD[TSA] bit is set to 1). If a TSALL transmission is aborted, then the CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit is
     also reset, but additionally the complete STB is marked as empty.

 15.1.4.7.4 Error Handling
     On one hand the CAN controller does automatic error handling which means that in the most cases the host
     controller does not care about errors. This includes automatic message retransmission and automatic
     deletion of received messages with errors. On the other hand, if required by the host, the CAN controller can
     optionally give detailed information about errors and signal every error to the host by an interrupt. This
     enables to run an application like a CAN bus monitor at the host.
     Every CAN node has 3 states of error handling:
      1. Error-Active: The node automatically transmits active error frames upon detection of an error.
      2. Error-Passive: The node transmits a passive error frame upon detection of an error. This means that it
         does not transmit a dominant value to the bus, but expects an error frame transmitted by other CAN
         nodes.
      3. Bus Off: After too many errors a node goes bus off where it stops touching the bus (refer to Section
         15.1.4.7.4.1 Bus Off State).
     To handle the 3 error states, every CAN node has two error counters: transmit and receive error counters.
     Both are incremented and decremented as defined by the CAN specification and the node enters the
     appropriate error state upon reaching a counter level defined by the CAN specification.
     The error counters are incremented if there are errors. Dangerous errors that are probably caused by this
     node results in incrementing the counter by 8, errors that are probably caused by other nodes results in
     incrementing the counter by 1. Valid frame transmission or valid receptions result in decrementing the
     counters. All this is defined by the CAN specification and handled automatically by the CAN controller.
     An error frame (an error flag) is different to a data frame. It is a dominant pulse for at least 6 consecutive
     dominant bits, which is a stuff bit violation for other nodes. The host controller cannot command to transmit
     an error frame. It is done fully automatically by the CAN controller.
     If the CAN controller is programmed to transmit a frame then it automatically tries retransmissions as fast as
     possible until the frame gets transmitted without error or the node goes bus off. If a frame is received and
     the CAN controller detects an error, then the received data is discarded. Because of the automatically
     transmitted error frame the sender of the frame retransmits the frame. Frames in RBUF are never
     overwritten by frames with errors. Only valid received frames results in RBUF overflow.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       615
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


 15.1.4.7.4.1 Bus Off State
     The bus off state is signaled using the CANFD_CFG_STAT[BUSOFF] status bit. A CAN node enters the bus off
     state automatically if its transmit error counter becomes greater than 255. The CAN node does not take part
     in further communications until it returns into the error-active state again. Setting the CANFD_CFG_STAT
     [BUSOFF] bit to 1 also sets the CANFD_RTIF[EIF] bit if the CANFD_RTIE[EIE] bit is enabled. A CAN node returns
     to an error-active state if it is reset by a POR or if it receives 128 sequences of 11 recessive bits (recovery
     sequences). Note that between each recovery sequence the bus may have a dominant state.
     In the bus off state, the CANFD_RECNT and CANFD_TECNT registers stay unchanged. Note that while entering
     bus off state, the CANFD_TECNT register rolls over and therefore may hold a small value. It is recommended
     to use the CANFD_TECNT register before the node enters bus off state and the CANFD_CFG_STAT[BUSOFF]
     bit afterwards.
     If the node recovers from bus off state then the CANFD_RECNT and CANFD_TECNT registers are
     automatically reset to 0.
     If a frame is pending for transmission but the CAN node has entered bus off state, then this frame is kept
     pending. If a node returns to error-active state after bus off, then the transmission of the pending frame is
     tried. If this is not desired, then the frame should be aborted by the host controller.

 15.1.4.7.5 Extended Status and Error Report
     During CAN bus communication, transmission errors may occur. The following features support detection
     and analysis of them. This can be used for extended bus monitoring.

 15.1.4.7.5.1 Programmable Error Warning Limit
     Errors during reception or transmission are counted by the CANFD_RECNT and CANFD_TECNT registers. A
     programmable error warning limit (CANFD_LIMIT[EWL]) can be used by the host controller for flexible
     reaction on those events. The limit values can be chosen in steps of 8 errors from 8 to 128:
                                                                                                               (15-1)
     The CANFD_RTIF[EIF] bit is set if enabled by the CANFD_RTIE[EIE] bit under one of the following conditions:
       n The border of the error warning limit has been crossed in either direction by the CANFD_RECNT or
         CANFD_TECNT.
       n The CANFD_CFG_STAT[BUSOFF] bit has been changed in either direction.


 15.1.4.7.5.2 Arbitration Lost Capture (ALC)
     The CAN controller is able to detect the exact bit position in the Arbitration Field where the arbitration has
     been lost. This event can be signaled by the CANFD_ERRINT[ALIF] bit if it is enabled. The value of ALC stays
     unchanged if the node is able to win the arbitration. Then ALC holds the old value of the last loss of
     arbitration.
     The value of ALC is defined as follows:
       n   A frame starts with the SOF bit and then the first bit of the ID is transmitted.
       n   This first ID bit has ALC value = 0, the second ID bit ALC value = 1 and so on.
     Refer to Figure 15-5 for the bit order in all types of CAN 2.0 and CAN FD frames.
     The arbitration is only allowed in the arbitration field. Therefore, the maximum value of ALC is 31 which is
     the RTR bit in extended frames.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                          616
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                E7 Series


     Additional hint: If a standard remote frame arbitrates with an extended frame, then the extended frame
     loses arbitration at the IDE bit and ALC is set to 12. The node transmitting the standard remote frame does
     not notice that an arbitration has been taken place, because this node has won.
     It is impossible to get an arbitration loss outside of the arbitration field. Such an event is a bit error.

 15.1.4.7.5.3 Kind Of Error (CANFD_EALCAP[KOER])
     The CAN controller recognizes errors on the CAN bus and stores the last error event in the CANFD_EALCAP
     [KOER] bit field. A CAN bus error can be signaled by the CANFD_ERRINT[BEIF] bit if it is enabled. Every new
     error event overwrites the previous stored value of the CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] bit field. Therefore, the host
     controller has to react quickly on the error event. The error codes are described in Table 15-8.
     The CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] bit field is updated with each new error. Therefore, it stays untouched when
     frames are successfully transmitted or received. This opens the opportunity for a delayed error investigation.

 15.1.4.7.5.4 Reception of All Data Frames (CANFD_RCTRL[RBALL])
     If the CANFD_RCTRL[RBALL] bit is set to 1 then all received data frames are stored even those with error. This
     holds also for Loop Back mode (for more details refer to Section 15.1.4.8.4 Loop Back Mode (LBM)). Only
     data frames are stored in RBUF. Error frames or overload frames are not stored.
     If CiA 603 time-stamping is enabled (CANFD_TIMECFG[TIMEEN] bit is set to 1) and the time-stamp is
     configured for the EOF (CANFD_TIMECFG[TIMEPOS]bit is set to 1) then in the case of an error the time-stamp
     is acquired at the start of the error frame.
     Most of the possible errors can only occur if the node is the transmitter of the frame. In this case a frame
     would only be stored in RBUF if a Loop Back mode is activated. Depending on the type of error parts of the
     frame stored in an RBUF slot may be valid while other parts are unknown. Table 15-8 lists the possibilities.
                            Table 15-8 CANFD_RCTRL[RBALL] and CANFD_EALCAP[KOER]
  CANFD_EALCAP[KOER]         Condition    Description
  No error                   All         Successful reception.
                             Receiver    Receiver can only occur in the ACK slot. All stored data are valid.
                                         The payload is always invalid. The header bits including the ID may be valid. In the
                                         arbitration phase, detection of a wrong bit is part of the arbitration and therefore
                                         not a BIT ERROR. But if a stuff bit in the arbitration phase is detected wrong by the
  BIT ERROR
                             Transmitter transmitter of the frame, then this is a BIT ERROR and in this case the header bits
                                         are invalid. Therefore, the header bits cannot be trusted, but if the header
                                         matches to an expected header of a frame, it can be used for further
                                         investigation.
                                         Only FORM ERRORs in a data frame are covered. This includes errors in the CRC
  FORM ERROR                 All
                                         delimiter, the ACK delimiter, or the EOF bits. All stored data are valid.
                             Receiver    The position of a STUFF ERROR is unknown. All stored data are invalid.
  STUFF ERROR
                             Transmitter Can only happen during arbitration. All stored data are invalid.
                             Receiver    Can only occur if the node is in Listen Only Mode (LOM). All stored data are valid.
  ACK ERROR
                             Transmitter Can only occur in Loop Back mode without self-ACK. All stored data are valid.
  CRC ERROR                  Receiver    All stored data are invalid.


     Note that even if Table 15-8 states that (parts of) the data are valid under certain conditions, then care must
     be taken. There is no guarantee for this and it depends on the reason for the error if this statement is
     correct.
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                 Alif Semiconductor
                                                           617
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                    www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


     Example: if the node has a bad bit timing configuration then there is no correct synchronization and
     therefore no valid data. Therefore, the statement that (parts of) the data is valid signals only the possibility
     that it is so.

 15.1.4.8 Extended Features

 15.1.4.8.1 Single Shot Transmission (SST)
     Sometimes an automatic retransmission is not desired. Therefore, the order to transmit a message only once
     can be set separately for the PTB by the CANFD_CFG_STAT[TPSS] bit and for the STB by the CANFD_CFG_
     STAT[TSSS] bit. In this case no retransmission is performed in the event of an error or arbitration lost if the
     selected transmission is active.
     In the case of an immediate successful transmission there is no difference to normal transmission. But in the
     case of an unsuccessful transmission the following happens:
       n The CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] bit gets set if enabled, the appropriate transmit buffer slot gets cleared.
       n In case of an error, the CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] bit field and the error counters get updated. The CANFD_
         ERRINT[BEIF] bit gets set if the CANFD_ERRINT[BEIE] bit is enabled and the other error interrupt flags act
         accordingly.
       n In case of a lost arbitration, the CANFD_ERRINT[ALIF] bit gets set if the CANFD_ERRINT[ALIE] bit is
         enable.
     Therefore, for SST, the CANFD_RTIF[TPIF] bit alone does not indicate if the frame has been successfully
     transmitted. The SST only be used together with the CANFD_ERRINT[BEIF] and CANFD_ERRINT[ALIF] bits.
     If SST is used with TSALL and there is more than one frame in the STB then for each frame a SST is done.
     Regardless if any of the frames is not successfully transmitted (for example, because of an ACK error) the
     CAN controller advances to the next frame and stops if the STB is empty. Therefore, in this scenario only the
     error counters indicate what has happened. This can be quite complex to evaluate because if one of two
     frames got errors the host cannot detect which one was the successful one.
     If the bus is occupied by another frame, if a SST is started, then the CAN controller waits till the bus is idle
     and then tries to transmit the single shot frame.

 15.1.4.8.2 Listen Only Mode (LOM)
     The Listen Only Mode (LOM) provides the ability of monitoring the CAN bus without any influence to the bus.
     The LOM by CAN controller is compatible to the bus monitoring feature defined in the CAN FD Specification.
     Another application is the automatic bit rate detection where the host controller tries different timing
     settings until no errors occur.
     Errors are monitored (through CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] and CANFD_ERRINT[BEIF] bit fields) in LOM.
     In LOM the core is not able to write dominant bits onto the bus (no active error flags or overload flags, no
     acknowledge). This is done using the following rules:
       n In LOM the protocol machine acts as if in error passive mode where only recessive error flags are
         generated. Only the protocol machine acts as if in error passive mode. All other components including
         the status registers are not touched.
       n In LOM the protocol machine does not generate a dominant ACK.
       n The error counters stay unchanged regardless of any error condition.

     Important facts regarding ACKs for LOM:



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                         618
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


       n If a frame is transmitted by a node then an ACK visible at the bus is only generated if at least one
         additional node is attached to the bus that is not in LOM. Then there is no error and all nodes (also those
         in LOM) receive the frame.
       n If there is an active or passive error flag after an ACK error, then the node in LOM is able to detect this as
         ACK error.
     Activation of LOM should not be done while a transmission is active. The host controller has to take care of
     this. There is not additional protection from the CAN controller.
     If LOM is enabled then no transmission can be started.
     The Loop Back mode (external) LBME (refer to Section 15.1.4.8.4 Loop Back Mode (LBM)) plays an important
     role for the behavior of LOM. If the LBME is disabled, then LOM acts as described above and the node cannot
     write any dominant bit to the bus. But if the LBME is activated, then the node is allowed to transmit a frame.
     The LBME allows only the transmission of an frame including the optional self-ACK (SACK), but the node does
     not respond with an ACK to frames from other nodes and does not generate error or overload frames. In
     summary the combination of LOM and LBME is a silent receiver, that is able to transmit if necessary.

 15.1.4.8.3 Bus Connection Test
     To check if a node is connected to the bus the following steps shall be done:
       n Transmit a frame. If the node is connected to the bus then its TX bits are visible on its RX input.
       n If there are other nodes connected to the CAN bus, then a successful transmission (including an
         acknowledge from the other nodes) is expected. No error is signaled.
       n If the node is the only node that is connected to the CAN bus (but the connection between the bus, the
         transceiver and the CAN controller is fine) then the first regular error situation occurs in the ACK slot
         because of no acknowledge from other nodes. Then a bus error interrupt (CANFD_ERRINT[BEIF] bit) is
         generated if enabled and the CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] bit field is set to 3'b100 (ACK Error).
       n If the connection to the transceiver or the bus is broken then immediately after the SOF bit the CANFD_
         ERRINT[BEIF] bit is set and the CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] bit field is set to 3'b001 (Bit Error).

 15.1.4.8.4 Loop Back Mode (LBM)
     The CAN controller supports two Loop Back Modes—Internal (LBMI) and External (LBME). Both modes result
     in reception of the own transmitted frame which can be useful for self-tests (see Figure 15-11).
     In LBMI the CAN controller is disconnected from the CAN bus and the TXD output is set to recessive. The
     output data stream is internally fed back to the input. In LBMI the node generates a self-ACK to avoid an ACK
     error.
     In LBME the CAN controller stays connected to the transceiver and a transmitted frame is visible on the bus.
     With the help of the transceiver, the CAN controller receives its own frame. In LBME the node does not
     generate a self-ACK when SACK = 0 but generates a self-ACK when SACK = 1. Therefore, in LBME with SACK =
     0 there are two possible results upon a frame transmission:
      1. Another node receives the frame too and generates an ACK. This results in a successful transmission and
         reception.
      2. No other node is connected to the bus and this results in an ACK error. To avoid retransmissions and
         incrementing the error counters it is recommended to use the CANFD_CFG_STAT[TPSS] or the CANFD_
         CFG_STAT[TSSS] bit if it is unknown if other nodes are connected.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        619
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


                                 Figure 15-11 Loop Back Mode: Internal and External
                                               CAN Bus                 CAN Bus

                                        Tranceiver              Tranceiver


                                       1         _


                                      TXD       RXD            TXD       RXD
                                          CAN                       CAN
                                        Controller               Controller    CANFD-010


                                          LBMI                     LBME

     In Loop Back mode the CAN controller receives its own message, stores it in the RBUF and sets the
     appropriate receive and transmit interrupt flags if enabled.
     The LBMI can be useful for software tests while LBME can test the transceiver and the connections to it.
     Activation of LBMI or LBME should not be done while a transmission is active. The host controller has to take
     care of this. There is not additional protection from the CAN controller.
     If the node is connected to a CAN bus then switching back from LBMI to normal operation must not be done
     by simply setting the CANFD_CFG_STAT[LBMI] bit to 0, because then it may be that this occurs just at the
     moment while another CAN node is transmitting. In this case switching back to normal operation shall be
     done by setting the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit to 1. This automatically clears the CANFD_CFG_STAT[LBMI]
     bit to 0. Finally the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit can be disabled and the core returns back to normal
     operation. The CANFD_CFG_STAT[LBME] bit can be disabled every time.
     The LBME can be used in combination with LOM (see Section 15.1.4.8.2 Listen Only Mode (LOM)).
     Receiving the own transmitted frame triggers the appropriate transmit and receive interrupts. The receive
     interrupt is set earlier, because a frame gets valid for a receiver at the last but one bit of EOF, but for a
     transmitter at the last bit of EOF.

 15.1.4.8.5 Transceiver Standby Mode
     Using the CANFD_TCMD[STBY] bit, the output standby signal (CAN_STBY) is driven. It can be used to activate
     a standby mode for a transceiver.
     Once standby is activated no transmission is possible and therefore the CANFD_TCMD[TPE], CANFD_TCMD
     [TSONE] and CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bits cannot be set. On the other hand the CAN controller does not allow
     the CANFD_TCMD[STBY] bit to be set if a transmission is already active (the CANFD_TCMD[TPE], CANFD_
     TCMD[TSONE] or CANFD_TCMD[TSALL] bit is set).
     If the CANFD_TCMD[STBY] bit is set the transceiver enters a low-power mode. In this mode it is unable to
     receive a frame at full speed but monitors the CAN bus for a dominant state. If RXD is low, the CAN controller
     automatically clears the CANFD_TCMD[STBY] bit to 0 which disables standby mode for the transceiver. This is
     done silently without an interrupt to the host controller.
     Switching from standby mode to active mode takes some time for the transceiver and therefore the initial
     wakeup frame cannot be received successfully. Therefore, the node recently being in standby does not
     respond with an ACK. If no CAN node at the bus responds to the wakeup frame with an ACK then this results
     in an ACK error for the transmitter of the wakeup frame. Then the transmitter automatically repeats the
     frame. During the repetition, the transceiver is back in active mode and the CAN controller receives the
     frame and responds with an ACK.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                         620
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


     In summary: One node transmits a frame for wakeup. If all others nodes are in standby mode, then the
     transmitter gets an ACK error and automatically repeats the frame. During the repetition, the nodes are back
     in active mode and respond with an ACK.
     The CANFD_TCMD[STBY] bit is not affected by the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit.

 15.1.4.8.6 Error Counter Reset
     According to the CAN and CAN FD standard, the CANFD_RECNT register counts the receive errors and the
     CANFD_TECNT register counts the transmit errors. After too many transmit errors a CAN node has to go to
     bus off state (see Section 15.1.4.7.4.1 Bus Off State). The CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit does not modify the
     errors counters or the bus off state. The CAN and CAN FD specification defines rules how to disable bus off
     state and to decrease the error counters. A good node recovers from all of this automatically if only a
     temporary error has caused the problems. The classic CAN 2.0B specification requires this automatic
     behavior without host controller interaction.
     The CAN FD specification relaxes this and allows the host controller to override the automatic error counter
     handling. But this should be used with extra care and is suggested to be used only for debugging purposes.
     Writing a 1 to the CANFD_CFG_STAT[BUSOFF] bit, resets the error counters and therefore forces the node to
     leave the bus off state. This is done without setting the CANFD_RTIF[EIF] bit.

 15.1.4.8.7 Software Reset
     If the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit is set to 1 then the software reset is active. Several components are
     forced to a reset state if the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit is set to 1 but no all components are touched by

 15.1.4.9 CAN Bit Time

 15.1.4.9.1 Data Bit Rates
     CAN 2.0B defines data bit rates up to 1 Mbit/s. For CAN FD there is no fixed limitation. For the real life
     systems the data rates are limited by the used transceiver and the achievable clock frequency for the
     CAN controller.
     The CAN controller can be programmed to arbitrarily chosen data rates only limited by the range of the bit
     settings in the appropriate bit timing and prescaler registers.
     The CAN Bit Time (BT) consists of several segments as shown in Figure 15-12. Each segment consists of a
     number of Time Quanta (TQ) units nTQ. The duration of a TQ is:

     match BTREAL as close as possible to BTIDEAL = 1/BR, where BR is the CAN bus baud rate:

     CAN FD core switches from slow nominal bit rate to fast data bit rate at the sample point in the BRS bit and
     switches back at the sample point in the CRC delimiter bit.

     Having the requirements from Table 15-11, the host controller has to define the length of segment 1,
     segment 2 and the SJW for the slow bit rate and if required for CAN FD for the fast bit rate:
     Useful rules:
       n Segment 1 must be slightly larger than segment 2. Then the sample point is in a little bit later than in the
         middle of the bit time.
       n The synchronization jump width must not be bigger than segment 2. If SJW is too small the CAN node
         may be too slow to resynchronize, if SJW is too big then the CAN node may resynchronize too often. SJW
         being half as long as segment 2 seems to be a suitable value.
       n All CAN nodes connected to the CAN bus should choose similar settings if possible.

     The fastest CAN bus speed can be configured using the minimum timing values. But there are some points
     that need to be considered:
       n If the prescalers are bigger than one then all other timing parameters could be set to zero, but this
         violates the rule tSeg_1 ≥ tSeg_2 + 2 (slow speed) respectively tSeg_1 ≥ tSeg_2 + 1 (fast speed) and therefore
         the CANFD_S_SEG_1 and CANFD_F_SEG_1 registers should be at least set to 1. But such a selecting of
         timing parameters works in theory, but may not be robust enough for real nets.
       n If the prescalers are set to one then synchronization becomes difficult. In general the CAN specification
         requires one bit time to be at least 8 TQ long for CAN 2.0 and CAN FD slow nominal bit rate. For the CAN
         controller one bit time of fast data bit rate needs to be also at least 8 TQ long if the fast prescaler is set
         to 1.
       n In summary the fastest CAN bus frequency is the CANFD_CLK frequency divided by 8: prescalers set to 1
         and 8 TQ bit time.

 15.1.4.9.2 Example Configuration
     This example refers to Figure 15-13. It is an example for CAN 2.0 (slow) bit rate configuration but all
     statements can be easily translated to CAN FD (fast) data bit rate.
     The following steps need to be carried for the configuration of the CAN controller:
      1. Set the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit to 1.
      2. Set the CANFD_S_SEG_1 and CANFD_S_SEG_2 registers:
         In the example the data rate on the bus fBUS = 1 Mbaud and the system clock is 16 MHz.
         The values of nTQ and nPRESCALER have to be selected to fit BTREAL as close as possible to BTIDEAL. In this
         example nPRESCALER = 2 and nTQ = 8 are chosen which results in a perfect match: BTIDEAL = BTREAL = 8 TQ.
         With BTREAL = tSeg_1 + tSeg_2 and the time segment definitions given in Section 15.1.4.9.1 Data Bit Rates,
         tSeg_1 = 5 TQ and tSeg_2 = 3 TQ can be chosen as suitable values which finally results in the CANFD_S_
         SEG_1 set to 3 and CANFD_S_SEG_2 set to 2 register settings.
      3. Load the acceptance code and mask registers (optional).
      4. Set the CANFD_S_SJW register:
         With tSeg_2 ≥ tSWJ one is free to chose tSWJ = 3 which finally results in 2.
      5. Load the clock prescaler register (CANFD_S_PRESC): nPRESCALER = CANFD_S_PRESC + 1 results in the
         CANFD_S_PRESC register set to 1.
      6. Set the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit to 0.
         The given order is not mandatory. It is necessary to set the CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit to 1 at the
         beginning, as it is otherwise not possible to load the bit timing, the CANFD_ACF_0_3_CODE[ACODE_X]
         and CANFD_ACF_0_3_MASK[AMASK_X] bit fields. The CANFD_CFG_STAT[RESET] bit set to 0 is required
         upon completion of the configuration. The CAN controller then waits for 8 recessive bits (frame end) and
         resumes its normal operation.
      7. Continue with configuration of interrupts, other configuration bits and execute commands.

 15.1.4.9.3 Bit Rate Switching and Sample Point
     In a CAN network when CAN FD frames with bit rate switching are used the exact position of the sample
     point is important and needs to be for all nodes as similar as possible.
     The bit rate is switched after the sample point of the BRS bit and the sample point of the CRC delimiter.
     Therefore, the lengths of these bits are intermediate. As can be seen in Figure 15-14 the position of the
     sample point makes a big difference for the absolute length of the BRS bit (1 TQ of the slow nominal bit rate
     may be much bigger than several TQs of the fast data rate). If the data rate is much higher than the nominal
     bit rate then an earlier or later sample point may lead to false samples at fast data bit rate.

 15.1.4.9.4 Bit Timing Configuration for CAN FD Nodes
     As stated in Section 15.1.4.9.3 Bit Rate Switching and Sample Point the position of the sample point is very
     important for bit rate switching. Therefore, there is the general recommendation for all CAN FD nodes to use
     exactly the same timing parameters in the CAN network. In contrast to classic CAN where only the data rate
     needs to be the same for all nodes, CAN FD requires the sample point at the same position. In others words
     segment 1 and segment 2 need to be configured to the same length for all nodes. Furthermore, it is
     recommended to use also the same length of one TQ to make synchronization for all nodes equal.
     This requirement can only be achieved if all nodes run with the same base clock frequency (CANFD_CLK for
     the CAN controller) or at least with compatible clock frequencies. The recommended settings are 20 MHz, 40
     MHz or 80 MHz.

 15.1.4.9.5 Bit Timing Recommendations
     The CAN FD timing configuration requires to use the same data rate and the same sample point for all nodes
     in a CAN network. Therefore, it is recommended to use 20 MHz, 40 MHz or 80 MHz as source for the CAN
     protocol machine (CANFD_CLK). In Table 15-13, Table 15-14 and Table 15-15 there are some
     recommendations for the bit timing settings that should apply to all nodes in a CAN FD network. These
     settings are recommendations from CAN in Automation (CiA).
                                                                  NOTE

       CANFD_CLK can be divided by using the CANFD_CTRL[CKDIV] bit field.


     Note that the bit time should be at least 8 TQ if the prescaler is set to 1 for a stable communication. Lower
     settings are possible, but may cause problems.
     The decision if TDC is used or not, depends on the CAN network. The tables only give a suggestion and TDC
     can be enabled or disabled as needed.
