 15.1.4.9.6 TDC and RDC
     For CAN FD nodes Transmitter Delay Compensation (TDC) can be optionally enabled while Receiver Delay
     Compensation (RDC) is automatically active. These features have the following background: for
     communication with CAN FD, data bit rate it may be that the delay of the transmitting transceiver or the
     delay of the bus is bigger than a bit time. This needs to be compensated. Without TDC, the bit rate in the
     data-phase of CAN FD frames is limited by the fact that the transmitter detects a bit error if it cannot receive
     its own transmitted bit latest at the sample point of that bit.
                                                      Figure 15-15 Transmitter Delay
                       Sample Point              Sample Point              Sample Point          Sample Point




               1 2 3 4 5 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 1 2 3


       TXD               A                            B

       TXD
                                                                                                                                  CANFD-014
                                                                                    A                      B
       Delay                       Transmi�er Delay
                                                                       SSP Oﬀset SSP                       SSP


     Figure 15-15 gives an example of the effect of a big transmitter delay. In this figure a TXD data stream is
     shown starting with A and B bits. One bit time consists of tSeg_1 = 5 TQ before the Sample Point (SP) and tSeg_
     2 = 3 TQ behind. In this example the transmitter delay is longer than 2 bit times. Therefore, the original SP
     cannot be used to sample the correct bit value and the CAN FD specification defines an additional Secondary
     Sample Point (SSP).
     If TDC is enabled with the CANFD_TDC[TDCEN] bit set to 1 then the CAN controller automatically determines
     the transmitter delay. The position of the SSP is the transmitter delay plus the SSP offset which is defined by
     the CANFD_TDC[SSPOFF] configuration bits. The CANFD_TDC[SSPOFF] bits must be given as a number of TQ
     and it is suggested to set tSeg_1 equal to the CANFD_TDC[SSPOFF] bit field value. Note that the CANFD_F_
     SEG_1 register defines tSeg_1 during data bit rate. Therefore, in the example given in Figure 15-15, the
     CANFD_TDC[SSPOFF] bit field set to 5 is chosen, because the CANFD_F_SEG_1 register is set to 3.
     ISO 11898-1:2015 requires to use only the CANFD_F_PRESC register set to 0 or 1 if that TDC is used. With this
     requirement the CAN controller is capable of automatically determining a transmitter delay of up to 3 bit
     times of the fast data bit rate.
     A delay bigger than a bit time needs to be taken into account also for receiving nodes. CAN FD defines an
     additional hard synchronization at the falling edge between FDF bit set to 1 and the following r0 bit (at this
     time the slow nominal bit rate is active). Synchronization for CAN and CAN FD is in general defined to operate

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                                631
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     in time steps of one TQ. But steps of one TQ at nominal bit rate may be to coarse for a synchronization for
     the fast data bit rate. Therefore, the additional hard synchronization at the FDF bit needs to violate this rule
     and needs to synchronize as exact as possible and only limited by the clock frequency of the system. The CAN
     controller uses this special synchronization and this is called RDC. RDC is automatically done during reception
     if FDF is 1, no matter if TDC is enabled or not.

 15.1.4.10 CANFD Clocks
     The CAN controller uses two clock domains: one for the host interface and one for the CAN protocol
     machine. This allows the CAN protocol machine to operate with a clock that fits best for the desired CAN bus
     data rates while the host is free to operate at a different (higher) clock speed.

 15.1.4.11 CANFD RBUF and TBUF Registers

 15.1.4.11.1 CANFD RBUF Registers
     The CANFD_RBUFn registers point the message slot with the oldest received message in the RB. All RBUF
     registers can be read in any order.
     The KOER bit field in an RBUF register has the same meaning as the CANFD_EALCAP[KOER] bit field. The
     KOER bit field in an RBUF register becomes meaningful if the CANFD_RCTRL[RBALL] = 0x1.
     The TX status bit in an RBUF register is set to 0x1 if the Loop Back mode is activated and the core has
     received its own transmitted frame. This can be useful if the CANFD_CFG_STAT[LBME] = 0x1 and other nodes
     in the network do also transmissions.

 15.1.4.11.2 CANFD TBUF Registers
     The CANFD_TBUFn registers point the next empty message slot in the STB if the CANFD_TCMD[TBSEL] = 0x1
     or to the PTB otherwise. All TBUF registers can be written in any order. For the STB it is necessary to set the
     CANFD_TCTRL[TSNEXT] bit to mark a slot filled and to jump to the next message slot.
     There is a gap inside the addressing range: from TBUF + 5 to TBUF + 7. This is for better address segment
     alignment. The memory cells in the gap can be read and written, but have no meaning for the CAN protocol.
     TBUF registers are 32-bit wide and must therefore be accessed through a 32-bit write only.

 15.1.4.11.3 CANFD RBUF and TBUF Control Bits
     Both RBUF and TBUF registers include some frame-individual control bits (see Table 15-20). For the RBUF
     registers, these bits signal the status of the appropriate CAN control field bits of the received CAN frame
     while for the TBUF these bits select the appropriate CAN control bit field for the frame that has to be
     transmitted.
                                      Table 15-20 Control Bits in RBUF and TBUF
        Bit                                                          Description
                   IDentifier Extension
        IDE        0x0: Standard Format: ID(10-0)
                   0x1: Extended Format: ID(28-0)
                   Remote Transmission Request
                   0x0: Data frame
                   0x1: Remote frame
       RTR         Only CAN 2.0 frames can be remote frames. There is no remote frame for CAN FD. Therefore, RTR is forced
                   to 0x0 if FDF = 0x1 in TBUF and RBUF.
                   If a CAN FD frame is received with RRS = 0x1, then this is ignored, a data payload is expected for reception
                   instead and RTR bit in RBUF is overridden but the CRC of the frame is calculated with RRS = 0x1.
                   CAN FD frame
       FDF         0x0: CAN 2.0 frame (up to 8 bytes payload)
                   0x1: CAN FD frame (up to 64 bytes payload)
                   Bit Rate Switch
                   0x0: Nominal/slow bit rate for the complete frame
       BRS
                   0x1: Switch to data/fast bit rate for the data payload and the CRC
                   Only CAN FD frames can switch the bitrate. Therefore, BRS is forced to 0x0 if FDF = 0x0.
                   Error State Indicator
                   This is a read-only status bit for RBUF and is not available in TBUF.
                   The protocol machine automatically embeds the correct value of ESI into transmitted frames. ESI is only
                   included in CAN FD frames and does not exist in CAN 2.0 frames.
        ESI
                   0x0: CAN node is error active
                   0x1: CAN node is error passive
                   ESI in RBUF is always low for CAN 2.0 frames.
                   The error state for transmission is shown with the CANFD_ERRINT[EPASS] bit.
                   Transmit Time-Stamp Enable
      TTSEN
                   For CiA 603 time-stamping the acquisition of a transmit time stamp (TTS) can be selected in the TBUF:

        Bit                                                            Description
                   0x0: No acquisition of a transmit time stamp for this frame
                   0x1: TTS update enabled

 15.1.4.11.4 CANFD RBUF and TBUF Data Length Code (DLC)
     The Data Length Code (DLC) in the RBUF and TBUF registers defines the length of the payload—the number
     of payload bytes in a frame (see Table 15-21).
     Remote frames (only for CAN 2.0 frames, where FDF = 0x0) are always transmitted with 0 payload bytes, but
     the content of the DLC is transmitted in the frame header. Therefore, it is possible to code some information
     into the DLC bits for remote frames. But then care needs to be taken if different CAN nodes are allowed to
     transmit a remote frame with the same ID. In this case all transmitters need to use the same DLC because
     otherwise this would result in an unresolvable collision.
                   Table 15-21 Definition of the DLC (According to the CAN 2.0 / FD Specification)
              DLC (binary)                                Frame Type                                   Payload in Bytes
              0000 to 1000                           CAN 2.0 and CAN FD                                     0 to 8
              1001 to 1111                                CAN 2.0                                              8
                 1001                                      CAN FD                                             12
                 1010                                      CAN FD                                             16
                 1011                                      CAN FD                                             20
                 1100                                      CAN FD                                             24
                 1101                                      CAN FD                                             32
                 1110                                      CAN FD                                             48
                 1111                                      CAN FD                                             64

    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                            The bit will be reset to the hardware reset value if the CANFD_
                                                            CFG_STAT[RESET] = 0x1, STBY = 0x1, (LOM = 0x1 and CANFD_CFG_
                                                            STAT[LBME] = 0x0).
                                                            If during a transmission the STB is loaded with a new frame then
                                                            the new frame will be transmitted too. In other words: a
                                                            transmission initiated by this bit is finished when the STB becomes
                                                            empty.
                                                            Note: Setting both TSONE and TSALL bits is meaningless. While the
                                                            TSALL bit is already set, it is impossible to set the TSONE bit and
                                                            vice versa. If both TSONE and TSALL bits are set simultaneously
                                                            then the TSALL bit wins and the TSONE bit is cleared by the CAN
                                                            controller.
                                                            Transmit Secondary Abort.
                                                            0x0: No abort
                                                            0x1: Aborts a transmission from STB which has been requested but
                                                            not started yet
                                                            The bit has to be set by the host controller and will be reset by the
                                                            CAN controller. Setting this bit, automatically de-asserts the
                                                            TSONE or TSALL bit respectively.
                                                            The host controller can set this bit to 0x1 but can not reset it to
                                                            0x0.
                                                            The bit will be reset to the hardware reset value if the CANFD_
                                                            CFG_STAT[RESET] = 0x1.
     0        TSA                     R/W         0x0
                                                            This bit should not be set simultaneously with the TSONE or TSALL
                                                            bit.
                                                            For a TSONE transmission, only one frame is aborted while for a
                                                            TSALL transmission, all frames are aborted.
                                                            One or all message slots will be released which updates the
                                                            CANFD_TCTRL[TSSTAT] bit field.
                                                            All aborted messages are lost because they are not accessible any
                                                            more.
                                                            If in priority mode a TSONE transmission is aborted, then it is not
                                                            clear which frame will be aborted if new frames are written to the
                                                            STB meanwhile.

                                                  0x1: ISO CAN FD mode (ISO 11898-1:2015)

     5     TSMODE            R/W        0x0       In priority decision mode the frame with the highest priority in the

                                                  the priority decision. A lower ID means a higher priority of a frame.
                                                  A frame in the PTB has always the highest priority regardless of

    1-0    TSSTAT             R         0x0       0x1: STB is less than or equal to half full

 15.2 Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) Calculation Unit

 15.2.1 CRC Overview
     The Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) calculation module can produce 8-, 16-, and 32-bit codes for variety of
     polynomials. This function is used to validate the integrity of a communication packet received or the
     integrity of a binary image that is an update candidate. This is achieved by computing and comparing the CRC
     code with the one received after the data packet transmission.
     The device includes up to two CRC modules.
     Each CRC module has the following main features:


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                             660
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                   E7 Series


       n Built-in support for the following CRC algorithms:
         l CRC-8-CCITT

         l CRC-16

         l CRC-16-CCITT

         l CRC-32

         l CRC-32C

       n Support of customized polynomials configured by register settings
       n 8- or 32-bits of data processed at a time
       n Configurable byte and bit swapping of data

     Figure 15-16 provides a high-level overview of the CRC implementation in the device.

 15.2.3.3 CRC Byte and Bit Swapping
     Some of the algorithms require a byte swap and/or a bit swapping of the checked value.
     One swap or the other (or both) can be done automatically after each word is written in, and the result is
     used in the CRC calculation. Bit swap is done on a byte basis.
     Figure 15-20 shows the process and the result of performing byte and bit swapping.

 15.2.4 CRC Programming Guide

 15.2.4.1 CRC Setup
     To set up the CRC the following steps should be performed:
      1. Write the CRC_CONTROL register to setup operation:
         a. Choose the CRC algorithm and size, 8-, 16-, or 32-bit via the CRC_CONTROL[ALGO_SIZE] and the CRC_
             CONTROL[ALGORITHM_SEL] bit fields.
         b. Program the byte and/or bit swapping (optional) by writing the CRC_CONTROL[BYTE_SWAP] and the
             CRC_CONTROL[BIT_SWAP] bits.
         c. Program the CRC result to be reflected across word or bit inverted when read. This should be done
             by writing the CRC_CONTROL[REFLECT_CRC] and the CRC_CONTROL[INVERT_CRC] bits.
         d. Write a seed for the desired algorithm via the CRC_SEED register.
         e. If a custom CRC is used, write the polynomial to the CRC_POLY_CUSTOM register. Also, if this step is
             done, the CRC_CONTROL[USE_CUSTOM_POLY] bit must be set.
          f. Write the CRC_CONTROL[INIT] bit to load the CRC accumulation register with the seed value.
      2. Write data to be accumulated into module:
         n Write 8-bit data to CRC_DATA_IN_8_n register—range to support AHB bursts
         n Write 32-bit data to CRC_DATA_IN_32_n register—range to support AHB bursts
      3. Once all data is written, read the CRC result from CRC_OUT register. For 8-bit accumulations the result is
         in the lowest 8-bits of the CRC_OUT register. For 16-bit accumulations the result is in the lowest 16-bits
         of the CRC_OUT register.

 15.3 Ethernet 10/100 Controller (ETH)

 15.3.1 ETH Overview
     The Ethernet Controller (ETH) enables the device to transmit and receive data over Ethernet in compliance
     with IEEE 802.3-2008.
     The device includes one ETH module.
     The ETH module supports the following main features:
       n Compliance with standards:
           IEEE 1588-2008 standard for precision networked clock synchronization
           l

         l RMII specification version 1.2 from RMII consortium

       n MAC features:
         l 10 and 100 Mbps data transfer rates with RMII interface to communicate with an external fast

           Ethernet PHY
         l Full-duplex operation:

           o IEEE 802.3x flow control automatic transmission of zero-quanta pause frame on flow control input

              de-assertion
           o Forwarding of received pause frames to the user application

         l Half-duplex operation:

           o CSMA/CD protocol support
           o Flow control using backpressure support

         l Preamble and Start of Frame Data (SFD) insertion in transmit path

         l Preamble and Start Frame Delimiter (SFD) deletion in the receive path

         l Automatic CRC and pad generation controllable on a per-frame basis

         l Automatic pad and CRC stripping options for receive frames

         l Programmable frame length to support standard or jumbo Ethernet frames of up to 16KB

         l Programmable Interframe Gap (IFG) (40-bit to 96-bit times in steps of 8)

         l Transmit frames with reduced preamble size

         l Separate 32-bit status for transmit and receive packets

         l IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tag detection for reception frames

         l Separate transmission, reception, and control interfaces to the application

         l Little-endian for transmit and receive paths

         l 64-bit data transfer interface on system-side

         l Detection of remote wake-up frames

         l Receive module for checksum off-load for received IPv4 and TCP packets encapsulated by the

           Ethernet frame (Type 1)
         l Receive module for checking IPv4 header checksum and TCP, UDP, or ICMP checksum encapsulated in

           IPv4 or IPv6 datagrams (Type 2)
         l MDIO master interface for PHY device configuration and management

         l Programmable watchdog timeout limit in the receive path

       n MAC Transaction Layer (MTL) features:
         l 2KB transmit FIFO with programmable threshold

         l 2KB receive FIFO with programmable threshold

         l Single-channel transmit and receive engines

         l Data transfers executed using simple FIFO protocol

         l Optimization for packet-oriented transfers with frame delimiters

         l Programmable burst length for starting a burst up to half the size of the MTL Rx and Tx FIFO

         l Insertion of receive status vectors into the receive FIFO after the EOF transfer




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                     668
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                        www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                  E7 Series


          lStore and forward mechanism for transmission to the MAC
         l Automatic generation of pause frame control or backpressure signal to the MAC based on receive

           FIFO-fill (threshold configurable) level
         l Automatic retransmission of collision frames for transmission

         l Discard frames on late collision, excessive collisions, excessive deferral, and under-run conditions

         l Software control to flush the transmit FIFO

       n DMA features:
         l Exchanges data between the MTL block and system memory

         l Single-channel transmit and receive engines

         l Optimization for packet-oriented DMA transfers with frame delimiters

         l Byte-aligned addressing for data buffer support

         l Descriptor architecture to allow large blocks of data transfer with minimum CPU intervention (each

           descriptor can transfer up to 8KB of data)
         l Comprehensive status reporting for normal operation and transfers with errors

         l Individual programmable burst size for transmit and receive DMA engines for optimal system bus

           utilization
         l Programmable interrupt options for different operational conditions

         l Per-frame transmit or receive complete interrupt control

         l Round-robin or fixed-priority arbitration between receive and transmit engines

       n Monitoring and testing features:
         l DMA states (Tx and Rx) as status bits

         l Status registers that give status of FSMs in transmit and receive data-paths and FIFO fill levels

         l Application abort status bits

         l Current Tx/Rx buffer pointer as status registers

         l Current Tx/Rx descriptor pointer as status registers

 15.3.4.2 ETH AXI Master Interface
     The DMA controller interfaces with the system through the AMBA 3 AXI interface which supports highly-
     effective data traffic throughput. Allowing simultaneous read and write transfers initiated from different
     DMA channels maximize the system bus utilization. For example, the Tx descriptor read and Rx descriptor
     write-back (status update) operation can happen simultaneously. However, the Tx descriptor read and Tx
     descriptor write-back operation cannot happen simultaneously because Tx DMA (or Rx DMA) does not
     initiate the next transfer unless the previous one is complete. The AXI master interface allows queuing of
     multiple numbers of burst requests for read or write operation.

 15.3.4.2.1 Burst Splitting and Burst Selection
     The AXI master interface splits the DMA requests into multiple bursts on the AXI system bus. The splitting is
     based on the DMA count and software-controllable burst enable bits (ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN16],
     ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN8], ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN4]). The AXI master interface also takes
     care of splitting the transfers that cross 4KB address boundary. The burst length select priority is in the
     following sequence: ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN16], ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN8], and ETH_DMA_
     SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN4].

 15.3.4.2.2 INCR Burst Type
     In cases where the DMA requests are not multiples of the maximum allowed burst length or because of 4KB
     address boundary crossing condition, the AXI master interface chooses a burst length of any value less than
     the maximum enabled burst length. For example, when only ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN16] and ETH_
     DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN4] are enabled, and the DMA requests a burst transfer of size 30 beats, then the
     AXI master interface splits it into two bursts of size 16 and 14 beats, respectively. When the DMA requests to
     transfer a burst, the AXI interface splits the requested bursts into multiple transfers by using only the enabled
     burst lengths. This splitting can occur either because the requested burst is not a multiple of the maximum
     enabled burst or because of 4KB address boundary crossing. If the AXI master interface cannot choose any of
     the enabled burst lengths, then it selects the burst length as 1. For example, when only ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_
     MODE[BLEN16] and ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[BLEN4] are enabled, and the DMA requests a burst transfer
     of size 30 beats, then the AXI master interface splits it into multiple bursts of size 16, 4, 4, 4, 1, and 1 beats,
     respectively. The sequence is in decreasing burst sizes.

 15.3.4.2.3 Outstanding Transactions
     The AXI master interface supports up to 4 read or write outstanding requests on the AXI bus. Software can
     also control these outstanding requests by programming the ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[WR_OSR_LMT] or


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                   Alif Semiconductor
                                                                      673
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[RD_OSR_LMT] bits. This is a useful workaround for any system-level issues with
     the handling of multiple requests.

 15.3.4.2.4 Priority of AXI Requests
     The descriptor transfers have higher priority than the data transfers. Therefore, if there are two requests, Rx
     Descriptor Read and Tx Data Read, then Rx Descriptor Read is given higher priority so that the next Rx Data
     Write (subsequent to Rx Descriptor Read) does not need to wait for the Tx Data Read transfer to complete. If
     there are descriptor read requests from both DMAs, then these requests are serviced based on the first-
     come first-serve basis. Rx DMA has higher priority if descriptor read requests are generated from both DMAs
     in the same clock. Similarly, in the write channel, descriptor writes from any DMA have higher priority than
     the data-write transfers for the Rx DMA.

 15.3.4.2.5 Error Response Handling
     Whenever there is an error response from an AXI slave, the respective DMA channel which generated the
     request gets disabled. The ETH_SBD_IRQ interrupt is asserted when the corresponding Fatal Bus Error
     interrupt is enabled. The host has to reset the ETH module to restart the DMA.

 15.3.4.2.6 AXI Low Power Interface
     The ETH module supports the low-power interface defined by AXI specifications. The ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_
     MODE[EN_LPI] and ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[LPI_XIT_PKT] bits control the behavior of the AXI master
     interface in low-power mode. When the ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[EN_LPI] bit is enabled and the host
     requests a low-power initiation, the AXI master interface checks for idle status of the data-paths before
     giving the response. In other words, when both the MAC transmitter and receiver are idle, both DMA engines
     are idle and there is no data in the transmit or receive FIFOs for a continuous period of 16 clock-cycles
     (ACLK), then it accepts the low-power request and goes into low-power mode in which the host can remove
     ACLK. If the MAC goes to an inactive state within 15 clocks after the request, then the AXI master interface
     waits for confirmation of the inactive state for a further period of 16 clocks before giving the response. If
     some activity is found in the MAC during this period of 16 clock cycles, it responds by denying the low-power
     request.
     In the low-power mode, AXI master interface can initiate a request to come out of low-power mode when
     any packet is being received by the MAC receiver or when a magic packet or remote wake-up frame is
     received as controlled by the ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[LPI_XIT_PKT] bit.

 15.3.4.3 ETH AHB Slave Interface
     The 32-bit AHB slave interface provides access to the DMA and MAC register spaces. When a reserved
     address in the MAC register space is read, it gives all zeros data. Similarly, when a reserved address is written,
     the ETH module ignores the write request.

 15.3.4.4 ETH DMA Controller
     The DMA has independent transmit and receive engines, and control and status register space. The transmit
     engine transfers data from system memory to the device port (MTL), while the receive engine transfers data
     from the device port to the system memory. The controller use descriptors to efficiently move data from
     source to destination with minimal host CPU intervention. The DMA is designed for packet-oriented data
     transfers such as frames in Ethernet. The controller can be programmed to interrupt the host CPU for
     situations such as frame transmit and frame receive transfer completion, and other normal or error
     conditions. The DMA and the host driver communicate through two data structures:

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        674
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


       n Control and status registers
       n Descriptor lists and data buffers

     The control and status registers are described in Section 15.3.6 ETH Registers Guide. The descriptors are
     described in Section 15.3.4.4.6 DMA Descriptors.
     The DMA transfers data frames received by the MAC to the receive buffer in the host memory, and data
     frames transmitted from the transmit buffer in the host memory. Descriptors that reside in the host memory
     act as pointers to these buffers.
     There are two descriptor lists. One is for reception, and one is for transmission. The base address of each list
     is written into the ETH_DMA_CH0_RXDESC_LIST_ADDRESS register and the ETH_DMA_CH0_TXDESC_LIST_
     ADDRESS register, respectively. A descriptor list is forward linked either implicitly or explicitly. The last
     descriptor may point back to the first entry to create a ring structure. Explicit chaining of descriptors is
     accomplished by setting the second address chained in both receive and transmit descriptors (RDES1[24] and
     TDES1[24]). The descriptor lists resides in the host physical memory address space. Each descriptor can point
     to a maximum of two buffers. This enables two buffers to be used, physically addressed, rather than
     contiguous buffers in memory.
     A data buffer resides in the host physical memory space, and consists of an entire frame or part of a frame,
     but cannot exceed a single frame. Buffers contain only data. Buffer status is maintained in the descriptor.
     Data chaining refers to frames that span multiple data buffers, but single descriptor cannot span multiple
     frames. The DMA skips to the next frame buffer when the end of frame is detected. Data chaining can be
     enabled or disabled.

 15.3.4.4.1 Initialization
     The initialization for the ETH module is as follows:
      1. Write to the ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE register to set host bus access parameters.
      2. Write to the ETH_DMA_CH0_INTERRUPT_ENABLE register to mask unnecessary interrupt causes.
      3. Create the transmit and receive descriptor lists, and then write to the ETH_DMA_CH0_RXDESC_LIST_
         ADDRESS register and the ETH_DMA_CH0_TXDESC_LIST_ADDRESS register, providing the DMA with the
         starting address of each list.
      4. Write to the ETH_MAC_PACKET_FILTER register for desired filtering options.
      5. Write to the ETH_MAC_CONFIGURATION register to configure the operating mode and enable the
         transmit operation (Bit 1).
      6. Program the ETH_MAC_CONFIGURATION[PS] and ETH_MAC_CONFIGURATION[DM] bits based on the
         line status received or read from the PHY status registers after auto-negotiation.
      7. Set the ETH_DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[ST] and ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[SR] bits to start
         transmission and reception.
      8. Enable the receive operation via the ETH_MAC_CONFIGURATION[RE] bit.
     The transmit and receive engines enter the running state and attempt to acquire descriptors from the
     respective descriptor lists. The receive and transmit engines then begin processing receive and transmit
     operations. The transmit and receive processes are independent of each other and can be started or stopped
     separately.

 15.3.4.4.1.1 Host Bus Burst Access
     The DMA attempts to execute fixed-length Burst transfers on the AXI master interface if configured to do so
     through the ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[FB] bit. The maximum burst length is indicated and limited by the
     ETH_DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[TXPBL] and ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[RXPBL] fields. The receive and
     transmit descriptors are always accessed in the maximum possible burst-size for the 16-bytes to be read.
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                        675
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     The transmit DMA initiates a data transfer only when sufficient space to accommodate the configured burst
     is available in MTL transmit FIFO or the number of bytes till the end of frame (when it is less than the
     configured burst length). The DMA indicates the start address and the number of transfers required to the
     AXI master interface. When the AXI interface is configured for fixed-length burst, then it transfers data using
     the best combination of INCR4, 8, or 16 and SINGLE transactions. Otherwise (no fixed length burst), it
     transfers data using INCR (undefined length) and SINGLE transactions.
     The receive DMA initiates a data transfer only when sufficient data to accommodate the configured burst is
     available in MTL Receive FIFO or when the end of frame (when it is less than the configured burst length) is
     detected in the receive FIFO. The DMA indicates the start address and the number of transfers required to
     the AXI master interface. When the AXI interface is configured for fixed-length burst, then it transfers data
     using the best combination of INCR4, 8, or 16 and SINGLE transactions. If the end-of frame is reached before
     the fixed-burst ends on the AXI interface, then dummy transfers are performed to complete the fixed-burst.
     Otherwise (ETH_DMA_SYSBUS_MODE[FB] bit is reset), it transfers data using INCR (undefined length) and
     SINGLE transactions.
     When the AXI interface is configured for address-aligned beats, both DMA engines ensure that the first burst
     transfer the AXI initiates is less than or equal to the size of the configured burst length. Thus, all subsequent
     beats start at an address that is aligned to the configured burst length. The DMA can only align the address
     for beats up to size 16 (for PBL > 16), because the AXI interface does not support more than INCR16.

 15.3.4.4.1.2 Host Data Buffer Alignment
     The transmit and receive data buffers do not have any restrictions on start address alignment. The start
     address for the buffers can be aligned to any byte. However, the DMA always initiates write transfers, with
     address aligned to the bus width, with dummy data (old data) in the byte lanes that are not valid. This
     typically happens during the transfer of the beginning or end of an Ethernet frame. Software should discard
     the dummy bytes based on the start address of the buffer and size of the frame.

 15.3.4.4.1.3 Buffer Size Calculations
     The DMA does not update the size fields in the transmit and receive descriptors. The DMA updates only the
     status fields (RDES and TDES) of the descriptors. Software has to perform the size calculations.
     The transmit DMA transfers the exact number of bytes towards the MAC indicated by buffer size field of
     TDES1. If a descriptor is marked as first (TDES1[FS] bit is set), then the DMA marks the first transfer from the
     buffer as the start of frame. If a descriptor is marked as last (TDES1[LS] bit), then the DMA marks the last
     transfer from that data buffer as the end-of-frame to the MTL.
     The receive DMA transfers data to a buffer until the buffer is full or the end-of-frame is received from the
     MTL. If a descriptor is not marked as last (RDES0[LS] bit), then the descriptor’s corresponding buffers are full
     and the amount of valid data in a buffer is accurately indicated by its buffer size field minus the data buffer
     pointer offset when the FS bit of that descriptor is set. The offset is zero when the data buffer pointer is
     aligned to the data bus width. If a descriptor is marked as last, then the buffer may not be full as indicated by
     the buffer size in RDES1. To compute the amount of valid data in this final buffer, software must read the
     frame length (RDES0[FL] field) and subtract the sum of the buffer sizes of the preceding buffers in this frame.
     The receive DMA always transfers the start of next frame with a new descriptor.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        676
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


                                                       NOTE

       Even when the start address of a receive buffer is not aligned to the data width of system bus, the
       system should allocate a receive buffer of a size aligned to the system bus width. For example, if the
       system allocates a 1,024-byte (1KB) receive buffer starting from address 0x1000, the software can
       program the buffer start address in the receive descriptor to have a 0x1002 offset. The receive DMA
       writes the frame to this buffer with dummy data in the first two locations (0x1000 and 0x1001). The
       actual frame is written from location 0x1002. Thus, the actual useful space in this buffer is 1,022
       bytes, even though the buffer size is programmed as 1,024 bytes, because of the start address offset.


 15.3.4.4.2 Transmission

 15.3.4.4.2.1 Tx DMA Operation: Default (Non-OSF) Mode
     The transmit DMA engine in default mode proceeds as follows:
      1. The host sets up the transmit descriptor (TDES0-TDES3) and sets the TDES0[OWN] bit after setting up
         the corresponding data buffers with Ethernet frame data.
      2. When the ETH_DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[ST] bit is set, the DMA enters run state.
      3. While in run state, the DMA polls the transmit descriptor list for frames requiring transmission. After
         polling starts, it continues in either sequential descriptor ring order or chained order. If the DMA detects
         a descriptor flagged as owned by the host (TDES0[OWN] = 0), or if an error condition occurs,
         transmission is suspended and both the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[TBU] and ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[NIS]
         bits are set, the transmit engine proceeds to step 9.
      4. If the acquired descriptor is flagged as owned by DMA (TDES0[OWN] = 1), the DMA decodes the transmit
         data buffer address from the acquired descriptor.
      5. The DMA fetches the transmit data from the host memory and transfers the data to the MTL for
         transmission.
      6. If an Ethernet frame is stored over data buffers in multiple descriptors, the DMA closes the intermediate
         descriptor and fetches the next descriptor. Steps 3, 4, and 5 are repeated until the end-of- Ethernet-
         frame data is transferred to the MTL.
      7. When frame transmission is complete, if IEEE 1588 timestamping was enabled for the frame (as
         indicated in the transmit status) the timestamp value obtained from MTL is written to the transmit
         descriptor (TDES2 and TDES3) that contains the end-of-frame buffer. The status information is then
         written to this transmit descriptor (TDES0). Because the TDES0[OWN] bit is cleared during this step, the
         host now owns this descriptor. If timestamping was not enabled for this frame, the DMA does not alter
         the contents of TDES2 and TDES3.
      8. The ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[TI] bit is set after completing transmission of a frame that has the TDES1
         [IC] bit set in its last descriptor. The DMA engine then returns to step 3.
      9. In suspend state, the DMA tries to reacquire the descriptor (and thereby return to step 3) when it
         receives a Transmit Poll Demand and the ETH_MTL_Q0_INTERRUPT_CONTROL_STATUS[TXUNFIS] bit is
         cleared. If the host stopped the DMA by clearing the ETH_DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[ST] bit, the DMA
         enters stop state.

 15.3.4.4.2.2 Tx DMA Operation: OSF Mode
     While in run state, the transmit process can simultaneously acquire two frames without closing the status
     descriptor of the first one if the ETH_DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[OSF] bit is set. As the transmit process finishes
     transferring the first frame, it immediately polls the transmit descriptor list for the second frame. If the
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       677
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     second frame is valid, the transmit process transfers this frame before writing the first frame’s status
     information. In OSF mode, the Run state Transmit DMA operates in the following sequence:
      1. The DMA operates as described in steps 1–6 of the Tx DMA (default mode).
      2. Without closing the previous frame’s last descriptor, the DMA fetches the next descriptor.
      3. If the DMA owns the acquired descriptor, the DMA decodes the transmit buffer address in this
         descriptor. If the DMA does not own the descriptor, the DMA goes into suspend mode and skips to step
         7.
      4. The DMA fetches the transmit frame from the host memory and transfers the frame to the MTL until the
         end-of-frame data is transferred, closing the intermediate descriptors if this frame is split across multiple
         descriptors.
      5. The DMA waits for the previous frame transmission status and timestamp. When the status is available,
         the DMA writes the timestamp to TDES2 and TDES3, if such timestamp was captured. The DMA then
         writes the status, with a cleared TDES0[OWN] bit thus closing the descriptor. If timestamping was not
         enabled for the previous frame, the DMA does not alter the contents of TDES2 and TDES3.
      6. If enabled, the transmit interrupt is set, the DMA fetches the next descriptor, then proceeds to step 3
         when status is normal. If the previous transmission status shows an underflow error, the DMA goes into
         suspend mode (step 7).
      7. In suspend mode, if a pending status and timestamp are received from the MTL, the DMA writes the
         timestamp (if enabled for the current frame) to TDES2 and TDES3, then writes the status to the
         corresponding TDES0. It then sets relevant interrupts and returns to suspend mode. If no status is
         pending and the host stopped the DMA by clearing the ETH_DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[ST] bit, the DMA
         enters the stop state.
      8. The DMA can exit suspend mode and enter run state (go to step 1 or step 2 depending on pending
         status) only after receiving a Transmit Poll Demand command.


                                                        NOTE

       The DMA fetches the next descriptor in advance before closing the current descriptor. Therefore, the
       descriptor chain should have more than two different descriptors for correct and proper operation.


 15.3.4.4.2.3 Transmit Frame Processing
     The transmit DMA expects that the data buffers contain complete Ethernet frames, excluding preamble, pad
     bytes, and FCS fields. The DA, SA, and Type/Length fields contain valid data. If the transmit descriptor
     indicates that the MAC must disable CRC or PAD insertion, the buffer must have complete Ethernet frames
     (excluding preamble), including the CRC bytes.
     Frames can be data-chained and can span several buffers. Frames must be delimited by the first descriptor
     (TDES1[29]) and the last descriptor (TDES1[30]), respectively.
     As transmission starts, the first descriptor must have the TDES1[29] bit set. When this occurs, frame data
     transfers from the host buffer to the MTL transmit FIFO. Concurrently, if the current frame has the last
     descriptor (TDES1[30]) clear, the transmit process attempts to acquire the next descriptor. The transmit
     process expects this descriptor to have the TDES1[29] bit cleared. If TDES1[30] is cleared, it indicates an
     intermediary buffer. If TDES1[30] is set, it indicates the last buffer of the frame.
     After the last buffer of the frame has been transmitted, the DMA writes back the final status information to
     the transmit descriptor 0 (TDES0) word of the descriptor that has the last segment set (TDES1[30]). At this

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                        678
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


     time, if TDES1[31] is set, the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[TI] bit is set, the next descriptor is fetched, and the
     process repeats.
     The actual frame transmission begins after the MTL transmit FIFO has reached either a programmable
     transmit threshold (the ETH_MTL_TXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[TTC] field), or a full frame is contained in the
     FIFO. There is also an option for store and forward mode (the ETH_MTL_TXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[TSF] bit).
     Descriptors are released (TDES0[OWN] clears) when the DMA finishes transferring the frame.


                                                         NOTE

       To ensure proper transmission of a frame and the next frame, the user must specify a non-zero buffer
       size for the transmit descriptor that has the last descriptor (TDES1[30]) set.


 15.3.4.4.2.4 Transmit Polling Suspended
     Transmit polling can be suspended by either of the following conditions:
       n The DMA detects a descriptor owned by the host (TDES0[31] = 0). To resume, the driver must give
         descriptor ownership to the DMA and then issue a Poll Demand command.
       n A frame transmission is aborted upon transmit error because of detected underflow. The appropriate
         TDES0 bit is set.
     If the DMA goes into suspend state because of the first condition, then both the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS
     [TBU] and ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[NIS] bits are set. If the second condition occurs, the ETH_DMA_CH0_
     STATUS[AIS] bit is set, and the information is written to TDES0, causing the suspension.
     In both cases, the position in the transmit list is retained. The retained position is that of the descriptor
     following the last descriptor closed by the DMA.
     The driver must explicitly issue a Transmit Poll Demand command after correcting the suspension cause.

 15.3.4.4.3 Reception
     The receive DMA engine’s reception sequence proceeds as follows:
      1. The host sets up receive descriptors (RDES0-RDES3) and sets the RDES0[OWN] bit.
      2. When the ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[SR] bit is set, the DMA enters run state. While in run state, the
         DMA polls the receive descriptor list, attempting to acquire free descriptors. If the fetched descriptor is
         not free (owned by the host), the DMA enters suspend state and jumps to step 9.
      3. The DMA decodes the receive data buffer address from the acquired descriptors.
      4. Incoming frames are processed and placed in the acquired descriptor’s data buffers.
      5. When the buffer is full or the frame transfer is complete, the receive engine fetches the next descriptor.
      6. If the current frame transfer is complete, the DMA proceeds to step 7. If the DMA does not own the next
         fetched descriptor and the frame transfer is not complete (EOF is not yet transferred), the DMA sets the
         RDES0[DE] bit unless flushing is disabled via the ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[RPF] bit. The DMA closes
         the current descriptor (clears the OWN bit) and marks it as intermediate by clearing the RDES0[LS] bit
         (marks it as last descriptor if flushing is not disabled), then proceeds to step 8. If the DMA does own the
         next descriptor but the current frame transfer is not complete, the DMA closes the current descriptor as
         intermediate and reverts to step 4.
      7. If IEEE 1588 timestamping is enabled, the DMA writes the timestamp (if available) to the current
         descriptor’s RDES2 and RDES3. It then takes the receive frame’s status from the MTL and writes the
         status word to the current descriptor’s RDES0, with the OWN bit cleared and the LS bit set. If the host

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                         679
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


         stopped the Rx DMA by clearing the ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[SR] bit, the DMA goes to stop state.
         Otherwise, the Rx DMA proceeds to the step 8.
      8. The receive engine checks the latest descriptor’s OWN bit. If the host owns the descriptor (OWN bit is 0),
         the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RBU] bit is set and the DMA receive engine enters suspend state (step 9). If
         the DMA owns the descriptor, the engine returns to step 4 and awaits the next frame.
      9. Before the receive engine enters suspend state, partial frames are flushed from the receive FIFO. The
         user can control flushing using the ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[RPF] bit.
     10. The Receive DMA goes to stop state if the host had cleared the ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[SR] bit.
         Otherwise, it exits suspend state when a Receive Poll demand is given or the start of next frame is
         available from the receive FIFO of the MTL. The engine proceeds to step 2 and re-fetches the next
         descriptor.
     The DMA does not acknowledge accepting the status from the MTL until it has completed the timestamp
     write-back and is ready to perform status write-back to the descriptor.
     If software has enabled timestamping, when a valid timestamp value is not available for the frame (for
     example, because the receive FIFO was full before the timestamp could be written to it), the DMA writes
     ones to all bits of RDES2 and RDES3. Otherwise (that is, if timestamping is not enabled), the RDES2 and
     RDES3 remain unchanged.

 15.3.4.4.3.1 Receive Descriptor Acquisition
     The receive engine always attempts to acquire an extra descriptor in anticipation of an incoming frame.
     Descriptor acquisition is attempted if any of the following conditions is satisfied:
       n The ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[SR] bit has been set immediately after being placed in run state.
       n The data buffer of current descriptor is full before the frame ends for the current transfer.
       n The controller has completed frame reception, but the current receive descriptor is not yet closed.
       n The receive process has been suspended because of a host-owned buffer (RDES0[31] = 0) and a new
         frame is received.
       n A Receive Poll demand has been issued.


 15.3.4.4.3.2 Receive Frame Processing
     The MAC transfers the received frames to the host memory only when the frame passes the address filter
     and frame size is greater than or equal to configurable threshold bytes set for the receive FIFO of MTL, or
     when the complete frame is written to the FIFO in the store-and-forward mode.
     If the frame fails the address filtering, it is dropped in the MAC block itself unless the ETH_MAC_PACKET_
     FILTER[RA] bit is set. Frames that are shorter than 64 bytes, because of collision or premature termination,
     can be removed from the MTL receive FIFO.
     After 64 (configurable threshold) bytes have been received, the MTL block requests the DMA block to begin
     transferring the frame data to the receive buffer pointed by the current descriptor. The DMA sets the RDES0
     [9] bit after the AXI master interface becomes ready to receive a data transfer (if DMA is not fetching
     transmit data from the host), to delimit the frame. The descriptors are released when the RDES0[OWN] bit is
     reset to 0, either as the data buffer fills up or as the last segment of the frame is transferred to the receive
     buffer. If the frame is contained in a single descriptor, both the RDES0[LS] and RDES0[FD] bits are set.
     The DMA fetches the next descriptor, sets the RDES0[LS] bit, and releases the RDES0 status bits in the
     previous frame descriptor. Then the DMA sets the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RI] bit. The same process repeats
     unless the DMA encounters a descriptor flagged as being owned by the host. If this occurs, the receive
     process sets the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RBU] bit and then enters suspend state. The position in the receive
     list is retained.
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                        680
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


 15.3.4.4.3.3 Receive Process Suspended
     If a new receive frame arrives while the receive process is in suspend state, the DMA re-fetches the current
     descriptor in the host memory. If the descriptor is now owned by the DMA, the receive process re-enters run
     state and starts frame reception. If the descriptor is still owned by the host, the DMA discards the current
     frame at the top of the MTL Rx FIFO and increments the missed frame counter. If more than one frame is
     stored in the MTL Rx FIFO, the process repeats.
     The discarding or flushing of the frame at the top of the MTL Rx FIFO can be avoided by disabling flushing via
     the ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_CONTROL[RPF] bit. In such conditions, the receive process sets the ETH_DMA_CH0_
     STATUS[RBU] bit and returns to suspend state.

 15.3.4.4.4 Interrupts
     Interrupts can be generated as a result of various events. The ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS register contains all
     the bits that cause an interrupt. The ETH_DMA_CH0_INTERRUPT_ENABLE register contains an enable bit for
     each of the events that can cause an interrupt.
     There are two groups of interrupts: normal and abnormal. Interrupts are cleared by writing 1 to the
     corresponding bit position. When all enabled interrupts within a group are cleared, the corresponding
     summary bit is cleared. When both summary bits are cleared, the interrupt signal ETH_SBD_IRQ is de-
     asserted.


                                                       NOTE

       The interrupt signal ETH_SBD_IRQ is asserted because of any event in the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS
       register only if the corresponding interrupt enable bit is set in the ETH_DMA_CH0_INTERRUPT_
       ENABLE register.


     Interrupts are not queued and if the interrupt event occurs before software has responded to it, no
     additional interrupts are generated. For example, the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RI] bit indicates that one or
     more frames were transferred to the host buffer. Software must scan all descriptors, from the last recorded
     position to the first one owned by the DMA.
     An interrupt is generated only once for simultaneous, multiple events. Software must scan the ETH_DMA_
     CH0_STATUS register for the cause of the interrupt. The interrupt is not generated again unless a new
     interrupt event occurs, after software has cleared the appropriate bit in the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS register.
     For example, the controller generates a receive interrupt (the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RI] bit is asserted) and
     software begins reading the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS register. Next, receive buffer unavailable interrupt
     occurs (the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RBU] bit is asserted). Software clears the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RI] bit
     but even then, the ETH_SBD_IRQ signal is not de-asserted, as the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RBU] bit is still
     asserted.
     The ETH_DMA_CH0_RX_INTERRUPT_WATCHDOG_TIMER[RWT] field is used as an interrupt timer for flexible
     control of the receive interrupts. When this interrupt timer is programmed with a non-zero value, it gets
     activated as soon as the Rx DMA completes a transfer of a received frame to system memory without
     asserting the receive interrupt because it is not enabled in the corresponding receive descriptor (RDES1[31]).
     When this timer runs out as per the programmed value, the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[RI] bit is set and the
     interrupt is asserted if the corresponding recieve interrupt is enabled in the ETH_DMA_CH0_INTERRUPT_


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                       681
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                   E7 Series


     ENABLE register. This timer gets disabled before it runs out, when a frame is transferred to memory and the
     receive interrupt is set because it is enabled for that descriptor.

 15.3.4.4.5 Error Response to DMA
     For any data transfer initiated by a DMA channel, if the slave replies with an error response, that DMA stops
     all operations and updates the ETH_DMA_CH0_STATUS[REB] field. The DMA controller can resume operation
     only after reset of the ETH module and reinitializing the DMA.

 15.3.4.5 ETH MAC Transaction Layer (MTL)
     The MAC transaction layer provides FIFO memory to buffer and regulates the frames between the
     application system memory and the MAC. It also enables the data to be transferred between the application
     clock domain and the MAC clock domains. The MTL layer has 2 data paths, namely the transmit path and the
     receive path. The MTL communicates with the application side with application transmit interface (ATI),
     application receive interface (ARI), and the MAC control interface (MCI).
     The MAC does not support direct access to the FIFO memory through the register slave interface.

 15.3.4.5.1 Transmit Path
     The DMA controls all transactions for the transmit path through the ATI. The Ethernet frames read from the
     system memory are pushed into the FIFO by the DMA. The frame is then popped out and transferred to the
     MAC when triggered. When the end of frame is transferred, the status of the transmission is taken from the
     MAC and transferred back to the DMA.
     The transmit FIFO has a depth of 2KB. FIFO-fill level is indicated to the DMA so that it can initiate a data fetch
     in required bursts from the system memory. The data from the AXI master interface is pushed into the FIFO
     with the appropriate byte lanes qualified by the DMA. The DMA also indicates the start of frame (SOF) and
     end of frame (EOF) transfers and controls the pad-insertion or CRC generation for that frame in the MAC.
     There are two modes of operation for popping data towards the MAC. In threshold mode, as soon as the
     number of bytes in the FIFO crosses the configured threshold level (or when the end of frame is written
     before the threshold is crossed), the data is ready to be popped out and forwarded to the MAC. The
     threshold level is configured using the ETH_MTL_TXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[TTC] field. In the store-and-
     forward mode, the MTL pops the frame towards the MAC only when one or more of the following conditions
     are true:
         n When a complete frame is stored in the FIFO
         n When the Tx FIFO becomes almost full
         n When the ATI watermark becomes low. The watermark becomes low when the requested FIFO does not
           have space to accommodate the requested burst length on the ATI.
     Therefore, the MTL never stops in the store-and-forward mode even if the Ethernet frame length is bigger
     than the Tx FIFO size.
     The application can flush the transmit FIFO of all contents by setting the ETH_MTL_TXQ0_OPERATION_MODE
     [FTQ] bit. This bit is self-clearing and initializes the FIFO pointers to the default state. If the FTQ bit is set
     during a frame transfer from the MTL to the MAC, then the MTL stops further transfer as the FIFO is
     considered to be empty. Hence an underflow event occurs at the MAC transmitter and the corresponding
     status word is forwarded to the DMA.

 15.3.4.5.1.1 Initialization
     Upon reset, the MTL is ready to manage the flow of data to and from the DMA and the MAC.
     There are no requirements for enabling the MTL. However, the MAC block and the DMA controller must be
     enabled individually through their respective registers.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                  Alif Semiconductor
                                                                689
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


 15.3.4.5.1.2 Single-Packet Transmit Operation
     During a transmit operation, the MTL block is a slave to the DMA controller. The general sequence of events
     for a transmit operation is as follows:
      1. If the system has data to be transferred, the DMA controller, if enabled, fetches data from the host
         through the AXI master interface and starts forwarding it to the MTL. The MTL pushes the data received
         from the DMA into the FIFO. It continues to receive the data until end-of-frame is transferred.
      2. The data is taken out of the FIFO and sent to the MAC by the FIFO controller engine. When the threshold
         level is crossed or a full packet of data is received into the FIFO, the MTL pops out the frame data and
         drives them to the MAC. The engine continues to transfer data from the FIFO until a complete packet
         has been transferred to the MAC. Upon completion of the frame, the MTL receives the status from the
         MAC and then notifies the DMA controller.

 15.3.4.5.1.3 Transmit Operation—Two Packets in the Buffer
     Because the DMA must update the descriptor status before releasing it to the host, there can be at most two
     frames inside a transmit FIFO. The second frame is fetched by the DMA and put into the FIFO only if the ETH_
     DMA_CH0_TX_CONTROL[OSF] bit is set. If this bit is not set, the next frame is fetched from the memory only
     after the MAC has completely processed the frame and the DMA has released the descriptors.
     If the OSF bit is set, the DMA starts fetching the second frame immediately after completing the transfer of
     the first frame to the FIFO. It does not wait for the status to be updated. The MTL, in the meantime, receives
     the second frame into the FIFO while transmitting the first frame. As soon as the first frame has been
     transferred and the status is received from the MAC, the MTL pushes it to the DMA. If the DMA has already
     completed sending the second packet to the MTL, it must wait for the status of the first packet before
     proceeding to the next frame.

 15.3.4.5.1.4 Retransmission During Collision
     If a collision occurs early in a transmission frame, a retry will be executed automatically using existing data in
     the FIFO (up to 96 bytes). If a collision occurs late in a transmission frame then the transmission is aborted.

 15.3.4.5.1.5 Transmit FIFO Flush Operation
     The ETH module provides a control to software to flush the transmit FIFO in the MTL layer through the ETH_
     MTL_TXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[FTQ] bit. The Flush operation is immediate and the MTL clears the Tx FIFO
     and the corresponding pointers to the initial state even if it is in the middle of transferring a frame to the
     MAC. The data which is already accepted by the MAC transmitter is not flushed. It is scheduled for
     transmission and results in underflow as Tx FIFO does not complete the transfer of rest of the frame. As in all
     underflow conditions, a runt frame is transmitted and observed on the line. The status of such a frame is
     marked with both frame flush and underflow events via TDES0[FF] and TDES0[UF] bits, respectively.


                                                         NOTE

       Before issuing the transmit FIFO flush command, make sure that the Tx FIFO is not empty, that is, the
       ETH_MTL_TXQ0_DEBUG[TXQSTS] bit is reset.


     The MTL layer also stops accepting any data from the application (DMA) during the flush operation. It
     generates and transfers transmit status words to the application for the number of frames flushed inside the


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                        690
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


     MTL including partial frames. Frames that are completely flushed in the MTL have the TDES0[FF] bit set. The
     MTL completes the flush operation when the DMA accepts all of the status words for the frames that were
     flushed, and then clears the ETH_MTL_TXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[FTQ] bit. At this point, the MTL starts
     accepting new frames from the DMA.

 15.3.4.5.1.6 Transmit Status Word
     At the end of transfer of the Ethernet frame to the MAC and after the MAC completes the transmission of
     the frame, the MTL outputs the transmit status to bits [17:0] of TDES0.
     If IEEE 1588 timestamping is enabled, the MTL returns specific frame’s 64-bit timestamp, along with the ATI’s
     transmit status. A valid timestamp is indicated by an active high on the TDES0[TTSS] bit.
     In addition, the 64-bit timestamp can also be read via the ETH_PTP_TMST1 and ETH_PTP_TMST0 registers.

 15.3.4.5.2 Receive Path
     This module receives the frames given out by the MAC and pushes them into the Rx FIFO. The status (fill
     level) of this FIFO is indicated to the DMA when it crosses the configured receive threshold via the ETH_MTL_
     RXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[RTC] field). The MTL also indicates the FIFO fill level so that the DMA can initiate
     pre-configured burst transfers towards the AHB interface.

 15.3.4.5.2.1 Receive Operation
     During an Rx operation, the MTL is a slave to the MAC. The general sequence of receive operation events is
     as follows:
      1. When the MAC receives a frame, it pushes in data along with byte enables. The MAC also indicates the
         SOF and EOF. The MTL accepts the data and pushes it into the Rx FIFO. After the EOF is transferred, the
         MAC drives the status word, which is also pushed into the same Rx FIFO by the MTL.
      2. When IEEE 1588 timestamping is enabled and the 64-bit timestamp is available along with the receive
         status, it is appended to the frame received from the MAC and is pushed into the Rx FIFO before the
         corresponding receive status word is written. Thus, in 32-bit data bus mode, two additional locations per
         frame are taken for storing the timestamp in the Rx FIFO, while in 64-/128-bit mode, one additional
         location is taken.
      3. The MTL_RX engine takes the data out of the FIFO and sends it to the DMA. In the default Cut-Through
         mode, when 64 bytes configured via the ETH_MTL_RXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[RTC] field or a full packet
         of data are received into the FIFO, the MTL_RX engine pops out the data and indicates its availability to
         the DMA. When the DMA initiates the transfer to the AXI interface, the MTL_RX engine continues to
         transfer data from the FIFO until a complete packet has been transferred. Upon completion of the EOF
         frame transfer, the MTL pops-out the status word and sends it to the DMA controller.
      4. In the Rx FIFO store-and-forward mode configured via the ETH_MTL_RXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[RSF] bit,
         a frame is read out only after being written completely into the receive FIFO. In this mode, all error
         frames are dropped (if the MAC is configured to do so) such that only valid frames are read out and
         forwarded to the application. In Cut-Through mode, some error frames are not dropped, because the
         error status is received at the end of frame, by which time the start of that frame has already been read
         out of the FIFO.

 15.3.4.5.2.2 Receive Operation Multiframe Handling
     The status is available immediately after the data. Therefore, the MTL is capable of storing any number of
     frames into the FIFO as long as it is not full.

 15.3.4.5.2.4 Error Handling
        If the MTL Rx FIFO is full before it receives the EOF data from the MAC, an overflow is declared, the whole
        frame (including the status word) is dropped, and the ETH_MTL_RXQ0_MISSED_PACKET_OVERFLOW_CNT
        [OVFPKTCNT] field is incremented. This is true even if the ETH_MTL_RXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[FEP] bit is set.
        If the start address of such a frame has already been transferred to the read controller, the rest of the frame
        is dropped and a dummy EOF is written to the FIFO along with the status word. The status indicates a partial
        frame because of overflow. In such frames, the Frame Length field is invalid. If the MTL receive FIFO is
        configured to operate in the store-and-forward mode and if the length of the received frame is more than
        the FIFO size, overflow occurs and all such frames are dropped.
        The MTL Rx control logic can filter error and undersized frames, if enabled by the ETH_MTL_RXQ0_
        OPERATION_MODE[FEP] and ETH_MTL_RXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[FUP] bits. If the start address of such a
        frame has already been transferred to the Rx FIFO read controller, that frame is not filtered. The start
        address of the frame is transferred to the read controller after the frame crosses the receive threshold set by
        the ETH_MTL_RXQ0_OPERATION_MODE[RTC] field.
        If the MTL receive FIFO is configured to operate in the store-and-forward mode, all error frames can be
        filtered and dropped.
        After the DMA flushes the error frame being read from the FIFO the MTL stops transferring data to the DMA.
        It internally reads out the rest of the frame and drops it. The MTL then starts the transfer of next frame, if it
        is available.

                                                                   692
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
