     The host accesses data, control, and status information of the OSPI through the 32-bit AHB interface. The
     AHB supports little-endian scheme for data transfer, and is used for both OSPI register access by an external
     AHB master and XIP operations.
     The OSPI module also has an interface to communicate with DMA controller, transmit and receive FIFO
     controllers, FSM controller, register block, shift control logic, and interrupt logic.
     The OSPI works as a serial master which initiates and controls all the serial transfers to the serial-slave
     peripheral device. The OSPI can either directly access the external SPI memory for read/write operations, or
     when OSPI is configured in XIP mode the incoming data can be optionally decrypted on-the-fly via the AES
     engine. The AES engine is accessed via the 32-bit AHB/APB interfaces.

 16.1.4.2 OSPI and AES Clocks
     The OSPI receives two clocks—the HCLK is the AHB bus clock and the OSPI_CLK is the OSPI internal core
     clock.
     The serial bit-rate clock, generated and controlled by the OSPI, is driven out on the OSPI_SCLK line. When
     OSPI is disabled (OSPI_ENR[OSPI_EN] = 0), no serial transfers can occur and OSPI_SCLK is held inactive.
     For OSPI Master mode of operation, the maximum frequency of the peripheral bit-rate clock (OSPI_SCLK) is
     one-half the frequency of OSPI clock (OSPI_CLK). This allows the shift control logic to capture data on one
     clock edge of OSPI_SCLK and propagate data on the opposite edge.
     The frequency of OSPI_SCLK can be derived from equation 16-1:

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                              1276
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                          www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


                                                                                                                 (16-1)

     where BAUDR is any even value between 2 and 65534. BAUDR = SCKDV × 2, and SCKDV can be set in the
     OSPI_BAUDR[SCKDV] bit field. If the OSPI_BAUDR[SCKDV] = 0, OSPI_SCLK is disabled.
     The OSPI_SCLK line toggles only when an active transfer is in progress, else, it is held inactive, as defined by
     the Motorola Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) protocol under which it operates (see Section 16.1.4.6
     OSPI Connection Interfaces).
     The AES engine receives the HCLK clock.

 16.1.4.3 OSPI and AES Interrupt Requests
     The OSPI supports a single interrupt request line (OSPI_IRQ) that is the combined (OR-ed) result of various
     internal OSPI interrupts after masking. The OSPI_IMR register controls the interrupt masking. The combined
     interrupt request is routed to the corresponding device interrupt controller through the Shared Interrupt
     Router. For more information, refer to Section 16.1.2 Cryptographic OSPI Internal Connections.
     The OSPI_IRQ line is active-high, level-sensitive, and can be triggered by any of the following interrupts:
       n Transmit FIFO Empty Interrupt (OSPI_TXE_IRQ)—Set when the transmit FIFO is equal to or below its
         threshold value and requires actions to prevent an under-run. The threshold value, set through the
         OSPI_TXFTLR register, determines the level of transmit FIFO entries at which an interrupt is generated.
         This interrupt is cleared by hardware when data are written into the transmit FIFO buffer, bringing it
         over the threshold level. To control the OSPI_TXE_IRQ interrupt, set the OSPI_IMR[TXEIM] bit. The OSPI_
         TXE_IRQ interrupt status can be read from the OSPI_ISR[TXEIS] and OSPI_RISR[TXEIR] bits.
       n Transmit FIFO Overflow Interrupt (OSPI_TXO_IRQ)—Set when an AHB access attempts to write into the
         transmit FIFO after it has been completely filled. When set, data written from the AHB is discarded. This
         interrupt remains set until software reads the transmit FIFO overflow interrupt clear register (OSPI_
         TXOICR). To control the OSPI_TXO_IRQ interrupt, set the OSPI_IMR[TXOIM] bit. The OSPI_TXO_IRQ
         interrupt status can be read from the OSPI_ISR[TXOIS] and OSPI_RISR[TXOIR] bits.
       n Transmit FIFO underflow Interrupt (OSPI_TXU_IRQ)—Set when the transmit FIFO goes empty. This
         interrupt remains set until the OSPI_TXEICR[TXEICR] bit is read.
       n Receive FIFO Full Interrupt (OSPI_RXF_IRQ)—Set when the receive FIFO is equal to or above its threshold
         value plus 1 and requires actions to prevent an overflow. The threshold value, set through the OSPI_
         RXFTLR register, determines the level of receive FIFO entries at which an interrupt is generated. This
         interrupt is cleared by hardware when data are read from the receive FIFO buffer, bringing it below the
         threshold level. To control the OSPI_RXF_IRQ interrupt, set the OSPI_IMR[RXFIM] bit. The OSPI_RXF_IRQ
         interrupt status can be read from the OSPI_ISR[RXFIS] and OSPI_RISR[RXFIR] bits.
       n Receive FIFO Overflow Interrupt (OSPI_RXO_IRQ)—Set when the receive logic attempts to place data
         into the receive FIFO after it has been completely filled. When set, newly received data are discarded.
         This interrupt remains set until software reads the receive FIFO overflow interrupt clear register (OSPI_
         RXOICR). To control the OSPI_RXO_IRQ interrupt, set the OSPI_IMR[XRXOIM] bit. The OSPI_RXO_IRQ
         interrupt status can be read from the OSPI_ISR[RXOIM] and OSPI_RISR[XRXOIS] bits.
       n Receive FIFO Underflow Interrupt (OSPI_RXU_IRQ)—Set when an AHB access attempts to read from the
         receive FIFO when it is empty. When set, zeros are read back from the receive FIFO. This interrupt
         remains set until software reads the receive FIFO underflow interrupt clear register (OSPI_RXUICR). To
         control the OSPI_RXU_IRQ interrupt, set the OSPI_IMR[RXUIM] bit. The OSPI_RXU_IRQ interrupt status
         can be read from the OSPI_ISR[RXUIS] and OSPI_RISR[RXUIR] bits.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1277
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     The AES engine supports a single interrupt request line (AESDEC_IRQ) that is the combined interrupt request
     from AES routed to the interrupt controllers in the device. The AES_INTERRUPT_MASK register controls the
     interrupt enabling.
     The AESDEC_IRQ line is active-high, level-sensitive, and can be triggered by any of the following interrupts:
       n SPI Error Response Interrupt (AES_SPI_ERR_RESP_IRQ)—Set when an error response is received from
         the OSPI through the AHB bus. To control AES_SPI_ERR_RESP_IRQ interrupt, set AES_INTERRUPT_MASK
         [SPI_ERR_RESP] bit. The AES_SPI_ERR_RESP_IRQ interrupt status can be read from the AES_INTERRUPT
         [SPI_ERR_RESP] bit.
       n Register Error Response Interrupt (AES_REG_ERR_RESP_IRQ)—Set when there is an access to an invalid
         OSPI register. To control AES_REG_ERR_RESP_IRQ interrupt, set AES_INTERRUPT_MASK[REGS_ERR_
         RESP] bit. The AES_REGS_ERR_RESP_IRQ interrupt status can be read from the AES_INTERRUPT[REGS_
         ERR_RESP] bit.

 16.1.4.4 OSPI DMA Requests

 16.1.4.4.1 DMA Handshaking Interface
     The OSPI supports a DMA handshaking interface to a DMA Controller (DMAC) at device level to request and
     control data transfers on the AHB bus.
     The OSPI uses two DMA channels, one for the transmit data and one for the receive data. Each OSPI DMA
     channel, if enabled, can issue DMA requests.
     To enable the DMA interface on the OSPI side, the DMA control register (OSPI_DMACR) should be
     configured. Writing a 1 into the OSPI_DMACR[TDMAE] bit field enables the OSPI transmit handshaking
     interface. Writing a 1 into the OSPI_DMACR[RDMAE] bit field enables the OSPI receive handshaking interface.
     The OSPI request signals for source and destination, DMA_TX_REQ and DMA_RX_REQ, are activated when
     their corresponding FIFOs reach the corresponding watermark levels.

 16.1.4.4.2 Transmit Watermark Level and Transmit FIFO Underflow
     During OSPI serial transfers, Tx FIFO requests are made to the DMAC whenever the number of entries in the
     Tx FIFO is less than or equal to the value of the OSPI_DMATDLR register. This is known as transmit
     Watermark Level (WL). The DMAC responds by writing a burst of data to the Tx FIFO buffer.
     Data should be fetched from the DMA often enough for the Tx FIFO to perform serial transfers continuously;
     that is, when the Tx FIFO begins to empty, another DMA request should be triggered. Otherwise, the Tx FIFO
     runs out of data (Tx FIFO underflow occurs).

 16.1.4.4.2.1 Choosing Transmit Watermark Level
     The goal in choosing a proper WL is to minimize the number of transactions per DMA block transfer, while at
     the same time keeping the probability of an underflow condition to an acceptable level. In practice, this is a
     function of the ratio of the rate at which the OSPI transmits data to the rate at which the DMA controller can
     respond to destination burst requests.
     Figure 16-7 and Figure 16-8 illustrate two example cases for different WL settings. In both examples the
     following assumptions are made:
       n   The needed Number of Burst Transactions (NBT) equals the DMA Transfer Block Size divided by the
           Number of Data Items (NDI) per DMA Burst, as defined by equation 16-2:

     WL, which improves bus utilization without compromising the probability of an underflow occurring.

 16.1.4.4.3 Receive Watermark Level and Receive FIFO Overflow
     During OSPI serial transfers, Rx FIFO requests are made to the DMA controller whenever the number of
     entries in the Rx FIFO is at or above the value of the OSPI_DMARDLR register plus 1. This is known as the
     receive WL. The DMA controller responds by fetching a burst of data from the Rx FIFO buffer.
     Data should be fetched by the DMA often enough for the Rx FIFO to accept serial transfers continuously; that
     is, when the FIFO begins to fill, another DMA transfer is requested. Otherwise, the FIFO fills with data
     (receive FIFO overflow).

 16.1.4.4.3.1 Choosing Receive Watermark Level
     Similar to choosing the transmit WL described in Section 16.1.4 Cryptographic OSPI Functional Description,
     the receive WL (OSPI_DMARDLR[DMARDL] + 1), should be set to minimize the probability of overflow, as
     shown in Figure 16-9. It is a trade-off between the number of DMA burst transactions required per block
     versus the probability of an overflow occurring.

 16.1.4.5 OSPI Transfer Modes
     This section describes the modes in which OSPI operates when transferring data on its serial bus.

 16.1.4.5.1 Transmit and Receive
     When the OSPI_CTRLR0[TMOD] = 0x0, both transmit and receive data are valid. Transmit data are popped
     from the transmit FIFO and sent through the TXD line to the target device, which replies with data on the
     RXD line. The receive data from the target device is moved from the receive shift register into the receive
     FIFO at the end of each data frame.

 16.1.4.5.2 Transmit Only
     When OSPI_CTRLR0[TMOD] = 0x1, the receive data are invalid. Transmit data are popped from the transmit
     FIFO and sent through the TXD line to the target device, which replies with data on the RXD line. At the end
     of the data frame, the receive shift register does not load its newly received data into the receive FIFO. The
     data in the receive shift register is overwritten by the next transfer.
     When this mode is entered, the interrupts originating from the receive logic should be masked.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                              1281
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


                                                        NOTE

       Transfer mode setting does not affect the duplex of the serial transfer.


 16.1.4.5.3 Receive Only
     When the OSPI_CTRLR0[TMOD] = 0x2, the transmit data are invalid. The TXD output remains at a constant
     logic level during the transmission. The receive data from the target device is moved from the receive shift
     register into the receive FIFO at the end of each data frame.
     When this mode is entered, the interrupts originating from the transmit logic should be masked.

 16.1.4.5.4 EEPROM Read
     When the OSPI_CTRLR0[TMOD] = 0x3, the transmit data is used to transmit an opcode and/or an address to
     an EEPROM device. Typically this takes three data frames (8-bit opcode followed by 8-bit upper address and
     8-bit lower address). During the transmission of the opcode and address, no data is captured by the receive
     logic (as long as the OSPI master is transmitting data on its TXD line, data on the RXD line is ignored). The
     OSPI master continues to transmit data until the transmit FIFO is empty. Therefore, the transmit FIFO should
     only have enough data frames to supply the opcode and address to the EEPROM. If more data frames than
     needed are in the transmit FIFO, then read data is lost.
     When the transmit FIFO becomes empty, the TXD output is held at a constant logic level and data on the RXD
     line is valid and stored in the receive FIFO. The serial transfer continues until the number of data frames
     received by the OSPI master matches the value of the OSPI_CTRLR1[NDF] bit field plus 1.

 16.1.4.6 OSPI Connection Interfaces
     The OSPI can be used only in a serial master mode of operation and can connect to any serial-slave
     peripheral device using Motorola Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI).

 16.1.4.6.1 Motorola Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI)
     The clock polarity determines whether the inactive state of the serial clock is high or low. To transmit data,
     both SPI peripherals must have identical serial clock phase (SCPH) and clock polarity (SCPOL) values. The data
     frame can be 4 to 32 bits.
     When SCPH = 0, data transmission begins on the falling edge of the slave select signal. The first data bit is
     captured on the first edge of the serial clock; therefore, valid data must be present on the TXD and RXD lines
     prior to the first serial clock edge.

 16.1.4.7 OSPI Data Transfers
     Data transfer starts when the following is met:
       n OSPI is enabled (OSPI_ENR[OSPI_EN] = 0x1)
       n Serial-slave device is enabled (OSPI_SER register is set)
       n Number of data entries in transmit FIFO is greater than the value of OSPI_TXFTLR[TXFTHR] bit field.

     While actively transferring the data, the OSPI_SR[BUSY] bit is set. Before attempting a new serial transfer,
     software should wait until the BUSY bit is cleared.


                                                        NOTE

       The BUSY status bit is not set when the data are written into the transmit FIFO. This bit gets set only
       when the target slave device has been selected and the transfer is underway. After writing data into
       the transmit FIFO, the shift logic does not begin the serial transfer until a positive edge of the OSPI_
       SCLK output signal is present. The delay in waiting for this positive edge depends on the baud rate of
       the serial transfer. Before polling the BUSY status bit, software should first poll the OSPI_SR[TFE]
       (waiting for 1) or wait for BAUDR × OSPI_CLK clock cycles.


 16.1.4.8 OSPI Enhanced SPI Modes
     Aside from the normal SPI mode of operation (Single SPI), the OSPI supports additional enhanced SPI
     modes—Dual, Quad, and Octal SPI. When Dual, Quad, or Octal mode is selected, the width of TXD, RXD, and
     SSI_OE_N signals changes to 2, 4, or 8, respectively. Hence, the data is shifted in/out on more than one line,
     increasing the overall throughput.
     For Dual, Quad and Octal SPI modes, all four combinations of the Serial Clock Polarity (SCPOL) and Serial
     Clock Phase (SCPH) are valid. They work same as in normal SPI mode, as described in Section 16.1.4.6.1
     Motorola Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) except with different width of TXD, RXD, and SSI_OE_N signals.
     Write or read mode of operation can be selected using the OSPI_CTRLR0[TMOD] bit field.

 16.1.4.8.1 Write Operation in Enhanced SPI Modes
     Dual, Quad, or Octal SPI write operations can be divided into the following phases:
       n Instruction phase
       n Address phase
       n Data phase

     An instruction takes one FIFO location and address can take more than one FIFO locations. Both the
     instruction and the address should be programmed in the OSPI_DRn register before OSPI starts write
     operation.
     The sending of instruction, address and data in Dual, Quad, or Octal mode is programmed through the OSPI_
     SPI_CTRLR0[TRANS_TYPE] and OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] bit fields.
     Figure 16-17 shows a typical write operation in Dual, Quad, or Octal SPI mode. The value of N is 7 if Octal
     mode is selected, 3 for Quad mode, and 1 for Dual mode. For one write operation, the instruction and

 16.1.4.8.2 Read Operation in Enhanced SPI Modes

       n Instruction phase
       n Address phase
       n Wait cycles
       n Data phase

     introduced for target slave to change their mode from input to output and the wait cycles can vary for
     different devices.

     data frames specified via the OSPI_CTRLR1[NDF] bit field. Then OSPI de-asserts the slave select signal (OSPI_

 16.1.4.9 OSPI Receive and Transmit FIFO Buffers
     The Tx FIFO is loaded by writing to the OSPI data register (OSPI_DRn) via the AHB interface. Data are popped
     (removed) from the Tx FIFO by the shift control logic into the transmit shift register. The Tx FIFO generates a
     FIFO empty interrupt request (OSPI_TXE_IRQ) when the number of entries in the FIFO is less than or equal to
     the FIFO threshold value. The threshold value, set through the OSPI_TXFTLR register, determines the level of
     FIFO entries at which an interrupt is generated. The threshold value allows early indication to the processor
     that the Tx FIFO is nearly empty. A Tx FIFO overflow interrupt (OSPI_TXO_IRQ) is generated if an attempt to
     write data into an already full Tx FIFO is made.
     Data are popped from the Rx FIFO by reading from the OSPI_DRn register via the AHB interface. The Rx FIFO
     is loaded from the receive shift register by the shift control logic. The Rx FIFO generates a FIFO-full interrupt
     request (OSPI_RXF_IRQ) when the number of entries in the FIFO is greater than or equal to the FIFO

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                              1291
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


     threshold value plus 1. The threshold value, set through the OSPI_RXFTLR register, determines the level of
     FIFO entries at which an interrupt is generated. The threshold value allows early indication to the processor
     that the Rx FIFO is nearly full. A Rx FIFO overrun interrupt (OSPI_RXO_IRQ) is generated when the receive
     shift logic attempts to load data into a completely full receive FIFO. However, this newly received data are
     lost. A Rx FIFO underflow interrupt (OSPI_RXU_IRQ) is generated if an attempt to read from an empty Rx FIFO
     is made. This alerts the processor that the read data are invalid.
     The Tx and Rx FIFO buffers are cleared when the OSPI is disabled (OSPI_ENR[OSPI_EN] = 0).


                                                         NOTE

     Data frames that are less than 32 bits in size must be right-justified when written into the transmit FIFO
     buffer.
     The shift control logic automatically right-justifies receive data in the receive FIFO buffer.


 16.1.4.10 OSPI Receive Data (RXD) Sample Delay
     The OSPI module includes a logic to delay the default sample time of the RXD signal helping it to increase the
     maximum achievable frequency on the serial bus.
     Round trip routing delays on the OSPI_SCLK output signal from the master and the RXD signal from the slave
     can mean that the timing of the RXD signal—as seen by the master—has moved away from the normal
     sampling time.
     The slave uses the OSPI_SCLK signal from the master as a strobe in order to drive RXD signal data onto the
     serial bus. Routing and sampling delays on the OSPI_SCLK signal by the slave device can mean that the RXD
     bit has not stabilized to the correct value before the master samples the RXD signal.
     With the RXD sample delay logic, a delay value can be dynamically programmed in order to move the
     sampling time of the RXD signal equal to a number of OSPI_CLK cycles from the default. The RXD sample
     delay logic uses both positive and negative edge of OSPI_CLK to sample the RXD signal. This increases the
     number of sampling points within an OSPI_SCLK period and meet timings in higher frequencies.
     OSPI uses the OSPI_RX_SAMPLE_DELAY register to change the sampling point of RXD signal.
       n If OSPI_RX_SAMPLE_DELAY[SE] = 0, OSPI delays the sampling point of RXD signal with a programmed
         number of OSPI_CLK cycles
       n If OSPI_RX_SAMPLE_DELAY[SE] = 1, OSPI delays the sampling point of RXD signal with a programmed
         number of OSPI_CLK cycles + 0.5 × (OSPI_CLK period). Thus, the sampling is done on the negative edge
         of the OSPI_CLK. This gives more sampling points within a single OSPI_SCLK clock period.

 16.1.4.11 OSPI Dual Data-Rate (DDR) Support
     In standard operations, data transfer in SPI modes occur on either the positive, or negative edge of the clock.
     For improved throughput, the dual data-rate transfer mode can be used for reading or writing to the
     memories.
     The DDR mode supports the following modes of the SPI protocol:
       n Mode 0—When the default serial clock phase and default serial clock polarity are not enabled (SCPH = 0
         and SCPOL = 0)
       n Mode 3—When the default serial clock phase and default serial clock polarity are enabled (SCPH = 1 and
         SCPOL = 1).

     DDR commands enable data to be transferred on both edges of clock. The different types of DDR commands
     are:
       n Address and data are transmitted (or received in case of data) in DDR format, while instruction is

 16.1.4.11.1 Transmitting Data in DDR Mode
     In DDR mode, data can be transmitted on both edges. The OSPI_DDR_DRIVE_EDGE[TDE] bit field is used to
     set the desired edge on which the data to be transmitted. This ensures that the receiver is able to get a
     stable data while sampling.
     The OSPI sends data with respect to the baud clock (OSPI_SCLK), which is an integral multiple of the internal
     clock (OSPI_SCLK = OSPI_CLK × BAUDR, see Section 16.1.4.2 OSPI and AES Clocks). The data needs to be
     transmitted within half-clock cycle (BAUDR/2), therefore the maximum value for OSPI_DDR_DRIVE_EDGE is
     equal to [(BAUDR/2) – 1]. If OSPI_DDR_DRIVE_EDGE = 0, data is transmitted edge-aligned with respect to


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                               Alif Semiconductor
                                                                 1293
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


     OSPI_SCLK (baud clock). If OSPI_DDR_DRIVE_EDGE = 1, data is transmitted two OSPI_CLK before the edge of
     OSPI_SCLK.

 16.1.4.12 OSPI Read Data Strobe Signal (OSPI_RXDS)
     To achieve high frequency, a data strobe signaling is used in read operations—OSPI_RXDS. Set the OSPI_SPI_
     CTRLR0[SPI_RXDS_EN] bit to 0x1 to sample incoming data with respect to the read data strobe signal.
     Otherwise, if the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[SPI_RXDS_EN] bit is not set to 0x1, the data is sampled based on the
     existing logic.
     When using the OSPI_RXDS signal, only Mode 0 (SCPH = 0 and SCPOL = 0) is supported. OSPI_RXDS signaling
     is only available for enhanced SPI transfers where the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] field is different than 0x0.
     To enable the OSPI_RXDS, DDR data transfer should be enabled in SPI format via the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_DDR_
     EN] bit.


                                                        NOTE

       The OSPI input data lines (RXD) are being delayed inside the device compared to the read data strobe
       (RXDS) line. The AES_RXDS_DELAY[RXDS_DELAY] register field provides the option a delay to be added
       to the RXDS line itself to overcome the delay of the data lines. The objective is to ensure that the
       RXDS line is delayed by ¼ OSPI clock cycle with respect to the leading edge of the valid data lines.
       The equation to determine the RXDS delay is:


                                                                                                             (16-6)

       For example, for internal RXD delay of 1.2 ns and 100 MHz OSPI clock, the RXDS delay = 1.2 ns + 0.25 x
       1/100 MHz = 1.2 ns + 2.5 ns = 3.7 ns. The RXDS delay code in the AES_RXDS_DELAY[RXDS_DELAY] field
       should be programmed to 0x8.
       The RXDS delay value may need to be calibrated for each specific application and may also depend on
       the pin multiplexing options selected for the OSPI data bus signals. For information on OSPI timing
       data, refer to Section OSPI Timing Characteristics of the device series-specific Datasheet.


 16.1.4.13 OSPI Data Mask
     The OSPI supports data mask feature used to mask the data only during write transactions in enhanced SPI
     DDR operations. This feature is enabled by setting to 0x1 the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[SPI_DM_EN] bit. When data
     mask is enabled, OSPI uses the TXD_DM signal to mask the data on the TXD line.
     The data mask value is derived from the incoming transactions on the AHB interface to the OSPI_DRn
     register. For example, if 4 bytes (D3, D2, D1, D0) with D3 as MSB and D2 masked need to be transmitted,
     software should divide the transfer into two transfers:
       n   First 16-bit transfer with D1 and D0 being written to the OSPI_DRn register.
       n   Second 8-bit transfer with D3 being written to the OSPI_DRn register.
     OSPI activates the TXD_DM signal while transmitting the third byte (D2) of the data which is not written in
     the SPI device.

 16.1.4.14 OSPI HyperBus Protocol
     The OSPI supports a HyperBus protocol that works on the principle of the SPI DDR interface. The DDR
     protocol transfers two data bytes per clock cycle on the input/output signals. HyperBus protocol is enabled
     through the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_HYPERBUS_EN] bit.
     In the HyperBus protocol, read and write transactions transfer complete 16-bit words of data. Read data
     words always contain two valid bytes. Write data words may have one or both bytes masked to prevent
     writing of individual bytes within a write burst.
     Command, address, and data information are transferred over the eight HyperBus signals (TXD[7-0]/RXD[7-
     0]). The HyperBus slave device uses the clock to capture information while receiving the command, address,
     or data on the DQ signals. The Command or Address values are center aligned with clock transitions.
     HyperBus uses 48-bit command-address (CA) to convey the instruction and address information, where:
       n Bit [47]—identifies whether the transaction is Read (1) or Write (0)
       n Bit [46]—indicates whether the read or write transaction accesses the memory (0) or register space (1).
       n Bit [45]—indicates whether the burst is linear (1) or wrapped (0).
       n Bits [44-16]—row and upper column component of the target address: system word address bits A31-A3
       n Bits [15-3]—reserved field
       n Bits [2-0]—lower column component of the target address: system word address bits A2-0 selecting the
         starting word within a half-page

 16.1.4.14.1 HyperBus Read Transactions
     The OSPI begins a HyperBus transaction by driving the slave select signal OSPI_SS low while the clock (OSPI_
     SCLK) is idle. Then, the clock starts toggling while CA words are transferred. Thereafter OSPI continues
     clocking for a number of cycles defined by the Initial Latency Count setting in a configuration register of the
     HyperBus slave device. Refer to the HyperBus device data sheet to determine the correct configuration
     register and Initial Latency Count. If the slave device drives the OSPI_RXDS signal (HyperBus RWDS line) low
     during the CA cycles, one latency count is inserted. If OSPI_RXDS is high during the CA cycles, an additional
     latency count is inserted. After these latency clocks are completed, the HyperBus slave device transitions the
     OSPI_RXDS and outputs the target data. Figure 16-29 shows a typical HyperBus read transaction .
                                          Figure 16-29 HyperBus Read Transaction (21)

           OSPI_SCLK

                                     LOW = 1x Latency count

 16.1.4.14.2 HyperBus Write Transactions
     The OSPI begins a HyperBus transaction by driving the slave select signal OSPI_SS low while the clock (OSPI_
     SCLK) is idle. Then, the clock starts toggling while CA words are transferred. Thereafter OSPI continues
     clocking for a number of cycles defined by the Initial Latency Count setting in a configuration register of the
     HyperBus slave device. Refer to the HyperBus device data sheet to determine the correct configuration
     register and Initial Latency Count. If the slave device drives the OSPI_RXDS signal (HyperBus RWDS line) low
     during the CA cycles, one latency count is inserted. If OSPI_RXDS is high during the CA cycles, an additional
     latency count is inserted. After these latency clocks are completed, OSPI starts to output the target data. The
     write data is center aligned with the clock edges. The first byte of data in each word is captured by the
     HyperBus memory on the rising edge of OSPI_SCLK and the second byte is captured on the falling edge of
     OSPI_SCLK.
     As can be seen on Figure 16-5 the RXDS input, the TXD_DM output, and the TXD_DM_OE_N output enable
     signals are used together to form the bi-directional OSPI_RXDS signal that is connected to the HyperBus
     RWDS line. The OSPI_RXDS is driven by the slave memory device during the CA phase to indicate if additional
     initial latency is required and during read transactions as a synchronous read data strobe. During write
     transactions OSPI drives the OSPI_RXDS signal which functions as a data mask.
     The HyperBus wait cycles can be configured using the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[WAIT_CYCLES] bit field. As the
     HyperBus protocol counts the wait cycles from the third CA cycle, OSPI sends OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[WAIT_
     CYCLES] – 1 wait cycles after the CA phase is complete. Figure 16-30 shows a typical HyperBus write
     transaction.

       SSI_OE_N[N:0]

                                     LOW = 1x Latency count

      TXD_DM_OE_N                output enable HIGH for RXDS signaling

 16.1.4.16 OSPI Execute-in-Place (XIP) Mode
     When OSPI operates in Dual, Quad, or Octal SPI mode, it supports a feature for direct memory read
     operation from AHB transaction—Execute-in-Place mode. In XIP mode, OSPI acts as a memory mapped
     interface to an SPI memory.
     Typically, an XIP operation consists of an address phase and a data phase. The programming flow to set-up
     an XIP transfer is as follows:
      1. Set the SPI frame format in the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] bit field.
      2. Set the Address length, Wait cycles, and transaction type in the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0 register.
     The instruction phase can also be included in XIP transfer by using the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[XIP_INST_EN] bit. In
     this case, the following registers should be set:
      1. Set length of instruction in the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0 register.
      2. Write the instruction opcodes in the OSPI_XIP_INCR_INST[INCR_INST] and the OSPI_XIP_WRAP_INST
         [WRAP_INST] registers.
     After the programming is complete, a read transaction through the AHB interface can be initiated and is
     transferred to the SPI peripheral using programmed values.
     When the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[XIP_DFS_HC] is set to 0x0, AHB control signals are used to derive the values of
     the Data Frame Size (DFS) and the Number of Data Frames (NDF) to be fetched from the slave device.
     When OSPI is operating in XIP mode, read data can optionally be decrypted via the AES engine operating in
     ECB mode using keys loaded by the host processor. For more details, see Section 16.1.4.17 OSPI Decryption
     Mode with AES.
     If OSPI is operating in XIP mode without AES decryption, then these steps should be followed:
      1. Set the AES_CONTROL[XIP_EN] bit to 0x1.
      2. Once the data transfer operation is completed, the AES_CONTROL[XIP_EN] bit may be written back to
         0x0 or OSPI can be left in XIP mode.

 16.1.4.16.1 XIP Transfers
     The OSPI first receives all the data and then transmits on the AHB interface. Once the required amount of
     data is fetched for a particular burst, the slave is de-selected. For each new burst request, address is sent
     again on AHB interface.

 16.1.4.16.2 Mode Bits Support
     The OSPI supports additional bits for serial transfer, referred to as Mode bits, enabled through the OSPI_SPI_
     CTRLR0[XIP_MD_BIT_EN] bit. The value of the Mode bits can be set by writing into the OSPI_XIP_MODE_BITS
     register. The length of the Mode bits is set using the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[XIP_MBL] or the OSPI_XIP_CTRL[XIP_
     MBL] bit field. Mode bits occur immediately after the address phase is completed and follow the same rules
     as for the address bits. Therefore, serial transfers consist of the following phases when Mode bit support is
     enabled:
     Instruction Phase > Address Phase > Mode Bits > Wait cycles > Data Phase
     Based on the value in the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] bit field, Mode bits are driven as follows:
       n If the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] is set to Dual, the Mode bits are sent on two data lines.
       n If the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] is set to Quad, the Mode bits are sent on four data lines.
       n If the OSPI_CTRLR0[SPI_FRF] is set to Octal, the Mode bits are sent on eight data lines.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1299
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


                                                        NOTE

       Mode bits support is available only when XIP support is enabled.


 16.1.4.16.3 XIP Write Model
     The OSPI executes the write transactions into the SPI memory without software intervention. There is no
     need to write the instruction and address separately inside the transmit FIFO. OSPI ends the transfer on the
     SPI interface when the transmit FIFO goes empty or when there is no further activity on the AHB bus during
     XIP write operation.


                                                        NOTE

       Before issuing an XIP write transfer on the OSPI AHB interface, the following conditions must be met:
       n OSPI is enabled (OSPI_ENR[OSPI_EN] = 0x1)
       n The transmit FIFO is empty
       n The OSPI_TXU_IRQ interrupt is cleared (read the OSPI_TXEICR[TXEICR] bit)




     If any of these conditions are not met, OSPI issues an error response for XIP write transfer.

 16.1.4.16.4 Concurrent XIP and Non-XIP Operation
     An XIP and non-XIP transfers are mutually exclusive. Hence, it is assumed that the receive and transmit FIFOs
     are empty when a new XIP or non-XIP transfer is initiated. Therefore, both transfers should be scheduled
     sequentially to ensure that there is no overlap or data loss during any of the transfers.
     To perform concurrent non-XIP (read or write) transaction with XIP transfers, OSPI has a separate FIFO for
     XIP data. In this way Tx FIFO and Rx FIFO does not need to be empty before requesting for a new XIP transfer,
     thus ensuring no data is corrupted. On the serial interface, only one transaction goes through at a time. OSPI
     prioritizes transactions on the first-come-first-served basis, which means that if a non-XIP transfer is already
     in progress on the SPI interface, then XIP transfer request does not go through until the current transfer is
     completed and vice-versa.
     A separate XIP configuration is available in the OSPI_XIP_CTRL register and a slave select in the OSPI_XIP_SER
     register. XIP transfers use the OSPI_XIP_CTRL register to define the XIP transfer. For non-XIP transfers, the
     OSPI_CTRLR0 and the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0 registers determine the SPI serial transfer.
     The OSPI provides maximum throughput when the following rules are applied:
       n Set the DMA control and DMA threshold registers in the OSPI module
       n Set the slave number for DMA transaction in the OSPI_SER register
       n Set the slave number for XIP transaction in the OSPI_XIP_SER register
       n Ensure that the DMA transaction length is equal to the OSPI_TXFTLR[TXFTHR] bit field value

     The OSPI waits for the data frames to be set in the OSPI_TXFTLR[TXFTHR] bit field before starting new
     transfer on SPI interface. A value equal to DMA transaction length must be set to ensure that whole DMA
     transaction goes through in a single attempt. OSPI accumulates the data for DMA transaction in Tx FIFO until
     the threshold level is reached. During this time, if Master-B requests any XIP transaction, it goes through
     immediately. Thus, removing any CPU involvement and polling.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1300
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     Once all the data required for DMA transaction is present in Tx FIFO, OSPI initiates a write transaction to the
     slave device only if the device is not BUSY. This transaction does not break until the FIFO is empty. During this
     time, if any XIP request is made to the device, it needs to wait until the write data transfer is complete.

 16.1.4.16.5 Continuous Transfer Mode in XIP Operation
     When OSPI receives an XIP request, address from the AHB interface is transmitted onto the SPI interface
     directly. Each new transfer (XIP Read) on the AHB interface is treated in the same manner. Therefore, for
     every request, a new address should be sent to the slave device thereby contributing to the latency of the
     system.
     If a memory device allows the stretching of slave select signal in between the XIP read transfers, then OSPI
     can be set in continuous XIP mode using the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[OSPI_XIP_CONT_XFER_EN] bit to achieve
     higher performance. Then OSPI functions as soon as first XIP command is received. For the first XIP transfer,
     the address (and instruction if is enabled by the OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[XIP_INST_EN] = 1) is sent on the SPI
     interface. After reception of requested data, OSPI continues to keep the slave selected and the output clock
     OSPI_SCLK remains in the default state. For subsequent XIP transfers on the AHB interface, OSPI resumes
     OSPI_SCLK clock and neither the command, nor the address is transmitted onto the SPI interface and the
     data is fetched from the memory device immediately (no dummy cycles).
     The OSPI goes out of continuous mode in one of the following conditions:
       n   A non-XIP command is received on an XIP interface.
       n   When the AHB transaction is to a non-consecutive address, the slave select is removed and OSPI initiates
           a new XIP request.

 16.1.4.16.6 Slave De-select in Continuous Transfer Mode
     During the continuous transfer, a lot of power is dissipated on the slave device since the slave is selected all
     the times. To avoid such condition, OSPI supports a watchdog timer to de-select the slave after the counter
     runs out.
     The OSPI can de-select the slave when the following conditions are available:
       n A non-XIP command is received on an XIP interface.
       n When the AHB transaction is to a non-consecutive address, the slave select is removed and then OSPI
         initiates a new XIP request.
       n OSPI does not detect any XIP transfer on AHB interface for the time-period specified in the OSPI_XIP_
         CNT_TIME_OUT register.
     The counter starts its operation after the last XIP transfer is completed, and then waits for a new request on
     the AHB interface. The OSPI_XIP_CNT_TIME_OUT register sets the count-down value for the IDLE period.
     When set to 0x0 the counter is disabled, and OSPI continues to wait for the next XIP request without de-
     selecting the slave.

 16.1.4.17 OSPI Decryption Mode with AES
     When OSPI is configured in XIP mode, the data read from the external memory can be decrypted on-the-fly
     with the help of the AES engine. Figure 16-33 shows a high-level overview of the OSPI with AES decryption.

                                                        1301
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                        E7 Series


                                    Figure 16-33 OSPI Decryption Mode with AES

                                                           Cryptographic OSPI




                                      Local Interconnect
                                                                                OSPI                       I/Os

                              AHB




                                                               APB                  AES
                                                             AHB Read
                                                                            ECB       Control
                                                             AHB Write     Engine      Logic

                                                                                                OSPI-049




     In the case when AES decryption of the read data is not required, all data transfers from the external
     memory initiated by OSPI pass directly through the local interconnect without any intervention from the AES
     engine. For more details on the normal OSPI operation in XIP mode, see Section 16.1.4.16 OSPI Execute-in-
     Place (XIP) Mode.
     When on-the-fly decryption of the read data is required, the AES pre-fetches data from the external
     SPI memory based upon the last read address from the host. Data is read 32 bits at a time from the memory
     via the OSPI, driven through the AES engine. Sequential host reads will have data returned via this pipeline.
     Non-sequential reads causes the pipeline to be flushed and new SPI data to be processed.
     To configure the OSPI to operate in XIP mode with AES decryption, these steps should be followed:
      1. Program the OSPI registers as required for operation in XIP mode.
      2. Set OSPI_SPI_CTRLR0[XIP_PREFETCH_EN] bit to reduce latency.
      3. The Secure Enclave shall write the 256-bit AES key within its private address space. The key is then
         automatically passed to the AES engine.
      4. Program AES_CONTROL[DECRYPT_EN] and [LD_KEY] bits to 0x1. This causes the host to read decrypted
         data rather than read the OSPI interface directly and also causes the AES key to be loaded into the AES
         engine and pre-processed.
      5. The Host can access now the full address range of the SPI memory. All reads must be on 32-bit address
         boundaries. Note that latency will be affected by the sequence of reads. Data is pre-fetched and
         decrypted by the AES engine, and non-sequential reads will cause this pipeline of data to be purged.
      6. Once data read transfer is completed, the AES_CONTROL[DECRYPT_EN] bit must be written to 0x0 to
         turn off decryption. This allows the access to the OSPI programming interface to be resumed. If XIP
         mode without encryption is needed, the AES_CONTROL[XIP_EN] must remain at 0x1.

                                                             (OSPI_SCLK) and waits for rest of the data until the programmed
                                                             amount of frames are transferred successfully.

           Offset           Access          Description

         0x10                               The register enables the individual slave select output line from the OSPI master.

 16.1.5.3.5 OSPI_BAUDR Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            OSPI Baud Rate Select
         0x14                               The register derives the frequency of the serial clock that regulates the data
                             R/W
     Base address                           transfer. A 16-bit field in this register defines the OSPI_CLK divider value. It is
                                            impossible to write to this register when the OSPI is enabled.


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
   31-16 RESERVED                      R           0x0        Reserved.
                                                              OSPI Clock Divider.
                                                              This field contains the MSB 15 bits of the 16-bit SPI_CLK divider
                                                              value. The LSB for this bit field is always set to 0 and is unaffected
                                                              by a write operation, which ensures the divider is always set to an
                                                              even value. If this field is set to all 0s, the serial output clock
                                                              (OSPI_SCLK) is disabled. The frequency of the OSPI_SCLK is derived
    15-1      SCKDV                   R/W          0x0        from the following equation:
                                                              FOSPI_SCLK = FOSPI_CLK/BAUDR
                                                              Where BAUDR is any even value between 2 and 65534, and
                                                              BAUDR = SCKDV × 2. For example, for FOSPI_CLK = 3.6864 MHz and
                                                              SCKDV = 1b’1:
                                                              BAUDR = 2 and FOSPI_SCLK = 3.6864/2 = 1.8432 MHz


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1308
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                         E7 Series


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
     0        RESERVED                 R          0x0        Reserved.

 16.1.5.3.23 OSPI_DRn Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            OSPI Data Register (n); n = 0 to 35.
                                            The OSPI data register is a 32-bit read/write buffer for the transmit/receive FIFOs.
                                            When the register is read, data in the receive FIFO buffer is accessed. When it is
                                            written, data are moved into the transmit FIFO buffer; a write can occur only when
   0x60 + (n × 0x4)                         OSPI is enabled. FIFOs are reset when OSPI is disabled. The data registers in the
                             R/W
    Base address                            OSPI occupies thirty-six 32-bit address locations of the memory map to facilitate
                                            AHB burst transfers. Writing to any of these address locations has the same effect
                                            as pushing the data from the write data bus into the transmit FIFO. Reading from
                                            any of these locations has the same effect as popping data from the receive FIFO
                                            onto the read data bus. The FIFO buffers on the OSPI are not addressable.


    Bits      Field Name             Access    Reset Value Description
                                                             Data Register (n). When writing to this register, the data must be
                                                             right-justified. Read data are automatically right-justified.
    31-0      DR                      R/W          0x0
                                                             Read = Receive FIFO buffer
                                                             Write = Transmit FIFO buffer

 16.1.5.6.4 AES_RXDS_DELAY Register
           Offset           Access          Description
         0x20
                              R/W           OSPI RXDS Delay Register
     Base address


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
    31-5      RESERVED                 R          0x0       Reserved.
                                                            A delay added to the OSPI read data strobe (RXDS) input line in
                                                            0.5-ns steps. The maximum allowed value to program is 16.
                                                            0x0: No delay
                                                            0x1: 0.5 ns delay
                                                            0x2: 2 × 0.5 ns delay
                                                            ...
                                                            0xF: 15 × 0.5 ns delay
                                                            0x10: 16 × 0.5 ns delay
                                                            0x11 to 0x1F: Reserved
                                                            Note: The delay should be set to overcome the internal delay of
                                                            OSPI input data lines (RXD) compared to the RXDS line. The
    4-0       RXDS_DELAY              R/W         0x0       objective is to ensure that the RXDS line is delayed by 1/4 OSPI
                                                            clock cycle with respect to the leading edge of the valid RXD data
                                                            lines.
                                                            Equation to determine RXDS delay value:
                                                            RXDS delay (ns) = RXD_delay (ns) + 0.25 × 1/FOSPI_SCLK
                                                            For example, for internal RXD delay of 1.2 ns and 100 MHz OSPI
                                                            clock, the RXDS delay = 1.2 ns + 0.25 x 1/100 MHz = 1.2 ns + 2.5 ns
                                                            = 3.7 ns. The RXDS_DELAY code should be programmed to 0x8.
                                                            This value may need to be calibrated for each specific application
                                                            and may also depend on the pin multiplexing options selected for
                                                            the OSPI data bus signals. For information on OSPI timing data,
                                                            refer to Section OSPI Timing Characteristics of the device series-
                                                            specific Datasheet.

 16.2 Secure Digital / Embedded Multimedia Card (SDMMC)

 16.2.1 SDMMC Overview
     The Secure Digital / MultiMediaCard (SDMMC) module provides an interface to embedded MultiMediaCard
     (eMMC™), Secure Digital® (SD®) card, and SD Input/Output (SDIO). The communication between the SDMMC
     module and eMMC/SD/SDIO device is performed according to the eMMC/SD/SDIO protocol.
     The device includes one SDMMC module.
     The SDMMC module supports the following main features:
       n SD card interface:
         l 4-bit data bus

         l Complaint with SD Host Controller Standard Specification v4.20

         l Complaint with SD Physical Layer Specification v6.00

         l Backward compatible with earlier SD card specifications

         l UHS-I mode

         l Speed modes:

           o Default-Speed (DS)
           o High-Speed (HS)
           o SDR12
           o SDR25

       n SDIO interface:
         l 4-bit data bus

         l Complaint with SD Specifications Part E1 SDIO Specification Version 4.10

         l SDIO read wait

         l SDIO card interrupts in both 1-bit and 4-bit modes

         l Wake-up on card interrupt

       n eMMC interface:
         l 4-bit/8-bit data bus

         l Complaint with JEDEC eMMC 5.1 Specification (JESD84-B51)

         l Backward compatible with earlier eMMC specifications

         l Speed legacy modes:

           o High Speed SDR

         l Boot operation and alternative boot operation

       n 32-bit slave AHB and 64-bit master AXI interface
       n Data transfer types for SD and eMMC:
         l CPU

         l SDMA

         l ADMA2

         l ADMA3

       n Clocking:
         l Supports independent clocks for the host controller, slave interface, and master interface

         l Supports gating of host controller base clock, if host controller is inactive

         l Supports context aware functional clock gates

       n Interrupt outputs:
         l Combined and separate interrupt outputs

         l Interrupt enabling and masking

       n Data buffering:
         l Automatic packing/unpacking of data to fit buffer width

 16.2.4 SDMMC Functional Description

 16.2.4.1 SDMMC Introduction
     The SDMMC module is a programmable high-performance host controller with Advanced eXtensible
     Interface (AXI) as a master interface for data transfer. The SDMMC is compliant with SD Host specifications
     and eMMC Host Controller Interface (HCI) specifications—the standard software drivers should work on the
     SDMMC.
     The SDMMC supports the following basic modes:
       n   SD mode—SD, SDIO, and UHS-I
       n   eMMC mode—eMMC version 5.1




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                          1334
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     Figure 16-37 presents a simplified diagram of the SDMMC main internal blocks and connections.
                                                    Figure 16-37 SDMMC Block Diagram(1)

    Device                                                                   SDMMC
                                         Master
                                        Interface            AXI Master               DMA
                                                              Interface              Engine
             Host
           Processor



                         Interconnect
                                          Slave

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The SDMMC has the following basic blocks:
       n Slave Interface
         The host processor accesses the SDMMC registers through the 32-bit AHB slave interface. The Slave
         Interface supports little-endian scheme for register accesses.
       n Master Interface
         The data transfers to and from the system memory are performed through the 64-bit AXI master
         interface. The Master Interface supports little-endian mode, does not support narrow transfers and
         always performs full data-width transfers.
       n SDMMC Host Controller Registers
         The SDMMC Host Controller Registers block includes a set of all used SDMMC registers. This block
         comprises standard SD host controller registers, as specified in the SD Specifications Part A2 SD Host
         Controller Standard Specification Version 4.20. For more information, refer to Section 16.2.5 SDMMC
         Registers Guide.
       n FIFO Controller
         The FIFO Controller controls the data transfers between the packet buffer (SPRAM), DMA Engine and
         SDMMC Host Controller Registers blocks.
       n DMA Engine
         The DMA Engine handles data transfers between the SDMMC and the system memory. The key features
         of this block are as follows:
         l Support of SDMA/ADMA2/ADMA3 modes

         l Support of pre-fetch data for back-to-back eMMC write commands

         l Support of write back of the received data packets to the system memory

         l DMA FIFO depth—4 levels

       n SPRAM



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                                1335
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                     E7 Series


         The Single-Port RAM (SPRAM) is used as a packet buffer. The packet buffer is the local storage used by
         the SDMMC to store data packets while carrying out data transfer to and from the card. The packet
         buffer depth is 512 levels.
         The received data from the SD/eMMC Unit is written into the packet buffer. When one block of data is
         received, the DMA Engine starts transmitting that data to the system by reading it from the packet
         buffer. For a card write transfer, the data flows in the reverse direction. The DMA Engine writes data
         into the packet buffer that is subsequently read by the SD/eMMC Unit. The DMA Engine and the
         SD/eMMC Unit can work simultaneously as read and write to the packet buffer can be interleaved.
       n SD/eMMC Unit
         l The SD Unit is responsible for managing SD interface protocols. The key features of this unit are:

           o Generates DS/HS/UHS-I command and data packets
           o Generates CRC and checks for command and data packets
           o Handles packet timeouts
           o Supports 1-bit DAT and 4-bit DAT modes
           o Handles SDIO card interrupt
           o Supports DS, HS, SDR12, and SDR25 speed modes

         l The eMMC Unit is responsible for managing eMMC interface protocols. The key features of this unit

            are:
           o Generates eMMC command and data packets
           o Generates CRC and checks for command and data packets
           o Handles packet timeouts
           o Supports 1-bit DAT, 4-bit DAT, and 8-bit DAT modes
           o Supports Legacy and HS Single Data Rate (SDR) modes

       n SD/eMMC Interface
         The SD/eMMC Interface includes all used interface pins. SD supports a 4-bit data bus and eMMC
         supports a 4-bit or 8-bit data bus. For more information, refer to Section 16.2.3 SDMMC External
         Connectivity.
       n Interrupt Requests
         The SDMMC is able to generate interrupt requests to the device Interrupt controller.

 16.2.4.3 SDMMC Standards Compliance
       n JEDEC eMMC 5.1 Specification—JESD84-B51, February 2015
         This specification describes the eMMC design guidelines, protocol, electrical interface, its environment,
         and handling.
       n SD Specifications Part A2 SD Host Controller Standard Specification Version 4.20, August 2015
         This specification describes guidelines for standard host controller drivers including the register maps
         and the descriptor structures as well as the various DMA modes.
       n SD Specifications Part A2 Host Controller Version 4.20, Supplementary Notes Version 1.00, Draft 0.60,
         December 2015
         This specification describes some clarifications and updates for the Host Controller Standard
         Specification Version 4.20, August 2015.
       n SD Specifications Part 1 Physical layer Specification Version 6.00, February 2017
         This specification describes the physical layer interface used by SD memory card.
       n SD Specifications Part E1 SDIO Specification Version 4.10, September 2014
         This specification defines the SD bus interface specification for SDIO and also provides register
         specification. SDIO is based on the Physical Layer Specification and the SDIO specification provides an
         extension and modification to the Physical Layer specification for SDIO card and device.
       n AMBA 2 for AHB slave port
         This specification describes the AMBA specification and explains AHB.
       n AMBA 3 for AXI master port
         This document describes the AMBA specification and explains AXI.

 16.2.4.4 SDMMC DMA and Slave Mode of Data Transfer
     The SDMMC is used to transfer data to and from storage devices (such as SD, eMMC). On the
     system/application side, the data can be transferred using either the high-performance master interface or

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                                1337
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                   E7 Series


     the slave interface as shown in Figure 16-39.
                                            Figure 16-39 System Side Data Transfer(1)

                 System                                                                 Interface
                 Memory
                                         AHB                       AHB                    Logic

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     When the master interface is used, the data is directly accessed from the system memory by AXI.
     When the slave interface is used, the data is accessed from the system memory by a separate AHB master
     and the SDMMC uses the SDMMC_BUF_DATA_R register. This type of transfer is also called Non-DMA
     transfer or Programmed Input Output (PIO) transfer.
     High throughput can be achieved using the master interface for data transfer. If the application does not
     need such a high throughput, then the slave interface can be used for data transfer.

 16.2.4.5 SDMMC Interrupt Requests
     In the SDMMC, the interrupts are generated based on various events.
     The SDMMC has two interrupt outputs:
       n INTR
       n WAKEUP_INTR

     The INTR signal must be used as an interrupt for different events during active mode. During standby mode,
     WAKEUP_INTR must be used to identify any wakeup event, such as card removal or insertion, or an SDIO
     card interrupt. The interrupts are of level type, that is, the interrupt remains asserted (high) until it is cleared
     by the host or the software.
     The interrupt status registers (SDMMC_NORMAL_INT_STAT_R and SDMMC_ERROR_INT_STAT_R) indicate
     the events that caused the interrupt generation. Each event can be prevented from asserting the interrupt
     on the interrupt signal by setting the corresponding mask bits.
     A bit in the interrupt status registers (SDMMC_NORMAL_INT_STAT_R and SDMMC_ERROR_INT_STAT_R) is
     set only if the corresponding interrupt status enable bit is set (SDMMC_NORMAL_INT_STAT_EN_R and
     SDMMC_ERROR_INT_STAT_EN_R) and the interrupt event is observed. Thus bit set in the interrupt status
     register asserts interrupt only if the corresponding bit in the interrupt signal enable register is set.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1338
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                      E7 Series


                                                                NOTE

       The host driver is responsible for enabling wakeup signals and disabling interrupt signals when the
       host system enters its standby mode, and for disabling wakeup signals and enabling interrupt signals
       when the host system goes into active mode. The host driver must not enable both at the same time.
       The interrupt signals are enabled using interrupt signal enable and wakeup signals are enabled using
       wakeup event enable.


     For information about interrupt wakeup events, refer to the SDMMC_NORMAL_INT_STAT_R, SDMMC_
     ERROR_INT_STAT_R and SDMMC_WUP_CTRL_R registers.

 16.2.4.6 SDMMC Error Detection
     The SDMMC is capable of detecting different types of errors in SD and eMMC transactions. An error is
     detected in either the command or data portion of the transaction. When an error is detected, an error
     interrupt in the Normal Interrupt Status register (SDMMC_NORMAL_INT_STAT_R) is set.
     If an error occurs in the SD or eMMC modes, one of the bits in the SDMMC_ERROR_INT_STAT_R register is
     set. Abort command is used to recover from an error detected during data transfer.
     In addition to the SDMMC_ERROR_INT_STAT_R register, there are two more error status registers, namely
     Auto CMD Status register (SDMMC_AUTO_CMD_STAT_R) and ADMA Error Status register (SDMMC_ADMA_
     ERR_STAT_R).
     Table 16-16 lists the error types and categories into which they can be grouped for both SD and eMMC
     modes.

 16.2.4.7 SDMMC Protocol Overview
     This section provides an overview of the protocols that are supported by SDMMC module in the SD and
     eMMC modes of operation. Additionally, this section provides information about important concepts of the
     standard applicable to the SDMMC.

     Compliance.

     The signals that connect the host controller and the slave device (card) are shown in Table 16-15.
     The number of data lines can be dynamically configured. By default, only the DAT0 line is power up, but the
     host can change the bus width (the number of active data lines).

 16.2.4.7.3 Bus Protocol
     This section discusses the bus protocol for the SD and eMMC modes.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                   Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1340
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                    E7 Series


 16.2.4.7.3.1 SD Bus Protocol
     In SD mode, the bus communication is based on command and data bit streams each bounded by a start bit
     and a stop bit.
     Command is a token that starts an operation and is sent by the host to one or more cards. The command is
     transferred through the CMD line. Response is a token that is sent by the addressed card or cards to the host
     as a reply to the previous command. The response is also transferred serially through the CMD line.
     Data can be set either by the host (Write operation) or by the card (Read operation) and can be transferred
     through the data lines. Data transfers in either direction are done in blocks. Each block has a CRC succeeding
     it. The transfers can either happen as a single or multiple block. The multiple block transmissions are
     terminated by the issue of a stop command on the command line.
     Figure 16-41 shows the command and data bit streams in the SD mode.
                                                  Figure 16-41 SD Mode of Operation(1)

     Host to                            Card to       Data from Card
      Card                               Host             to Host
                                                                                                         Stop CMD
  CMD          cmd               resp
                                                                                                  cmd                resp

   DAT
                                  data block 1     CRC        data block 2   CRC   data block 3   CRC


                        Block Read
                                                                                                        Data Stop
                                                   Mul�ple Block Read


                                                                                                                                SDMMC-007




     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.



 16.2.4.7.3.2 eMMC Bus Protocol
     An eMMC bus data transfer contains a command, a response, and data block tokens. Each data transfer is
     considered as a bus operation that always contains a command and a response token. Additionally, certain
     bus operations also contain a data token. Data sent on the data line can be transferred in one bit (single data
     rate) or in two bits (dual data rate) per clock cycle.
     Similar to the SD bus protocol, the command and data bit streams are bound by a start bit and a stop bit.
     Data transfer occurs in the form of blocks that are followed by CRC bits and the data is transferred in single
     or multiple blocks. While a single/multiple read block is terminated by a stop command on the CMD line, a
     single/multiple write block is terminated by a busy signal on the DAT0 line. Figure 16-42 and Figure 16-43
     show the eMMC block read and write operations, respectively.

     The slave device (card) addressing is implemented using a session address, assigned during the initialization
     phase, by the bus host to the connected card. A card is identified by its Card IDentification (CID) number. This
     method requires the card to have a unique CID number. To ensure uniqueness of CIDs, the CID register
     contains 24 bits (Manufacturer ID (MID) and Original Equipment Manufacturer Identification (OEMID or OID)
     fields) that are defined by JEDEC/MMCA.
     Every device manufacturer is required to apply for an unique MID (and optionally OID) number.

 16.2.4.7.4 Application Layer Data Flow
     The host controller communicates to the software driver using the system bus interface and to the card using
     the SD bus interface. Figure 16-44 presents the high-level data flow through the host controller.
                                             Figure 16-44 Host Controller Data Flow(1)


                                                                      Applica�on Bus


                                                          DMA Interface


                                                 Registers                 Buﬀers



                                               CMD Control             Data Control


                                                   CMD                     DAT[3-0]
                                                                                       SDMMC-010
                                                         SD Bus Interface

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The host driver can transfer data using either a Programmed I/O (PIO) method or using any of the defined
     DMA methods.
     In the PIO method of data transfer, data is transferred to the system memory by the host driver. For SD and
     eMMC modes, it is done on a block basis. In a card write, the controller provides Buffer Write Ready
     interrupt when it has space for one block. Based on this interrupt, the host driver must transfer one block of
     data from the system memory to the SDMMC buffer through the SDMMC_BUF_DATA_R register. After that
     block is sent to the card by the controller, the same mechanism is used in the reverse direction in the case of
     card read using the Buffer Read Ready interrupt.
     The PIO mode is much slower and burdens the processor. It is recommended not to use the PIO mode for
     large transfers.
     The SDMMC module supports the following DMA methods:
       n Single operation DMA (SDMA)
       n Advanced DMA-2 (ADMA2)
       n Advanced DMA-3 (ADMA3)

     The capabilities register defined by the standard provides the information of the type of DMA support
     provided by the particular controller.
     The DMA supports both single block and multi-block transfers. The control bits in the SDMMC_BGAP_CTRL_R
     register are used to Stop and Restart a DMA operation.
     The SDMA mode is used for short data transfer as it generates interrupts at page boundaries.
     The ADMA2 and ADMA3 modes are used for long data transfers and use scatter-gather algorithms. The
     ADMA2 supports a single Read/Write SD operation at a time while the ADMA3 supports multiple Read/Write
     SD operations at a time.
     The SD mode command generation is done by writing into the following registers:
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1343
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                              E7 Series


       n System address registers (SDMMC_SDMASA_R, SDMMC_ADMA_SA_LOW_R)
       n Block size register (SDMMC_BLOCKSIZE_R)
       n Block count register (SDMMC_BLOCKCOUNT_R)
       n Transfer mode register (SDMMC_XFER_MODE_R)
       n Command register (SDMMC_CMD_R)


 16.2.4.7.4.1 ADMA2 Operation
     Figure 16-45 shows the ADMA2 data transfer between the host controller and the system memory and the
     descriptor table that is created by the host driver. A 32-bit address descriptor table is used for a system with
     32-bit addressing and a 64-bit address descriptor table is used for a system with 64-bit addressing. In the
     descriptor table, each line contains information about an address, its length, and attributes that specify the
     operation of the descriptor line. The ADMA2 uses the 64-bit ADMA address register for the descriptor
     pointer. An ADMA2 transfer is triggered by writing to the command register and the ADMA2 processes each
     line in the descriptor table.

 16.2.4.7.4.2 ADMA3 Operation
     The ADMA3 operations can be considered as multiple ADMA2 operations. This is achieved by using an
     integrated descriptor structure which in turn consists of a pair of Command Descriptor and ADMA2
     descriptor. This pair is programmed for a multi-block data transfer from the system memory to the SD card.
     In ADMA2, the host driver issues an SD command using the Host Control registers (SDMMC_HOST_CTRL1_R,
     SDMMC_HOST_CTRL2_R), whereas the ADMA3 uses the Command Descriptors to issue an SD command.
     Figure 16-47 shows a sample ADMA3 data transfer to write three data blocks (Data A, Data B, and Data C) to
     different areas of an SD card.
