 16.2.4.7.5 SDIO Read Wait
     The host device controls the SD_CLK (card clock) to stop the read data block output from a card executing a
     multiple read command when the host cannot accept more data. For the duration of time when the host has
     stopped the SD_CLK, CMD52 cannot be issued. This limitation causes a problem—the host device cannot
     perform the I/O command during a multiple read cycle.
     To overcome this limitation, the SDMMC supports the read wait feature to signal the card that is executing
     multiple read (CMD53) operations to temporarily pause data transfer while allowing the host to send
     commands to any other function within the card. The read wait function is optional for SDIO cards.
     If the card supports read wait, then the SDMMC controller can stall the read data from the card by issuing
     read wait using the SD_D2 output at the block boundary instead of stopping the card clock. The SDMMC
     controller asserts read wait during the Network Access Control (NAC) period of the data block if:
       n   The controller is configured to stop at block gap and read wait is enabled.
       n   The packet buffer of the controller does not have sufficient space to contain the next block of data and
           read wait is enabled.
     The read wait feature is optional for the SDIO cards. This feature is defined only for the SD 1-bit and 4-bit
     modes.

 16.2.4.7.6 SDIO Card Interrupt
     The SD interface supports the interrupt function to allow an SDIO card to interrupt the host. The SDIO card
     provides a level-sensitive interrupt to the SDMMC using the SD_D1 interrupt input in SD mode. This interrupt
     is used to inform the host about error status and also about normal information, such as function Ready.
     This interrupt is also used as a source of wakeup event to inform the host to resume from standby mode. The
     card interrupt is cleared when the card (slave device) stops asserting the interrupt, that is, when the
     application services the interrupt condition.
     For SD 1-bit mode, there are no timing constraints for interrupt.
     For SD 4-bit mode, the SDMMC samples the card interrupt only during the interrupt period that is defined as
     follows:
       n   The interrupt period ends from the end bit of a command that transfers the data block.
       n Resumes two clocks after the completion of the last data block transfer.
       n Within the data block gap, 2-clock interrupt period begins 2 clocks after the end bit of the data blocks.
       n While the SDIO specification defines that the asynchronous interrupt period starts 4 clocks from the
         start of the synchronous interrupt period and ends 1 to 3 clocks from the beginning of the end bit of
         data command, the SDMMC module does not distinguish between the synchronous and asynchronous
         interrupt periods.
       n In case of abort CMD, the interrupt period ends 2 clocks after the end bit of abort CMD and resumes 2
         clocks after the end bit of the response.
     An asynchronous interrupt is effective in the SD 4-bit mode. The asynchronous interrupt generated from the
     slave device while the card clock is stopped (to save the power) is delivered to the host system.

 16.2.4.8 SDMMC Programming Model
     The following programming steps are required before initiating data transfer with the card:
      1. Provide SYST_HCLK to SDMMC.
      2. Read SDMMC_PSTATE_REG to check if the card is already inserted. This step is needed for a removable
         card. If the card is already inserted, then go to Step 4.
      3. Wait for the card insertion interrupt (SDMMC_NORMAL_INT_STAT_R[CARD_INSERTION]). This step is
         necessary for handling removable cards. Card detection sequence is described in Section 16.2.4.8.1
         Programming to Detect the Card.
      4. Set up the basic settings for SDMMC as described in Section 16.2.4.8.2 Programming the Host
         Controller. Separate setup sequences are provided for SD (Section 16.2.4.8.2.1 SD Interface) and eMMC
         (Section 16.2.4.8.2.2 eMMC Interface) cards. This step can also be executed immediately after Step 1.
      5. Enable input clocks (other than SYST_HCLK) that are available in the SDMMC. Internal clocks (ACLK,
         BCLK, and TMCLK) are enabled first, followed by the card clocks (CCLK_TX and CCLK_RX) as discussed in



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                             1349
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                 E7 Series


           the programming sequence in Section 16.2.4.8.3.1 Host Controller Clock Setup Sequence. At this stage,
           SDMMC is ready to communicate with the card.
        6. Set up the SD card connected to SDMMC as explained in the programming sequence in Section
           16.2.4.8.4.1 SD Card Interface Setup. If SDMMC is connected to an eMMC card, follow the programming
           sequence outlined in Section 16.2.4.8.4.2 eMMC Card Interface Setup. This is a simplified sequence
           specifically for an eMMC card, as the card type is always known. Both programming sequences provide
           power and clock to the cards.
        7. After powering up the card, the card is initialized. The appropriate sequence, as shown in Table 16-18,
           must be followed depending on the type of connected card.

 16.2.4.8.6 Programming Terminate Transaction
     A terminate command can be issued to the card to end an ongoing data transaction. To terminate a
     transaction on an SD/eMMC card, CMD12 is issued, while CMD52 is used for terminating a transaction on an
     SDIO card.
     The following are scenarios when a terminate command must be issued:
       n To stop an infinite block transfer
       n To halt a transfer upon a request from an application
       n To stop a transfer due to error detection

     The sequence to issue a terminate command is shown in Section 16.2.4.8.6.1 Terminate Command
     Sequence. A terminate command can be issued either synchronously or asynchronously during data transfer.
     In an asynchronous terminate, the command is issued at any time, regardless of the data transfer state, as a
     subcommand. In a synchronous terminate, the data transfer is stopped (at the block gap) before the
     terminate command is issued. Both methods are explained in Section 16.2.4.8.6.2 Asynchronous Terminate,
     and Section 16.2.4.8.6.3 Synchronous Terminate, respectively.

     For optimal performance during card read/write DMA operations, it is recommended to set the End bit on
     the final transfer descriptor. Additionally, the End bit must always be set on a descriptor of type Tran.
     Possible descriptor types are provided in Table 16-20 for quick reference.
                                                Table 16-20 Descriptor Types
   Act2 Act1 Act0 Symbol            Comment        ADMA2 descriptor address
    0      0       0      NOP     No Operation Do not execute the current line and proceed to the next line.
    0      1       0      RSV       Reserved     Same as NOP: Do not execute the current line and proceed to the next line.
    1      0       0      Tran    Transfer Data Transfer data of one descriptor line.
    1      1       0      Link   Link Descriptor Link to another descriptor.

                                                               1371
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                           www.alifsemi.com

                                                                  NOTE

       The descriptor type recommendation is applicable only to ADMA2 and ADMA3 transfers.

     The following are the descriptor requirements for an ADMA3 CMD:
       n Setting infinite data transfer (SDMMC_XFER_MODE_R[BLOCK_COUNT_ENABLE] = 0) is not allowed
         except for single block transfer (SDMMC_XFER_MODE_R[MULTI_BLK_SEL] = 0).
       n As ADMA3 only supports 32-bit, the SDMMC_XFER_MODE_R[BLOCK_COUNT_ENABLE] is set to 1 and
         SDMMC_BLOCKCOUNT_R[BLOCK_CNT] is set to 0000h. Setting Stop Count (32-bit Block Count SDMMC_

                                                               1372

         SDMASA_R[BLOCKCNT_SDMASA] = 0) is not allowed, except for single block transfer (SDMMC_XFER_
         MODE_R[MULTI_BLK_SEL] = 0).
       n Setting no data transfer (Block Size SDMMC_BLOCKSIZE_R[XFER_BLOCK_SIZE] = 0) is not allowed, except
         for no data transfer command in the Command Descriptor (CDEnd = 1).
       n In the case of memory data transfer command, SDMMC_XFER_MODE_R[AUTO_CMD_ENABLE] = 0x3) is
         used to ensure that the Command Descriptor is independent of whether the card supports CMD23. For
         other commands (including SDIO), SDMMC_XFER_MODE_R[AUTO_CMD_ENABLE] = 0 is used to disable
         Auto CMD.
     During card read/write DMA operations, it is recommended that the very last transfer descriptor also has the
     End bit set for marginal performance improvement. The End bit should always be set in descriptors of type
     Tran.

 16.2.4.8.8.11 Terminate Mandatory Boot
     Figure 16-84 shows the programming sequence for terminating a mandatory boot when the application
     needs to exit the boot prematurely, either due to an error or upon receiving sufficient boot data.
     However, a mandatory boot is typically exited by SDMMC automatically pulling the CMD line high once the
     boot data is successfully transmitted to the system memory and the transfer complete interrupt is
     generated. Note that command inhibit can be asserted while the CMD line is pulled low, and the command
     complete interrupt can be generated when exiting the mandatory boot.

 16.2.4.8.8.12 Initiating Alternate Boot
     Alternate boot is a command-based boot operation and can be initiated by issuing CMD0 with the
     0xFFFFFFFA argument. For the programming sequence for initiating an alternate book, see Section
     16.2.4.8.7.5 Issuing CMD with Data Transfer, Section 16.2.4.8.7.7 Issuing CMD with Data Transfer (Using
     SDMA), and Section 16.2.4.8.7.8 Issuing CMD with Data Transfer (Using ADMA2) with the following
     exceptions:
       n If boot acknowledgement is expected, SDMMC_BOOT_CTRL_R can be programmed to set the timeout
         counter for boot acknowledgement before setting the SDMMC_CMD_R register.
       n Response check cannot be performed as CMD0 has no response.
       n Terminating the alternate boot operation follows Section 16.2.4.8.8.13 Terminate Alternate Boot
         instead of CMD12 for other data transfer operations.
     When the boot is initiated, the device state is assumed to be in pre-boot state and 74 clock cycles has expired
     after power is stable before issuing CMD0.

 16.2.5.3 SDMMC Registers Description

 16.2.5.3.1 SDMMC_SDMASA_R Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            SDMA System Address Register
         0x0                                This register is used to configure a 32-bit Block Count or an SDMA System Address
                             R/W
     Base address                           based on the SDMMC_HOST_CTRL2_R[HOST_VER4_ENABLE] bit. This register is
                                            applicable for both SD and eMMC Modes.


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                            32-bit Block Count—SDMA System Address.
                                                            SDMMC_HOST_CTRL2_R[HOST_VER4_ENABLE] = 0x0: The
                                                            BLOCKCNT_SDMASA bit field contains the system memory address
                                                            for an SDMA transfer in the 32-bit addressing Mode. When the
                                                            host controller stops an SDMA transfer, this bit field points to the
                                                            system address of the next contiguous data position. It can be
                                                            accessed only if no transaction is executing. Reading this bit field
                                                            during data transfers may return invalid value.
                                                            32-bit Block Count
                                                            SDMMC_HOST_CTRL2_R[HOST_VER4_ENABLE] = 0x1: From the
                                                            host controller version 4.10 specification, the BLOCKCNT_SDMASA
    31-0      BLOCKCNT_SDMASA         R/W         0x0       bit field is redefined as 32-bit Block Count. The host controller
                                                            decrements the block count of this bit field for every block transfer
                                                            and the data transfer stops when the count reaches zero. This bit
                                                            field must be accessed when no transaction is executing. Reading
                                                            this bit field during data transfers may return invalid value.
                                                            0xFFFFFFFF: 4GB—1 Block
                                                            ...
                                                            0x00000002: 2 Blocks
                                                            0x00000001: 1 Block
                                                            0x00000000: Stop count
                                                            Note: For the SDMMC_HOST_CTRL2_R[HOST_VER4_ENABLE] =
                                                            0x0, the host driver does not program the system address in this

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                              1390
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                      E7 Series


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             bit field while operating in ADMA mode. The system address must
                                                             be programmed in the ADMA System Address register (SDMMC_
                                                             ADMA_SA_LOW_R).
                                                             For the SDMMC_HOST_CTRL2_R[HOST_VER4_ENABLE] = 0x0, the
                                                             host driver programs a non-zero 32-bit block count value in this bit
                                                             field when Auto CMD23 is enabled for non-DMA and ADMA
                                                             modes. Auto CMD23 cannot be used with SDMA.
                                                             This bit field must be programmed with a non-zero value for data
                                                             transfer if the 32-bit Block Count register is used instead of the 16-
                                                             bit Block Count register (SDMMC_BLOCKCOUNT_R).



 16.2.5.3.2 SDMMC_BLOCKSIZE_R Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            Block Size Register
         0x4
                             R/W            This register is used to configure an SDMA buffer boundary and the number of
     Base address

    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
     15       RESERVED                 R           0x0       Reserved.
                                                             SDMA Buffer Boundary.
                                                             These bits specify the size of a contiguous buffer in the system
                                                             memory. The SDMA transfer waits at every boundary specified by
                                                             these bits and the host controller generates the DMA interrupt to
                                                             request the host driver to update the SDMMC_SDMASA_R
                                                             register.

   14-12 SDMA_BUF_BDARY               R/W          0x0       0x1: 8KB Bytes SDMA buffer boundary

                                                             0x3: 32KB Bytes SDMA buffer boundary
                                                             0x4: 64KB Bytes SDMA buffer boundary
                                                             0x5: 128KB Bytes SDMA buffer boundary
                                                             0x6: 256KB Bytes SDMA buffer boundary
                                                             0x7: 512KB Bytes SDMA buffer boundary
                                                             Transfer Block Size.
                                                             These bits specify the block size of data transfers. In case of
                                                             memory, it is set to 512 bytes. It can be accessed only if no
                                                             transaction is executing. Read operations during transfers may
    11-0      XFER_BLOCK_SIZE         R/W          0x0

 17 Camera Interfaces

 17.1 Camera Parallel Interface (CPI)

 17.1.1 CPI Overview
     The digital Camera Parallel Interface (CPI) enables pixel data reception from external CMOS sensors and
     camera modules, or from the internal MIPI CSI controller. The data transfer rate is limited by the maximum
     supported pixel clock and data bus width.
     The device includes:
       n One CPI controller in Shared Peripherals. The CPI receives parallel data from either of the following
         sources:
         l External camera sensor (up to 16-bit data bus)

         l Internal MIPI CSI controller (16-bit or 48-bit IPI data bus)

       n One Low-Power CPI (LPCPI) controller in the RTSS-HE. The LPCPI receives parallel data from an external
         camera sensor (up to 8-bit data bus).
     Each CPI controller supports the following main features:
       n Up to 60 MHz pixel clock
       n Programmable polarity for the pixel clock, horizontal and vertical synchronization signals
       n Single frame capture snapshot mode only (automated streaming mode is not supported)
       n Pixel clock output to external camera sensor

     Each CPI controller supports the following specific features depending on the pixel data source and bus
     width:
       n External camera sensor source:
         l Data modes: 1-, 2-, 4-, 8-bit (CPI and LPCPI), and 16-bit (CPI only)

         l Data mask for 16-bit data mode (CPI only)

         l Programmable MSB/LSB selection

         l Transfer 10-bit pixel encoding over 8-bit wide data bus

       n MIPI CSI controller source:
         l Data modes: 8-, 16-, 32-, 64-bit

         l Halt function to prevent FIFO overflow




                                                        NOTE

       All Low Power peripherals are single-master accessible, including LPCPI. Ensure that application
       software manages access to these LP peripherals such that no more than one bus master (CPU or
       DMA) attempts access at a time, using semaphores or similar techniques.


     Figure 17-1 provides a high-level overview of the CPI implementation in the device.

 17.1.4 CPI Functional Description


                                                                   NOTE

       All information related to CPI in this section also applies to LPCPI, unless stated otherwise.


 17.1.4.1 CPI Introduction
     Figure 17-6 presents a simplified diagram of the CPI controller main internal blocks and connections.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                     Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1445
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                                   E7 Series


                                                     Figure 17-6 CPI Block Diagram(1)
                                                                     CPI Controller

                 CAM_D
                                             Input
                               Mux            FIFO
            CSI_PIXDATA

                                                                                                                   AXI
              CAM_PCLK                                          Control               Output              AXI
                                     PIXEL_CLK                   Logic                 FIFO           Bus Master
                               Mux
              CSI_PIXCLK

           CAM_V/HSYNC

            CSI_V/HSYNC
                                                                                  Control Registers
                                                                                                                         CPI-001




     1. Input from MIPI CSI controller is not supported for LPCPI.


     The data flow within the CPI controller comprises of the following main steps:
      1. The input pixel data is sampled on the input PIXEL_CLK clock and written into the input FIFO.
      2. Data is read from the input FIFO and formatted based on CPI registers configuration, and then written to
         the output FIFO.
      3. Finally, the processed data is transferred from the output FIFO to a system memory location specified by
         SW, via the AXI interface.

 17.1.4.2 CPI Clocks
     The CPI controller receives the following clocks:
       n PCLK: APB register configuration clock.
       n ACLK: AXI interface clock for data write to system memory.
       n CAM_PCLK: Pixel clock for data received on the external camera sensor interface
       n CSI_PIXCLK: Pixel clock for data received on the MIPI CSI interface

     The CPI controller also supports a XVCLK pixel clock output to an external camera sensor.

 17.1.4.3 CPI Reset
     The CPI controller can be reset by software in the CAM_CTRL[SW_RESET] register bit.

 17.1.4.4 CPI Interrupt Requests
     The CPI controller supports a single output IRQ line. A number of events can be mapped to the IRQ line. Each
     interrupt event can be enabled/disabled individually in the CAM_INTR_ENA register.
     The status of the interrupt events can be read in the CAM_INTR register. Once set by hardware, each
     interrupt status register bit sticks to high until the software writes one to clear it.

 17.1.4.5 CPI DMA Requests
     The CPI controller supports two output DMA request lines, VSYNC_DMA_REQ and HSYNC_DMA_REQ.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                                     1446
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                            www.alifsemi.com

 17.1.4.6 CPI Configuration Sequence
     Figure 17-7 summarizes the CPI controller configuration steps.
                                          Figure 17-7 CPI Configuration Flow


                                                Enable CPI Controller



                                               Conﬁgure CPI Controller



                                             So�ware Reset CPI Controller



                                                 Start CPI Controller



                                                  Wait for Interrupt           CPI-002




      1. Enable the clock supplies for the CPI controller, as explained in Section 17.1.2 CPI Internal Connections.
      2. Program the following registers inside the CPI controller:
         n CAM_INTR, CAM_INTR_ENA, CAM_CFG, CAM_FIFO_CTRL, CAM_VIDEO_FCFG
         n Program CAM_CSI_CMCFG if pixel data is sourced from the MIPI CSI interface
         n Program CAM_FRAME_ADDR for the start address of frame buffer in system memory
      3. Follow the register configuration steps below to apply soft reset to the CPI controller:
         a. Set CAM_CTRL = 0—prepare for soft reset
         b. Set CAM_CTRL = 0x100—activate soft reset by setting bit [SW_RESET]
         c. Set CAM_CTRL = 0—stop soft reset
         d. Set CAM_CTRL = 0x1011—start the CPI controller by setting bit [START], selecting external camera
             clock through bit [FIFO_CLK_SEL], and setting the operation mode with bit [SNAPSHOT]
      4. Stop the CPI controller in the interrupt service routine:
         n Set CAM_CTRL = 0
         n Once CAM_CTRL[START] register bit is cleared to zero, the CPI controller will not stop immediately—it
            always captures a full frame of data then stops on the [START] bit being cleared.

 17.1.4.7 CPI Input Data from External Camera Sensor
     Program CAM_CFG[MIPI_CSI] = 0 to select the external camera sensor interface to be the source of pixel
     data.
     The following bit fields in the CAM_CFG register control the data mode:
       n The [DATA_MODE] field defines the number of active data pins from the external camera sensor
         interface
       n The [MSB] field selects how data is stored in memory—MSB or LSB first
       n The [CODE10ON8] field enables the transfer of 10-bit encoded pixel data on 8 data pins
       n When [DATA_MODE] = 16-bit (16 data pins), the [DATA_MASK] field is used to select the data mask

                                                        1447

     interface:
                 Table 17-6 CPI Data Mode Dependencies for External Camera Sensor Interface
           Data Mode                   MSB/LSB First               10 Bits on 8 Pins               Data Mask
                1                           Yes                           No                            No

                4                           Yes                           No                            No

 17.1.4.7.1 Data Mode = 1
     Camera sensor sending out encoded pixel data on 1 data pin.
     Every 8 data received in 8 PIXEL_CLK cycles are stored into a byte of memory space.
     Received data order (each Dn is 1 bit):
       n   D0, D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, … , D0, D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D7
     When CAM_CFG[MSB] = 0, which selects LSB mode, data is stored in memory in below order:
       bit 0          bit 1         bit 2          bit 3          bit 4          bit 5         bit 6             bit 7
        D0             D1            D2             D3             D4             D5            D6                D7


     When [MSB] = 1, which selects MSB mode, data is stored in memory in below order:
       bit 0          bit 1         bit 2          bit 3          bit 4          bit 5         bit 6             bit 7
        D7             D6            D5             D4             D3             D2            D1                D0


 17.1.4.7.2 Data Mode = 2
     Camera sensor sending out encoded pixel data on 2 data pins.
     Every 4 data received in 4 PIXEL_CLK cycles are stored into a byte of memory space.
     Received data order (each Dn is 2 bits):
       n   D0, D1, D2, D3, … , D0, D1, D2, D3
     When CAM_CFG[MSB] = 0, which selects LSB mode, data is stored in memory in below order:
       bit 0          bit 1         bit 2          bit 3          bit 4          bit 5         bit 6             bit 7
               D0                           D1                            D2                              D3


     When [MSB] = 1, which selects MSB mode, data is stored in memory in below order:

 17.1.4.7.3 Data Mode = 4

                                                                   NOTE

       The CPI always stores data to memory in double-word 64-bit unit. Thus, Byte 0 in above table is the
       LSB byte of a 64-bit double-word memory space.


     If the number of data received from a camera sensor for an image frame is not the integer multiple of
     double-word (64-bit), the remainder will occupy a full double-word.
     For example, if an image size is 6402 bytes, the CPI will store it to memory and occupy 6404 bytes of memory
     space.

 17.1.4.7.5 Data Mode = 8 (10-bit on 8-pin Mode Enabled)
     Camera sensor sending out encoded pixel data on 8 data pins. Every 2 data received in 2 PIXEL_CLK cycles are
     stored into a half-word (16-bit) of memory space. For each half-word, the MSB bits [15:10] are always zero.
     For CAM_CFG[MSB] = 0, the received data order is as follows:
       n   D0[9:2], D0[1:0], D1[9:2], D1[1:0], …
     For [MSB] = 1, received data order is as follows:
       n   D0[1:0], D0[9:2], D1[1:0], D1[9:2], …
     CPI stores data in memory in below order:
   bit 0   bit 1   bit 2    bit 3   bit 4        bit 5   bit 6   bit 7   bit 8   bit 9   bit 10 bit 11 bit 12 bit 13 bit 14 bit 15

   bit 0   bit 1   bit 2    bit 3   bit 4        bit 5   bit 6   bit 7   bit 8   bit 9   bit 10 bit 11 bit 12 bit 13 bit 14 bit 15
     D1 [0:1]                                      D1 [2:9]                                0      0      0      0        0       0
   bit 0   bit 1   bit 2    bit 3   bit 4        bit 5   bit 6   bit 7   bit 8   bit 9   bit 10 bit 11 bit 12 bit 13 bit 14 bit 15
     D2 [0:1]                                      D2 [2:9]                                0      0      0      0        0       0
   bit 0   bit 1   bit 2    bit 3   bit 4        bit 5   bit 6   bit 7   bit 8   bit 9   bit 10 bit 11 bit 12 bit 13 bit 14 bit 15

 17.1.4.9 CPI Timings and Frame Configuration

 17.1.4.9.1 Horizontal Timing
     The CPI controller takes HSYNC input signal as data enable, and captures input data only when HSYNC is high.
     In Figure 17-8, DATA_EN is alias to HSYNC.
     In ideal case, the rising edge of the data clock driven by the camera sensor is supposed to be center-aligned
     to the pixel data. The data clock can be either free running or gated (only valid when DATA_EN is high).
     In case the rising edge of the data clock is edge-aligned to the pixel data, there is an option to invert the data
     clock by programming the CAM_CFG[PCLK_POL] register bit:
       n [PCLK_POL] = 0—Do not invert data clock input
       n [PCLK_POL] = 1—Invert data clock input

                                                Figure 17-8 CPI Horizontal Timing

                                                                  LIne N
                                 DATA_EN

                                   DATA          D0     D1       D2        .....................   Dn



                                    CLK                                                                     CPI-003




 17.1.4.9.2 VSYNC and HSYNC Polarity
     The CPI controller requires both VSYNC and HSYNC input signals to be valid high. If these signals come from
     the camera sensor in active low state, then program the CAM_CFG[VSYNC_POL] and [HSYNC_POL] register
     bits to invert them, as follows:
       n       [VSYNC_POL] = 0—Do not invert VSYNC input
       n       [VSYNC_POL] = 1—Invert VSYNC input


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1457
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                        www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                               E7 Series


       n [HSYNC_POL] = 0—Do not invert HSYNC input
       n [HSYNC_POL] = 1—Invert HSYNC input


 17.1.4.9.3 Data Enable Configuration
     The CPI controller takes HSYNC input signal as data enable and captures input data only when HSYNC is high,
     as already covered in Section 17.1.4.9.1 Horizontal Timing.
     For some camera sensors, VSYNC input signal is used as additional data enable. In such cases, the CPI
     controller captures input data when both VSYNC and HSYNC are high. This option is controlled by the CAM_
     CFG[VSYNC_EN] register bit, as follows:
       n [VSYNC_EN] = 0—Capture input data when HSYNC is high
       n [VSYNC_EN] = 1—Capture input data when both HSYNC and VSYNC are high

     When [VSYNC_EN] = 1, the VSYNC signal stays high to cover all the valid pixel data, as depicted in Figure 17-9.
     Here, DATA_EN is alias to HSYNC.
                                       Figure 17-9 CPI Data Enable Configuration

                   VSYNC                    Frame N                           Frame N+1



                 DATA_EN           Line 0      Line 1    Line N      Line 0      Line 1    Line N

                                                                                                     CPI-004
                    DATA           Data        Data      Data        Data        Data       Data




 17.1.4.9.3.1 Scenario #1, VSYNC and HSYNC are Aligned
     The rising edge of VSYNC and DATA_EN (alias to HSYNC) are aligned, see Figure 17-10. In this case, set CAM_
     CFG[WAIT_VSYNC] = 0, to start video capture without waiting for VSYNC signal.
                                     Figure 17-10 CPI VSYNC Aligned with HSYNC

                    DATA           Data        Data      Data        Data        Data       Data




 17.1.4.9.3.2 Scenario #2, VSYNC and HSYNC are Not Aligned
     The rising edge of VSYNC comes at least 3 data clock cycles prior to DATA_EN (alias to HSYNC), see Figure 17-
     11. In this case, set CAM_CFG[WAIT_VSYNC] = 1, to start video capture on rising edge of VSYNC signal.

 17.1.4.9.4 Frame Size
     Configure the image frame size through the following CAM_VIDEO_FCFG register fields:
       n   [ROW]: Defines the number of rows/lines of an image frame minus one
       n   [DATA]: Defines the amount of data in a single row/line. This value must match the camera output.
     Example: Image size = 640 (data) x 480 (lines)
       n Program [ROW] = 480 – 1 = 479
       n Program [DATA] = 640



                                                        NOTE

       The term “pixel” does not always represent the actual data transferred with the data clock. The
       definition of “pixel” varies across camera sensors. Refer to the camera sensor’s documentation for
       detailed information.


     For example, a pixel might be comprised of 4 data of “R, G, G, B” which have been sent out of the camera
     sensor on 4 data clock cycles. In this case, 1 pixel = 4 data .
     At the CPI controller side, the “data” does not equal to “pixel”; it is one data captured by one clock cycle.

 17.1.4.10 CPI FIFO Settings

 17.1.4.10.1 FIFO Types and AXI Interface
     There are 2 types of FIFO in the CPI controller:
       n      The input FIFO is used to synchronize incoming data from the camera sensor interface / MIPI CSI
              clock domain to the AXI interface clock domain. The input FIFO is not programmable.
       n      The output FIFO is used to store the captured data and then write it to the memory space via AXI
              interface. The watermark of output FIFO can be programmed based on the use case scenarios.
     The output FIFO is 32 (depth) x 64 (bit width) in size. The data writes on AXI is always 64-bit wide.
     The CPI controller hardware can handle the AXI write crossing the 4KB boundary of AXI address space. Thus,
     there’s no limitation on software to allocate the memory space for buffering the image data.

 17.1.4.10.2 Output FIFO Almost Empty Watermark
     The settings of FIFO almost empty watermark determine the AXI burst length.
     An AXI write will not start until the FIFO almost empty goes invalid, which means there is a certain amount of
     data accumulated in the output FIFO.
     The FIFO almost empty watermark can be programmed in the CAM_FIFO_CTRL[RD_WMARK] register field
     with recommended range = [4 ÷ 16].
     For example, if [RD_WMARK] = 10, when there is 10 or more data accumulated in the output FIFO, the CPI
     controller will initiate an AXI burst write with length = 10, data width = 64-bit.
     At the end of each frame, there might be few data left in the output FIFO, which is less than 10. In this case,
     the CPI controller will initiate an AXI burst write with length = (left data amount), data width = 64-bit.
     The CPI controller hardware can predict a burst crossing the 4KB boundary and break it down to avoid
     violation of AXI protocol.
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1459
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                          E7 Series


 17.1.4.10.3 Output FIFO Almost Full Watermark
     When MIPI CSI is selected as data source, the FIFO almost full watermark can be used to generate halt signal
     on the CSI IPI interface to prevent output FIFO overflow. For more information of the CSI IPI halt function,
     see IPI Halt Functionality.
     The FIFO almost full watermark can be programmed in the CAM_FIFO_CTRL[WR_WMARK] register field with
     recommended range = [16 ÷ 28]. The control of the halt signal is controlled by the CAM_CFG[CSI_HALT_EN]
     register bit.
     For example, if [WR_WMARK] = 24 and [CSI_HALT_EN] = 1 (halt function enabled), when data accumulated in
     the output FIFO reaches 24, the CPI controller will generate halt signal on the CSI IPI interface. If the halt
     function is disabled (that is, [CSI_HALT_EN] = 0), then [WR_WMARK] setting has no effect and the output
     FIFO might overflow.

 17.2 MIPI Camera Serial Interface 2 (CSI)

 17.2.1 CSI Overview
     The MIPI Camera Serial Interface (CSI) facilitates the data reception from a MIPI CSI-2 compliant camera
     sensor. The interface is realized through a MIPI CSI-2 host controller that implements the protocol functions
     defined in the MIPI CSI-2 Specification, and a MIPI D-PHY module acting as the physical layer.
     The device includes a single CSI implementation.
     The CSI supports the following main features:
       n Conformity to MIPI standards:
         l MIPI Alliance Specification for Camera Serial Interface 2 (CSI-2), Version 1.2, January 2014

         l MIPI Alliance Specification for D-PHY, Version 1.2, September 2014

       n PHY Protocol Interface (PPI) between the CSI-2 host controller and the D-PHY receiver
       n Up to two D-PHY RX data lanes
       n Up to 2.5 Gbps throughput per lane
       n Dynamically configurable multi-lane merging
       n Long and short packet decoding
       n Virtual channel extension—up to 16 interleaved virtual channels
       n Timing accurate signaling of frame and line synchronization packets
       n Several frame formats:
         l General frame or digital interlaced video with or without accurate sync timing

         l Data type (packet or frame level) and virtual channel interleaving

       n Primary and secondary data formats:
         l YUV420: 8-bit (legacy)/8-bit/10-bit/8-bit (CSPS)/10-bit (CSPS)

         l YUV422: 8-bit/10-bit

         l RGB: RGB888/RGB666/RGB565/RGB555/RGB444

         l RAW: RAW6/RAW7/RAW8/RAW10/RAW12/RAW14/RAW16

         l Generic 8-bit long packet data types

         l User-defined byte-based data

         l Embedded data (RAW16)

       n Error detection and correction at PHY, packet, line and frame level
       n Up to four Data IDs (VC/DT pairs) for simultaneous error monitoring
       n Data scrambling for Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) and Radio Frequency Interference (RFI)
         mitigation
       n Configurable Image Pixel Interface (IPI) to system level that provides:
         l Conversion of CSI-2 packets data from byte to pixel format

         l 16- or 48-bit output parallel data bus, operating at pixel clock rate and delivering either one color

            component at a time or one pixel (or pair of pixels) per pixel clock cycle, respectively
         l Vertical and horizontal timing accurate video synchronization signals

         l 1024-entry FIFO for data storage and synchronization

       n APB slave configuration interface

     The CSI does not provide support for RAW data type decompression.
     Figure 17-12 provides a high-level overview of the CSI implementation in the device.

 17.2.4 CSI Functional Description

 17.2.4.1 CSI Introduction
     Figure 17-15 presents a simplified diagram of the CSI controller main internal blocks and connections.

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The CSI controller includes the following main blocks:
       n Pipeline: The pipeline registers the PPI high-speed related signals received from the D-PHY RX to avoid
         possible timing constraints in the device.
       n Descrambler: This block exploits the linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) seeds, already used by the
         camera sensor transmitter, to convert the PPI scrambled data to its original value.
       n PHY Adaptation Layer: This block is responsible for managing the PHY interface, including PHY error
         handling.
       n Packet Analyzer: This blocks handles the data lane merging, alongside with header decoding, error
         detection and correction, frame size error detection, and CRC error detection.
       n Image Pixel Interface (IPI): This interface converts the input data, within the received CSI-2 packets, from
         byte to pixel format, and then (similarly to an RGB interface) outputs a 16-bit or 48-bit pixel data bus
         enriched with vertical and horizontal synchronism information.
       n Error Management: This block notifies and monitors the error conditions on the CSI-2 link.
       n Register Bank: The register bank is accessible through an APB slave interface, which enables access to
         the CSI controller registers, both for controller configuration and control. There is also a fully
         programmable interrupt generator to inform the system about certain events.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1471
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


 17.2.4.2 CSI Clocks
     For most part, the CSI controller works on the high-speed byte clock, RXBYTECLKHS, provided by the D-PHY
     RX module. The RXBYTECLKHS rate is 1/4th of the DDR clock on the D-PHY clock lane.
     The PCLK is the input clock signal on the APB slave interface. It is used for internal register configuration.
     The PIXCLK is the IPI interface output pixel clock. The parallel pixel data is delivered to system level on this
     clock.
     The clock frequencies of CSI controller based on clock domains are as follows:
       n RXBYTECLKHS: This frequency is 1/8th of the serial D-PHY bitrate:
         l 1.0 Gbps: Maximum frequency of RXBYTECLKHS = 125.0 MHz

         l 1.5 Gbps: Maximum frequency of RXBYTECLKHS = 187.5 MHz

         l 2.5 Gbps: Maximum frequency of RXBYTECLKHS = 312.5 MHz

       n PCLK: The minimum required frequency is 20 MHz.
       n PIXCLK: There is no protocol limitation for this clock frequency.


 17.2.4.3 CSI Resets
     The CSI controller can be reset in software by writing to the CSI_CSI2_RESETN[CSI2_RESETN] register bit.

 17.2.4.4 CSI Interrupt Requests
     The CSI controller generates a single interrupt signal, CSI_IRQ, to system level.
     The CSI_INT_ST_<group> registers are associated with error condition reporting. These registers trigger the
     CSI_IRQ which is synchronous with the PCLK clock.
     The triggering of the CSI_IRQ can be masked by programming the CSI_INT_MSK_<group> mask registers. By
     default all error events are masked. When any bit of these registers is set to 1, it enables the interrupt for a
     specific error. The error bit is always set in the respective the CSI_INT_ST_<group> registers. The CSI_INT_ST_
     <group> registers are always cleared after a read operation.
     The CSI_INT_FORCE_<group> registers are used for test purposes and allow triggering interrupt events
     individually, without the need to activate the conditions that trigger the interrupt sources. Setting any bit of
     these registers to 1 triggers the corresponding interrupt.
     Figure 17-16 shows the main parts of the interrupt mechanism.

 17.2.4.5 CSI Supported Resolutions and Frame Rates
     The MIPI CSI-2 Specification does not define the supported standard resolutions or frame rates. Camera
     sensor resolution, blanking periods, synchronization events, frame rates, and pixel color depth play a
     fundamental role in the required bandwidth. All these variables make it difficult to define a standard
     procedure to estimate the minimum lane rate and the minimum number of lanes that support a specific CSI-
     2 device.

 17.2.4.6 CSI Pipeline
     The pipeline interface includes a buffer (1024-entry FIFO) that is added to a the following subset of PPI
     signals:
       n RXDATAHS
       n RXVALIDHS
       n ERRSOTHS
       n ERRSOTSYNCH

     The buffering helps avoiding possible timing constraints in the device.

 17.2.4.7 CSI Descrambler
     Data scrambling is used to mitigate the effects of EMI and RF self-interference by spreading the information
     transmission energy of the link over a possibly large frequency band, using a data randomization technique.
     Transmitted data is scrambled with a Pseudo-Random-Bit-Stream (PRBS) to reduce the likelihood of a
     repetitive pattern on a lane basis.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1475
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                E7 Series

     generator polynomial, shown in equation 17-1:
                                                                                                                      (17-1)

     16-bit LSFR seed by the CSI_SCRAMBLING_SEED1 (for data lane 0) and CSI_SCRAMBLING_SEED2 (for data
     lane 1) registers. The descrambling feature can be enabled in the CSI_SCRAMBLING[SCRAMBLE_ENABLE]
     register bit.

 17.2.4.8 CSI Virtual Channel Extension
     The CSI controller supports multiple independent input data streams of up to 32 peripherals. The data stream
     for each peripheral can be a virtual channel. These data streams can be interleaved and sent as sequential
     packets, with each packet dedicated to a particular peripheral or channel.
     The CSI controller supports up to 16 interleaved virtual channels on the same D-PHY link.
     Setting the CSI_VC_EXTENSION[VSX] bit to 1 selects a legacy mode, where the virtual channel extension
     feature is disabled and the corresponding field on the packet header is ignored by the CSI controller.

 17.2.4.9 CSI Image Pixel Interface (IPI)

 17.2.4.9.1 IPI Overview
     IPI is a parallel interface that delivers:
       n    Timing information
       n    16-bit or 48-bit pixel data


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                 Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1476
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                   www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                    E7 Series


     The IPI contains a 2-port RAM 1024-entry FIFO that allows the CSI controller to buffer the incoming data until
     it is necessary to process pixels to the output.
     The IPI monitors packets that match the Virtual Channel, programmed in the CSI_IPI_VCID register. All other
     Virtual Channel identifier packets are ignored. This interface interprets Frame Start, Frame End, Line Start,
     Line End, and Blanking packets to gather timing information. The IPI only accepts one of the following data
     types received from the camera:
       n RGB
       n RAW
       n Embedded data

     The selected data type is programmed in the CSI_IPI_DATA_TYPE register, and all other data types are
     ignored.

 17.2.4.9.2 IPI Operating Modes
     The IPI has two different operating modes for the generation of frame timing signals: camera timing mode
     and controller timing mode. The operating mode can be selected in the CSI_IPI_MODE[IPI_MODE] register
     bit.
     Camera Timing Mode
     In camera timing mode, the frame timing signals, vertical and horizontal synchronism, are generated based in
     the information of the packets such as Frame Start, Line Start, and Blanking packets. Figure 17-20 illustrates
     the generation of the frame timing signals.
     To ensure the correct generation of events from the received packets, the following expression must be met,
     where MIN_TIME_BETWEEN_PACKETS represents the minimum time that may occur between two
     consecutive received packets.

                              DATAEN

     Controller Timing Mode
     In controller timing mode, the IPI generates frame timing signals based on the programed configuration.
     After a Frame Start is received, the IPI generates the frame ignoring all other synchronism packets.
     The following registers configure the frame:

     n RAW data types: The interface transfers two or more pixels in parallel reducing the number of clock cycles that is necessary to send the same

     n RGB data types: Deliver one pixel per clock cycle.

     n All empty bits (table cells) that do not carry information from a color component (represented with white color) are filled with 0's.
     n Indexes are used along with a letter identifying the color component to distinguish different pixels of the same data type. This does not apply
       to RGB data types because the R, G, and B components all belong to the same pixel.
     n For RAW data types, two pixels are present for each clock cycle and there is a distinction between odd and even lines.

 17.2.4.9.4 IPI 2-Port RAM
     Synchronous 2-port RAMs are used by the CSI controller to implement FIFOs for pixel buffering and data
     movement between CSI-2 link clock and pixel clock domains. The size of RAM is selected to accommodate
     the difference between the two clock domains and frame buffering requirements.
     Camera Mode
     There are two possible situations in camera mode:
       n The distance between the data packets in camera throughput is lesser than or equal to the HLINE period
         in IPI.
       n The distance between the data packets in camera throughput is greater than the HLINE period in IPI.

     When camera HLINE is greater than or equal to IPI HLINE period (that is, camera throughput is slower), all the
     data is transferred before a new line arrives (see Figure 17-21). For this scenario, RAM only needs to store
     one line.

     When camera HLINE is lesser than the IPI HLINE (that is, camera throughput is faster), the memory must
     accommodate all data that is overlapped with the next line (Figure 17-22). For this scenario, RAM needs to
     store one line plus the pixels that are not transmitted in the previous line (red zone).

     Controller Mode
     The minimum memory required in the CSI controller depends on:
       n   The memory required to store the camera incoming data before IPI starts to drive pixels to the output.
       n   Accommodating extra data if CSI-2 link speed is higher than IPI.
     When camera HLINE is greater than or equal to the IPI HLINE period (that is, camera throughput is slower), it
     means that all data is transferred before a new line arrives. So, the minimum memory has to be able to
     buffer all camera data until IPI starts to output pixels information. In this example, a memory that can buffer
     three lines ensure that an overflow never occurs.

 17.2.4.9.5 IPI Vertical Timing
     The presence of vertical timing information in the CSI-2 link is mandatory according to the MIPI CSI-2
     specification, so camera devices should transmit respective vertical frame synchronization packets on every
     frame. When a Frame Start packet is received for the virtual channel programmed in the CSI_IPI_VCID
     register, the HSYNC and VSYNC signals are simultaneously triggered according to the programming of the
     CSI_IPI_HSD_TIME and CSI_IPI_HSA_TIME registers. Frame End packets are ignored by this interface. In the
     Camera Mode, by default, VSYNC and HSYNC are not triggered when frame start packet is received. Frame
     Start can be configured to trigger a sync event by setting the CSI_IPI_ADV_FEATURES[IPI_SYNC_EVENT_
     MODE] bit to 1.

 17.2.4.9.6 IPI Horizontal Timing
     The presence of horizontal timing information in a CSI-2 link is optional according to the MIPI CSI-2
     specification. Therefore, when horizontal timing information is not used, the horizontal timing signals are
     reconstructed by the IPI through the blanking and data packets. The IPI interface timing can work in two
     different modes, camera timing and controller timing. The active mode is selected in the CSI_IPI_MODE[IPI_
     MODE] register bit.

 17.2.4.9.6.1 Camera Timing
     In this mode, IPI generates timing information based on packets. The number of video lines and blanking
     periods (vertical and horizontal) are defined by the camera. If the horizontal timing information is absent, the
     blanking or video packets trigger the line generation at the IPI output. This different IPI behavior is selected
     automatically.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1486
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com

     Without Horizontal Timing Information
     In this mode, IPI builds a line after receiving a valid video packet as per the CSI_IPI_VCID and CSI_IPI_DATA_
     TYPE registers configuration. The video packet is stored in the RAM and the reception of this packet is
     signaled. At this point, HSYNC (with pulse width defined in the CSI_IPI_HSA_TIME register) is sent after the
     time defined in the CSI_IPI_HSD_TIME register. Meanwhile, payload is received in parallel in RXBYTECLKHS
     clock domain and is stored into the FIFO until the end of the packet.
     After the completion of the time interval defined in the CSI_IPI_HBP_TIME register, pixel data starts to be
     retrieved from the FIFO and is delivered through IPI.
     This behavior is illustrated in Figure 17-29.

 17.2.4.9.6.2 Controller Timing
     In this mode, IPI generates the timing based on the IPI registers. After a Frame Start packet, IPI builds a frame
     exactly as configured in the IPI registers ignoring any other event generated by the camera traffic (horizontal
     information and video reception). The start of the frame at IPI interface is delayed by the value set in the
     CSI_IPI_HSD_TIME register in PIXCLK cycles. The generated frame is illustrated in Figure 17-33.
     Figure 17-33 shows the parallelism between the IPI registers and the generated frame. The only exceptions
     are Video zone and HFP:
       n   Video zone is the time IPI takes to transmit all the video.
       n   HFP is time remaining in the line time (as configured in the CSI_IPI_HLINE_TIME register) from the
           moment the video is transmitted.
     The software must ensure that the configuration matches the camera frame or there is available memory to
     accommodate the mismatch.

 17.2.4.9.7 IPI Memory Flush
     The CSI_IPI_MEM_FLUSH register is used to flush the memory, in case the memory is corrupted. Following
     are the two ways to flush the memory:
       n Manual:
         l Set CSI_IPI_MEM_FLUSH[IPI_FLUSH] register bit to 1.

       n Automatic:
         l Set CSI_IPI_MEM_FLUSH[IPI_AUTO_FLUSH] bit to 1. The IPI memory is flushed when a VSYNC (frame

           start) is received. When bit IPI_AUTO_FLUSH is set, it is not possible to overlap frames (that is, start
           buffering a new frame before the previous frame is transmitted).

 17.2.4.9.8 IPI Halt Functionality
     The backpressure mechanism is enforced using the IPI_HALT signal. Upon assertion of this signal, the CSI
     controller stops transmitting (sync events and payload) in the IPI interface.
     After the de-assertion of the IPI_HALT, the data transmission is resumed.

 17.2.4.9.8.1 Controller Timing
     If a new line starts and the data from the previous line is not transmitted, the CSI controller delays the sync
     events and payload, but asserts an error (PIXEL_IF_HLINE_ERR) indicating that the frame generated by the IPI
     interface has been changed. Upon this, CSI controller transmits the programed frame.
     The following examples demonstrate the behavior of the IPI interface under different scenarios.
     IPI_HALT Asserts during PIXEN Duration
     The CSI_IPI_HSA_TIME, CSI_IPI_HBP_TIME, and CSI_IPI_HLINE_TIME registers are not affected by the IPI_
     HALT signal. However, the HFP duration is smaller than expected.
     The CSI controller still transmits valid pixel data information during the HALT_PIXENZ interval (in PIXCLK
     cycles).
     When IPI_HALT deasserts (see Figure 17-35), the CSI controller needs HALTZ_PIXEN interval (in PIXCLK cycles)
     to resume the transmission.

 17.2.4.9.8.2 Camera Timing
     In Camera mode, the back-pressure can be applied without restrictions. The time that system can assert the

 17.2.4.9.9 IPI Cut-Through Functionality
     The IPI Cut-Through mode allows the pixel stream to be non-continuous. This means that if the pixel
     interface FIFO becomes empty during pixel transmission, the operation is suspended. Transmission is
     resumed as soon as the memory has valid pixels as shown in Figure 17-38.
                                                Figure 17-38 CSI IPI Cut-Through Functionality(1)

        WRITE_CLK

                                 P3             X             X         X           X         X                    X

         READ_CLK

                 PIXEN

           PIXDATA          P1    P2       P3       P4   P5        P6          P7        P8                   PN
                                                                                                                          CSI-013




     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     Figure 17-38 shows an example where the READ_CLK (PIXCLK) frequency is twice that of WRITE_CLK
     (RXBYTECLKHS). When the FIFO is empty, CSI controller stops pixel transmission and PIXEN signal is set to 0.
     This feature requires that the synchronization events have the same latency as that of the data stored in the
     memory. To ensure this, the IPI_HSD_TIME value set in the CSI_IPI_HSD_TIME register should be according to
     equation 17-11:
                                                                                                                                (17-11)

                                                                        1493

     Note that, with Cut-Through mode, video transmission starts after IPI buffering. Consequently, IPI_HBP_TIME
     (configured in the CSI_IPI_HBP_TIME register) could be higher than the time visible on the PPI interface.

 17.2.4.9.10 IPI Advanced Features

 17.2.4.9.10.1 Data Type Overwrite
     The Data Type Overwrite feature changes how the IPI process receives the data. When the feature is active
     (CSI_IPI_ADV_FEATURES[IPI_DT_OVERWRITE] bit is set to 1), the IPI data is decoded using the data type
     configured in the CSI_IPI_ADV_FEATURES register instead of the received data type from the camera. At the
     same time, the CSI_IPI_DATA_TYPE register must be still configured with the data type received from the
     camera.
     To ensure a proper decoding, the configured data types must respect the relation present in Table 17-19.

 17.2.4.9.11 IPI End Frame Signal
     IPI interface provides an END_FRAME signal to indicate when the frame is transmitted. The CSI controller
     determines the end of the current frame and generates a pulse indicating that.

 17.2.4.9.12 IPI Support for Embedded Data
     According to the MIPI CSI-2 specification, it is possible to embed extra lines containing additional information
     to the beginning and/or to the end of each picture frame.
     In camera timing mode, with this feature is active, the CSI controller is able to transmit embedded data at the
     IPI interface. To differentiate pixel data from embedded data the signal IPI_EMBEDDED is used in the IPI
     interface. This feature is active when the CSI_IPI_DATA_TYPE[EMBEDDED_DATA] register bit is set to 1.

 17.2.4.9.14 IPI Enabling
     The IPI stores the received data in memory. Upon retrieving data from memory, it reorganizes the data in a
     pixel stream format. This stream is then conveyed to the interface through a pixel data bus and additional
     Frame timing signals containing vertical and horizontal information. IPI uses an externally supplied pixel
     clock.

 17.2.4.9.15 IPI Pixel Data
     The 16-bit pixel data information is delivered by IPI_DATAEN and IPI_DATA[47:32] interface lines.
     The assertion of IPI_DATAEN signal means that IPI_DATA[47:32] is containing pixel data information.

       n Line errors such as incorrect line sequence and mismatch between Line Start and Line End

 17.2.4.10.1 Data ID Monitors
     According to the MIPI CSI-2 Specification, each CSI-2 line contains information regarding Data Type (DT) and
     Virtual Channel (VC) identification. Yet, each CSI-2 frame is identified uniquely by its virtual channel. In fact, a
     frame can contain different lines using different data types.
     This fact imposes some restriction on how errors are monitored for CSI-2 lines. To have a mechanism to
     identify these errors, it is required to have the knowledge of the DT and VC pairs that are active on the CSI- 2
     link. The CSI controller includes CSI_DATA_IDS_1 and CSI_DATA_IDS_VC_1 registers to store this information,
     creating the possibility to program up to four Data IDs (VC/DT pairs) for simultaneous monitoring.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1499
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com

                          DIN        ...    DI8     DI7        DI6     DI5   DI4    DI3        DI2   DI1   DI0

                                    DVX                   VC                              DT


                                Virtual Channel Iden�ﬁer (VC)                      Data Type (DT)

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The CSI_DATA_IDS_1 and CSI_DATA_IDS_VC_1 registers must be programmed during CSI controller
     initialization only.
     For further details, detect the protocol layer errors and report the errors as follows:
       n Analyze the data type field of the headers of short and long packets, and raise an error whenever an
         unrecognized or unimplemented one is found. This corresponds to ERR_ID and is reported for each
         virtual channel, independently (ERR_ID_VS* fields of the CSI_INT_ST_PKT register).
       n Take note of the occurrence of payload CRC error detections in any of the packets that are received
         between a Frame Start and its corresponding Frame End. When the Frame End is received, the ERR_
         FRAME_DATA error is raised for the virtual channel where the frame has been received, if at least one
         payload CRC error has been detected in some packet of that frame (ERR_FRAME_DATA_VC* fields of the
         CSI_INT_ST_FRAME_FATAL register).
       n Analyze the headers of short packets, aiming to match Frame Start with Frame End and Line Start with
         Line End packets by the corresponding Frame Number or Line Number.
         l If there are two consecutive Frame Start packets or two consecutive Frame End ones, or even if the

            Frame Number of a Frame End packet is not the same as for the last received Frame Start (all verified
            in the same virtual channel), then the ERR_F_BNDRY_MATCH error is raised (ERR_F_BNDRY_MATCH _
            VC* fields of the CSI_INT_ST_FRAME_FATAL register).
         l If the frame number in a Frame Start packet is not incremented by 1 relatively to the previous one, for

            some virtual channel, then the ERR_F_SEQ error is raised. The exception is that if the Frame Number
            is 0, frame numbering is inactive; if it is 1, the frame numbers restart. Therefore the error is not raised
            in these exceptions (ERR_F_SEQ_VC* fields of the CSI_INT_ST_FRAME_FATAL register).
         l If there are two consecutive Line Start packets or two consecutive Line End ones, or even if the line

            number of a Line End packet is not the same as for the last received Line Start (all verified in the same
            virtual channel), an ERR_I_BNDRY_MATCH error is raised for each data ID of long packets that have
            been received in between and that match the data IDs that are programmed in the register bank
            (ERRR_I_BNDRY_MATCH_DI* fields of the CSI_INT_ST_LINE register, where DI* corresponds to the
            data ID programmed in CSI_DATA_IDS_1 and CSI_DATA_IDS_VC_1 registers).
         l The line number of each Line Start packet is saved, according to its virtual channel. Later, when a long

            packet is received for the same virtual channel, if its data ID is programmed in the register bank and if
            that Line Number is out of the expected sequence for that data ID, an ERR_l_SEQ error is raised for
            that data ID. Prior to raising any ERR_l_SEQ error, the increment between successive lines, for a given
            data ID has to be determined. For that, at least two consecutive lines of a given data ID must be
            received without errors after each frame starts, so that the difference between those two line
            numbers can be used to determine the increment of the line numbers to expect for that data ID (ERR_
            l_SEQ_DI* fields of the CSI_INT_ST_LINE register, where DI* corresponds to the data ID programmed
            in CSI_DATA_IDS_1 and CSI_DATA_IDS_VC_1 registers).

                                                                     1500

     All the errors described previously can trigger the CSI_IRQ interrupt signal. Any of these errors can be
     independently masked to inhibit the generation of interrupt.

 17.2.4.11 CSI D-PHY RX Operation

 17.2.4.11.1 D-PHY RX Introduction
     The CSI D-PHY RX module implements the physical layer for the MIPI D-PHY interface. The PHY comprises of
     two data lanes and one clock lane. The PHY is used in slave applications where it receives the high-speed
     clock. The lane modules are unidirectional with high-speed receiver (HS-RX), low-power receiver (LP-RX) and
     low-power contention detector (LP-CD) functions.
     The PHY provides high-speed digital serial data reception between the device and an external MIPI-compliant
     camera module supporting a maximum effective bit rate of 2.5 Gbps (per lane in forward direction). The
     assembled two data lanes system enables up to 10 Gbps aggregated communication throughput.
     The PHY interfaces with the CSI controller through the PHY Protocol Interface (PPI). The CSI controller
     implements all protocol functions defined in the MIPI CSI-2 Specification. This provides an interface between
     the system and the PHY, which allows the communication with the external MIPI-compliant camera sensor.

 17.2.4.11.2 D-PHY RX HS Equalizer
     The PHY includes an HS RX Equalizer up to 3 dB.
     To mitigate package signal impairments, a fixed emphasis level for the RX path can be selected through the
     built-in Equalizer. This allows high robustness to degraded input signals and the use of a wider range of
     package types.
     The HS RX Equalizer is disabled by default and set to the no gain impact.
     RX control registers at address offset 0x509 and 0x709 (for Lane 0 and Lane 1, respectively) can be used to
     override the Equalizer setting. By default the Equalizer is set to 3'b000. Increasing the equalizer setting will
     increase the respective equalizer gain up to a maximum of 3 dB.

 17.2.4.11.3 D-PHY RX External Resistor Calibration
     The PHY contains a low-speed digital logic with sub-blocks responsible for PHY power up and calibration
     algorithms.
       n   The resistor termination calibration logic relies on external resistor Rext (200 Ω with 1% spread). The
           logic is responsible to guarantee that the following PHY parameters meet the specification:
           l HS Differential input impedance Zid

           l HS Single ended output impedance Zos

           l HS Single ended output impedance mismatch – ΔZos


     The Rext is used only on calibration procedures during D-PHY initialization meaning that it can be
     disconnected afterwards (after the PHY has reached idle mode). On this context, each PHY modile can use it
     when required, as long as there is no more than one using it and forcing current across the resistor at the
     same time. For instance, if there are two D-PHYs sharing the Rext, the first PHY must power up and second
     one must only be powered up when bit[4] of test control register with address offset 0x0C9 of the first PHY is
     asserted. When Rext is not used, the current is disabled and Rext net is in high impedance (Hi-Z).




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1501

       The CSI and DSI controllers share a single Rext at device package level.
