 17.2.4.11.4.1 No Power Mode
     The No Power mode is characterized by the non-existence of any supply voltage applied to the PHY. In order
     to get to the powered modes, proper voltages should be applied sequentially to the PHY. This task is usually
     done by the device power management.

 17.2.4.11.4.2 Shutdown Mode
     This mode is the lowest power consumption mode, where all analog blocks are disabled, and digital logic is
     reset. The current consumption is given by the analog standby current and the digital logic leakage current.
     The mode is entered asynchronously when CSI_DPHY_RSTZ and CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ register bits are in
     low state. It should be ensured that the CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] bit is asserted by default, as it
     acts as an active high reset to the control block responsible for the configuration values preset. In this mode,
     the clock and data differential lines are Hi-Z.
     All necessary MIPI D-PHY configurations to set the desired operation should be made with the PHY on this
     mode, before Start-up.

 17.2.4.11.4.3 HS-RX DDL Tunning
     A Digital Delay Line (DDL) is used on the clock and data path to support the deskew mechanism introduced in
     MIPI D-PHY 1.2 specification and part of the D-PHY RX implementation. The same mechanism is also


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                               Alif Semiconductor
                                                                1502
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     exercised during MIPI D-PHY 1.1 compatibility mode operation but with no pattern training sequence
     requirements. There is a seprate DDL for the clock (clock received from the clock lane) and a DDL for the data
     path.
     The DDL for the data path is only exercised when D-PHY is working in backwards compatibility mode for
     operating frequency resulting in lower than 1.5 Gbps throughput.
     The implemented deskew algorithm for MIPI D-PHY 1.2 deskew compensation requires the DDL minimum
     length to be 2 UI, so that is guaranteed that the clock shift during the deskew calibration process will capture
     2 data edges and be able to decide the optimum DDL step to center the clock when sampling the data.
     To meet this requirement, the DDL lenght is tuned during PHY Start-up such that the 2 UI DDL length is met.
     If the selected operating bitrate is ≤ 1.5 Gbps, the DDL is always tuned to the same oscillation frequency and
     step size independent of the selected bitrate. This step size selection is the recommended for MIPI D-PHY 1.1
      compatibility mode deskew algorithm.
     If the selected operating bitrate is > 1.5 Gbps, the DDL length is tuned to > 2 UI @ the defined bitrate and for
     the configured DDL oscillation frequency.
     The DDL tuning configuration should be configured before the PHY Start-up sequence globally for all lanes at
     the same time or for each lane independently through the following PHY RX test control registers:
       n Global control over all lanes through registers at address 0xE2, 0xE3, 0xE4
       n Independent Lane 0 control through registers at address 0x60A, 0x60A, 0x60A
       n Independent Lane 1 control through registers at address 0x80A, 0x80A, 0x80A

     For the DDL oscillation target frequency configuration for each bitrate, see Table 17-33.
     Increasing the oscillation target frequency counter of the DDL through the test control registers identified
     above will result in smaller DDL step size and decreasing in a more coarse step size.
     The DDL tuning algorithm is run over the clock DDL and the same settings applied to the data DDL, which has
     a length of 1 UI after it is properly configured.
     The clock DDL has 32 steps, the data DDL has 16 steps and the average DDL step is > 2.0 UI / 32.

 17.2.4.11.4.4 Deskew for MIPI D-PHY 1.1 Compatibility Mode (≤ 1.5 Gbps)
     When the PHY is operating at or below 1.5 Gbps it is not mandatory to support High-Speed deskew
     calibration for compatibility with TX that do not support this mode - no clock pattern calibration sequence is
     sent through lines by protocol request.
     When compatibility mode is enabled, the PHY makes use of an algorithm that is supported by the data and
     clock DDL that is tuned at PHY Start-up.
     The algorithm exercises the data and clock lanes with CFG_CLK as there will not be a deskew pattern being
     exercised externally from a D-PHY Transmitter. This backwards compatibility algorithm will be able to
     compensate for internal intrinsic static skew between data lanes. The DDL will be exercised to shift clock vs
     data on each data lane until the location of data edge transitions is identified and the DDL logic configured
     for this location. During this calibration, both clock and data lanes are exercised with the same input stimuli
     while during a normal HS data reception, the clock will be shifted 0.5 UI when compared to data transitions,
     this places the clock lane on the optimum location for the internal static skew compensation and maximum
     operating margin for correct data sampling and HS reception.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1503
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


 17.2.4.11.4.5 Control Mode
     Control mode is the default PHY operating mode. After the initialization is completed, the PHY remains in this
      default mode until a request is made either by the protocol layer, or directly through the sequence of low
     power signals in the lanes in case of RX. While in control mode, the transmitter side sets the LP-11 state in
     the lines - this is also called the Stop state.
     The receiver side remains in control mode while receiving LP-11 in the lines. Any request must start from and
     end in Stop state. Following a request, a lane can leave control mode for either high-speed data transfer
     mode, Escape mode, or Ultra Low Power state.

 17.2.4.11.4.6 High-Speed mode
     Once the initialization sequence is completed, the PHY remains in control mode, which is the default
     operating mode, until some request appears. High-speed is one of the possible requests at this point. High-
     speed data transfer occurs in bursts. Only during these bursts the lane is in high-speed mode. A high-speed
     burst must start from and return to a Stop state (control mode). A high-speed burst allows for the
     transmission of payload data by the data lanes.
     Inherent to such data transmission is the existence of a valid DDR clock in the clock lane.

 17.2.4.11.4.7 High-Speed Data Reception (Slave, Forward Mode)
     When the PHY is configured as slave, it is expecting to receive high-speed data bursts start synchronously in
     all data lanes (one UI difference in HS-SYNC is tolerated), but may end independently of the state of the
     remaining data lanes due to an unequal amount of received bytes per data lane. For a clock lane, processing
     the high-speed starts with the reception of a low-power sequence (LP11 -> LP01 -> LP00) to enable HS-RX line
     termination followed by a HS-0 during TCLK-ZERO to enable the HS-RX clock receiver.
     For a data lane, the high-speed entry sequence is the similar as for clock lanes, that is low-power sequence to
     enable HS-RX line termination followed by a HS-0 during THS-ZERO to enable the HS-RX data receiver.
     The RX side will wait for TCLK-SETTLE and THS-SETTLE to expire in order to neglect transition effects on clock and
     data, respectively.
     Before the payload data there is a leader sequence (HS-SYNC value 1’h1D) that allow for the receiver
     synchronization. The transmission of such sequence requires the existence of a valid high-speed clock signal
     in the clock lane.
     The clock lane will enter the high-speed mode before a high-speed data transmission (TCLK-PRE) begins and it
     must not leave this state before all the lanes finish their respective high-speed. The operation sequence
     when leaving the high-speed mode is slightly different for data and clock lanes. For a clock lane, the high-
     speed transfer always ends with a HS-0 state, this absence of clock transitions will be detected by RX (TCLK-
     MISS) followed by the disabling of the HS-RX of the clock lane.
     As for a data lane, transmission ends with the differential state opposite to the last bit transmitted and then
     Stop state is observed in the lines (LP11) and the PHY returns to Control mode.


                                                         NOTE

     When PHY is working in non-continuous clock mode, the TCLK-POST might need to be increased beyond the
     MIPI specification minimum (60 + 52 UI) in order to provide enough RXBYTECLKHS cycles for the CSI
     controller to process the received data correctly.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1504
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series




 17.2.4.11.4.8 High-Speed Deskew Calibration (Slave, Forward Mode, > 1.5 Gbps)
     In order to achieve data rates in the High-Speed Data mode (higher than 1.5 Gbps) a calibration mode was
     introduced in D-PHY 1.2 Specification. The implemented algorithm will be exercised while the PHY is in idle
     mode, that is, after Start-up and is triggered by a defined pattern sent by the external D-PHY TX module.
     This mode intends to allow the RX to compensate the skew introduced by TX, by the channel and by
     differences on RX on clock and data RX paths. High-Speed deskew calibration results in additional margin to
     correctly sample receiving data for higher data rate. The lines sequence for deskew calibration is very similar
     to High-speed transfer mode entry. For clock lane the entry sequence and exit sequence is exactly the same
     as in normal HS mode. As for the data lanes the entry is the same as for the normal HS except for:
      1. The leader sequence that is different (value 16’hFFFF for calibration mode) and allows for receiver to
         distinguish from a normal operation or calibration.
      2. A deskew pattern (clock pattern) is received in the data lanes during a minimum and maximum time
         defined by the specification. An initial high-speed deskew calibration should be done by the transmitter
         when operating above 1.5 Gbps, prior to the first High-Speed Data burst.
     When working as a slave, the PHY reports the state of the deskew calibration in the CSI_PHY_CAL
     [RXSKEWCALHS] register bit. When the bit is high, it represents that the PHY is in deskew calibration mode.
     The maximum skew that the algorithm will be able to compensate is ±0.5 UI between data and clock lanes
     and 1 UI between data lanes.
     This algorithm is supported by the PHY clock DDL that is tuned at D-PHY Start-up for a minimum length of 2
     UI. The DDL will be exercised to shift clock versus data on each data lane until the location of both data
     transition edges is identified. At this point, the algorithm can set the proper configuration to the existing DDL
     logic to compensate for the internal static skew and maximum operating margin for correct data sampling
     and HS reception.

 17.2.4.11.4.9 Temperature Change Sensitivity
     When RX operates in MIPI D-PHY 1.2 mode and the junction temperature changes > 10 °C, compared to the
     temperature in the first deskew sequence, this means that:
       n   The PHY requires DDL re-calibration
       n   TX needs to re-send deskew pattern
     The reason for this requirement is the fact that DDL block is sensitive to supply and power variations.
     In the applications where re-calibration of DDL is not possible, and being exposed only to temperature
     variations, TX should periodically re-send the deskew sequence in order to allow RX to adjust its timings.

 17.2.4.11.4.10 Power Supply Change Sensitivity
     When RX operates in MIPI D-PHY 1.1/1.2 mode and average power supply voltage changes more than 3%
     (ignoring power supply noise), compared to power supply value at the first deskew sequence, this means
     that:
       n The PHY requires DDL and RX offset cancellation re-calibration.
       n TX needs to re-send deskew pattern.

     The reason for this requirement is the fact that DDL block is sensitive to the power variation.

AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com

 17.2.4.11.4.11 Escape Mode
     Escape mode is a special mode of operation that uses the data lanes to communicate using the low-power
     states at low-speed. The PHY supports this mode in both directions for all data lanes. A data lane enters the
     Escape mode through an Escape mode entry procedure (LP-11, LP-10, LP-00, LP-01, LP-00). If an LP-11 is
     detected before reaching LP-00 state, the entry is aborted and the receiver returns to the Stop state. Once
     the sequence is correctly completed, the transmitter sends an 8-bit command to indicate a requested action.
     Table 17-32 shows the Escape mode supported actions. If the entry command is not valid, it is ignored, a
     PHY_ERRESC error is triggered, and the receiver waits until the transmitter returns to the Stop state. The PHY
     applies Spaced-One-Hot encoding (a Mark state is interleaved with a Space state) on commands and data.
     Each symbol consists of the following two parts:
       n One-Hot phase
       n Space state to transmit one bit, a Mark-1 should be sent followed by the Space state. In the case of a
         zero bit, a Mark-0 should be sent followed by Space state.
                   Table 17-32 CSI D-PHY RX Possible Escape Mode Sequences for Data Lanes(1)
                                        Entry Command Pattern (First Bit to Last Bit to be
      Escape Mode Action                                                                               Command Type
                                                       Transmitted)
  Low-Power Data
                                   11100001                                                  Mode
  Transmission
  Ultra- Lower Power State         00011110                                                  Mode
  Reset Trigger                    01100010                                                  Trigger
  Unknown - 3                      01011101                                                  Trigger
  Unknown - 4                      00100001                                                  Trigger
  Unknown - 5                      10100000                                                  Trigger
     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     Low-Power Data Transmission (LPDT)
     In LPDT mode, the data can be transmitted by the protocol at low speed in Low-Power mode—high-speed
     receivers are off and low-power receivers are on. During LPDT, the protocol can pause by maintaining a
     Space state on the lines. The last state before exiting Escape mode is Mark-1—not considered as 1 bit—
     because it is followed by the Stop state.
     Data shall be encoded on the lines with the same Spaced-One-Hot code as used for the Entry Commands.
     This encoding allows data to be self-clocked and does not rely on the clock lane.
     Remote Trigger
     This mode allows the protocol to send a flag to the receiving side, on request of the transmitting side. If the
     Entry Command Pattern matches the Reset-Trigger Command (01100010) a Trigger is flagged to the protocol
     at the receive side via the logical PPI. Any bit received after a Trigger Command but before the Lines go to
     Stop state shall be ignored. Therefore, dummy bytes can be concatenated in order to provide clock
     information to the receive side.
     Ultra Low Power State (ULPS)
     This mode has the lowest power consumption, excluding the Shutdown mode. For data lanes, this mode is
     entered by sending an Ultra Lower Power state entry command (00011110), after the Escape mode entry
     command. During this mode, the lines are in the Space state (LP-00). Although the clock lane does not
     support regular Escape mode, the clock lane supports ULPS.

                                                               1506
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                   www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                                E7 Series


     To exit ULPS, the transmitter side drives a Mark-1 followed by a Stop state. The twakeup time must be ensured
     by the protocol layer.

 17.2.4.11.5 D-PHY RX Control Registers Configuration

 17.2.4.11.5.1 Overview
     The PHY has a test control interface that is primarily used for the PHY configuration of its normal operating
     modes. The interface can be driven through the following CSI registers and fields: CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_
     TESTCLK],[PHY_TESTCLR] and CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN],[PHT_TESTDOUT],[PHY_TESTDIN].

 17.2.4.11.5.2 Registers Configuration Procedure
     The standard procedure for configuring a test control register in the PHY is two-folded; first the necessary
     control register address is programmed and then the related data is set.
     All PHY related configurations that impact its functional operation need to be done with the PHY in shutdown
     mode. The correct operation of the PHY may be compromised if the test and control interface is used during
     active modes to change the PHY operation configuration. It is allowed to use the test and control interface
     during active modes for debugging purposes and signals observability only. At the first PHY start-up, it is
     recommended to apply an interface reset (through setting CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 0x1) before
     any other test control register is set.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                                 1507
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


     Each control register address is composed by a 4-bit word (test code MSB) and an 8-bit word (test code LSB),
     referred to as 'offset'. With an 8-bit test and control interface, to access each control register, it is necessary
     to perform two write operations to respectively set the 12-bit control register address (test code MSB + test
     code LSB). For example, to access control register at offset 0x270, first the test code MSBs (value 0x2) need
     to be written and then the test code LSBs (value 0x70).
     The test code programming is done using the following steps:


                                                         NOTE

       For a back-to-back read from multiple registers, execute steps #1 and #2 (only).


      1. For writing the 4-bit test code MSB:
         a. Ensure that CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] and CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] register
            bits are set to 0x0.
         b. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x1
         c. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x1
         d. Place 0x00 in CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN] field
         e. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
         f. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x0
         g. Place the 8-bit word corresponding to the test code MSB in CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN]
         h. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x1
      2. For writing the 8-bit test code LSB:
         a. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
         b. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x1
         c. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x1
         d. Place the 8-bit word corresponding to the test code LSB in CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN]
         e. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
         f. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x0
      3. For writing the test data:
         a. Place the 8-bit word test data in CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN]
         b. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
     The CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDOUT] register field reflects the test code or test data, as soon as it is
     written in the [PHY_TESTDIN] field.
     It is only required to write the 4-bit test code MSBs if they change for the next test code to be written. If not,
     they don't need to be written again. This represents executing steps #2 and #3 above.
     The steps above for writing the data can be repeated for different test data to be written to the same test
     code.
     Repeat the above procedure to program subsequent test codes. Additionally, a test reset procedure (CSI_
     PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 1) is only needed if there is a need for the PHY configuration to be reset to
     its default values and override any changes made meanwhile.
     After a test code is effectively programmed, CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDOUT] asynchronously reflects
     the relevant data for that specific control register.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1508
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


 17.2.4.11.5.3 Start-Up Sequence
     Before PHY start-up, it needs to be properly configured for the desired operation. This needs to be done with
     the PHY in Shutdown mode and it is assumed that such configurations are static or at least are stable prior to
     leaving the Shutdown mode.

     the 12-bit OSC_FREQ_TARGET field in PHY registers at address offsets 0xE2[7-0], 0xE3[3-0] and 0xE2[0].
     The DDL target oscillation frequency needs to be configured for the desired operating frequency according to

     By default, the PHY Start-up sequence performs termination calibration considering the presence of an
     external termination resistor.
     The PHY consists of two data lanes, but the applications can use two or lesser number data lanes. The lane
     enables must not be changed during operation. They should be set while the PHY is in power-down
     (STOPSTATE).




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1510
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


                                                         NOTE

     If only a single lane is to be enabled, that lane must be Lane 0.


     After the resets (in CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ and CSI_DPHY_RSTZ registers) are released, the PHY begins an
     initialization sequence that allows its correct operation. Programming CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ should precede
     CSI_DPHY_RSTZ; it is also assumed that the CFG_CLK signal is available and stable by that time. The
     initialization sequence determines that the bandgap and biasing blocks are enabled first. After the current
     references get settled, a second step is triggered where the internal calibrations are performed.
     This includes:
      1. Termination resistors calibration
      2. Data and clock lane offset compensation
      3. Digital Delay Line (DDL) tunning calibration
      4. For operating frequencies < 1.5 Gbps (MIPI D-PHY1.1 backwards compatibility mode), an internal
         deskew compensation algorithm is executed
     The deskew algorithm selection is done automatically based on the high-speed clock range but can be
     overridden through the PHY test control registers, as well as all other Start-up calibration algorithms. When
     the second step is complete, the control is passed to the lanes, which handle the power management for
     LP/HS requests, enabling or disabling the corresponding receivers. All initialization steps are complete once
     the data/clock lane bits in CSI_PHY_STOPSTATE register get asserted (if the D-PHY Transmitter is driving
     LP11). For operating frequencies > 1.5 Gbps, a deskew compensation calibration algorithm can be executed
     (enabled by default for operating frequencies > 1.5 Gbps), if the PHY is triggered through a defined pattern
     sent by the TX after the PHY is already powered-up and in STOPSTATE.
     If there are no test or configuration operations to be performed, the CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR]
     register bit can be kept at logic high level. Otherwise, the testclr must be de-asserted to bring the control
     logic out of reset and allow for the necessary configuration steps through the control interface.
     The MIPI D-PHY specification has many timing intervals which have to be followed to ensure proper
     operation. The initialization sequence ends when STOPSTATE LP11 is driven in the lanes and the PHY reaches
     Control Mode state.
     The initialization period (TINIT) is a protocol dependent parameter with a minimum 100 μs defined by the
     MIPI specification. The PHY does not set any limit to the initialization period, meaning it starts decoding the
     LP commands after the AFE initialization in RX mode. It is up to the CSI controller or the upper layers to
     ensure the proper initialization times through the correct handling of the PHY configuration. This time must
     conform to MIPI D-PHY specification and obey the minimum specified 100 μs value.

 17.2.4.11.5.4 Configuration Example
     For PHY configuration purposes, the test and control interface must be exercised after a transition from 0 to
     1 of the CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] register bit and before PHY leaves shutdown mode (de-
     assertion of CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ and CSI_DPHY_RSTZ bits) and start Start-up sequence.
     While CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ and CSI_DPHY_RSTZ are de-asserted, the PHY remains in POWERDWN state. If
     the PHY properly reached the end of its startup sequence, it will be in IDLE state.
     Example (Slave; Operating Rate 1 Gbps; External Rext; CFG_CLK = 27 MHz; MIPI D-PHY 1.1 Backwards
     Compatibility Mode):



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1511
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


      1. Set CSI_DPHY_RSTZ = 0
      2. Set CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ = 0
      3. Set TX_RXZ = 0
      4. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 1
      5. Wait for 15 ns
      6. Set CSI_PHY_TEST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 0
      7. Configure RX register at address 0x307 to set bit [7], [RXCLK_RXHS_PULL_LONG_CHANNEL_IF_RW] to 1
      8. Refer to Table 17-33, and configure RX registers at address 0xE2, 0xE3 with the appropriate DDL target
         oscillation frequency. Enable override to configure the DDL target oscillation frequency on bit [0], [DDL_
         OSC_FREQ_TARGET_OVR_EN_RW] of register at address 0xE4.
      9. Apply CFG_CLK signal with the appropriate 27 MHz frequency
     10. Wait for 15 ns
     11. Set the desired number of active lanes in CSI_N_LANES register
     12. Wait 5 ns
     13. Set CSI_PHY_SHUTDOWNZ = 1
     14. Wait 5 ns
     15. Set CSI_DPHY_RSTZ = 1
     16. Wait until the respective clock/data lane bits in the CSI_PHY_STOPSTATE register are asserted indicating
         PHY is receiving LP11 in enabled data lanes and clock lane.


                                                       NOTE

     For an operating rate of 80 Mbps, if the master drives a spec minimum THS-PREPARE + THS-ZERO time (145 ns +
     10 UI), the THS-SETTLE default counter value should be adjusted by programming PHY RX register at address
     0xF1 to 10000101.

 17.2.4.12.2 CSI Programming Flow
     The following are the main tasks performed when a CSI-2 system captures a still image of an image video
     from a camera device:
       n Start up CSI controller: Setting CSI and PHY with the default values.
       n Initialize CSI controller: Configuring CSI for the proper operation mode and configuring PHY for the
         required frequency range.
       n Configure IPI: Setting up CSI to output the data through the pixel interface.
       n Start the High Speed Reception Mode: Setting up CSI and PHY to be ready to receive high-speed
         information.
       n Detect Errors: Detecting where an error occurs.
       n Stop the High Speed Reception Mode: Disabling CSI and PHY.
       n Enter and Exit ULPM: Entering and exiting Ultra Low Power Mode (ULPM). This sequence is optional.


 17.2.4.12.2.1 Start up CSI Controller
     Follow the programming steps below to start up CSI:
      1. Release CSI from reset
      2. Configure CSI
      3. Set or clear PHY Reset
      4. Release PHY test codes from reset

 17.2.4.12.2.2 Initialize CSI Controller
     Follow the programming steps below to initialize CSI:
      1. Release PHY test codes from reset
      2. Configure the PHY frequency range
      3. Perform additional PHY test code configuration (optional)
      4. Set or clear PHY from reset
      5. Configure the number of active lanes
      6. Configure the data ID values (optional)
      7. Define error to be masked
      8. Release CSI from reset
      9. Check that data lanes are in stop state


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                     Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1518
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                       www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


 17.2.4.12.2.3 Configure IPI
     Follow the programming sequence below to configure IPI. This task should be done during initialization.
      1. Select virtual channel and data type to be processed by IPI.
      2. Select the IPI operating mode (camera timing or controller timing).
      3. Configure IPI horizontal frame information.
      4. In case of IPI controller timing mode selected, configure also IPI vertical frame information.

 17.2.4.12.2.4 Examples of Configuring IPI
     In this section, some examples of configuring IPI for various situations are provided.
     It is assumed that IPI_HSD_TIME value is always less than one line. If not, extra buffering may be required.


                                                         NOTE

       The IPI configuration examples in this section assume that CSI D-PHY RX supports 4 or more data
       lanes.
       However, the D-PHY RX implementation in the device supports 2 data lanes only. Therefore, some
       equations in the examples shall be re-calculated accordingly.

     1498 (IPI_HLINE = IPI_HLINE_TIME in controller timing mode) = 0 (buffering is not required)
     BUFFERED_LINES = IPI_VSA_LINES + IPI_VBP_LINES - NUMBER_OF_CAMERA_BLANKING_LINES = 1 + 2 - 0 = 3
                                                                                                                 (17-30)



     Where,
     HLINE_MISSMATCH = 1 - Decimal part of (CAMERA_HLINE_PIX) = 1 - Decimal part of (1497.6) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4
                                                                                                                 (17-31)

     Therefore,
     Memory required = 300 + 0 + 3 × 300 + 90 = 1290
     But, 1290 is more than 1024, which means there is not enough memory to transmit the frame. Therefore, it
     is necessary to reconsider some of the configurable values.
     For example, if the number of IPI_VBP_LINES is reduced to 1:
     BUFFERED_LINES = 1 + 1 - 0 = 2
     BUFFERED_MEMORY_PER_FRAME = 24 × 0 × (600 - 0) = 0
     Therefore,
     Memory required = 300 + 0 + 2 × 300 + 90 = 990

     But the available memory is 1024. Therefore, the required memory (990) is less than the available memory.

 17.2.4.12.2.5 Start the High-Speed Reception Mode
     To start with, set up the camera device to start high-speed clock transmission. At the end of this sequence,
     CSI is ready to receive high-speed data.
      1. Check that clock lane is in HS mode
      2. Start the camera image capture
      3. Monitor the interruption for error reports

 17.2.4.12.2.6 Detect Errors
     To detect why the CSI_IRQ interrupt signal is triggered:
      1. Read CSI_INT_ST_MAIN register
      2. Read CSI_INT_ST_<group> registers
     An unmasked errors triggers the CSI_IRQ interrupt signal.
     CSI_INT_ST_MAIN: Clear on read register. Read this register to know from which group the interruption
     comes from. Reading this register clears the CSI_IRQ signal.
     Read CSI_INT_ST_<group>: Clear on read registers. Read these registers in order to know which error
     occurred. Reading these registers does not clear the CSI_IRQ.
     For descriptions of all errors that CSI can identify, see Section 17.2.4.10 CSI Error Detection.

 17.2.4.12.2.7 Stop the High-Speed Reception Mode
     After the image or video has been completely received, the CSI-2 system is turned off.
      1. Stop the camera image capture
      2. Set up the camera to stop HS clock transmission
      3. Check that the clock lane is not in HS mode
      4. Request the camera to enter ULPM (optional)

 17.2.4.12.2.8 Enter and Exit ULPM
     After the image or video has been completely received, the CSI-2 system is turned off.
     For Enter ULPM:
      1. Request the camera device to enter ULPM (clock and/or data lanes)
      2. Check that the CSI controller reports ULPM active (clock and/or data lanes)
     For Exit ULPM:
      1. Request the camera device to exit ULPM (clock and/or data lanes)
      2. Check that the CSI controller reports ULPM is not active (clock and/or data Lanes)

 17.2.5.3.62 CSI_SCRAMBLING Register
           Offset           Access          Description
        0x300                               Descrambling Control Register
                             R/W
     Base address                           This register configures the descrambler block.


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description

 18 Display Interfaces

 18.1 Display Parallel Interface (DPI) Controller

 18.1.1 DPI Controller Overview
     The Display Parallel Interface (DPI) provides a 24-bit RGB data bus either directly to LCD and TFT panels with
     a resolution of up to WXGA (1280 × 800) or to the MIPI DSI Controller. In addition to the 24 data lines, the
     interface includes pixel clock up to 50 MHz, horizontal and vertical synchronization pulses, and data enable
     signals with configurable polarity.
     The device includes a single Configurable DPI Controller (CDC).
     The CDC supports the following main features:
       n Configurable resolution and refresh rate
       n Two display layers
       n Programmable background color
       n Color Look-Up Table (CLUT) with 256 × 24-bit entries per layer for indexed pixel formats
       n Flexible blending between the layers using alpha value (pixel alpha or constant alpha)
       n Color keying: defining transparent color for pixel formats without alpha channel
       n Windowing: blending a programmable rectangular area of one layer into the other
       n Gamma correction
       n Dithering (2 bits per color component): providing softer color transitions for displays with less color
         depth
       n Multiple input pixel formats selectable per layer:
         l ARGB8888, RGBA8888, RGB888, RGB565, ARGB1555, ARGB4444

         l AL44 (4-bit alpha + 4-bit luminance) and L8 (8-bit luminance)

       n RGB888 output pixel format
       n Master Bus Interface (MBI): 64-bit AXI interface used for pixel data transfer
       n Slave Bus Interface (SBI): 32-bit APB interface used for configuration

     Figure 18-1 provides a high-level overview of the DPI implementation in the device.

                       The CDC fetches pixel data from the device system memory (framebuffer) through its Master Bus Interface
                       (MBI), performs various pixel processing and video layer tasks (such as gamma correction, blending, overlay,
                       dithering), and then outputs the processed pixels via an RGB digital parallel interface. The internal timing
                       generator logic generates the output interface signals for horizontal and vertical synchronization. The CDC
                       also includes a Slave Bus Interface (SBI) for registers configuration, and an internal interrupt controller.
                       The Configuration Status Controllers (CSC) handle the read and write accesses to the registers. There is a CSC
                       for each clock domain. Only the slave CSC is connected to the interconnect bus. It forwards read- or write-
                       requests to the master and pixel CSC if necessary. Each CSC contains all configuration registers needed in its
                       clock domain (for example, the framebuffer addresses are stored in the master CSC domain only).
                       The CDC can be globally enabled/disabled via the CDC_GLB_CTRL[CDC_EN] register bit.

 18.1.4.2 CDC Clocks
                       The CDC receives a number of clocks that define the internal clock domains:
                        n ACLK is the interface clock on the CDC AXI master port. The pixel data transfer from memory runs on this
                          clock.
                        n PCLK is the interface clock on the CDC APB slave port. The CDC global registers and interrupts
                          configuration run on this clock.
                        n PIXEL_CLK is the pixel data clock. The CDC internal pixel data processing and the output parallel interface
                          signals generation run on this clock. The output pixel clock (CDC_PCLK) is a feed-through of the PIXEL_

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                                                  Alif Semiconductor
                                                                                                1571
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


           CLK with a register programmable inverter. The pixel clock should be configured based on the display
           panel requirements.
     When the complete CDC or a single layer are deactivated, the respective logic parts are clock-gated. In
     addition, during blanking times, the pixel pipelines are also clock-gated and once the internal FIFOs are filled
     (prefetch finished) the master bus interface is also gated during these times.

 18.1.4.3 CDC Interrupts
     The CDC supports a number of interrupt events. Each event is mapped to a dedicated interrupt line going to
     system level.
       n CDC_SCANLINE0_IRQ: Line interrupt. The interrupt is generated at the first pixel (start of horizontal
         sync) of a programmed line number. The line number is programmed in the CDC_LINE_IRQ_POS and
         CDC_SLINE_IRQ_POS registers.
       n CDC_FIFO_UNDERRUN0_IRQ: Layer FIFO underrun interrupt. The interrupt is generated when a pixel
         needs to be read from a layer FIFO, but the FIFO is empty. Implies that the available bus bandwidth has
         not been sufficient and visual artifacts have appeared on the screen. Should not occur under normal
         circumstances. If it does occur, the bus bandwidth situation needs to be improved (for example, disable
         layers, disable other masters, improve bus arbitration settings, and so forth) and the CDC needs to be
         reset and re-initialized as soon as possible to avoid display of visual artifacts.
       n   CDC_FIFO_WARNING0_IRQ: FIFO underrun warning interrupt. The interrupt is generated if one of the
           layer FIFOs is empty and pixel data is read from the FIFO. This can occur if the color framebuffer length is
           not defined properly or the master bus performance is too low, such that the pixel data cannot be read
           in.
       n   CDC_BUS_ERROR0_IRQ: Bus error interrupt. The interrupt is generated when any error occurs at the
           master bus. Normally implies that the CDC has performed a read access to an invalid bus address, but
           depends on the external bus infrastructure. Should only happen when an invalid address has been
           programmed to the CDC by the driver/application. A reset and re-initialization of the CDC is required
           after the problem has been solved.
       n   CDC_REG_RELOAD0_IRQ: Register reload interrupt. The interrupt is generated when the shadowed
           registers have been automatically reloaded (if a vertical blanking reload has been programmed via the
           CDC_SRCTRL register and the first line after the active area reached). Typically used when implementing
           multi-buffer display schemes. In this case the IRQ means that the framebuffer previously used by the
           CDC is now free for image generation purposes again, without the risk of seeing visual artifacts. No
           specific response time requirements from CDC point of view.
     The CDC internal interrupt controller handles the IRQ enabling and clearing.
       n Each interrupt can be enabled/ disabled independently by configuring the CDC_IRQ_MASK0 register.
       n The status of each interrupt can be read from a dedicated bit in the CDC_IRQ_STATUS0 register.
       n The interrupts stay asserted until they are cleared by writing in the corresponding bit of the CDC_IRQ_
         CLEAR0 register.

 18.1.4.4.1 Input Pixel Data Formats
     The CDC supports the following input pixel formats which are used for the data stored in the framebuffer of a
     layer:
       n   RGB: ARGB8888, RGBA8888, RGB888, RGB565, ARGB1555, ARGB4444
       n   AL44 (4-bit alpha + 4-bit luminance) and L8 (8-bit luminance)
     The CDC internal pixel format is ARGB8888. The pixel data is read from the framebuffer and then
     transformed to the internal format as follows:
       n Color components which have a width of less than 8 bits get expanded to 8 bits in hardware by bit
         replication: The selected bit range is concatenated multiple times until it is longer than 8 bits. Of the
         resulting vector, the 8 MSB bits are chosen.
       n Color components, which have a width of 0, need to be set to all '1' in case of alpha and all '0' in case of
         color components.
     The selection of the pixel format for each layer is done in the CDC_Ln_PIX_FORMAT register.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                          1573
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


 18.1.4.4.2 Data Fetch from Memory
     The video data for the layers is located in several framebuffers and is loaded via bus master accesses using
     burst transfers. There is one color framebuffer per layer that holds the RGB pixel color components.
     An MBI arbiter arbitrates the layer MBI ports to a single external MBI port. The arbitration strategy is a
     round-robin scheme through all enabled layers. The arbiter allows prefetching of multiple reads from
     multiple layers.
     Data fetch units control the MBI for each layer and fill the layer FIFOs with the framebuffer data. The FIFO
     Read/Format Converter (FC) blocks control the reading from the FIFOs and mux out the pixels from the data
     words according to the currently selected input pixel format of that layer. When the CDC is disabled, no new
     bus accesses are started, returning read data is discarded and the FIFOs are flushed.
     The fetching for a new frame starts with the beginning of the last blanking line prior to the active area.
     Prefetching of multiple bursts is done when multiple bursts fit into the FIFO.
     When a layer is enabled, data is fetched from the framebuffer, that is, the address, number of lines, line
     length, and pitch settings have to be consistent. When a layer is disabled, the configured default color for
     that layer (ARGB format) is used for all pixels.
     When reading data from the framebuffer, the number of words per burst can be modified by programming
     the CDC_Ln_FB_BCTRL register. The default burst length, which is also the maximum value, is 16 words.
     Framebuffer start address:
       n   Every layer has a start address for the color framebuffer that should be programmed in the CDC_Ln_
           CFB_ADDR register.
     Framebuffer length:
       n The total line length setting for the color buffer in bytes for each layer is set in the CDC_Ln_CFB_LENGTH
         [LLENGTH] register field.
       n The number of lines in the framebuffer for every layer is set in the CDC_Ln_CFB_LINES register.
       n The line length and number of lines settings are used to stop prefetching of data to the layer FIFO at the
         end of the framebuffer:
         l If it is set to less bytes than actually required, then a FIFO underrun warning interrupt is generated, if

            enabled.
         l If it is set to more bytes than actually required, then an undefined data may be read from the

            respective FIFO that is discarded and not displayed.
     Framebuffer pitch:
       n   Every layer has a configurable pitch for the color buffer, which is the distance between the start of one
           line and the beginning of the next line in bytes. It is set in the CDC_Ln_CFB_LENGTH[PITCH] register field.

 18.1.4.4.3 Layer Windowing
     Each layer supports a windowing feature, meaning that every layer can be positioned and resized inside the
     active video area.
     The window position and size can be configured through the top-left and bottom-right X/Y positions. These
     positions are in coordinates of the internal timing generator, that is, they include the sync and back porch
     sizes:
       n   The horizontal position (first and last pixel) of the layer window is defined in the CDC_Ln_WIN_HPOS
           register. The first visible pixel of a line is the value of register field CDC_BP_CFG[AHBP] + 1. The last
           visible pixel of a line is the value of CDC_ACTW_CFG[AAW] register field.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                         1574
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


       n   The vertical position (first and last line) of the layer window is defined in the CDC_Ln_WIN_VPOS
           register. The first visible line of a frame is the value of register field CDC_BP_CFG[AVBP] + 1. The last
           visible line of a frame is the value of CDC_ACTW_CFG[AAH] register field.

 18.1.4.4.4 Color Look-Up Table (CLUT)
     CDC supports a color look-up table (CLUT) feature for Layer 1 only. The CLUT is realized as a single ported
     RAM of 256 x 24-bit RGB entries.
     The CLUT is loaded by a write to the CDC_Ln_CLUT_WRACC register with the R, G and B values that replace
     the original R, G, B values of a given pixel (indexed color). Each color (RGB value) has its own address that is
     the position within the CLUT.
     When the CLUT feature is enabled in the CDC_Ln_CTRL[CLUT_EN] register bit, the blue component of the
     color framebuffer pixel after conversion to the internal pixel format is used to look up an RGB value in the
     table. The RGB value loaded in the register replaces the original RGB value of that pixel.
     Write accesses to the CLUT have a higher priority than read accesses, therefore the CLUT should only be
     configured during blanking or if the layer is not enabled.

 18.1.4.4.5 Default Color
     Every layer can have a default color (ARGB format), which is used instead of the per-pixel color, when the
     layer is disabled. When the layer window is configured, the default color is also used for pixels of that layer,
     which lie outside of the window.
     The default color can be set in the CDC_Ln_DFLT_COLOR register. Blending with the default color has to be
     enabled in the CDC_Ln_CTRL[DFLT_CBLEND_EN] register bit for the CDC_Ln_DFLT_COLOR register to have an
     effect.
     It is possible to disable the blending with the default color. In this case the sub-adjacent layers color is
     unmodified for pixels outside of the window or when the current layer is disabled.

 18.1.4.4.6 Blending
     The CDC includes a blending logic that is used to combine the color values (RGB) of one layer with the
     combined blending results of the sub-adjacent layers.
     To calculate one blended pixel as many steps as layers are needed. This is achieved internally through the
     Alpha Blending Pipeline (ABP) which delivers one pixel per clock. The length of the ABP is the same as the
     number of steps of calculation. If two layers are enabled, as shown in Figure 18-7, first Layer 1 is blended
     with the Background (BG) color, then Layer 2 is blended with the result of blended color of Layer 1 and the
     Background.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                         1575
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                            E7 Series

                                                             Top

                                                                                                   Layer 1 +
                       Layer 2                          Layer 2                                    BG

                       Layer 1                        Layer 1 + BG

                      Background

                                                            Down                                                  DPI-007




     Figure 18-8 shows an example alpha blending pipeline with fixed layer order. Each ABP stage receives the
     resulting color from the previous alpha blending.
                                            Figure 18-8 CDC Blending Pipeline

                                                                        ARGB from
                                                            Color +     Blending Control
                                     Background              Alpha
                                        Color               Layer 1
                                    Alpha Blending

                                               Sync                     ARGB from
                                                            Color +     Blending Control
                                         Stage 1             Alpha
                                                            Layer 2
                                    Alpha Blending
                                                                        Synchroniza�on
                                               Sync
                                         Stage n                        RGB
                                                                                         DPI-008




     The default layer order is ascending (bottom -> top):
     Background color -> Layer 1 -> Layer 2
     The blending technique uses 8 × 8-bit multiplications with a 8-bit result. The general blending formula is as
     follows:


                                              c’ = f1 × c + f2 × cs ,                                                           (18-1)
     where:
     c’ = blended color
     f1 = blend factor 1
     c = current layer color
     f2 = blend factor 2
     cs = subjacent layers blended color
     For f1 the following factors, that can be selected in the CDC_Ln_BLEND_CFG[F1_SEL] register field, are
     available:

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                           1576
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                        www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                              E7 Series


       n Constant alpha; field value = 4
       n Pixel alpha × constant alpha; field value = 6

     For f2 the following factors, that can be selected in the CDC_Ln_BLEND_CFG[F2_SEL] register field, are
     available:
       n 1.0—constant alpha; field value = 5
       n 1.0—(pixel alpha × constant alpha); field value = 7

     If a factor, which is not usable/available, is selected via the registers, the respective default (reset) factor is
     effectively used internally.
     If for either f1 or f2 a factor with ‘constant alpha’ is selected, a constant alpha value can be programmed for
     the blending in the CDC_Ln_CONST_ALPHA register.
     The background color, which is used for blending with the bottom layer, can be configured in the CDC_
     BACKGND_COLOR register.

 18.1.4.4.7 Shadowed Registers Reload
     Some CDC registers are double-buffered, meaning that they are shadowed. The shadow registers values can
     be transferred in one go to the actual working registers (reload) upon a certain event: either triggered by a
     register write (immediate reload) or at the beginning of the vertical blanking (delayed reload).
     The reset values of the shadow registers is the same as for the respective working registers. Reading from a
     shadowed register returns the actual working register value, that is, the new value can only be read after the
     reload has taken place.
     The CDC provides shadow registers reload control for each layer through the CDC_Ln_REL_CTRL register.
     Writing to this register triggers an immediate or delayed update of the active registers from their associated
     shadow register values. If the CDC_Ln_REL_CTRL[SH_VBLANK] bit is set to '1', the registers are updated at the
     beginning of the first line after the active area. If the CDC_Ln_REL_CTRL[SH_IM] is set to '1', the registers are
     updated immediately.
     The shadowed registers are all layer registers, except the CDC_Ln_CLUT_WRACC register.

 18.1.4.5 CDC Video Output Configuration

 18.1.4.5.1 Timings Generation
     The timing generator generates the Horizontal Synchronization (HSYNC), Vertical Synchronization (VSYNC)
     and Data Enable (DE) timing signals for the display output interface.
     The current display screen coordinates are sent to the Alpha Blending Control (ABC) units of each layer to
     allow correct windowing. To correctly display a picture, the video data must be synchronous to the sync and
     DE signals of the timing generator. To guarantee a synchronous output, all synchronization signals are
     pipelined through the Alpha Blending Pipeline (ABP).
     The timing generator supports resolutions up to 2K at different refresh rates. The maximum possible
     resolutions are effectively further constrained by the available bandwidth and the operating pixel clock
     frequency.
     Figure 18-9 shows the configurable video timing parameters for both directions (horizontal, vertical) of the
     total and active video areas.

                                                         1577
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                           E7 Series


                                           Figure 18-9 CDC Video Timing Parameters

                                       HSYNC Width     HBP                                 HFP
                                                                         Ac�ve Width


                      VSYNC Height             (0,0)              Display Panel
                                VBP                                                    x


                                                                                                 Total Height
                            Ac�ve Height                                Ac�ve Region



                                                             y
                                 VFP

                                                                                                           DPI-009
                                                                  Total Width


     The HSYNC width (horizontal sync pixels minus 1) and the VSYNC height (number of vertical sync lines minus
     1) are defined in the CDC_SYNC_SIZE_CFG register.
     The accumulated width number of HSYNC and Horizontal Back Porch (HBP) pixels minus 1 and the
     accumulated height number of VSYNC and Vertical Back Porch (VBP) lines minus 1 are defined in the CDC_
     BP_CFG register.
     The accumulated width number of HSYNC, VBP and active pixels minus 1 and the accumulated height
     number of VSYNC, VBP and active lines minus 1 are defined in the CDC_ACTW_CFG register.
     The total width number of HSYNC, HBP, active area and Horizontal Front Porch (HFP) pixels minus 1 and the
     total height number of VSYNC, VBP, active area and Vertical Front Porch (VFP) lines minus 1 are defined in
     the CDC_TOTALW_CFG register.
     When the CDC is enabled, the internal timing generator starts with positions X,Y = (0,0) as the first horizontal
     sync pixel in the vertical sync area. Following are the back porch, the active area and the front porch.
     When the CDC is disabled, the timing generator is reset to positions X = TOTAL_WIDTH - 1, Y = TOTAL_
     HEIGHT - 1, and held (that is, at the last pixel before the vertical sync phase). Thus, only blanking data is
     output continuously while the CDC is disabled. The layer FIFOs are flushed.
     The VSYNC signal is asserted and de-asserted synchronously with the leading edge of the HSYNC signal. The
     polarity of the HSYNC, VSYNC, DE and PCLK output signals can be configured via the CDC_GLB_CTRL[HSPOL]
     [VSPOL][BLPOL][PCLKPOL] register bits, respectively. The current X and Y positions are indicated in the CDC_
     POS_STAT register.
     The HSYNC, VSYNC and DE signals status can be read from the corresponding bits of the CDC_SYNC_BLANK_
     STAT register. Here, the polarity does not depend on the polarity configuration of the corresponding output
     signals in the CDC_GLB_CTRL register. During blanking periods, the RGB data lines output all-zeros.

 18.1.4.5.2 Gamma Correction
     The CDC supports a gamma correction feature on its output, which maps the incoming RGB values to
     different output values. All output pixels are forwarded unchanged when the gamma correction is not used

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                                 1578
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                              www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     or not enabled.
     The gamma correction CLUTs are loaded by writing to the CDC_GAMMA_CORR register.
     By default, the gamma correction logic is bypassed. It can be enabled in the CDC_GLB_CTRL[GAMMA_EN]
     register bit.
     The gamma correction unit uses 9 grid points (nodes) for each color and implements linear interpolation
     among the node values. The upper 3 bits from input colors select the nodes from the CDC_GAMMA_CORR
     register-based tables, and the lower 5 bits are used for interpolation.
     The following lines show the gamma correction algorithm in a simplified manner:
     color_i = Input color (one of R/G/B)
     reg_table = Register based table for the concerned color
     node_idx = Index of the node from a register based table = color_i(7 down to 5)
     inter = Interpolation bits = color_i(4 down to 0)
     color_o = Output color (one of R/G/B)
     vl = Lower node value from the register based table = reg_table(node_idx)
     vh = Higher node value from the register based table (incremented by 1 if node at address 255)
     = reg_table(node_idx + 1) + 1 when node is at address 255;
     = reg_table(node_idx + 1) otherwise;
     color_o = gamma corrected color value = (((vh – vl)/32) x inter) + vl

 18.1.4.5.3 Dithering
     The dither unit at the CDC video output, when enabled in the CDC_GLB_CTRL[DITHER_EN] register bit, adds
     a small threshold value to each pixels color channel (R, G, or B) value, thus rounding up the MSB part in some
     cases instead of only truncating them.
     The dither unit implements an ordered dithering algorithm using a predefined Bayer matrix of 4×4 4-bit
     threshold values. The dithering technique is the same as comparing LSBs against a threshold value and
     adding a 1 to the MSB part only, if the LSB part is greater than or equal to the threshold. The LSBs are
     typically dropped after dithering has been applied.
     The number of bits to be dithered (that is, the width of the threshold values to be added) for each R, G and B
     color channel is fixed at 2 bits. After adding the threshold values, the resulting color values are clamped to
     0xFF, so that no overflow can occur.
     When the CDC is enabled, the dithering algorithm starts running with the first active pixel and from then on
     runs continuously, even during blanking times and when dithering is switched off. The dithering algorithm is
     always reset when the CDC is disabled.

 18.2 MIPI Display Serial Interface (DSI)

 18.2.1 DSI Overview
     The MIPI Display Serial Interface (DSI) facilitates the communication and data transfer to a MIPI DSI
     compliant display panel. The interface is realized through a MIPI DSI host controller that implements the
     protocol functions defined in the MIPI DSI Specification, and a MIPI D-PHY module acting as the physical
     layer.
     The device includes a single DSI implementation.
     The DSI supports the following main features:
       n Conformity to MIPI standards:
           lMIPI Alliance Specification for Display Serial Interface (DSI) Version 1.2—16 June 2014
         l MIPI Alliance Standard for Display Pixel Interface v2.00 (DPI-2)—15 September 2005

         l MIPI Alliance Specification for Stereoscopic Display Formats (SDF) v1.0—22 November 2011

         l MIPI Alliance Specification for D-PHY v1.2, 01 August 2014

       n PPI between the DSI host controller and the D-PHY transmitter
       n Up to two D-PHY TX data lanes
       n Up to 2.5 Gbps throughput per lane
       n Bidirectional communication and escape mode support through data lane 0
       n End of Transmission Packet (EoTp)
       n ECC and checksum capabilities
       n Fault recovery schemes
       n Stereoscopic (3D) image data transmission
       n Video mode only
       n Configurable MIPI Display Pixel Interface (DPI) to system level that provides:
         l Data transfer in Video mode:

           o Real-time pixel stream
           o Shut Down Peripheral and Color Mode commands

         l 24-bit RGB color coding

         l Programmable polarity of all DPI interface signals

         l The maximum resolution and frame rate are limited by the pixel clock and the available DSI physical

            link bandwidth (defined by the number of lanes and the maximum speed per lane)
       n Slave interface used for the transmission of generic commands
       n Independently programmable virtual channel ID for the DPI and slave interfaces
       n DPI payload FIFO with 1024 × 32-bit slots depth
       n Generic command FIFO with 16 × 32-bit slots depth
       n Generic payload FIFO with 128 × 32-bit slots depth
       n Generic read FIFO with 32 × 32-bit slots depth
       n Video mode pattern generator with the following capabilities:
         l Vertical and horizontal color bar generation without DPI stimuli

         l PHY Bit-Error Ratio (BER) pattern without DPI stimuli


     The DSI does not support the following features:
       n Command mode
       n VESA® Display Stream Compression (DSC) standard

     Figure 18-10 provides a high-level overview of the DSI implementation in the device.

 18.2.4 DSI Functional Description

 18.2.4.1 DSI Introduction
     Figure 18-13 presents a simplified diagram of the DSI main internal blocks and connections.

     The DSI controller captures pixel data and control signals on the DPI interface and conveys them to two
     internal FIFOs (one for video control signals and another one for the pixel data). This data is then used to
     build video packets when the DSI controller is configured in Video mode.
     The PHY Interface Control block manages the PHY PPI interfaces. It acknowledges the current operation and
     enables low-power transmission/reception or a high-speed transmission. It also performs data splitting
     between available PHY lanes for high-speed transmission.
     The Packet Handler block schedules the activities inside the link. It performs several functions for the DPI
     interface based on the video transmission mode that is used (burst mode or Non-Burst mode with sync
     pulses or sync events). It builds long or short packet generating correspondent ECC and CRC codes. This block
     also performs the following functions:
       n Packet reception
       n Validation of packet header by checking the ECC
       n Header correction and notification for single-bit errors
       n Termination of reception
       n Multiple header error notification
       n Routing the output data to the Generic port based on the virtual channel of the incoming packet




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                               Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1602
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                 www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                           E7 Series


     The APB-to-Generic block bridges the APB operations into FIFOs holding the Generic commands. The block
     interfaces with the Command FIFO, Write payload FIFO and the Read payload FIFO.
     The Error management block notifies and monitors the error conditions on the DSI link. It controls the timers
     used to determine if a timeout condition occurred, performing an internal soft reset and triggering an
     interruption notification.
     The DSI configuration and control registers are accessible through the APB slave interface. There is also a
     fully programmable interrupt generator to inform the system about certain events.
     The DSI controller includes also a Video mode pattern generator. The video pattern generator allows the
     transmission of an auto-generated horizontal/vertical color bar pattern image and PHY BER testing pattern.

 18.2.4.2 DSI Clocks
     The DSI controller uses the following clocks:
       n PCLK: This is the input clock signal on the APB slave interface. It is used for internal register configuration
         and also for generic packets transmission.
       n DPIPCLK: This is the input clock signal on the DPI interface. The reception of pixel data stream and
         synchronization signals happens on this clock.
       n RXCLKESC: This is the lane 0 low-power RX Escape Mode input clock signal received from the D-PHY TX.
       n TXCLKESC: This is the lane 0 low-power TX Escape Mode output clock signal sent to the D-PHY TX.
       n LANEBYTECLK: This is the input PHY lane byte clock received from the D-PHY TX. The frequency of this
         clock is 1/8th of the D-PHY maximum speed. The minimum operational frequency should be three times
         RXCLKESC. The maximum speed that can be used is determined as follows:
         l 1.0 Gbps D-PHY: Maximum frequency of LANEBYTECLK = 125 MHz

         l 1.5 Gbps D-PHY: Maximum frequency of LANEBYTECLK = 187.5 MHz

         l 2.5 Gbps D-PHY: Maximum frequency of LANEBYTECLK = 312.5 MHz



 18.2.4.3 DSI Reset
     The DSI controller can be reset in software by writing to the DSI_PWR_IP[SHUTDOWNZ] register field.

 18.2.4.4 DSI Interrupt Requests
     The DSI controller outputs a single interrupt signal, DSI_IRQ, to system level. The DSI_IRQ is set to active
     state when an error occurs in either the DSI_INT_ST0 or the DSI_INT_ST1 register. For more details on the DSI
     errors, see Section 18.2.4.10 DSI Error Handling.

 18.2.4.5 DSI DPI Interface
     The DPI interface follows the MIPI DPI specification with pixel data bus width of 24 bits. It is used to transmit
     information in Video mode, in which the transfers from the host processor to the peripheral take the form of
     a real-time pixel stream.
     The DPI interface is used with displays that support the Video mode. The Video mode display device requires
     a continuous stream of pixel data and synchronization signals to be provided through the DSI link with
     accurate timing precision. The Video mode display has very low control capability. It can support only two
     commands ShutDown (SD) and ColorMode (CM) and does not support the read commands. The Slave
     Generic Interface can be used to complement the DPI interface, in order to transfer additional commands
     (for example, to initialize the display).




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                            Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1603
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


 18.2.4.5.1 DPI Interface Enabling
     The DPI interface captures the data and control signals and conveys them to the FIFO interfaces that transmit
     them to the DSI link. Two different streams of data are presented at the interface: video control signals and
     pixel data. The interface color coding is RGB and the pixel data is disposed throughout 24-bit data bus. The
     interface pixel color coding is DPIPIXDATA[23:16] = Red component, DPIPIXDATAD[15:8] = Green component,
     DPIPIXDATA[7:0] = Blue component. One entire pixel is received per DPIPCLK pixel clock cycle.
     The DPI interface provides flexible programming options:
       n Polarity control: All the control signals are programmable to change the polarity depending on system
         requirements.
       n After reset of the DSI the controller, the DPI interface waits for the first VSYNC active transition to start
         signal sampling, including pixel data, thus avoiding starting the transmission of the image data in the
         middle of a frame.
       n To avoid FIFO underflows and overflows, the configured number of pixels is assumed to be received at
         all times. This happens even if the DPIDATAEN signal is active for more or less time than necessary. A set
         of bits in the DSI_VID_PKT_STATUS register report the status of the FIFOs and internal buffers associated
         with DPI interface support.
       n To keep the memory organized with respect to the packet scheduling, the number of pixels per packet
         parameter is used to separate the memory space of different video packets.
     For the 24-bit data type, the number of pixels of payload is restricted to be a multiple of 1.

 18.2.4.5.2 Video Mode with Stereoscopic (3D) Image Data
     A short packet consists of the bytes shown in Table 18-14.
                                        Table 18-14 DSI Bytes in a Short Packet(1)

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.

     packet is sent with Data 0 byte set to 0x08, as bit 3 indicates that the 3D control payload is present in data 1
     byte (the other bits of data 0 are reserved). The data 1 includes a copy of the 3D control configuration that is
     defined in the DSI_SDF_3D[5-0] register bits.
