     The 3D control is also used to indicate that the 2D mode is on. When switching from a 3D mode to 2D mode
     (via the DSI_SDF_3D[MODE_3D] register field), the next VSS packet contains data 0 set to 0x08 and data 1
     has the two LSB set to '00' to indicate that the 3D and the 2D modes are not on.
     If the DSI_SDF_3D[SEND_3D_CFG] register bit is set, the 3D control configuration is automatically sent in
     every VSS packet. If not, the VSS with 3D information is only sent in the next frame.
     If 3D mode is disabled and the DSI_SDF_3D register is updated without activating the 3D information, the
     next VSS does not have the 3D information. This behavior ensures compatibility with display devices that do
     not understand this packet.

 18.2.4.5.3 Video Transmission Modes
     The following video transmission modes are supported:
       n   Burst mode
       n   Non-Burst mode
           l Non-Burst mode with sync pulse

           l Non-Burst mode with sync event



 18.2.4.5.3.1 Burst Mode
     In this mode, the entire active pixel line is buffered into a FIFO and transmitted in a single packet with no
     interruptions. This transmission mode requires that the DPI Pixel FIFO has the capacity to store a full line of
     active pixel data inside it. This mode is optimally used if there is a big difference between the pixel required
     bandwidth and DSI link bandwidth. This enables the DSI controller to quickly dispatch the entire active video
     line in a single burst of data and then return to low-power mode.

 18.2.4.5.3.2 Non-Burst Mode
     In this mode, the host processor uses the partitioning properties of the DSI controller to divide the video line
     transmission into several DSI packets. This is done to match the pixel required bandwidth with the DSI link
     bandwidth. With this mode, the DSI controller configuration does not require a full line of pixel data to be
     stored inside the DPI Pixel FIFO. It requires only the content of one video packet.

 18.2.4.5.3.3 Guidelines for Selecting the Burst or Non-Burst Mode
     Selecting the Burst and Non-Burst mode is mainly dependent on the system configuration and the display
     device requirements. The video transmission mode that suits the application scenario should be chosen. The
     Burst mode is more beneficial because it increases the probability of the link spending more time in the low-
     power mode, thus decreasing power consumption. However, the following conditions should be met for
     availing the maximum benefits from the Burst mode of operation:
       n The DSI controller should have sufficient pixel memory to store an entire pixel line to avoid the overflow
         of the internal FIFOs.
       n The display device should support receiving a full pixel line in a single packet burst to avoid the overflow
         on the reception buffer.
       n The DSI output bandwidth should be higher than the DPI system interface input bandwidth in a relation
         that enables the link to go to low-power state once per line.
     If the system cannot meet these requirements, it is likely that the pixel data is lost causing the malfunctioning
     of the display device while using the Burst mode. These errors are related to the capabilities of the system to
     store the temporary pixel data.



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1605
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                             E7 Series


     If all the conditions for using the Burst mode cannot be met, use the Non-Burst mode to avoid the errors
     caused by the Burst mode. The Non-Burst mode provides a better matching of rates for pixel transmission,
     enabling:
       n Only a certain amount of pixels to be stored in the memory and not requiring a full pixel line (lesser DPI
         RAM requirements in the DSI controller)
       n Operation with display devices that support only a small amount of pixel buffering (less than a full pixel
         line)
     The Non-Burst mode should be configured in such way that the DSI output pixel ratio matches with the DPI
     input pixel ratio, reducing the memory requirements on both host and/or display device side. This is achieved
     by dividing a pixel line into several chunks of pixels and optionally interleaving them with null packets.
     The following equations show how the DSI controller transmission parameters should be programmed in
     Non-Burst mode to match the DSI link pixel output ratio (left hand side of the "=" sign) and DPI pixel input
     (right hand side of the "=" sign).
       n When the null packets are enabled:
         LANEBYTECLK_period × DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS (DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE × bytes_per_pixel + 12 + DSI_VID_
         NULL_SIZE) / number_of_lanes = pixels_per_line × DPICLK_period
       n When the null packets are disabled:
         LANEBYTECLK_period × DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS (DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE × bytes_per_pixel + 6) / number_of_
         lanes = pixels_per_line × DPICLK_period

 18.2.4.5.4 Updating the DPI Configuration Dynamically
     It is possible to update the DPI configuration on the fly without impacting the current frame. It is done with
     the help of shadow registers. This feature is controlled by the DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL register.
     The new configuration is only used when the system requests for it.
     To update the DPI configuration during the transmission of a video frame, the configuration of that frame
     needs to be stored in the auxiliary registers. This way, the new frame configurations can be programmed in
     the registers without corrupting the current frame.
     By default, this feature is disabled. To enable this feature, set the DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL[VID_SHADOW_
     EN] register bit to 1. When this feature is enabled, the system supplies the configuration stored in the
     auxiliary registers. Figure 18-14 shows the necessary steps to update the DPI configuration.
                   Figure 18-14 DSI Flow to Update the DPI Configuration using Shadow Registers(1)

                               Read VID_SHADOW_CTRL                          Start Video Engine

 18.2.4.5.4.1 Immediate Update
     When the shadow register feature is active, the auxiliary registers require the DPI configuration before the
     video engine starts. This means that, after a reset, the DPI registers content is immediately copied to the
     auxiliary registers.
     In situations when it is required to immediately update the active registers without the reset, ensure that the
     DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL[VID_SHADOW_EN] and [VID_SHADOW_REQ] register bits are set to 0.

 18.2.4.5.4.2 Updating the Configuration During the Transmission of a Frame
     To update the DPI configuration during the transmission of a frame, the steps listed below should be
     followed:
       n Ensure that the DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL[VID_SHADOW_EN] register bit is set to 1.
       n Set the DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL[VID_SHADOW_REQ] bit to 1.
       n Monitor the DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL[VID_SHADOW_REQ] bit. This bit is set to 0 when the update is
         complete.

 18.2.4.5.4.3 Requesting a Configuration Update
     It is possible to request for the DPI configuration update at any part of the frame. The DSI controller waits
     until the end of the frame to change the configuration. However, sending the update request during the first
     line of the frame should be avoided, because the data must propagate between clock domains.

 18.2.4.6 DSI APB Slave Generic Interface
     The APB slave interface allows the transmission of generic read/write short and long packets based on
     registers configuration. The format and interpretation of the contents of these packets can be specific to the
     manufacturer of the display panel. The slave generic interface can operate concurrently with the DPI
     interface. The DPI interface does not support vendor-specific commands that are generally required to
     perform display initialization
     The DSI_GEN_PLD_DATA register has two distinct functions based on the operation. Writing to this register
     sends the data as payload, while reading this register returns the payload of a read-back operation. The DSI_
     GEN_HDR register contains the packet header type and header data. Writing to this register triggers the
     transmission of the packet implying that for a long packet, the packet payload needs to be written in advance
     in the DSI_GEN_PLD_DATA register.
     The valid packets available to be transmitted through the generic interface are as follows:
       n Generic Write Short Packet 0 Parameters
       n Generic Write Short Packet 1 Parameters
       n Generic Write Short Packet 2 Parameters
       n Generic Read Short Packet 0 Parameters
       n Generic Read Short Packet 1 Parameters
       n Generic Read Short Packet 2 Parameters
       n Maximum Read Packet Configuration
       n Generic Long Write Packet

     A set of bits in the DSI_CMD_PKT_STATUS register report the status of the FIFOs associated with generic
     interface support.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1607
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                  E7 Series


     Generic interface packets are transported using the DSI Video transmission mode. If Video mode is not
     selected in the DSI_MODE_CFG[CMD_VIDEO_MODE] register bit, the packets are not transmitted through
     the link and the related FIFOs can eventually get overflowed.
     The transfer of packets through the APB bus is based on the following conditions:
       n The write and read procedure takes two clock cycles each to be executed. This means that the maximum
         input data rate through the APB interface is always half the speed of the APB clock.
       n The data input bus has a maximum width of 32 bits. This allows for a relation to be defined between the
         input APB clock frequency and the maximum bit rate achievable by the APB interface.
       n The DSI link pixel bit rate when using solely the APB interface is equal to: APB_clock_frequency × 16
         Mbps.
       n When using only the APB interface, the theoretical DSI link maximum bit rate is given by the following
         formula:
         DSI link maximum bit rate = PCLK (in MHz) × 32 / 2 Mbps
         In the formula, the number 32 represents the APB data bus width. The division by two is because each
         APB write procedure takes two clock cycles to be executed.
       n The bandwidth is dependent on the APB clock frequency (PCLK); the available bandwidth increases with
         the clock frequency.
     While writing the packet information, first the payload of a given packet should be written into the payload
     FIFO using the DSI_GEN_PLD_DATA register. When the payload data is for the command parameters, the first
     byte to be transmitted should be placed in the least significant byte position of the APB data bus. For more
     information, see the DSI_GEN_PLD_DATA register. After writing the payload, the packet header should be
     written into the command FIFO. For more information about the packet header organization and its proper
     storage inside the Command FIFO on the 32-bit APB data bus, see the DSI_GEN_HDR register.

 18.2.4.7 DSI Transmission of Commands

 18.2.4.7.1 Transmission of Commands in Video Mode
     The DSI controller supports the transmission of commands, both in high-speed and low-power, while
     configured in Video mode. The DSI uses Blanking or Low-Power (BLLP) periods to transmit commands
     inserted through the APB Generic interface. Those periods correspond to the shaded areas of Figure 18-15.
                         Figure 18-15 DSI Command Transmission Periods within the Image Area(1)

                               VSS or                           BLLP                 VSA and
                                HSS                                                  VPB lines




                               HSS + HBP             RGB           BLLP in    HFP    VACT lines
                                                                 Burst Mode



                                HSS                              BLLP                VFP lines    DSI-006




     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     Commands are transmitted in the blanking periods after the following packets/states:
       n   Vertical Sync Start (VSS) packets, if the Video Sync pulses are not enabled
       n   Horizontal Sync End (HSE) packets, in the VSA, VBP, and VFP regions
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                   Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1608
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                     www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                             E7 Series


       n Horizontal Sync Start (HSS) packets, if the Video Sync pulses are not enabled in the VSA, VBP, and VFP
         regions
       n Horizontal Active (HACT) state

     Only one command per line is transmitted in low-power mode. In high-speed mode, the DSI controller can
     send more than one command, as many as it determines to fit in the available time.
     The DSI controller avoids sending commands in the last line because it is possible that the last line is shorter
     than the other ones. For instance, the line time (tL) could be half a cycle longer than the tL on the DPI
     interface, that is, each line in the frame taking half a cycle from time for the last line. This results in the last
     line being (½ cycle) × (number of lines – 1) shorter than tL.
     The commands that can be sent in Video mode are are DSI data types Color Mode On, Color Mode Off, Shut
     Down Peripheral, and Turn on Peripheral. These commands should not be sent in the VACT region. If the DSI_
     VID_MODE_CFG[LP_CMD_EN] register bit is 1, these commands are sent in low-power mode. In low-power
     mode, the DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] register field is used to determine if these
     commands can be transmitted. It is assumed that the [OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] field value is greater than or
     equal to four bytes (number of bytes in a short packet), because the DSI controller does not transmit these
     commands on the last line.
     If the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[FRAME_BTA_ACK_EN] register field is set, a BTA is generated by the DSI
     controller after the last line of a frame. This may coincide with a write command or a read command.

 18.2.4.7.2 Transmission of Commands in Low-Power Mode
     The DSI controller can be configured to send the low-power commands during the high-speed video mode
     transmission. This feature is enabled by setting the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[LP_CMD_EN] register bit to 1. In this
     case, it is necessary to calculate the time available, in bytes, to transmit a command in low-power mode to
     Horizontal Front Porch (HFP), Vertical Sync Active (VSA), Vertical Back Porch (VBP), and Vertical Front Porch
     (VFP) regions.
     The [13-8] LP_* bits of the DSI VID_MODE_CFG register indicate if the DSI controller can go to low-power
     mode when in idle. If the [LP_CMD_EN] bit is set (1'b1) and non-video packets are in queue, the DSI
     controller ignores the low-power configuration and transmits low-power commands, even if it is not allowed
     to enter low-power in a specific region. After the low-power commands transmission, the DSI controller
     remains in low power until a sync event occurs.
     For example, in the case of VFP being selected as high-speed region (LP_VFP_EN = 1'b0) with LP_CMD_EN set
     as a command to transmit in low-power in the VPF region, this command is transmitted in low-power, and
     the line stays in low-power until a new HSS arrives.

 18.2.4.7.2.1 Calculating the Time to Transmit Commands in Low-Power Mode in the VSA, VBP, and
 VFP Regions
     The DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] register field indicates the time available (in bytes) to
     transmit a command in low-power mode (based on the escape clock) on a line during the VSA, VBP, and the
     VFP regions.
     The calculation of [OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] value depends on the video mode used. Figure 18-16 illustrates
     the timing intervals for the Video mode in Non-Burst with sync pulses and Figure 18-17 illustrates the timing

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     This time is calculated as follows:
     OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME = (tL - (tH1 + tHS->LP + tLP->HS + tLPDT + 2tESCCLK)) / (2 × 8 × tESCCLK)
     Where,
       n tL = Line time
       n tH1 = Time of the HSA pulse for sync pulses mode (see Figure 18-16) or the time to send the HSS packet,
         including EoTp (see Figure 18-17).
       n tHS->LP = Time to enter the low-power mode
       n tLP->HS = Time to leave the low-power mode
       n tLPDT = PHY timing related with Escape Mode Entry, LPDT Command, and Escape Exit. According to the
         MIPI D-PHY Specification, this value is always 11 bits in low-power (or 22 TXCLKESC clock cycles).
       n tESCCLK = Escape clock period as programmed in the DSI_CLKMGR_CFG[TX_ESC_CLK_DIVISION] register
         field
       n 2tESCCLK = Delay imposed by the DSI controller implementation

     In the previous equation, division by eight is done to convert the time available to bytes. Division by two is
     done because one bit is transmitted once in every two escape clock cycles. The DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM
     [OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] field can be compared directly with the size of the command to be transmitted to
     determine if there is enough time to transmit the command. The maximum size of a command that can be
     transmitted in low-power mode is limited to 255 bytes by this field. This register should be programmed to a
     value greater than or equal to 4 bytes for the transmission of the DSI controller commands, such as Color
     Mode On, Color Mode Off, and Shut Down Peripheral in low-power mode.
     Example
     This is an example of a frame with 12.4 μs per line and an escape clock frequency of 20 MHz and a lane bit
     rate of 800 Mbits. In this case, it is possible to send 124 bits in escape mode (that is, 124 bits = 12.4 μs × 20

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                        Alif Semiconductor
                                                                                       1610
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                                                     E7 Series


     MHz / 2). Also, it should be taken into consideration the PHY protocol and D-PHY timings. The following are
     the assumptions:
          n LANEBYTECLK period is 10 ns (800 Mbits per lane)
          n Escape clock period is 50 ns (DSI_CLKMGR_CFG[TX_ESC_CLK_DIVISION] register field value = 5)
          n Video is transmitted in Non-Burst mode with sync pulses bounded by HSS and HSE packets
          n The DSI interface is configured for two lanes
          n D-PHY takes 180 ns to transit from low-power to high-speed modes (DSI_PHY_TMR_CFG[PHY_LP2HS_
            TIME] register field value = 18)
          n D-PHY takes 200 ns to transit from high-speed to low-power modes (DSI_PHY_TMR_CFG[PHY_LP2HS_
            TIME] register field value = 20)
          n tHSA = 420 ns

     In this example, a 13-byte command can be transmitted as follows:
     DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] = (12.4 μs - (420 ns + 180 ns +200 ns + (22 × 50 ns + 2 × 50
     ns))) / (2 × 8 × 50 ns) = 13 bytes

     The calculation of DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[INVACT_LPCMD_TIME] register field value depends on the the
     video mode used. Figure 18-18 shows the timing intervals for video mode in Non-Burst with sync pulses.
     Figure 18-19 shows the timing intervals for video mode in Non-Burst with sync events. Figure 18-20 shows

     This DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[INVACT_LPCMD_TIME] register field value is calculated as follows:
     INVACT_LPCMD_TIME = (tL - (tHSA + tHBP + tHACT + tHS->LP + tLP->HS + tLPDT + 2tESCCLK)) / (2 × 8 × tESCCLK)
     Where,
          n tL = Line time
          n tHSA = Time of the HSA pulse (set in the DSI_VID_HSA_TIME register)
          n tHBP = Time of Horizontal Back Porch (set in the DSI_VID_HBP_TIME register)
          n tHACT = Time of Video active. For Burst mode, the Video active is time compressed and is calculated as
            follows:
            l t
                HACT = VID_PKT_SIZE × Bytes_per_Pixel / Number_of_Lanes × tLANEBYTECLK
          n tESCCLK = Escape clock period as programmed in the DSI_CLKMGR_CFG[TX_ESC_CLK_DIVISION] register
            field
     The DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[INVACT_LPCMD_TIME] field value can be compared directly with the size of the
     command to be transmitted to determine if there is time to transmit the command.
     Example
     This is an example of a frame with 16.4 μs per line and an escape clock frequency of 20 MHz and a lane bit
     rate of 800 Mbits. In this case, it is possible to send 420 bits in escape mode (that is, 164 bits = 16.4 μs × 20
     MHz / 2). Because this is the Vertical Active region of the frame, the HSA, HBP, and HACT timings should be
     considered apart from the D-PHY protocol and D-PHY timings. The following is assumed:
          n Number of active lanes is 4
          n LANEBYTECLK period is 10 ns (800 Mbits per lane)
          n Escape clock period is 50 ns (DSI_CLKMGR_CFG[TX_ESC_CLK_DIVISION] = 5)
          n PHY takes 180 ns to transit from low-power to high-speed modes (DSI_PHY_TMR_CFG[PHY_LP2HS_
            TIME] = 18)
          n PHY takes 200 ns to transit from high-speed to low-power modes (DSI_PHY_TMR_CFG[PHY_LP2HP_
            TIME] = 20)
          n tHSA = 420 ns
          n tHBP = 800 ns
          n tHACT = 12800 ns to send 1280 pixel at 24 bpp
          n Video is transmitted in Non-Burst mode
          n DSI controller is configured for four lanes

     The video is sent in Non-Burst mode. The DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[INVACT_LPCMD_TIME] field value is
     calculated as follows:
     INVACT_LPCMD_TIME = (16.4 μs - (420 ns + 800 ns + 12.8 μs + 180 ns +200 ns + (22 × 50 ns + 2 × 50 ns)) / (2 ×
     8 × 50 ns) = 1 byte
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1612
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                  www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                      E7 Series


     Only one byte can be transmitted in this period. A short packet (for example, generic short write) requires a
     minimum of four bytes. Therefore, in this example, commands are not sent in the VACT region.
     If Burst mode is enabled, more time is available to transmit the commands in the VACT region, because HACT
     is time compressed. In this case:
     INVACT_LPCMD_TIME = (16.4 μs - (420 ns + 800 ns + (1280 × 3 / 4 × 10 ns) + 180 ns + 200 ns + (22 × 50 ns + 2
     × 50 ns) / (2 × 8 × 50 ns) = 5 bytes
     For Burst mode, the DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM[INVACT_LPCMD_TIME] is 5 bytes and a 4-byte short packet can
     be effectively sent.

 18.2.4.7.3 Transmission of Commands in High-Speed Mode
     If the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[LP_CMD_EN] register bit is set to 0, the commands are sent in high-speed in
     video mode. In this case, the DSI controller automatically determines the area where each command can be
     sent and no programming or calculation is required.

 18.2.4.7.4 Read Command Transmission
     The DSI_PHY_TMR_RD_CFG[MAX_RD_TIME] register field configures the maximum amount of time required
     to perform a read command in LANEBYTECLK cycles. It is calculated as follows:
     [MAX_RD_TIME] = Time to transmit the read command in low-power mode + Time to enter and leave low
     power mode + Time to return the read data packet from the peripheral device.
     The time to return the read data packet from the peripheral depends on the number of bytes read and the
     escape clock frequency of the peripheral, not the escape clock of the host. The DSI_PHY_TMR_RD_CFG[MAX_
     RD_TIME] field is used in both high-speed and low-power modes to determine if there is time to complete a
     read command in a BLLP period.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                       Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1613
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


     In high-speed mode (DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[LP_CMD_EN] = 0), the DSI_PHY_TMR_RD_CFG[MAX_RD_TIME]
     value is calculated as follows:
     MAX_RD_TIME = (tHS->LP + tLP->HS + tread + 2 × tBTA) / LANEBYTECLK_period
     In low-power mode (VID_MODE_CFG[LP_CMD_EN] = 1), the [MAX_RD_TIME] value is calculated as follows:
     MAX_RD_TIME = (tHS->LP + tLP->HS + tLPDT + tlprd + tread + 2 x tBTA) / LANEBYTECLK_period
     Where,
       n tHS->LP = Time to enter the low-power mode
       n tLP->HS = Time to leave the low-power mode
       n tLPDT = PHY timing related to Escape mode entry, LPDT command, and Escape mode exit. According to
         the PHY specification, this value is always 11 bits in low-power (or 22 TX escape clock cycles).
       n tlprd = Read command time in low-power mode (64 × TXCLKESC)
       n tread = Time to return the read data packet from the peripheral
       n tBTA = Time to perform a bus turnaround (D-PHY dependent)

     It is recommended to keep the maximum number of bytes read from the peripheral to a minimum to have
     sufficient time available to issue the read commands in a line time. It must be ensured that:
      [MAX_RD_TIME] x LANEBYTECLK_period < [OUTVACT_LPCMD_TIME] x 16 x TXCLKESC_period
     Otherwise, the read commands are dispatched on the last line of a frame. If it is necessary to read a large
     number of parameters (> 16), the DSI_PHY_TMR_RD_CFG[MAX_RD_TIME] can be increased while the read
     command is being executed. When the read has completed, the DSI_PHY_TMR_RD_CFG[MAX_RD_TIME] ca
     be decreased to a lower value.

 18.2.4.7.5 Clock Lane in Low-Power Mode
     To reduce the power consumption of the D-PHY, the DSI controller, when not transmitting in the high-speed
     mode, allows the clock lane to enter into the low-power mode. The controller automatically handles the
     transition of the clock lane from high-speed (clock lane active sending clock) to low-power state without
     direct intervention by the software. This feature can be enabled by configuring the [PHY_TXREQUESTCLKHS]
     and [AUTO_CLKLANE_CTRL] bits of the DSI_LPCLK_CTRL register.
     In video mode, the DSI controller uses its internal video and D-PHY timing configurations to determine if
     there is time available for the clock line to enter the low-power mode and not compromise the video data
     transmission of pixel data and sync events.
     Along with a correct configuration of the video mode (see Section 18.2.4.5 DSI DPI Interface), the DSI
     controller needs to know the time required by the clock lane to go from high-speed to low-power and from
     low-power to high-speed.
     The DSI_PHY_TMR_LPCLK_CFG register should be programmed with the following values:
       n [PHY_CLKHS2LP] = Time from high-speed to low-power in clock lane / Byte clock period in high-speed
         (LANEBYTECLK)
       n [PHY_CLKHS2HS] = Time from low-power to high-speed in clock lane / Byte clock period in high-speed
         (LANEBYTECLK)
     Based on the programmed values, the DSI controller calculates if there is enough time for the clock lane to
     enter the low-power mode during inactive regions of the video frame.
     The DSI controller decides the best approach to follow regarding power saving out of the following three
     possible scenarios:

     Figure 18-22

 18.2.4.8 DSI Virtual Channels
     The DSI controller supports choosing the Virtual Channel (VC) for use for each interface. Using multiple
     Virtual Channels, the system can address multiple displays at the same time, when each display has a
     different VC identifier.
     When the DPI interface is configured for a particular VC, it is possible to use the APB Slave Generic interface
     to issue the commands while the video stream is being transmitted. With this, it is possible to send the
     commands through the ongoing video stream, addressing different VCs and thus enable the interface with
     multiple displays. During the Video mode, the video stream transmission has the maximum priority.
     Therefore, the transmission of sideband packets such as the ones from the Generic Interface are only
     transported when there is time available within the video stream transmission. The DSI controller identifies
     the available time periods and uses them to transport the Generic interface packets. Figure 18-25 illustrates

     stream delivered by the DPI interface.

     It is also possible to address the multiple displays with only the Generic interface using different VCs. Because
     the Generic Interface is not restricted to any particular VC through configuration, it is possible to issue the
     packets with different VCs. This enables the interface to time-multiplex the packets to be provided to the
     displays with different VCs.
     The DSI_DPI_VCID register configures the DPI Virtual Channel ID that is indexed to the Video mode packets.
     The DSI_GEN_HDR register configures the Packet Header (which includes the VC ID to be used) for
     transmissions using the APB Slave Generic interface.

 18.2.4.9 DSI Pattern Generator
     The Pattern Generator allows the transmission of horizontal/vertical color bar and PHY BER testing pattern
     without any stimuli. It is used in Video mode operation.
     The frame requirements must be defined in the following video registers:
       n DSI_VID_MODE_CFG = Video mode configuration
       n DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE = Video packet size
       n DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS = Number of chunks
       n DSI_VID_NULL_SIZE = Null packet size
       n DSI_VID_HSA_TIME = Horizontal Sync Active (HSA) time
       n DSI_VID_HBP_TIME = Horizontal Back Porch (HBP) time
       n DSI_VID_HLINE_TIME = Line time
       n DSI_VID_VSA_LINES = Vertical Sync Active (VSA) period
       n DSI_VID_VBP_LINES = Vertical Back Porch (VBP) period
       n DSI_VID_VFP_LINES = Vertical Front Porch (VFP) period
       n DSI_VID_VACTIVE_LINES = Vertical resolution

 18.2.4.9.1 Color Bar Pattern
     The color bar pattern comprises eight bars of the colors white, yellow, cyan, green, magenta, red, blue, and
     black.
     Each color width is calculated by dividing the line pixel size (vertical pattern) or the number of lines
     (horizontal pattern) by eight. In the vertical color bar mode (see Figure 18-26), each single color bar has a
     width of the number of pixels in a line divided by eight. In case the number of pixels in a line is not divisible
     by eight, the last color (black) contains the remaining pixels. In the horizontal color bar mode (see Figure 18-
     26), each color line has a color width of the number of lines in a frame divided by eight. In case the number
     of lines in a frame is not divisible by eight, the last color (black) contains the remaining lines.

 18.2.4.10 DSI Error Handling

 18.2.4.10.1 Errors Raised by Timeouts
     The DSI controller implements a set of timers and conditions to notify the errors. The controller has a set of
     registers to control the timers that are used to determine if a timeout has occurred. It also contains a set of
     interruption status registers that are cleared upon a read operation. Optionally, these registers also trigger
     an interrupt signal that can be used by the system to be activated when an error occurs within the DSI
     connection.
     The DSI_INT_ST1[TO_HS_TX] register field is set when a high-speed transmission timeout occurs (see Figure
     18-30), rising an interrupt. The timeout is configured in the DSI_TO_CNT_CFG[HSTX_TO_CNT] register field. A
     16-bit counter measures the time during which the high-speed mode is active. If that counter reaches the
     value defined by the DSI_TO_CNT_CFG[HSTX_TO_CNT] field, the DSI_INT_ST1[TO_HS_TX] field is asserted
     and an internal soft reset is generated to the DSI controller.
                            Figure 18-30 DSI High-Speed Transmission Errors Raised by Timeouts(1)

           LANEBYTECLK

             TOCLK_ENA

        HS_TX_COUNTER                              0          HSTX_TO_CNT-4 HSTX_TO_CNT-3   HSTX_TO_CNT-2       HSTX_TO_CNT-1   HSTX_TO_CNT     0

               TO_HS_TX                                                                                                                                       DSI-021

     The DSI_INT_ST1[TO_LP_RX] register field is set to flag the contention detection when a low-power reception
     timeout occurs, rising an interrupt (see Figure 18-31). The timeout is configured in the DSI_TO_CNT_CFG
     [LPRX_TO_CNT] register field. A 16-bit counter measures the time during which the low-power reception is
     active. If that counter reaches the value defined by the [LPRX_TO_CNT] field, the [TO_LP_RX] field is asserted
     and an internal soft reset is generated to the DSI controller.

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     Time units for these 16-bit counters are configured in cycles defined in the DSI_CLKMGR_CFG[TO_CLK_
     DIVISION] register field. The value written to the [TO_CLK_DIVISION] field defines the time unit for the
     timeout limits using the LANEBYTECLK as input. This mechanism increases the range to define these limits.

 18.2.4.10.2 Error Control
     The DSI_INT_ST0 and DSI_INT_ST1 registers are associated with error condition reporting. These registers
     can trigger the DSI_IRQ interrupt signal to inform the system about the occurrence of errors.
     The triggering of the interrupt can be masked by programming the DSI_INT_MSK0 and DSI_INT_MSK1 mask
     registers. By default all errors are masked. When any bit of these registers is set to 1, it enables the interrupt
     for a specific error. The error bit is always set in the respective DSI_INT_ST0/DSI_INT_ST1 register. The DSI_
     INT_ST0 and DSI_INT_ST1 registers are always cleared after a read operation. The DSI_IRQ interrupt is
     cleared if all registers that caused the interrupt are read.
     The interrupt force registers, DSI_INT_FORCE0 and DSI_INT_FORCE1, allow triggering the interrupt events
     individually without the need to activate the conditions that trigger the interrupt sources. Setting any bit of
     these registers to 1 triggers the corresponding interrupt.
     Figure 18-32 illustrates the location of some of the errors. For information about the causes of the errors and
     the action to be taken, see Section 18.2.4.10.3 Causes of Errors and Recovery.

 18.2.4.12 DSI D-PHY TX and PLL Operation

 18.2.4.12.1 D-PHY TX Introduction
     The DSI D-PHY TX module implements the physical layer for the MIPI D-PHY interface. The PHY comprises of
     two data lanes and one clock lane. Data lane 0 is bidirectional, while data lane 1 is unidirectional. The PHY is
     used in master applications where it transmits the High-speed (HS) clock and data in the forward direction.
     The lane modules support HS-TX, HS-RX, LP-TX, LP-RX, and LP-CD functions. The PHY also includes a clock
     multiplier PLL for the HS clock generation.
     The PHY provides high-speed digital data transmission from the device to an external MIPI DSI-compliant
     display module supporting a maximum effective bit rate of 2.5 Gbps (per lane in forward direction). The
     assembled two data lanes system enables up to 10 Gbps aggregated communication throughput. An
     additional low-power data reception mode with reduced throughput is supported through data lane 0.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1627
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                             E7 Series


     The PHY interfaces with the DSI controller through the PHY Protocol Interface (PPI). The DSI controller
     implements all protocol functions defined in the MIPI DSI specification. This provides an interface between
     the system and the PHY, which allows the communication with the external MIPI DSI-compliant display
     module.

 18.2.4.12.2 D-PHY TX PLL Description

 18.2.4.12.2.1 PLL Overview
     The PLL features a flexible clock-multiplying architecture to support changes in the lane bit-rate requirements
     of the D-PHY TX depending on the application. The PLL uses a VCO comprised of a pseudo-differential
     oscillator ring. The VCO output frequency is divided by a programmable counter before being compared to a
     crystal-based input reference frequency by means of a three-state phase-frequency detector (PFD) with no
     dead-zone. The digital PFD commands a charge-pump, which in turn delivers a charge to the loop filter or,
     alternatively, extracts a charge from the filter.
     The PLL generates quadrature clocks CLKOUT0, CLKOUT90, CLKOUT180 and CLKOUT270 to support the D-PHY
     TX operations.
     The proper configuration of the PLL for the desired frequency operation depends on the relation between
     the PLL output clock phases and the D-PHY data rate. The data rate is given by the double of the PLL output
     clock phases frequency: Data rate (Gbps) = PLL Fout (GHz) × 2. For example, for 2 Gbps operating frequency,
     the VCO output frequency is 1 GHz.
     The PLL can be configured through the D-PHY or through its dedicated system configuration interface. All PLL
     configurations for the desired operating frequency need to be done before D-PHY power-up.
     Figure 18-33 shows a functional diagram of the PLL system.
                                   Figure 18-33 DSI D-PHY TX PLL Functional Diagram(1)

 18.2.4.12.2.2 PLL Features
     The PLL has the following main features:
       n Flexible input clock reference (CLKIN): 2 MHz to 64 MHz
       n VCO oscillating range: 320 – 1250 MHz
       n Output frequency range (CLKOUT): 40 – 1250 MHz
       n Agile clocking and direct device control/observability
       n Low-power bypass mode


 18.2.4.12.2.3 PLL Power Down Mode
     In Power Down mode, the control voltage of the VCO is actively pulled high, forcing the VCO oscillation to
     stop. Also, the Charge Pump current is cut off. The reference clock (CLKIN) is also internally disabled, thus
     reducing the power dissipation to a minimal value.
     It is recommended that during power down, reference clock is stopped and all control registers are cleared
     to their reset default values.
     This mode also behaves as a reset sequence for the PLL, forcing it to start its lock acquisition from a low
     output frequency.

 18.2.4.12.2.4 PLL Initialization
     All power supplies and CLKIN reference clock should be stable before PLL power-up.
     All PLL related control registers configuration and changes should occur while the PLL is powered down or
     during agile clocking.
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL1[PLL_SOC_M]—Feedback multiplication ratio M [9:0]
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL1[PLL_SOC_N]—Input frequency division ratio N [3:0]
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL2[PLL_SOC_VCO_CNTRL]—VCO operating range [5:0]
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL2[PLL_SOC_CPBIAS_CNTRL]—Charge Pump bias control [6:0]
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_GMP_CNTRL]—Effective loop-filter resistance control [1:0]
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL2[PLL_SOC_INT_CNTRL]—Integral Charge Pump control [5:0]
       n DPHY_PLL_CTRL2[PLL_SOC_PROP_CNTRL]—Proportional Charge Pump control [5:0]

     For control of the PLL through shadow registers (DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_SHADOW_CONTROL] = 0), the
     following procedure needs to be respected:
       n Program the DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_SHADOW_CLEAR] register bit to 0x1 to set shadow registers to
         their reset default value.
       n Input (N), feedback (M) dividers and other required PLL configurations should be set to appropriate
         values prior to initialization of PLL block.
       n After programming all registers, set the DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_UPDATEPLL] bit to 0x1 to update the
         PLL configuration.

 18.2.4.12.2.5 PLL Frequency Change
     The architecture allows on-the-fly switching between generated frequencies being that the maximum
     allowed frequency change is 5%. The change occurs due to an update of M and N division factors, and it is
     triggered by setting the DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_UPDATEPLL] register bit to 0x1.
     The agile clocking and relock mode cannot be exercised until PLL is locked on a generated frequency. Before
     updating PLL output selection to the updated generated frequency, it is required that the PLL lock is asserted.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1629

     UPDATEPLL] bit until lock is acquired and PLL is relocking.
     Setting the [PLL_SOC_UPDATEPLL] bit reads in values and, for a new configuration, another write to the [PLL_
     SOC_UPDATEPLL] bit is required; refer to Figure 18-35. A minimum Tsetup for [PLL_SOC_UPDATEPLL] is
     necessary in order to ensure that PLL input values are stable in shadow registers.

 18.2.4.12.2.6 PLL Relock Counter Operation
     During a frequency change, the DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_LOCK] register bit changes its state to 0. It flags a lock
     after several microseconds. During a relock phase, the [PHY_LOCK] bit changes to 1 only when the internal
     lock detector flags the lock. The [PHY_LOCK] bit—the internal lock indicator for a PHY operation—stays at 1
     during a relock operation. The relock circuit is gated until the PLL receives the first lock through the lock
     detector circuit, after which the circuit is reinitialized whenever the DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_UPDATEPLL]
     register bit is set to 0x1.

     PLL Bypass Mode
     The PLL can be bypassed by configuring the DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_CLKSEL] register field according to
     Table 18-25.

                                                                1633

                                                                                                       E7 Series

                 CLKSEL[1:0]                                                       CLKOUT
                    2b'00                     Clocks stopped
                    2b'01                     Clock generation
                    2b'10                     Buffered CLKEXT (PLL bypass clock)

     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     The D-PHY TX requires 4 clock phases generated by the PLL. In bypass mode, the phases are generated using
     internal divider. The PLL output frequency will be 2, 4, or 8 times slower than CLKEXT input frequency. The
     division factor depends on DPHY_PLL_CTRL2[PLL_SOC_VCO_CNTRL] register field settings as shown in Table
     18-26.
                      Table 18-26 DSI D-PHY TX PLL Division Factors Based on VCO Setting(1)
              VCO_CNTRL[5:4]                                                CLKOUT frequency
                    2b'0x                                                          Fin / 2
                    2b'10                                                          Fin / 4
                    2b'11                                                          Fin / 8
     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     Changing VCO_CNTRL[5:4] dynamically without stopping output clocks or resetting PLL can generate a glitch
     on the output. This puts a constraint on usage of bypass functionality during relock. To generate the
     expected bypass frequency, a 2, 4 or 8 times higher frequency (depending on VCO_CNTRL[5:4] setting) needs
     to be applied on CLKEXT, as explained in the following examples:
     Example 1: 1.5 Gbps data rate with agile clocking transition for 800 Mbps
       n VCO_CNTRL = 000011
       n PLL output clock frequency = CLKEXT / 2
       n Data rate = PLL output clock frequency × 2
       n Data rate (Gbps) = CLKEXT (GHz)
       n CLKEXT = 800 MHz for 800 Mbps data rate

     Example 2: 320 Mbps data rate with agile clocking transition for 200 Mbps
       n VCO_CNTRL = 100111
       n PLL output clock frequency = CLKEXT / 4
       n Data rate = PLL output clock frequency × 2
       n Data rate (Gbps) = CLKEXT / 2 (GHz)
       n CLKEXT = 400 MHz for 200 Mbps data rate

     Bypass mode is operational during PLL power down. In this case, the output frequency is twice lower than
     input CLKEXT. That is, for example, for 800 Mbps data rate operation, a CLKEXT frequency of 800 MHz shall
     be input for a PLL output clocks frequency of 400 MHz.

 18.2.4.12.5 D-PHY TX Calibration
     The PHY contains low-speed digital logic with blocks responsible for PHY power up and calibration
     algorithms.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                       Alif Semiconductor
                                                                1635
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


       n The resistor termination calibration logic relies on external resistor Rext (200 Ω with 1% spread). The
         logic is responsible to guarantee that the following PHY parameters meet the specification:

       n HS termination impedance can be calibrated to 45 Ω through control of CB_EN_45_OHM_RW field of

     The Rext is used only on calibration procedures during D-PHY initialization meaning that it can be
     disconnected after wards (after the PHY has reached idle mode). On this context, each PHY module can use it
     when required, as long as there is no more than one using it and forcing current across the resistor at the
     same time. For instance, if there are two D-PHYs sharing the Rext, the first PHY must power up and second
     one must only be powered up when bit[4] of test control register 0x0C9 of the first PHY is asserted. When
     Rext is not used, the current is disabled and Rext net is in High-Z.

 18.2.4.12.6.1 No Power Mode
     The No Power mode is characterized by the non-existence of any supply voltage applied to the PHY. In order
     to get to the powered modes, proper voltages should be applied sequentially to the PHY. This task is usually
     handled by the device power management routines.

 18.2.4.12.6.2 Shutdown Mode
     This mode is the lowest power consumption mode, where all analog blocks are disabled, and digital logic is
     reset. The current consumption is given by the analog standby current and the digital logic leakage current.
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                              Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1637
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     The mode is entered asynchronously when DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_RSTZ] and DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ]
     register bits are in low state. It should be ensured that the DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] bit is asserted
     by default, as it acts as an active high reset to the control block responsible for the configuration values
     preset. In this mode, the clock and data differential lines are Hi-Z.
     All necessary MIPI D-PHY configurations to set the desired operation should be made with the PHY on this
     mode, before Start-up.

 18.2.4.12.6.3 Control Mode
     Control mode is the default PHY operating mode. After the initialization is completed, the PHY remains in this
      default mode until a request is made either by the protocol layer, or directly through the sequence of low-
     power signals in the lanes in case of RX. While in control mode, the transmitter side sets the LP-11 state in
     the lanes - this is also called the Stop state.
     The receiver side remains in control mode while receiving LP-11 in the lines. Any request must start from and
     end in Stop state. Following a request, a lane can leave control mode for either high-speed data transfer
     mode, Escape mode, or Ultra Low Power state.

 18.2.4.12.6.4 High-Speed Mode
     Once the initialization sequence is completed, the PHY remains in control mode, which is the default
     operating mode, until some request appears. High-speed is one of the possible requests at this point. High-
     speed data transfer occurs in bursts. Only during these bursts the lane is in high-speed mode. A high-speed
     burst must start from and return to a Stop state (Control mode). A high-speed burst allows for the
     transmission of payload data by the data lanes.
     Inherent to such data transmission is the existence of a valid DDR clock in the clock lane.

 18.2.4.12.6.5 High-Speed Data Transmission (Master, Forward mode)
     When the PHY is configured as master, it only supports forward mode of operation. In this mode, high-speed
     is entered when a TX HS request is received (assuming that the PHY is in Stop state, the PLL is enabled and
     locked; otherwise, the TX HS request is not allowed if these conditions are not met). This request is
     processed in a slightly different way for clock and data lanes.
     For a clock lane, processing the high-speed starts with the transmission of a low-power sequence (LP01 and
     LP00). Only after generating this sequence the low-power driver is disabled, and the high-speed driver
     enabled. After the time necessary to settle TCLK-ZERO, the transmission of the high-speed DDR clock starts.
     For a data lane, the high-speed entry sequence is the same as for clock lanes (that is, LP01 (TLPX) followed by
     LP00 (THS-PREPARE) and by THS-ZERO), but in addition, before the payload data there is a leader sequence
     (THS-SYNC value 8’h1D) that allow for the receiver synchronization. The transmission of such sequence
     requires the existence of a valid high-speed clock signal in the clock lane. When the high-speed request input
     is disabled, each lane leaves the high-speed data transmission mode. It is important that a clock lane must be
     in high-speed mode during the complete high-speed data transmission state of all the lanes. The clock lane
     must enter the high-speed mode before a high-speed data transmission (TCLK-PRE) begins and it must not
     leave this state before all the lanes finish their respective high-speed (TCLK-POST).
     The operation sequence when leaving the high-speed mode is also slightly different for data and clock lanes.
     For a clock lane, the high-speed transmission always ends with a HS-0 state (TCLK-TRAIL), followed by the
     disabling of the high-speed driver, and enabling of low-power driver. As for a data lane, the transmission
     ends with the differential state opposite to the last bit transmitted (THS-TRAIL), followed by the disabling of



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1638
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     the high-speed driver, and enabling of the low-power driver driving Stop state in the lanes (LP11) and
     returning to Control mode.

 18.2.4.12.6.6 Escape Mode
     Escape mode is a special mode of operation that uses the data lanes to communicate using the low-power
     states at low-speed. The PHY supports this mode in both directions for all data lanes. A data lane enters the
     Escape mode through an Escape mode entry procedure (LP-11, LP-10, LP-00, LP-01, LP-00). If an LP-11 is
     detected before reaching LP-00 state, the entry is aborted and the receiver returns to the Stop state. Once
     the sequence is correctly completed, the transmitter sends an 8-bit command to indicate a requested action.
     Table 18-29 shows the Escape mode supported actions. If the entry command is not valid, it is ignored,
     ERRESC error flag goes high, and the receiver waits until the transmitter returns to the Stop state. The PHY
     applies Spaced-One-Hot encoding (a Mark state is interleaved with a Space state) on commands and data.
     Each symbol consists of the following two parts:
       n   One-hot phase
       n   Space state to transmit one bit, a Mark-1 should be sent followed by the Space state. In the case of a
           zero bit, a Mark-0 should be sent followed by Space state.
                  Table 18-29 DSI D-PHY TX Possible Escape Mode Sequences for Data Lanes(1)
                                                       Entry Command Pattern
      Escape Mode Action                                                                       Command Type
                                               (First Bit to Last Bit to be Transmitted)
  Low-Power Data
                                                             8b'11100001                            Mode
  Transmission
  Ultra Low Power State                                      8b'00011110                           Mode
  Reset Trigger                                              8b'01100010                           Trigger
  Unknown—3                                                  8b'01011101                           Trigger
  Unknown—4                                                  8b'00100001                           Trigger
  Unknown—5                                                  8b'10100000                           Trigger
     1. Contains Synopsys proprietary information. Used with permission.


     Low-Power Data Transmission (LPDT)
     In LPDT mode, the data can be transmitted by the protocol at low speed in Low-Power mode—high-speed
     receivers are off and low-power receivers are on. During LPDT, the protocol can pause by maintaining a
     Space state on the lines. The last state before exiting Escape mode is Mark-1—not considered as 1 bit—
     because it is followed by the Stop state.
     Data shall be encoded on the lines with the same Spaced-One-Hot code as used for the Entry commands.
     This encoding allows data to be self-clocked and does not rely on the clock lane.
     Remote Trigger
     This mode allows the protocol to send a flag to the receiving side, on request of the transmitting side. If the
     Entry Command Pattern matches the Reset-Trigger Command (01100010) a Trigger is flagged to the protocol
     at the receive side via the logical PPI. Any bit received after a Trigger Command but before the Lines go to
     Stop state shall be ignored. Therefore, dummy bytes can be concatenated in order to provide clock
     information to the receive side.
     Ultra Low Power State (ULPS)
     This mode has the lowest power consumption, excluding the Shutdown mode. For data lanes, this mode is
     entered by sending an Ultra Lower Power state entry command (00011110), after the Escape mode entry

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1639
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                         E7 Series


     command. During this mode, the lines are in the Space state (LP-00). Although the clock lane does not
     support regular Escape mode, the clock lane supports ULPS.
     To exit ULPS, the transmitter side drives a Mark-1 followed by a Stop state. The twakeup time must be ensured
     by the protocol layer.
     If PLL is disabled during ULPS and PLL configuration is being done through the PLL registers at device level,
     the DPHY_PLL_CTRL0[PLL_SOC_UPDATEPLL] register bit shall be set to 1 before exiting from ULPS.

 18.2.4.12.6.7 Turnaround
     The PHY allows the transmission direction of a data lane to be swapped by means of a turnaround request.
     The sequence of a turnaround operation occurs in this way:
      1. Transmitter side
         a. Starts when TX_DPHY_CTRL1[TURNREQUEST] bit is set to 0x1 on transmitter side, assuming the PHY
            is in Stop state
         b. Transmitter sends specific low-power sequence—LP11, LP10, LP00, L10, L00
      2. Receiver side
         a. After receiving complete low-power sequence, receiver enables low-power driver
         b. Transmits LP00, indicating change by setting DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_DIRECTION] bit to '0'
         c. Overlapping LP00 transmitted by initial transmitter
         d. Initial receiver side transmits LP10, followed by LP11, returning to Control mode


                                                        NOTE

       The turnaround procedure is the same for a Forward-to-Reverse direction or Reverse-to-Forward
       direction. For a Turnaround operation, it is necessary that the TXCLKESC signal is available on both the
       transmitter and receiver sides.


 18.2.4.12.7 D-PHY TX Lane Polarity Swap
     The PHY provides a polarity change control for the clock and data lanes. There is a dedicated test control
     register bit for each lane. When a control bit is set to 0x1, the polarity of the corresponding lane is swapped
     from P/N to N/P:
       n Clock lane: DPHY4TXTESTER_DIG_RDWR_TX_CLKLANE_LANE_6[0] POLARITY_CLKLANE bit, offset 0x307
       n Data lane 0: DPHY4TXTESTER_DIG_RDWR_TX_LANE0_LANE_6[0] POLARITY_LANE0 bit, offset 0x507
       n Data lane 1: DPHY4TXTESTER_DIG_RDWR_TX_LANE1_LANE_6[0] POLARITY_LANE1 bit, offset 0x707

     For more information on accessing the test control registers, see Section 18.2.4.12.8 D-PHY TX Control
     Registers Configuration.

 18.2.4.12.8 D-PHY TX Control Registers Configuration

 18.2.4.12.8.1 Overview
     The PHY has a test control interface that is primarily used for the PHY configuration of its normal operating
     modes. The interface can be driven through the following DSI registers and fields: DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_
     TESTCLK], [PHY_TESTCLR] and DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN], [PHT_TESTDOUT], [PHY_TESTDIN].




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1640
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                            E7 Series


 18.2.4.12.8.2 Registers Configuration Procedure
     The standard procedure for configuring a test control register in the PHY is two-folded; first the necessary
     control register address is programmed and then the related data is set.
     All PHY related configurations that impact its functional operation need to be done with the PHY in shutdown
     mode. The correct operation of the PHY may be compromised if the test and control interface is used during
     active modes to change the PHY operation configuration. It is allowed to use the test and control interface
     during active modes for debugging purposes and signals observability only. At the first PHY start-up, it is
     recommended to apply an interface reset (through setting DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 0x1) before
     any other test control register is set.
     Each control register address is composed by a 4-bit word (test code MSB) and an 8-bit word (test code LSB),
     referred to as 'offset'. With an 8-bit test and control interface, to access each control register, it is necessary
     to perform two write operations to respectively set the 12-bit control register address (test code MSB + test
     code LSB). For example, to access control register at offset 0x270, first the test code MSBs (value 0x2) need
     to be written and then the test code LSBs (value 0x70).
     The test code programming is done using the following steps:


                                                         NOTE

       For a back-to-back read from multiple registers, execute steps #1 and #2 (only).


      1. For writing the 4-bit test code MSB:
         a. Ensure that DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] and DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] register bits
            are set to 0x0.
         b. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x1
         c. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x1
         d. Place 0x00 in DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN] field
         e. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
         f. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x0
         g. Place the 8-bit word corresponding to the test code MSB in DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN]
         h. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x1
      2. For writing the 8-bit test code LSB:
         a. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
         b. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x1
         c. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x1
         d. Place the 8-bit word corresponding to the test code LSB in DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN]
         e. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
         f. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTEN] to 0x0
      3. For writing the test data:
         a. Place the 8-bit word test data in DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDIN]
         b. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLK] to 0x0
     The DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDOUT] register field reflects the test code or test data, as soon as it is
     written in the [PHY_TESTDIN] field.
     It is only required to write the 4-bit test code MSBs if they change for the next test code to be written. If not,
     they don't need to be written again. This represents executing steps #2 and #3 above.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                             Alif Semiconductor
                                                        1641
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                               www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                       E7 Series


     The steps above for writing the data can be repeated for different test data to be written to the same test
     code.
     Repeat the above procedure to program subsequent test codes. Additionally, a test reset procedure (DSI_
     PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 1) is only needed if there is a need for the PHY configuration to be reset to
     its default values and override any changes made meanwhile.
     After a test code is effectively programmed, DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1[PHY_TESTDOUT] asynchronously reflects
     the relevant data for that specific control register.

 18.2.4.12.8.3 Start-Up Sequence
     Before PHY Start-up, it needs to be properly configured for the desired operation. This has to be done with
     the PHY in Shutdown mode and it is assumed that such configurations are static or at least are stable prior to
     leaving the Shutdown mode.
     Before PHY power-up, set test control register 0x16A, bits[1-0] to 2'b11. These control bits can be configured
     to 2'b00 when in ULPS or power-down for reduced power consumption.
     The following PHY configurations need to be applied for the desired operation.
     The PHY operating frequency and input reference clock frequency can be programmed in the following
     register fields:
       n   PHY operating frequency: TX_DPHY_CTRL0[HSFREQRANGE]
       n   Input reference clock frequency: TX_DPHY_CTRL0[CFGCLKFREQRANGE]
     The input reference CFG_CLK frequency shall be programmed according to the following formula:
                                                                                                            (18-14)
     To configure the bit rate operation, the [HSFREQRANGE] field shall be directly configured for the desired
     frequency range. [HSFREQRANGE] can be programmed only before the D-PHY start-up and cannot be
     changed during active operation.
     The desired operating frequency configuration is required to meet the D-PHY specification global timing
     parameters and intervals, to ensure proper operation.


                                                       NOTE

     When PHY is operating as master, for data rates below 450 Mbps, CLKDIV_CLK_EN must be enabled. This can
     be achieved by writing 1'b1 in PHY test configuration register 0x1AC, bit [4].

     By default, the D-PHY Start-up sequence performs termination calibration considering the presence of an
     external termination resistor.
     The PHY consists of two data lanes, but the applications can use two or lesser number of data lanes. The lane
     enables must not be changed during operation. They should be set while the PHY is in power-down
     (STOPSTATE).


                                                                NOTE

       If only a single lane is to be enabled, that lane must be lane 0.


     After the resets (programmable by DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ], [PHY_RSTZ] register bits) are released,
     the PHY begins an initialization sequence that allows its correct operation. Programming [PHY_SHUTDOWNZ]
     should precede [PHY_RSTZ]; it is also assumed that the CFG_CLK signal is available and stable by that time.
     The initialization sequence determines that the bandgap and biasing blocks are enabled first. After the
     current references get settled, a second step is triggered where the internal calibrations are performed.
     This includes:
      1. Termination resistors calibration
      2. Data and clock lane offset compensation
      3. For operating frequencies < 1.5Gbps (D-PHY 1.1 backwards compatibility mode), an internal deskew
         compensation algorithm is executed with internal stimuli provided to data and clock lanes.
     The deskew algorithm selection is done automatically based on TX_DPHY_CTRL0[HSFREQRANGE]
     configuration. When this second step is complete, the control is passed to the lanes, which handle the power
     management for LP/HS requests, enabling or disabling the corresponding receivers. All initialization steps are
     complete once the DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_STOPSTATE1LANE], [PHY_STOPSTATE0LANE], [PHY_
     STOPSTATECLKLANE] register get asserted (if D-PHY TX is driving LP11).
     After the PLL is configured, the D-PHY is responsible for the power-up and power-down of the PLL within its
     power sequence logic. After DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ][PHY_RSTZ] register bits are released, the D-
     PHY starts its Start-up sequence and, with it enabled, the PLL will lock to the configured operation. It is
     assumed that all register configurations are static or at least are stable prior to leaving the Shutdown mode.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1644
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                            www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                          E7 Series


     If there are no operations through the test configuration interface to be performed, the DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0
     [PHY_TESTCLR] register bit can be kept at '1'. Otherwise, the [PHY_TESTCLR] must be de-asserted to bring the
     control logic out of reset and allow for the necessary configuration steps through the control interface.
     The MIPI D-PHY specification has many timing intervals which have to be followed to ensure proper
     operation. The initialization sequence ends when STOPSTATE LP11 is driven in the lanes and the PHY reaches
     Control mode state.
     The initialization period (TINIT) is a protocol dependent parameter with a minimum 100 μs defined by the
     MIPI specification. The PHY does not set any limit to the initialization period, meaning it starts decoding the
     LP commands after the AFE initialization in RX mode. It is up to the DSI controller or the upper layers to
     ensure the proper initialization times through the correct handling of the PHY configuration. This time must
     conform to MIPI D-PHY specification and obey the minimum specified 100 μs value.

 18.2.4.12.8.4 Configuration Example
     For PHY configuration purposes, the test and control interface must be exercised after a transition from 0 to
     1 of the DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] register bit and before PHY leaves shutdown mode (de-assertion
     of DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ], [PHY_RSTZ] bits) and start Start-up sequence.
     While [PHY_SHUTDOWNZ] and [PHY_RSTZ] are de-asserted, the PHY remains in POWERDWN state. If the PHY
     properly reached the end of its Start-up sequence, it will be in IDLE state.
     Example (Master; Operating Rate 1 Gbps; CFG_CLK = 27 MHz; Slew Rate Calibration Enabled):
      1. Set DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_RSTZ] = 0
      2. Set DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ] = 0
      3. Set TX_DPHY_CTRL0[TXRXZ] = 1
      4. Set DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0[PHY_TESTCLR] = 1
      5. Wait for 15 ns
      6. Set [PHY_TESTCLR] = 0
      7. Set TX_DPHY_CTRL0[HSFREQRANGE] = 0001010
      8. Configure TX test control register 0x16A to set field PLL_MPLL_PROG_RW[1-0] to 11
      9. Configure TX test control register 0x1AB to set field CB_SEL_VREF_LPRX_RW[1-0] to 10
     10. Configure TX test control register 0x1AA to set field CB_SEL_VREFCD_LPRW_RW[6-5] to 10
     11. Configure TX test control register 0x402 to set fields TXCLK_TERM_LOWCAP_LP00_EN_OVR_EN and
         TXCLK_TERM_LOWCAP_LP00_EN_OVR[1-0] to 10
     12. Refer to Table 18-27 and configure TX test control registers with appropriate values for the specified
         rise/fall time
     13. Set bits [5-4] of TX control register 0x272 to 01 to enable slew rate calibration. Lanes that are disabled
         should not run slew-rate calibration algorithm. For the disabled lanes, set bits SR_FINISHED_OVR_EN =
         1’b1, SR_FINISHED_OVR = 1’b1, SRCAL_EN_OVR_EN = 1’b1 through test control registers 0x310, 0x50B,
         0x70B.
     14. Set TX_DPHY_CTRL0[CFGCLKFREQRANGE] = round[(FCFG_CLK(MHz) - 17) × 4] = 00101000
     15. Apply CFG_CLK signal with the appropriate 27 MHz frequency
     16. Configure PLL operating frequency as described in Section 18.2.4.12.2 D-PHY TX PLL Description
     17. Set TX_DPHY_CTRL0[BASEDIR] = 0
     18. Set TX_DPHY_CTRL1[FORCERXMODE] = 0
     19. Wait for 15 ns
     20. Set DSI_PHY_IF_CFG[N_LANES] and DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_ENABLECLK] = 1
     21. Wait 5 ns
     22. Set DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ] = 1
     23. Wait 5 ns
Hardware Reference Manual                                                                           Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1645
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                     E7 Series


     24. Set DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_RSTZ] = 1
     25. Wait until DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_STOPSTATE1LANE][PHY_STOPSTATE0LANE][PHY_STOPSTATECLKLANE]
         registers bits are asserted indicating PHY is driving LP11 in enabled data lanes and clock lane
