 18.2.4.13 DSI Programming Guide

 18.2.4.13.1 General Programming Flow
     The following list summarizes the procedure and actions to program the DSI controller:
       n   Initialize DSI controller for the required operation:
           l Configure the DPI interface.

           l Set up the D-PHY to send and receive low-power and high-speed data at the desired frequency.


       n Set up the DSI controller to output a video pattern.
       n Set up a new DPI configuration without resetting the DSI controller.
       n Configure the DSI controller to enter and exit ULPM.


 18.2.4.13.2 Initializing the DSI Controller
     Follow the programming sequence to build a DSI-compliant system:
      1. Reset the DSI controller, either via the system-level reset or through the DSI_PWR_UP[SHUTDOWNZ]
         register bit.
      2. Configure the DSI_PHY_IF_CFG[N_LANES] register field to define the number of lanes with which the
         controller can perform high-speed transmissions.
      3. Assert a bit corresponding to the error that is supposed to trigger an interrupt into the DSI_INT_MSK0 or
         DSI_INT_MSK1 register.
      4. Configure DPI interface according to the programming sequence described in Section 18.2.4.13.4
         Configuring the Display Pixel Interface
      5. Initialize the D-PHY by following the programming sequence in Section 18.2.4.13.5 Initializing the D-PHY.
      6. Assert the DSI_PWR_UP[SHUTDOWNZ] register bit to power-up the DSI controller.

 18.2.4.13.3 Configuring the DPI Using Shadow Registers
     To update the DPI configuration without resetting the DSI controller or impacting the current frame, follow
     the programming sequence:
      1. Initializing sequence:
         a. Configure the DPI registers.
         b. Use immediate update to make the configuration active, by using the following register setting: DSI_
             VID_SHADOW_CTRL = 9’h101.
      2. Change the DPI configuration:
         a. Set the DPI registers with next configuration, as follows:
             n DSI_DPI_VCID
             n DSI_DPI_COLOR_CODING
             n DSI_DPI_LP_CMD_TIM
             n DSI_VID_MODE_CFG
             n DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE
             n DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS
             n DSI_VID_NULL_SIZE



Hardware Reference Manual                                                                          Alif Semiconductor
                                                       1649
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                             www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                     E7 Series


             n DSI_VID_HSA_TIME
             n DSI_VID_HBP_TIME
             n DSI_VID_HLINE_TIME
             n DSI_VID_VSA_LINES
             n DSI_VID_VBP_LINES
             n DSI_VID_VFP_LINES
             n DSI_VID_VACTIVE_LINES
             n DSI_SDF_3D
          b. To make the configuration active after the next Vsync, set register DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL = 9'h101.
          c. Wait until the update is concluded by verifying that DSI_VID_SHADOW_CTRL = 9’h001.

 18.2.4.13.4 Configuring the Display Pixel Interface
     Follow the sequence to configure the DPI:
      1. Configure the DPI interface to define how the DPI interface interacts with the DSI controller:
         n Configure DSI_DPI_VCID register: This field configures the virtual channel that the packets generated
           by the DPI interface is indexed.
         n Configure DSI_DPI_COLOR_CODING: This field configures the bits per pixel (bpp) that the interface
           transmits and also the variant configuration of each bpp.
         n Configure DSI_DPI_CFG_POL[DATAEN_ACTIVE_LOW]: This bit configures the polarity of the
           DPIDATAEN signal and sets it to be active low.
         n Configure DSI_DPI_CFG_POL[VSYNC_ACTIVE_LOW]: This bit configures the polarity of the DPIVSYNC
           signal and sets it to be active low.
         n Configure DSI_DPI_CFG_POL[HSYNC_ACTIVE_LOW]: This bit configures the polarity of the DPIHSYNC
           signal and sets it to be active low.
      2. Select the video transmission mode to define how the software requires the video line to be transported
         through the DSI link:
         n Configure the low-power transitions bits in DSI_VID_MODE_CFG register: Defines the video periods
           which are permitted to go to low-power if there is time available to do so.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[FRAME_BTA_ACK_EN] bit: Specifies if the DSI controller should
           request the peripheral acknowledge message at the end of frames.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[LP_CMD_EN] bit: Specifies that commands are to be transmitted
           in low-power.
         n Burst mode settings. For more details about Burst mode, see Section 18.2.4.5.3 Video Transmission
           Modes.
           l Configure the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[VID_MODE_TYPE] register field with value 2'b1x.

           l Configure the DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE register with the size of the active line period, measured in pixels.

           l The DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS and DSI_VID_NUM_SIZE registers are ignored by the DSI controller.

         n Non-Burst mode settings. For more details about Non-Burst mode, see Section 18.2.4.5.3 Video
           Transmission Modes.
           l Configure the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG[VID_MODE_TYPE] register field with 2'b0x.

           l Configure the [VID_MODE_TYPE] field with 0x0 to enable the transmission of sync pulses.

           l Configure the [VID_MODE_TYPE] field with 0x1 to enable the transmission of sync events.

           l Configure the DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE register with the number of pixels to be transmitted in a single

              packet. Selecting this value depends on the available memory of the attached peripheral, if the
              data is first stored, or on the memory size of the FIFOs in the DSI controller.
           l Configure the DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS register with the number of packets to be transmitted per

              video line. The value of DSI_VID_PKT_SIZE × DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS is the number of pixels per
              line of video, except if DSI_VID_NUM_CHUNKS is 0, which disables the multi-packets. If DSI_VID_

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                     1650
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                     E7 Series


              NUM_CHUNKS register is set to 1, there is still only one packet per line, but it can be part of a
              chunk, followed by a null packet.
           l Configure the DSI_VID_NULL_SIZE register with the size of null packets to be inserted as part of the

              chunks. Setting it to 0, disables null packets.
      3. Define the DPI horizontal timing configuration as follows:
         n Configure the DSI_VID_HLINE_TIME register with the time taken by a DPI video line measured in
           cycles of the LANEBYTECLK clock. When the periods of DPIPCLK and LANEBYTECLK clocks are not
           multiples, the value to program the DSI_VID_HLINE_TIME needs to be rounded. A timing mismatch is
           introduced between the lines due to the rounding of configuration values. If the DSI controller is
           configured for not to go to low-power, this timing divergence accumulates on every line, introducing a
           significant amount of mismatch towards the end of the frame. The reason for this is that the DSI
           controller cannot re-synchronize on every new line because, it transmits the blanking packets when
           the horizontal sync event occurs on the DPI interface. However, the accumulated mismatch should
           become extinct on the last line of a frame, where, according to the MIPI DSI specification, the link
           should always return to a low-power regaining synchronization, when a new frame starts on a vertical
           sync event. If the accumulated timing mismatch is greater than the time in low-power on the last line,
           a malfunction occurs. This phenomenon can be avoided by configuring the DSI controller to go to low-
           power once per line.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_HSA_TIME register with the time taken by a DPI HSA period measured in cycles
           of LANEBYTECLK.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_HBP_TIME with the time taken by the DPI Horizontal Back Porch period
           measured in cycles of LANEBYTECLK. Special attention should be given to the calculation of this
           parameter.
      4. Define the vertical line configuration:
         n Configure the DSI_VID_VSA_LINES register with the number of lines existing in the DPI VSA period.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_VBP_LINES register with the number of lines existing in the DPI VBP period.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_VFP_LINES register with the number of lines existing in the DPI VFP period.
         n Configure the DSI_VID_VACTIVE_LINES register with the number of lines existing in the DPI VA period.


 18.2.4.13.5 Initializing the D-PHY
     Follow the programming sequence to initialize the D-PHY:
      1. Power-up and reset the D-PHY using the DSI_PHY_RSTZ register.
      2. Configure the D-PHY PLL clock frequency through the test interface. For more details on the test
         interface and test codes, see Section 18.2.4.12 DSI D-PHY TX and PLL Operation.
         a. Write 32'h00000000 into DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0 register to enable the interface to write new values to
             the D-PHY internal registers.
         b. Write 32'h000100XX into DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1 register. This operation initiates the configuration
             process of the test code number 0xXX.
         c. Write 32'h0000002 into DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0 followed by writing 32'h00000000 to latch a new test
             code.
         d. Write 32'h000000XX into DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL1. This operation prepares the interface to load the test
             code 0xXX.
         e. Write 32'h00000002 into DSI_PHY_TST_CTRL0 followed by writing 32'h00000000 into PHY_TST_
             CTRL0 to latch a new content data to the configured test code.
      3. The TXCLKESC frequency must be configured between 2 to 20 MHz. This is done by writing into the DSI_
         CLKMGR_CFG[TX_ESC_CLK_DIVISION] register field. This field divides the LANEBYTECLK clock and
         generates a TXCLKESC clock for the D-PHY.


Hardware Reference Manual                                                                      Alif Semiconductor
                                                     1651
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                         www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                        E7 Series


      4. Clear the DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_SHUTDOWNZ] and [PHY_RSTZ] register fields to put the D-PHY in the reset
         state. Set the [PHY_SHUTDOWNZ] and [PHY_RSTZ] to remove the D-PHY from reset state.
      5. Verify that D-PHY active lanes are in Stop state, by reading the following DSI_PHY_STATUS register bits:
         n [PHY_STOPSTATECLKLANE] = 1’b1
         n [PHY_STOPSTATE0LANE] = 1’b1
         n [PHY_STOPSTATE1LANE] = 1’b1


 18.2.4.13.6 Configuring the Video Mode Pattern Generator
     The DSI controller can transmit a color bar pattern without horizontal or vertical color bar and D-PHY BER
     testing pattern without any kind of stimulation. Follow the programming sequence to send a test pattern:
      1. Configure the DSI_MODE_CFG register to enable Video mode.
      2. Configure the DSI_DPI_COLOR_CODING register.
      3. Configure the frame parameters using the registers shown in Figure 18-37. The number of pixels of
         payload is restricted to be a multiple of 1.
      4. In the DSI_VID_MODE_CFG register, configure the pattern generation mode in the [VPG_MODE] bit and
         the pattern orientation in [VPG_ORIENTATION] bit, and then enable the generator through the [VPG_
         EN] bit.

 18.2.4.13.7 Entering and Exiting the ULPM
     There are two ways to configure the software to enter and exit the ULPM:
       n Enter and exit the ULPM with the D-PHY PLL running. This is a faster process.
       n Enter and exit the ULPM with the D-PHY PLL turned off. This is a more efficient process in terms of
         power consumption.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                    Alif Semiconductor
                                                               1652
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                      www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                   E7 Series


                                                                NOTE

       Software has to assert the DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_FORCEPLL] register bit before activating the ULPM.


 18.2.4.13.7.1 Process Flow to Enter the ULPM
     Software can implement the process flow, shown in Figure 18-38, to enter the ULPM on both clock lane and
     data lanes.
      1. Set the register DSI_PHY_ULPS_CTRL = 4'h5 to enter ULPM in the data and clock lanes.
      2. Verify that all the data lanes has entered in ULPM using the DSI_PHY_STATUS register.
      3. The DSI controller is now in ULPM. Perform step 4 and step 5 to turn off the D-PHY PLL.
      4. Turn off the D-PHY PLL by setting DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_FORCEPLL] = 1'b0.
      5. Verify that the D-PHY PLL is unlocked by checking that DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_LOCK] = 1'b0.

 18.2.4.13.7.2 Process Flow to Exit the ULPM
     Software can implement the process flow, shown in Figure 18-39, to exit the ULPM on both clock lane and
     data lanes.
      1. If the D-PHY PLL is already locked (DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_LOCK] = 1'b1), go to step 4, else continue.
      2. Turn on the D-PHY PLL by setting DSI_PHY_RSTZ[PHY_FORCEPLL] = 1'b1.
      3. Verify that D-PHY PLL is turned on: DSI_PHY_STATUS[PHY_LOCK] = 1'b1.
      4. Without de-asserting the ULPM request bits, assert the Exit ULPM bits by setting DSI_PHY_ULPS_CTRL =
         4'hF.
      5. Verify that all D-PHY lanes are not in ULPM using DSI_PHY_STATUS register.
      6. Wait for 1 millisecond.
      7. De-assert the ULPM requests and the ULPM exit bits by setting DSI_PHY_ULPS_CTRL = 4'h0.
     The DSI controller should be in Stop state and the D-PHY PLL should be locked.

 18.2.4.13.8 Delivery of 3D Content in Video Mode
     One of the following ways can be used to transmit the 3D content in the Video mode:
       n Temporal mode
       n Spatial mode, Frame-based
       n Spatial mode, Line-based
       n Spatial mode, Pixel-based

     The following sections illustrate the transmission of 3D content in different ways using as an example a
     960×540 3D frame. In this example, a pair of views having 960×540 pixels each has to be transmitted. The left
     view is sent first and the image is landscape oriented. This is also valid for sending the right view first, or
     changing to a different resolution or orientation.

 18.2.4.13.8.1 Temporal Mode
     To transmit the amount of information mentioned in the example using the Temporal mode, follow these
     general steps:
      1. Program all video parameters registers and provide the pixel data at the DPI interface the same way as
         for normal 2D frames of 960×540.
      2. Configure the DSI_SDF_3D register to 3D Temporal mode by setting the [SECOND_VSYNC] bit to 1 and
         the [FORMAT_3D] field to 0x1.
     This way, the DSI controller sends all the views as if they are normal 2D frames, keeping the timing that has
     been set, with the only difference that it has previously notified the display to interpret them as pairs of
     views of a 3D scene. Because it is configured to send frames with 540 lines, a VSYNC pulse is generated
     between the left and the right views, as required for 3D Temporal mode. This scenario is illustrated in Figure
     18-40.
                        Figure 18-40 DSI Configuration of a 960×540 3D Scene in Temporal Mode(1)

                                        540        Le� Eye View




                                        540                                 Right Eye View

 18.2.4.13.8.2 Spatial Mode, Frame-Based
     For this mode, the complete content of the left view is sent first and then the right view, without any
     interruption along the entire 3D frame. To use the mode, follow these general steps:

      1. Program twice the number of lines (that is, 1080 lines), while setting the video parameters.
      2. Configure the DSI_SDF_3D register accordingly, by setting the [SECOND_VSYNC] field to 0x0 and
         [FORMAT_3D] field to 0x1, and provide the two views without any additional blanking between them
         through the DPI interface.
     This way, the DSI controller sends each pair of views as if it was a single 2D frame with twice the number of
     lines, having previously notified the display of the way to interpret this data, using a VSS packet. This scenario
     is illustrated in Figure 18-41.

 18.2.4.13.8.3 Spatial Mode, Line-Based
     In this mode, each video line conveys the contents from the left view at its position, followed by the
     corresponding contents of the right view. To use the mode, follow these general steps:
      1. Program twice the number of pixels per line (that is, 1920 pixels) while setting the video parameters.
      2. Configure the DSI_SDF_3D register for this mode, by setting the [FORMAT_3D] field to 0x0, and also
         provide the pairs of lines merged without blanking in the middle through the DPI interface.
     Once again, the DSI controller sends the contents as if it was a single 2D frame with lines twice as long,
     having previously notified the display of the way to interpret them, using a VSS packet. This scenario is
     illustrated in Figure 18-42.

 18.2.5.3.26 DSI_TO_CNT_CFG Register
           Offset           Access          Description
                                            Timeout Counter Configuration Register
         0x78                               This register configures counters that trigger timeout errors. These are used to
                             R/W
     Base address                           warn the system of a failure, through an interrupt, and restart the DSI controller in
                                            case of unexpected situations that cause deadlock conditions.


    Bits      Field Name             Access   Reset Value Description
                                                             This field configures the timeout counter that triggers a high-speed
                                                             transmission timeout contention detection (measured in DSI_
                                                             CLKMGR_CFG[TO_CLK_DIVISION] cycles).
                                                             If using non-burst mode and there is not sufficient time to switch
                                                             from high-speed to low-power and back in the period which is
                                                             from one line data finishing to the next line sync start, the DSI link
                                                             returns low-power state once per frame, then the DSI_CLKMGR_
                                                             CFG[TO_CLK_DIVISION] and HSTX_TO_CNT fields should be
                                                             configured to satisfy the following formula:
                                                             HSTX_TO_CNT × LANEBYTECLK_period × TO_CLK_DIVISION ≥ the
   31-16 HSTX_TO_CNT                  R/W          0x0       time of one FRAME data transmission × (1 + 10%)
                                                             In burst mode, RGB pixel packets are time-compressed, leaving
                                                             more time during a scan line. So if in burst mode and there is
                                                             sufficient time to switch from high-speed to low-power and back
                                                             in the period of time from one line data finishing to the next line
                                                             sync start, the DSI link can return low-power mode and back in this
                                                             time interval to save power. If this case, the DSI_CLKMGR_CFG
                                                             [TO_CLK_DIVISION] and HSTX_TO_CNT fields should be configured
                                                             to satisfy the following formula:
                                                             HSTX_TO_CNT × LANEBYTECLK_period × TO_CLK_DIVISION ≥ the
                                                             time of one LINE data transmission × (1 + 10%)
                                                             This field configures the timeout counter that triggers a low-power
    15-0      LPRX_TO_CNT             R/W          0x0       reception timeout contention detection (measured in DSI_
                                                             CLKMGR_CFG[TO_CLK_DIVISION] cycles).

 19 Analog Peripherals

 19.1 Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC12 and ADC24)

 19.1.1 ADC Overview
     The Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) modules are 12-bit/24-bit, multi-input units used for analog signals
     conversion into digital values.
     The device includes three ADC12 modules and one ADC24 module.
     ADC12 modules support the following main features:
       n 12-bit Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC
       n Conversion rate of up to 1.25 MSPS
       n 6 external inputs and two internal inputs:
         l 6 external pins may be configured to 6 single-ended or 3 differential inputs

         l One input from the on-chip temperature sensor (TSENS)

         l One input from internal voltage reference


     ADC24 supports the following main features:
       n 24-bit Sigma-Delta ADC
       n Conversion rate of up to 16 kSPS
       n 4 external differential inputs

     ADC12 and ADC24 common features:
       n Programmable gain instrumentation amplifier (up to 38 dB gain)
       n On-chip offset calibration and factory calibrated gain error
       n Widely programmable sample time
       n Hardware averaging option (up to 256 samples) for enhanced Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)
         l ADC12 must use hardware averaging at all times, with a minimum of two samples per average


       n Flexible digital user interface:
           lProgrammable input scan modes:
           o Single-shot or continuous conversions
           o A sequencer can be programmed to loop over a selection of inputs

         l Conversions can be triggered also externally by UTIMER events or QEC pins

         l Conversion results can be stored into sample registers and to SRAM via DMA

         l Hardware data shift:

           o 1 to 12 bits left shift
           o 1 to 12 bits right shift (up to 8 bits for the averaging function plus 4 bits more)

         l Threshold and window detection options. A comparator logic can generate interrupts when an input

            signal passes programmable thresholds
       n Designed for low power operation:
         l ADC sample rate is selectable via a clock divider

         l ADC power consumption decreases as sample rate decreases

       n The ADC12, ADC24, as well as other analog peripherals, are powered from a dedicated internal 1.8-V
         LDO

 19.1.4.1 ADC Introduction
     Figure 19-6 presents a diagram of the ADC main internal blocks and their connections.

                                                                                                                                                                       ADC12-001

                                                                                            PCLK




     ADC—This is the 12-bit/24-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter.
     Sequencer and AMUX—An analog input for conversion can be selected (through the internal analog
     multiplexer) by software, or automatically by the sequencer hardware. The sequencer loops over a
     predefined selection of analog inputs thus reducing software intervention. Analog inputs can be either single-
     ended, or differential, selected by software. ADC24 inputs are differential only.
     Programmable Gain Instrumentation Amplifier— The PGA allows to monitor small signals with
     programmable gain of up to 42 dB.
     Sample Pulse Generator—Generates a Sample signal duration in PCLK clocks. ADC conversion phase starts
     right after the Sample pulse end, that is, after sampling phase end.
     External Start Triggers—A pulse detected on a selected input will trigger an ADC conversion. The pulses may
     be generated by other modules such as UTIMER.
     Averaging—This block will cause ADC to take up to 256 samples and then load the result register with the
     averaged value of all samples.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                                         Alif Semiconductor
                                                                                         1701
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                                           www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                        E7 Series


     Word Shift—This block participates in the averaging function and must be programmed accordingly. It can
     also shift the resulting value left or right, if the application requires it.
     Comparators A and B—These are two digital comparators with programmable thresholds. Additionally, the
     two comparators can operate in tandem to implement a window comparator function. Comparators can
     generate interrupts when a threshold is reached.

 19.1.4.2 ADC Basic Programming Sequence
     The following sequence shows the basic steps required to configure a start of ADC conversions:
      1. Program the ADC_REG1 register. Note that this register contains settings for all instances of ADC12 and
         is accessible from ADC120 memory map only. Enable ADC24 via the PMU_PERIPH[ADC24_EN] bit, if
         needed.
      2. Program PMU_PERIPH to enable the PGA, if needed. DIFFERENTIAL_EN in the ADC_REG1 must be set to
         1 if PGA has to be enabled.
      3. Program the ADC_CLK_DIVISOR register to the desired value, ADC clock = PCLK / [2 to 16].
      4. If Threshold-detect function is desired:
         a. Write the ADC_COMP_THRESH_A and ADC_COMP_THRESH_B values.
         b. Write the ADC_CONTROL[INT_CTRL] bit field to select the Threshold detection mode.
      5. Write the ADC_SAMPLE_WIDTH register with the desired duration of the Sample signal to the analog
         portion in PCLK clocks. The minimum pulse duration allowed is 1.5 divided clocks (see step 3).
      6. Write the ADC_AVG_NUM register to program the number samples for averaging (must be a power of
         2): 2 – 256 for ADC12, 1 – 256 for ADC24.
      7. To calculate the sample average, program the ADC_SHIFT_CONTROL register with the number of bits to
         shift right based upon the number of samples taken:
         n 1 sample: no shift
         n 2 samples: shift right 1 bit
         n 4 samples: shift right 2 bits
         n 8 samples: shift right 3 bits
         n 16 samples: shift right 4 bits
         n 32 samples: shift right 5 bits
         n 64 samples: shift right 6 bits
         n 128 samples: shift right 7 bits
         n 256 samples: shift right 8 bits
         If any additional shift left or right is desired, it should be added or subtracted from the averaging shift
         above, and the resulting value programmed into the ADC_SHIFT_CONTROL register.
      8. Write the ADC_SEQUENCER_CTRL register to indicate which of the ADC inputs are used (either selected
         by the sequencer or by software). For example, if ADC12 inputs IN0, IN1, and TSENS are to be
         monitored, write 9b110111100 to MASKED and 0 to MODE bit fields.
      9. Enable desired interrupts in the ADC_INTERRUPT_MASK register.
     10. Write the ADC_START_SRC to select the starting trigger (source). For example, bit 6 = 1 enables
         continuous operations.
     11. Wait for interrupt.
     12. Read the ADC_SAMPLE_REG_n (n = 0 to 8) registers if interrupt is Averaged sample ready (DONE0) or All
         samples taken (DONE1). The next sample register number to be updated can read from the ADC_SEL
         register.
     13. Write 1 to the ADC_INTERRUPT register to clear the interrupt.
     14. Go to step 11 or write 0x0000 to the ADC_START_SRC register to stop operation.

 19.2 Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC12)

 19.2.1 DAC12 Overview
     The Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC12) module converts 12-bit digital values into analog voltage signals.
     The analog output range is between 0 V and 1.8 V in LP mode.
     The device includes two DAC12 modules.
     Each DAC12 module supports the following main features:
       n Up to 1 kHz conversion rate at 12-bit resolution
       n Accepts unsigned binary or two’s complement signed digital data
       n Programmable output current up to 1.5 mA
       n Programmable load capacitance compensation
       n Internal 1.8-V voltage reference
       n Excellent high-frequency Power Supply Rejection Ratio (PSRR)
       n Maximum current output up to 1.5 mA
       n Software-selectable low-power (LP) or high-performance (HP) modes
         l HP mode handles larger resistive load at the expense of higher power consumption

         l LP mode handles slow sample rate and light resistive load for power savings


     Figure 19-7 provides a high-level overview of the DAC12 implementation in the device.
                                                       Figure 19-7 DAC12 Overview

                                                       DAC120/DAC121

                PCLK

 19.3 High-Speed Comparator (CMP)

 19.3.1 CMP Overview
     The High-Speed Comparator (CMP) module is a rail-to-rail, multi-input, analog comparator with
     programmable reference voltage and hysteresis.
     The device includes up to four CMP modules.
     Each CMP module supports the following main features:
       n Reference voltage from DAC6, internal Vref, or external pins
       n Programmable hysteresis
       n Windowing (gating) driven by one of four events from UTIMER and QEC
       n Comparator result inverter
       n Configurable number of taps for filtering
       n Interrupt generation after filtering
       n Response time: < 5 ns
       n Power supply from internal 1.8-V LDO (LDO-5)

 19.3.4 CMP Functional Description

 19.3.4.1 CMP Introduction
     Figure 19-11 presents a simplified diagram of the CMP main internal blocks and connections.




Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                     Alif Semiconductor

                                     COMP_REG1                        CMP[0-3]

                                                                                                FILTER_CTRL        INTERRUPT_MASK
                         AMUX             [HYST]

                 DAC6   3                                              0     1          2   3

                                                                       Windowing Events             PCLK                                            CMP-001




     CMP's main block is an analog comparator with a programmable hysteresis. The analog comparator produces
     a logic '1' when the voltage on the positive input (+) is higher than the voltage on the negative input (-),
     otherwise it outputs a logic '0'. If the two voltages are very close to each other, the comparator output may
     switch too often. If this phenomenon is not desired, a programmable hysteresis may be applied.
     Each CMP module can compare one of four external signals versus an internal Vref, DAC6 output, or two
     external reference pins.
     The analog inputs may be monitored continuously or in a time frames defined by external modules such as
     QEC inputs, or UTIMER intervals.
     The comparator result may be filtered out to eliminate any high-frequency glitches. Then, upon a filtering
     event, that is, the filtered result switches from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0, an interrupt may be generated and
     resulted is sent to the device event router and also to a device pin, CMPn_OUT.

 19.3.4.2 CMP Basic Programming Sequence
     The following sequence shows the basic steps required to configure start ADC conversions:
      1. Program CMP_COMP_REG1 to define the inputs (both positive and negative) to be compared. Enable
         the comparator hysteresis, if required.
      2. Write CMP_POLARITY_CTRL[0] to 1 if the inverted result of the comparator is required. That is, result
         becomes 1 when (-) signal is higher than (+) signal. When inverting function is not enabled, the result will
         be = 0.
      3. Write CMP_WINDOW_CTRL to 0x0n01, where n = 0 to 3. n selects one of the 4 inputs which will control
         the windowing (gating) function. If windowing is not required, skip this step.
      4. Write CMP_FILTER_CTRL to 0x0301 to enable the filtering function and define the number of filter taps
         to be 3.
      5. Write CMP_PRESCALER_CTRL to 0x0010 to cause CMP[0-3]_IN inputs to be evaluated into the taps every
         16 clocks.
      6. Enable the comparator by writing 1's in the respective CMP_COMP_REG1[COMP_HS_EN] bit.
      7. Run as long as necessary.

Hardware Reference Manual                                                                                                     Alif Semiconductor
                                                                    1721
AHRM0005 v2.9—June 2025                                                                                                        www.alifsemi.com
                                                                                                                       E7 Series


      8. Wait for FILTER_EVENT interrupt if it was enabled in the CMP_INTERRUPT_MASK register. By default,
         interrupt generation is disabled.

 19.4 Low-Power Comparator (LPCMP)

 19.4.1 LPCMP Overview
     The Low-Power Comparator (LPCMP) module is a low power, rail-to-rail, analog comparator with selectable
     reference voltage and hysteresis.
     The device includes a single LPCMP module located in the PD0 domain.
     The LPCMP supports the following main features:
       n Up to four external pins for voltage monitoring
       n Voltage reference from:
         l Internal AON 0.8-V voltage reference or

         l External VREF pins

       n Programmable hysteresis
       n Power supply from VDD_IO_1V8 pin
       n Response time: < 10 µs
       n The LPCMP interrupt can be used as a wake-up source from STANDBY and STOP low-power modes



                                                       NOTE

       All Low Power peripherals are single-master accessible, including LPCMP. Ensure that application
       software manages access to these LP peripherals such that no more than one bus master (CPU or
       DMA) attempts access at a time, using semaphores or similar techniques.


     Figure 19-12 provides a high-level overview of the LPCMP implementation in the device.

 19.5 Temperature Sensor (TSENS)

 19.5.1 TSENS Overview
     The Temperature Sensor (TSENS) generates a voltage VTEMP that varies incrementally with silicon die's
     temperature.
     The TSENS is connected internally to input channel 6 of each ADC12 module. ADC12 can convert the sensor
     output voltage into a digital value. The real temperature can be translated using temperature.h C header file
     available in the Alif Ensemble CMSIS pack.
     The sensor provides good linearity and accuracy of better than 2.4 °C. Additional calibration can be applied to
     improve accuracy.

 20 Debug Infrastructure

 20.1 Debug Overview
     To support the debug of multiple cores running simultaneously, the device provides an extensive debug
     infrastructure, compliant with the Arm® Debug Interface Architecture Specification ADIv6.0. The debug
     features include:
       n JTAG debug support
       n Serial Wire Debug (SWD) support
       n External debug of SE, APSS, RTSS-HP or RTSS-HE by an off-chip debugger
       n Debug through power down for APSS, RTSS-HP and RTSS-HE
       n Debug from reset for all systems
       n Support for single or multi-system debug
       n Trace and cross trigger capabilities

     For more information about trace and cross trigger support in the device, contact Alif Semiconductor:
     contact@alifsemi.com.


                                                       NOTE

       For managing software configurations of device resources, power, pins, clocks, DMA requests,
       interrupts, and various other additional settings, refer to the Alif Conductor tool.

 20.3.2 External Debug Bus
     The External Debug Bus provides support for an off-chip debugger to access all debug resources and CPU
     cores on the device. It consists of:
       n Debug Port (DP)—Provides access to an off-chip JTAG/SWD debugger
       n Debug Port ROM (DP ROM)—ROM table for DP, pointing to EXTDBG ROM and GPIO Control
       n External Debug ROM (EXTDBG ROM)—ROM table for all components on the External Debug Bus, except
         for GPIO Control
       n GPIO Control—Debug component providing control to general-purpose inputs and outputs
       n Debug APB ports to:
         l APSS AXI-AP Debug

         l A32 Debug

         l RTSS-HP Debug

         l RTSS-HE Debug

         l SE Debug



 20.3.3 APSS AXI-AP
     The AXI-AP and the associated AXI ROM table provide direct access to the APSS memory map. The AXI-AP
     ROM provides power control for the power domains of the device, which can be accessed via the APSS AXI-
     AP.

 20.3.4 A32 Debug
     The A32 debug logic includes:
       n Debug APB-AP
       n CoreSight (CS) ROM
       n Cortex-A32 debug and trace


 20.3.5 SE Debug
     The SE debug logic includes:
       n Debug AHB-AP
       n CoreSight (CS) ROM
       n SE CPU debug


 20.3.6 RTSS-HP Debug
     The RTSS-HP debug logic includes:
       n Debug AHB-AP
       n CoreSight (CS) ROM
       n M55-HP debug and trace


 20.3.7 RTSS-HE Debug
     The RTSS-HE debug logic includes:
       n   Debug AHB-AP
       n   CoreSight (CS) ROM

 21.4 Register Access Definitions
      Table 21-1 lists the abbreviations used in the register descriptions:
                                      Table 21-1 Registers Access Abbreviations
         Access                                                      Description
  R/W               Read/Write. Software can read and write to this bit.
  R                 Read only. Software can only read this bit.
  W                 Write only. Software can only write to this bit.
  RC                Read to Clear. Software can read this bit. Reading this bit automatically clears it to 0.
  W1C               Write 1 to Clear. Software clears the bit by writing 1 to it.
  W1S               Write 1 to Set. Software sets the bit by writing 1 to it.
  W1T               Write 1 to Toggle. Software toggles (1->0 or 0->1) the bit by writing 1 to it.
  R/W1C             Read / Write 1 to Clear. Software can read this bit and write 1 to it to clear it.
  RAZ/WI            Read As Zero / Writes are Ignored.
